[h1] Good morning Mr. Freeman. Looks like you're running late. [/h1] I'll admit. I've never actually played any games in the Half-Life series prior to 2026, let alone beat any of them. Once I actually tried out and beat this version of the game for the first time, I was surprised with how well the original Half-Life has aged. When I say that this game was essential for the first-person-shooter genre, that is not an exaggeration. For those who are getting into the series for the first time and are split between trying out the original Half-Life first or trying out the official fan-made reimagining of the game through [url=store.steampowered.com/app/362890/Black_Mesa/] Black Mesa, [/url] I'd highly recommend trying this game first before giving Black Mesa a shot. Even as someone who wasn't there when the original game was released, I still see the value in trying this game out first before playing Black Mesa. [h1] Positives [/h1] There are a lot of praises I can give this game, but I'll only highlight the biggest ones briefly. For starters, the gameplay is very different from what I'm normally used to. Half-Life heavily relies on your ability to use your brain to solve puzzles, make decisions on which weaponry to use when fighting enemies, and how you move around different hazards. Whenever I died in this game, it genuinely makes me feel like an idiot for underestimating a situation I faced instead of feeling upset when dying to something that was out of my control. You are constantly on edge when traversing through the facility, because you never know when another headcrab might jump out at you. I always felt like I was in control with my actions and how I approached a situation, which is one of the many big praises I can give this game. It's especially impressive for a game that came out toward the end of the 90s. The weaponry in this game is also really great. In terms of weaponry, they felt very good to use and each of them have their own pros and cons. A lot of them work great in most situations, but there may come a moment where you'll need to use something else instead. The sound design for the weapons, alongside plenty of other elements in the game, are pretty badass. The atmosphere and story were also really good. Visuals are something that have obviously gotten better over time, but in the context of this game (alongside other games that came out during its time), the way the atmosphere was handled and executed is amazing. It doesn't feel like I'm in the world of another video game. It genuinely feels like I'm in another world. The story, while vague in how it's presented in a lot of areas, is also really good. And who could forget about [url=store.steampowered.com/app/323130/HalfLife_Soundtrack/] the soundtrack? [/url] The soundtrack is very good, especially the closing credits theme and the extended version of the iconic Valve intro. I can go on and on about how great the game is, but there would be way to many things to list off in this review. So much that I probably wouldn't have enough room to put everything in. But as for the negatives, it thankfully isn't as long. [h1] Negatives [/h1] Like I said before, this game has aged surprisingly well. So much that the only only problems I have aren't that drastic and can be seen more as nitpicks than actually problems. The only real problem I have with this game are the last few chapters in the game, and how they can be a bit of a pain to navigate without either dying a lot or getting confused as to how you're supposed to progress. As for the nitpicks, I only have a few. When using ladders, expect them to be the true final boss of Half-Life as the Black Mesa scientists are still trying to figure out how the hell they're this bad. It can be very weird to climb ladders in this game, which can sometimes lead to unintentional deaths via fall damage. It doesn't happen that often, but when it does, it sucks. Another nitpick I have is that, while there are plenty of great weapons, there are a few that I hardly found any uses for because they were either difficult to understand or were meant to be used in very specific scenarios that I often forget that I had them. [h1] Conclusion [/h1] Despite this game being out for nearly 3 decades now, I still believe there is a lot of value in playing this game today. Once you actually beat this game, I'd highly recommend you show some love to the fan-made remake of the game, Black Mesa. The reason why I suggest playing the original Half-Life and then playing Half-Life 2 first is so that it makes the transition between games feel a lot more natural. I also feel that playing Black Mesa first could negatively impact how you would feel about Half-Life 2, due to how outdated the latter would feel when compared to the former. Half-Life is one of those games that every person that has Steam should play at least once in their life, because there are hardly any other games like it.

(Ignore my playtime, I've played this for years) Half-Life is probably the most important game of my life. It's one of the very first games I remember playing. Back then I just knew it as the game with the big scary elevator and falling headcrabs. It wasn't until college I rediscovered HL and played through it. I have fond memories of enjoying every part of the adventure (yes, even Xen). I've played tons of mods since then and will always play some form of this game for the rest of my life, whether it's replaying it or checking out a new mod. What sets Half-Life apart from every game that came before it, and even many games that came after it, is the quality of its story. The iconic opening tram ride introduces us to Gordon Freeman, the protagonist, and Black Mesa, his workplace. Once you arrive at work you interact with goofy scientists, blow up someone's lunch in a microwave, and equip your HEV suit. And that's just the first 15 minutes. It sounds simple now but back then this was revolutionary when every shooter was just a dude blasting bad guys and looking for keycards. The best comparison I can make is Half-Life reinvented the FPS genre the same as how The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time reinvented the action-adventure genre. Ironically they came out two days apart! HL released November 19th and OoT released November 21st in 1998. The gameplay has mostly aged well. It's a nonlinear shooter with some simple puzzles thrown in. HL introduced many mechanics we take for granted today, such as refilling your health and armor at stations, destroying boxes for supplies, working with NPC allies, and enemies talking to each other and coordinating their attacks to take you down. In my opinion, the game's at its best during the science parts such as Blast Pit and Questionable Ethics. Your mileage may vary with certain chapters. On A Rail and Surface Tension are love/hate depending on who you ask (yes I enjoy On A Rail and I won't apologize for it). Residue Processing and Interloper suck. Kelly Bailey's soundtrack adds ambience to this scientific adventure. The graphics, while they've aged, are very cozy. The GoldSrc engine has a certain vibe to it only matched by the Quake 2 engine. Black Mesa's environments are industrial; the surface is bright yet chaotic, and Xen feels like a H.R. Giger painting come to life. There's a lot to dislike about Xen, but it does a great job of making the player feel like they're in a desolate, alien world where they don't belong. If you can't stomach the graphics, the Black Mesa remake solves that problem. But I strongly recommend you play HL first. If HL is vanilla ice cream, BM is a hot fudge sundae with sprinkles and whip cream. Sometimes just vanilla is better. If you're interested in experiencing retro FPS games, this is an absolute must play. If you want to replay the campaign and mix things up: I recommend MMod, Brutal HL, and Half-Payne. Both the Opposing Force and Blue Shift expansions are worth playing. There's a lot of great mods but some of my favorites are They Hunger, Intensity Field, Delta Particles, and Gunman Chronicles which is an abandonware total conversion. The 25th anniversary update is the definitive way to play HL and I've confirmed the listed mods run well in that version.

Half-Life holds up as one of the best games of all time, let alone one of the best first-person shooters. It revolutionized the medium and proved that video games can not just tell a great story, but tell it in an engaging way that makes you feel like it's happening to YOU in a way only video games can. It has impeccable atmosphere and game design that feels seamless and smooth; progression through the story feels natural and logical as you fight to survive, the game effortlessly guiding you as you make your way through the facility in a desperate attempt to escape the aftermath of an experiment gone wrong. The game's final chapters, which take place in the alien border world Xen, rely a little too heavily on the wow factor of a new, novel environment and the gameplay slogs a little near the end, but the momentum is kept well enough to no drag on too long. Overall, a fantastic experience that holds up remarkably well 27 years later. If you're doing your homework on gaming history, this game can't be left out.

Half-Life begins with a tram ride through the incomprehensibly large and mysterious Black Mesa complex. To a new player, this five-or-so-minute sequence is a promise of an immersive world, a colossal underground network of laboratories and metal corridors and who knows what else. Every turned corner provides some new intrigue, asks some new question that the game may or may not answer later. There's a guy in a suit with a briefcase, staring. A scientist tries to pull a door open a little too desperately. Half-Life never stops doing this. It's a game built upon showing you all of the things you're not supposed to see. Black Mesa itself is a cavernous labyrinth of exhaust vents, pipelines, scaffolding, and elevator shafts that seem to go on infinitely below. There is a terrifying pervasive feeling throughout the game that something much bigger is going on, something that cannot be understood, and the seeds of that feeling are planted at the very start. But to protagonist Gordon Freeman, this intro is just another commute to the office. Freeman is a fascinating hero, managing to consistently surprise the player without saying a single word. What sort of background must this lab assistant have to be the absolute killing machine he is? Upon arriving to work, Freeman is told to put on his hazard suit, and while of course he knows exactly where that is, a new player doesn't have a clue. Right away, the dissonance between what the player knows vs. what the protagonist knows establishes Freeman as being competent and respected (necessary facets of the character if the entire plot is to be believable) while also introducing the kind of player agency and freedom that makes Half-Life so great. Freeman knows exactly where to go and what to do, but *I* get to explore. There's no NPC nagging me about me where my suit is, no cutscene panning to it in the next room over. I've got to search around and find the thing. On a second playthrough, I can dash right over to my suit, sure, but I have to earn that. This scene is a microcosm of what makes the game feel so rewarding to play. Half-Life may be a very linear game, but I always felt like I was exploring. Whereas progression provides a feeling of freedom through self-paced exploration, it's the brilliant combat that lets the player truly express themselves. I have not been into shooters for very long, but DOOM (the 1993 one) and Quake are some of my favorite games, period. And while they are by no means devoid of strategic gameplay, strategy there is more about keeping up pace, swapping weapons on the fly and retreating to grab a health pack real quick before running back in guns blazing. The entire language can be learned pretty quick. In Half-Life, even an empty room could pose a never-before-seen threat: a headcrab zombie crashes through an unassuming wall, for example. Scripted sequences like these never failed to surprise me and instill a sense of horror about whatever might come next. My favorite threats to deal with, though, were the ones you *could* see coming: the soldier rooms, lined with turrets and sandbag forts and stealth corridors and vantage points. In the spirit of Gordon Freeman, a nerd, these sequences require careful, deliberate planning. Do I toss a grenade to flush enemies out, maybe set some tripmines to lure them into? Do I stealthily take em out one-by-one via crossbow? Or can I actually save ammo by just picking off the guy manning the turret, then use it gun down the rest? Freeman's weapons arsenal is so well-balanced, and enemy encounters so carefully constructed, that there are always a multitude of ways to approach these "combat puzzles" but never so much freedom that you don't need to choose your approach carefully. And just about every weapon feels great to use. My favorite, the revolver, can take most enemies out at long-range with a headshot, but is balanced by the scarcity of its ammo and an awfully slow reload. Also, I may be crazy but I mostly loved the platforming. It's awkward, no doubt, but perfectly responsive if you actually engage with its systems (there's a walk function, people, you don't have to slide around everywhere!). The slower-paced platform segments break up the combat well and let atmosphere take center stage. Tragically, the tutorial had me excited about that long jump and then you use it maybe twice. Oh well.. Anyways, I think I paid one dollar for this? What a phenomenal game.

Writing a review for the first Half Life feels strange, because this is where everything began. Not just a game series, but a completely new way of telling stories in games. Half Life does not start with action. It starts with routine. A quiet train ride. You just sit there and watch Black Mesa pass by. No rush, no forced excitement. And when everything goes wrong, it does not feel scripted. It feels inevitable. What makes Half Life special is how grounded it is. You are not a soldier. You are not a hero. You are a scientist who survived something that never should have happened. The game never lets you forget that. Every weapon feels desperate. Every hallway feels unsafe. Progress always feels earned. There are no cutscenes taking control away from you. The disaster happens while you are still inside it. Scientists panic. Guards try to hold things together. Alarms echo through empty corridors. You are not watching a catastrophe. You are trapped in one. The enemies are not just targets. They feel confused, aggressive, out of place. Just like you. As the game slowly shifts from scientific horror into full invasion, it never loses that feeling of uncertainty. Silence is one of the strongest parts of Half Life. Long corridors. Broken labs. Distant sounds. The game knows when to shut up, and that is exactly why it works. And then there is the G-Man. No explanation. No answers. Just observation. Even at the very beginning, Valve understood something many games still do not. Mystery is stronger than explanation. Half Life is not old. It is foundational. It did not follow rules. It created them. If you are waiting for Half-Life 3... Prepare for unforeseen consequences!

From the beginning of the game you're witness to a logistical marvel: the daily operations of Black Mesa; cogs of modern machinery in full whir as you pass by sections of a world that can't stop turning. From there, chaos ensues, and the foundation set by the intro is as steady in the mind as the crowbar in your hand. Half-Life was groundbreaking for its continuous narrative. No boring-ass cutscenes - you can walk, run, even leap during important dialogue. NPCs are organic pieces in the facility: scanning you through doorways, hiding in nooks and crannies, shooting alongside you, and unfortunately dying. Parts of the building crumble, soldiers advance on the facility; labs are designed for actual function rather than a playground for the player. It all contributes to a sense of place that FPS games to this day dream of emulating. Playing it still feels buttery smooth, the only qualms being some awkward weapon swapping, bugs, and some stretched out sections. The momentum from that first third does slow a little as the game goes on, but there's a few drastic shake-ups to keep things interesting. Xen towards the end is infamous, but I quite like games that feel alien, even if it's only a portion of this one. So if you've never played Half-Life, what are you waiting for? Gordon Freeman is silently waiting for just the right person to come along and make him long jump into the void. Perhaps he's waiting for you.

Half-Life: Why Its Design Is Still the Gold Standard Half-Life is often called a classic, but replaying it today makes it clear why its design still outperforms many modern shooters. Even after decades of FPS evolution, it feels smarter, more confident, and more focused than a lot of current titles. Returning to it doesn't feel like nostalgia; it feels like a design lesson that still holds up. Valve didn't just create another shooter. They created a game that trusts the player. There are no long cutscenes or forced explanations; everything is understood through play. The story unfolds as you move, shoot, and explore, without ever taking control away from you. A decision that seems obvious today is still executed better here than in many modern games. Pacing is what truly keeps you engaged. Half-Life knows exactly when to apply pressure and when to let you walk in silence through Black Mesa, listening to your own footsteps and anticipating danger. It never overwhelms you, but it never fully relaxes either. It constantly pushes you forward, even when doing so quietly. Every weapon has a clear purpose. They aren't there just to look cool, but to solve specific situations. As you progress, you don't just gain new tools. You gain a better understanding of how the game works and how to approach each encounter. That constant sense of learning is what makes it satisfying even today. The immersion works because the game never breaks its own internal logic. Everything happens seamlessly. What you know about the disaster is discovered through gameplay. Even after multiple playthroughs, small details in level design and sound continue to reinforce the feeling of isolation and tension. Not everything has aged perfectly. The AI, impressive for its time, can behave inconsistently and occasionally break immersion. There are also jumping sections, especially near the end, where collisions feel imprecise and a bit frustrating. These are real flaws worth mentioning. Still, Half-Life remains an honest single-player FPS. It doesn't rely on modern gimmicks or empty spectacle to stand out. Its strength lies in clear, coherent design that respects the player. If you enjoy story-driven shooters that focus on smart design over flashy presentation, Half-Life is still absolutely worth your time. Pros • Excellent pacing • Storytelling that never interrupts gameplay Cons • Inconsistent AI in some moments • Jumping sections feel clunky by today's standards

Half-Life is a surprisingly well-aged game for something that came out in 1998. The controls are all very responsive and smooth, although I feel the movement is just a bit too slippery, especially considering all the platforming. The difficulty is also surprisingly manageable, but still suffers from the random spike most older games have. Despite it, save states will still help things from getting into "genuinely insufferable" territory. The enemy A.I. is also quite complex for such an old game. They'll take cover, throw grenades to fish you out, and even retreat if they're wounded. It made gameplay feel much more dynamic than if they only pushed. I will say that the bosses leave a lot to be desired, and some chapters I feel drag out for too long (I was not fond of On A Rail). I also didn't find myself using many other guns besides the submachine gun and shotgun, and sometimes the laser gun for tougher enemies. This could totally be on me though. Overall, I would recommend this game, even if you aren't a big fan of older titles. Just a little skill and a lot of patience can get you through this game on Medium.

Half Life 1 is a whole different kind of legendary. This is one of those games you don't rush for explosions or chaos. You load it up to chill, to exist in its world, and to feel that specific vibe no other game has. I used to speedrun this game, and that's how you really learn to respect it. You start noticing the movement, the map flow, the little tricks, and how smooth everything feels once you know what you're doing. Running through Black Mesa at full speed is satisfying in a way that's hard to explain. But even when you're not speedrunning, Half Life 1 hits different. The atmosphere is quiet, eerie, and immersive. No cutscenes breaking the flow, no hand holding. You're just Gordon Freeman moving through labs, corridors, and alien-infested areas while everything slowly goes to hell around you. The sound design, the level design, and the pacing give it that calm but unsettling feeling. It's not loud like modern shooters. It's smart, focused, and confident. You can play it seriously or just boot it up and relax, and it still works. Final verdict Half Life 1 is timeless. Whether you're speedrunning it or just chilling and soaking in the vibe, it's a game you never really forget. It's not about hype. It's about atmosphere. And it nails it perfectly.

Counter-Strike Condition Zero is a follow up to the original Counter-Strike game. It was released in 2004 and uses the Half-Life engine. This version adds a single player mission pack which gives players a chance to learn maps, guns and game modes without the pressure of online play. I have around 2500 hours in CSGO/CS2, but I have not played Condition Zero extensively and tried it mainly to experience how the gameplay worked. The campaign can be completed in about four hours on Normal difficulty, and higher difficulties provide additional challenge. The game includes a squad management system. At the start of each mission, you can select which squad members to take. Each member has different stats which can affect gameplay. You begin with three members and can expand to a full squad of eight. Each mission also has objectives and challenges, such as completing tasks in a set time or using specific weapons. These challenges help players practice different guns and strategies. The graphics are dated but still clear and functional. The difficulty levels can be adjusted to match experience. Normal mode is suitable for learning the game, while higher difficulties simulate online match conditions. Overall, Counter-Strike Condition Zero provides a structured way to practice and understand the game before playing online.

Developed by Ritual Entertainment and bundled as a bonus in Counter-Strike: Condition Zero, Deleted Scenes is a legit single-player scripted campaign for the Counter-Strike series, released in 2004 on the GoldSrc engine. Instead of the insane multiplayer matches of CS 1.6, you play as a counter-terrorist special forces operative in linear but varied missions all over the world: Middle East, Russia, Latvia, Colombia, Italy, Arctic Ocean on an icebreaker, Argentina, USA, Northern Ireland, Turkmenistan, Iraq. Neutralize terrorists, rescue hostages, defuse bombs, neutralize missiles, hunt down narco-traffickers, shoot down helos or fighter jets, you'll have your hands full taking down the global terrorist threat! The objectives also give off a Rainbow Six vibe at times and occasionally a hint of GoldenEye 64, with staging that packs a serious punch despite the engine's tech limits. The training is in the same vein as Half-Life and Opposing Force, teaching you the game mechanics as well as the use of special weapons and tools available during your missions: the blowtorch to melt locks and open doors, remote-controlled bombs usable like Half-Life's C4, the camera to capture key evidence to send back to HQ, the fiber optic camera to spy on the sly like in Splinter Cell, and the radio to communicate with your brothers in arms. While these gadgets add a welcome tactical touch, they're mostly for scouting the terrain before gunning down all the terrorists and blowing up their installations. The gameplay perfectly mixes the essence of old-school Counter-Strike, with its precise yet satisfying ballistics, and Half-Life's environmental puzzles. You'll have to push or pull crates and climb on them to reach otherwise inaccessible spots, activate levers or valves to unlock doors, use or destroy turrets, and heal up at med stations. The missions, loosely based on iconic CS 1.6 maps, are relatively varied in their settings and objectives. You go from classic hostage rescues and bomb defusals to sniping, controlled demolitions, recon, etc... Unlike CS multiplayer where you're limited to two firearms, here you can sometimes carry a massive arsenal during missions. I've had up to six primary weapons on me at once, maybe more, not counting gear! In addition to the weapons from 1.6/CZ, Deleted Scenes offers the M60 machine gun that sprays the battlefield relentlessly, and straight-up the M72 LAW rocket launcher to shred enemy vehicles and even their infantry if you're in the mood. The only annoying thing is you can't pick up weapons or ammo from dead enemies; you're stuck with your basic loadout and the guns strategically placed by the devs for you to grab. Like a rocket launcher near a tank, or a sniper rifle on a rooftop. Also, don't expect to buy weapons in this game, it doesn't work like that here. The staging is pretty impressive for a GoldSrc game, with beautifully scripted scenes featuring aerial bombardments, chain explosions, etc. The art direction is pleasing and coherent but doesn't hide the very dated graphics and animations for 2004, especially knowing that Half-Life 2 and Counter-Strike: Source came out the same year! Zak Belica's music is epic and fits the serious special forces vibe perfectly. That said, the French dub is super caricatural with ultra-exaggerated foreign accents, which makes the dialogue hilarious at times. Fun fact, in the French version, you can easily recognize the voice actors for Wallace Breen, Eli Vance, and Barney Calhoun from Half-Life 2! In the end, Counter-Strike: Condition Zero - Deleted Scenes is a solid underrated or even forgotten tactical FPS, with a real solo mode that brings together the best of old-school Counter-Strike gameplay and the cult classic first-gen Half-Life games. If you like old-school FPS and accessible military shooters, don't hesitate!

If you have difficulties in the walktrough, this guide will be very useful: [/b] https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3561496240 [h1] Category: Really weird games [/h1] I hadn't really talked much about the "legendary" Counter-Strike 1.6 before, since I didn't see much point in it. Essentially, Condition Zero isn't a new wrap for the series, and calling this chunk of code an add-on is a stretch. Sure, there's an attempt to introduce a storyline and add missions with specific conditions instead of just bot training. But honestly, it's all done pretty poorly, and that's putting it mildly. Everyone knows that Counter-Strike originally started as a huge mod for Half-Life 1, which grew and changed over time. It's clear that many of the people playing it now (including me, born in 2006) weren't even around back then. But even from a boomer's perspective, it's hard to get why CS 1.6 is such a big deal. Sadly, Condition Zero doesn't make the already so-so original game any better. The character models are the same, the weapons are the same (though mostly useful, like being able to customize a ready-made weapon loadout), and there are even fewer maps, supposedly to focus on the 'story mode.' As for that, the player has to complete all objectives on each of the 19 maps, keeping at least a three-round edge over the terrorists (I played the whole game on medium difficulty and seriously regret it!!!). Some of the perks include not just mindlessly fighting bots, but actually doing different tasks, like "take out this many terrorists with this weapon" or "get the hostages out." There's also a feature to tweak the bot squad you play with. Their stats are split into "morale," "skill," and "teamwork," which might seem kind of arbitrary. But sometimes you really have to juggle your choice of teammates to actually pull off a win. It's worth mentioning that you can only play the scenarios as special forces, and the whole politics and censorship argument from back then doesn't apply - you can't play as the terrorists in the story missions. Now to the main thing that will make you scream louder and angrier than Sashko Fokin out of rage. Bot behavior is NOT just bad - it's a FUCKING nightmare. Yeah, the game is old, but the bots (terrorists), frankly, cheat on any of the four difficulty levels. They spot the player three seconds before appearing, shoot, and kill through concrete objects. Ally behavior is a whole other story: sometimes they literally jump off high places, don't follow orders, and the one thing that could have been a major plus (AI) turns into a huge minus. Sometimes bots intentionally lose, stretching the gameplay with their dumb actions. And no matter how hard you try, killing bots with the local AWP or point-blank with a shotgun can be impossible - they shoot faster and aim 'better'. Plus, speaking about the bot cluster: on medium difficulty, for example, not all of them even become active. The sound design is pretty bad too: bot chatter, grenade bangs, and gunfire are really harsh on the ears. CS 1.6 had the same problem. The graphics are super lame and blocky, and the environment textures are blurry. With all the effects, sometimes it's totally unclear where to run, who to shoot, or if you even did any damage to the enemy. As for online play, there's almost none. Right now, you can't find full servers with lots of players. Sure, everyone hangs out in 1.6, Source, or CS2, but why didn't they just make Condition Zero purely a story-driven game, without taking up extra hard drive space, and actually work on Steam Cloud and achievements? Undoubtedly, CS Condition Zero is the weirdest game in the Counter-Strike lineup. While it offers something new, it doesn't improve the gameplay either visually or technically. This game might only be of interest if you never played CS 1.6 back in the day. If you're a sane person, a couple of hours with Condition Zero will leave you genuinely annoyed and kill any desire to play the older Counter-Strike games (except maybe Source and CS2). https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3612049014 [h3] P. Condition Zero feels like Valve looked at Counter-Strike and said, "What if… hear me out… we gave you homework?" I launched it expecting CS with a twist. The twist is: You're playing CS, but your teammates are bots who all share **one brain cell** and it's on cooldown. --- ### Pros: * It's Counter-Strike… kind of. Guns go pew, terrorists go boom, hostages complain. * "Mission objectives" like: "Win a round with a shield" and "Get 3 headshots with a FAMAS" - basically Steam achievements before Steam achievements. * Bot names like "Enzo," "Wolf," and "Snake" who play like they're legally blind and using a trackpad. * Deleted Scenes is like a fanfic campaign where you're a one-man anti-terror PowerPoint presentation. ### Cons: * Playing vs bots that either aimbot you from across the map or stare at a wall having an existential crisis. No in-between. * Your squad: all-in on knife rush. Enemy squad: stacked with Olympic-level sharpshooters. * Hostages have the pathfinding of a Roomba with a concussion. * Feels like a CS mod that snuck into the family photo as a full game. --- **Overall:** Condition Zero is that weird cousin of CS: not the favorite, not the best, but somehow always at the reunion. 10/10 Launched it "just to check it out," got yelled at by bots, went back to 1.6 anyway.

Condition Zero is kind of the "forgotten cousin" of the Counter-Strike series, but honestly, I had a lot of fun with it. The big difference here is the single-player campaign (Tour of Duty), which lets you lead your own CT squad through different missions. It's cool being able to experiment with weapons you don't normally touch in multiplayer, and the objective-based gameplay keeps things interesting. That said, the AI can be a pain. Early on, it feels balanced enough, but later missions get brutal. Enemies will snap onto your head the instant you peek, and sometimes it feels completely down to luck whether you survive or not. On top of that, you end up fighting your own teammates for kills just to complete challenges, which kind of kills the whole "teamwork" vibe. Still, I loved the idea of organizing a squad - it really makes me wish Valve had fleshed this out more. Imagine a modern version where your squad gains experience and you can actually issue tactical commands. That would be amazing. Then there's Deleted Scenes, which is basically a full single-player CS campaign. It's goofy, over the top, and the voice acting is hilariously cheesy, but it's also super fun. Honestly, it deserves a remake on Source or something, because there's nothing else like it. Sure, the graphics are old, and yeah, the game can be buggy or frustrating at times. But underneath all that, there's a really unique Counter-Strike experience here. Multiplayer is basically classic CS and community servers have kept it alive even today. Condition Zero isn't perfect, but it's definitely not the "bad" game people used to make it out to be. It tried something new, and while it didn't fully land back then, it's still a hidden gem that I'd recommend if you're a fan of old-school FPS games. Counter-Strike: Condition Zero on Steam presents a compelling evolution of the classic tactical shooter franchise, blending refined gameplay mechanics with a variety of game modes that cater to both new players and seasoned veterans. Building upon the foundation established by the original Counter-Strike, Condition Zero introduces a more polished experience, featuring improved graphics, enhanced AI, and a broader range of missions and multiplayer options. The game's visual design, while not pushing the boundaries of contemporary graphics, effectively captures the gritty, military-inspired aesthetic that has become synonymous with the series. The environments are detailed enough to immerse players in intense combat scenarios, and the sound design-ranging from weapon effects to ambient noises-adds a layer of realism that enhances the tactical gameplay experience. The core gameplay of Condition Zero remains faithful to the classic Counter-Strike formula: team-based combat where strategy, communication, and precise shooting are vital. The game offers a variety of modes, including the traditional bomb defusal, hostage rescue, and a single-player campaign that serves as both a tutorial and a story-driven experience. The single-player missions are well-designed, providing structured objectives that challenge players to employ different tactics and adapt to various scenarios. The AI opponents are notably smarter than in some earlier entries, making single-player and cooperative modes more engaging and less predictable. Multiplayer remains the heart of Counter-Strike: Condition Zero, with a robust community and a wide array of community-hosted servers offering custom maps, mods, and gameplay rules, ensuring longevity and replayability. One of the most significant upgrades in Condition Zero is the introduction of the "Deleted Scenes" campaign, which features a series of missions designed to showcase improved AI and more complex objectives. While some purists prefer the simplicity and rawness of the original Counter-Strike, the campaign provides a more structured and cinematic experience, with a narrative that ties the missions together. The game's mechanics-ranging from weapon recoil, movement, and economy management-are all finely tuned, providing a realistic yet accessible shooting experience. The controls are responsive, and the game strikes a good balance between arcade-style fun and tactical depth. The matchmaking and server browsing systems are straightforward, although at times they can suffer from latency issues or server availability, which is common in multiplayer-focused shooters of this era. The game's community support and modding scene have also played a significant role in maintaining its appeal. Players have created custom maps, skins, and game modes that keep the experience fresh long after the initial release. Additionally, the game's longevity is partly due to the enduring popularity of Counter-Strike's core gameplay loop-teamwork, map knowledge, and precise aiming. However, some players may find the game's graphics and interface somewhat dated, especially when compared to more modern shooters, which can slightly detract from the overall immersion. Still, the gameplay mechanics remain solid and reliable, making it a worthwhile experience for those who appreciate tactical shooters rooted in skill and strategy. Overall, Counter-Strike: Condition Zero on Steam is a worthy entry in the series that offers a blend of refined single-player content and the timeless appeal of competitive multiplayer. While it may not revolutionize the franchise, it successfully modernizes and polishes the classic formula, providing a balanced experience for fans of tactical shooters. Its emphasis on teamwork, map control, and precise shooting continues to resonate, and its community-driven content ensures that it remains relevant long after its initial release. For players seeking a game that combines strategic depth with fast-paced action in a multiplayer setting, Counter-Strike: Condition Zero remains a solid choice, especially for those interested in experiencing a more narrative-driven take on the foundational gameplay of Counter-Strike. Rating: 9/10

I'll be clear immediately: I'm a very casual fan of this series. I really don't care for Counter-Strike 2, how it outright replaced CSGO, how it essentially killed CSGO's casual content (all custom and most official), and its seemingly even further hardlined esports direction. I don't exactly enjoy the playerbase """communication""" in this series either, so there's basically no incentive for me to bother at this point. So then, somehow, Condition Zero has stood the test of time even though infamously nobody cared about it. It stands up just because it simply has by far the best singleplayer offerings in the series. This is the only entry to have an Unreal Tournament style singleplayer (Tour of Duty) where you'll be given a checklist of normal bot matches with multiple challenges to complete in order to win per match. The bots could be better (it should be noted though the bots use "voice chat" to communicate what they're doing and planning, which you can also use chat commands to somewhat influence them too) but this mode turned out to be a very respectable way of keeping the series alive for me. There's a bunch of mission pack mods to extend the playtime of Tour of Duty too, so it massively adds value to Condition Zero. Bizarrely too it contains a proper traditional singleplayer campaign via a series of singleplayer missions via "Deleted Scenes"; mildly comparable to Half-Life (only because Deleted Scenes plays much more like as if it's just another Half-Life expansion pack, rather than being true Counter-Strike). I'm not even going to pretend your time isn't probably much better spent on just playing the entire Half-Life collection or the Tour of Duty mode instead, but it does exist. Of course there's multiplayer too, but nobody's playing it. It does seem to have benefited from HL1's anniversary update, so it doesn't look like it would take much to run a server for friends at least. I recommend this one just for the fact it's the most reasonable game for singleplayer in the series, even if you don't care about Deleted Scenes.

Considering this game comes bundled with CS 1.6, I'm not really gonna talk about the multiplayer, I'm gonna talk about the single-player Campaign, Deleted Scenes. Deleted Scenes is comprised of multiple missions, each one being a different scenario where you play as a Counter-Terrorist Operator from one of the many CT factions depending on the mission's context. The best way to describe the level design is that it's sort of a hybrid between Medal of Honor and Half-Life. You'll be doing a lot of crawling through vents and tight areas like Half-Life, and there's a lot of corridor-style shooting with the game spawning enemies in areas you have to backtrack through after completing an objective like Medal of Honor. You're commonly doing 1-man infiltration missions, with a few sequences here and there with friendly NPCs. There's unfortunately no squad management type of gameplay like Rainbow Six, which in my opinion is a missed opportunity since they should've drawn more inspiration from it instead of Medal of Honor. The game still uses Counter-Strike's shooting mechanics, and the enemies seem to have the health of an armored opponent in the normal PvP (example being that M4 takes 2 headshots to kill while the AK takes 1). The game's setpieces are nice, and it's overall a fun older 2000s shooter that feels similar to Medal of Honor, while also having the blood and gibbing effects of Half-Life. This game was dropped and picked back up by a couple of different developers which is probably why it's as basic as it is. I honestly think they should drop an update for this game that merges it with the normal Condition Zero executable, and just sidelines that crappy bot "Campaign" the base game has. Overall it's worth playing to experience the novelty of a single-player CS game that has a similar charm to those community made Half-Life mods, but in the context of a neat Counter-Terrorism game. This sort of shooter genre needs to come back, because Rainbow Six is basically a shadow of its former self these days. I should also mention that the Campaign doesn't play through every mission, so it's worth checking out the World Map for the couple of missions it doesn't play.

A Nostalgic Journey with Some Hidden Gems Alright, let's talk about Counter-Strike: Condition Zero. I'm sure a lot of you probably know it's the "odd one out" in the Counter-Strike series, sandwiched between the original and Source. And yeah, it's got its flaws, but I can't help but feel a sense of nostalgia whenever I load it up. First off, this game has that classic Counter-Strike feel. If you've played 1.6, you'll instantly feel at home. The core mechanics are there: team-based, tactical gameplay, bomb planting, hostage rescues, all that good stuff. There's a reason CS became a staple in the FPS world, and Condition Zero carries that legacy well, even though it wasn't as big as its predecessors. Now, here's the thing about Condition Zero-it introduced a single-player component that was actually kind of fun. You get these little AI matches where you can practice your skills or just mess around. Sure, the bots aren't the brightest, but they do provide a decent challenge if you're looking to warm up or just want to play at your own pace without the pressure of online matches. The real hidden gem here, though, is the Deleted Scenes campaign. It's not perfect, but it was an interesting attempt to give Condition Zero a single-player story mode (something the franchise didn't have before). You go through different missions that range from stealthy approaches to all-out gunfights. The voice acting is... well, let's just say it's not going to win any awards, but it's got that goofy charm you can appreciate if you're into retro FPS campaigns. I won't lie, the AI is a little clunky, and the missions can get repetitive, but there's something oddly satisfying about taking on terrorists in a more structured way than the usual match-based chaos. For people who loved CS but wanted something different, Deleted Scenes was kind of an underappreciated bonus. Now, let's be real for a second. Condition Zero doesn't hold up to Counter-Strike: Source or Global Offensive. It's got that weird in-between vibe, where it's not as polished or fluid as Source, and the graphics-while decent for its time-look pretty dated now. The bots can be hilarious (in a bad way), and the online community was smaller than in the CS 1.6 days, which made it tough to get a full, active match going. Also, it had this weird mix of being too "arcade" for the hardcore competitive scene but not casual enough to be a proper "fun" game for people who just want to jump in and shoot stuff. It's like Condition Zero didn't really know what it wanted to be, and as a result, it kinda fell into this awkward middle ground that wasn't as well-received by the wider community. For me, though, Condition Zero is still a solid pick if you're a fan of Counter-Strike. It may not be the top dog in the series, but it's got that old-school charm. The maps feel classic, and the gunplay still holds up, even if it doesn't have the same polish as its successors. Plus, if you're into the history of Counter-Strike, this game is like a weird little snapshot of where the series was trying to go before Source changed everything. If you're into retro FPS games and enjoy diving deep into older titles that didn't quite make it, Condition Zero is worth checking out. Just don't expect it to dethrone CS 1.6 or Source.

Counter-Strike Condition Zero is a follow up to the original Counter-Strike game. It was released in 2004 and uses the Half-Life engine. This version adds a single player mission pack which gives players a chance to learn maps, guns and game modes without the pressure of online play. I have around 2500 hours in CSGO/CS2, but I have not played Condition Zero extensively and tried it mainly to experience how the gameplay worked. The campaign can be completed in about four hours on Normal difficulty, and higher difficulties provide additional challenge. The game includes a squad management system. At the start of each mission, you can select which squad members to take. Each member has different stats which can affect gameplay. You begin with three members and can expand to a full squad of eight. Each mission also has objectives and challenges, such as completing tasks in a set time or using specific weapons. These challenges help players practice different guns and strategies. The graphics are dated but still clear and functional. The difficulty levels can be adjusted to match experience. Normal mode is suitable for learning the game, while higher difficulties simulate online match conditions. Overall, Counter-Strike Condition Zero provides a structured way to practice and understand the game before playing online.

Developed by Ritual Entertainment and bundled as a bonus in Counter-Strike: Condition Zero, Deleted Scenes is a legit single-player scripted campaign for the Counter-Strike series, released in 2004 on the GoldSrc engine. Instead of the insane multiplayer matches of CS 1.6, you play as a counter-terrorist special forces operative in linear but varied missions all over the world: Middle East, Russia, Latvia, Colombia, Italy, Arctic Ocean on an icebreaker, Argentina, USA, Northern Ireland, Turkmenistan, Iraq. Neutralize terrorists, rescue hostages, defuse bombs, neutralize missiles, hunt down narco-traffickers, shoot down helos or fighter jets, you'll have your hands full taking down the global terrorist threat! The objectives also give off a Rainbow Six vibe at times and occasionally a hint of GoldenEye 64, with staging that packs a serious punch despite the engine's tech limits. The training is in the same vein as Half-Life and Opposing Force, teaching you the game mechanics as well as the use of special weapons and tools available during your missions: the blowtorch to melt locks and open doors, remote-controlled bombs usable like Half-Life's C4, the camera to capture key evidence to send back to HQ, the fiber optic camera to spy on the sly like in Splinter Cell, and the radio to communicate with your brothers in arms. While these gadgets add a welcome tactical touch, they're mostly for scouting the terrain before gunning down all the terrorists and blowing up their installations. The gameplay perfectly mixes the essence of old-school Counter-Strike, with its precise yet satisfying ballistics, and Half-Life's environmental puzzles. You'll have to push or pull crates and climb on them to reach otherwise inaccessible spots, activate levers or valves to unlock doors, use or destroy turrets, and heal up at med stations. The missions, loosely based on iconic CS 1.6 maps, are relatively varied in their settings and objectives. You go from classic hostage rescues and bomb defusals to sniping, controlled demolitions, recon, etc... Unlike CS multiplayer where you're limited to two firearms, here you can sometimes carry a massive arsenal during missions. I've had up to six primary weapons on me at once, maybe more, not counting gear! In addition to the weapons from 1.6/CZ, Deleted Scenes offers the M60 machine gun that sprays the battlefield relentlessly, and straight-up the M72 LAW rocket launcher to shred enemy vehicles and even their infantry if you're in the mood. The only annoying thing is you can't pick up weapons or ammo from dead enemies; you're stuck with your basic loadout and the guns strategically placed by the devs for you to grab. Like a rocket launcher near a tank, or a sniper rifle on a rooftop. Also, don't expect to buy weapons in this game, it doesn't work like that here. The staging is pretty impressive for a GoldSrc game, with beautifully scripted scenes featuring aerial bombardments, chain explosions, etc. The art direction is pleasing and coherent but doesn't hide the very dated graphics and animations for 2004, especially knowing that Half-Life 2 and Counter-Strike: Source came out the same year! Zak Belica's music is epic and fits the serious special forces vibe perfectly. That said, the French dub is super caricatural with ultra-exaggerated foreign accents, which makes the dialogue hilarious at times. Fun fact, in the French version, you can easily recognize the voice actors for Wallace Breen, Eli Vance, and Barney Calhoun from Half-Life 2! In the end, Counter-Strike: Condition Zero - Deleted Scenes is a solid underrated or even forgotten tactical FPS, with a real solo mode that brings together the best of old-school Counter-Strike gameplay and the cult classic first-gen Half-Life games. If you like old-school FPS and accessible military shooters, don't hesitate!

If you have difficulties in the walktrough, this guide will be very useful: [/b] https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3561496240 [h1] Category: Really weird games [/h1] I hadn't really talked much about the "legendary" Counter-Strike 1.6 before, since I didn't see much point in it. Essentially, Condition Zero isn't a new wrap for the series, and calling this chunk of code an add-on is a stretch. Sure, there's an attempt to introduce a storyline and add missions with specific conditions instead of just bot training. But honestly, it's all done pretty poorly, and that's putting it mildly. Everyone knows that Counter-Strike originally started as a huge mod for Half-Life 1, which grew and changed over time. It's clear that many of the people playing it now (including me, born in 2006) weren't even around back then. But even from a boomer's perspective, it's hard to get why CS 1.6 is such a big deal. Sadly, Condition Zero doesn't make the already so-so original game any better. The character models are the same, the weapons are the same (though mostly useful, like being able to customize a ready-made weapon loadout), and there are even fewer maps, supposedly to focus on the 'story mode.' As for that, the player has to complete all objectives on each of the 19 maps, keeping at least a three-round edge over the terrorists (I played the whole game on medium difficulty and seriously regret it!!!). Some of the perks include not just mindlessly fighting bots, but actually doing different tasks, like "take out this many terrorists with this weapon" or "get the hostages out." There's also a feature to tweak the bot squad you play with. Their stats are split into "morale," "skill," and "teamwork," which might seem kind of arbitrary. But sometimes you really have to juggle your choice of teammates to actually pull off a win. It's worth mentioning that you can only play the scenarios as special forces, and the whole politics and censorship argument from back then doesn't apply - you can't play as the terrorists in the story missions. Now to the main thing that will make you scream louder and angrier than Sashko Fokin out of rage. Bot behavior is NOT just bad - it's a FUCKING nightmare. Yeah, the game is old, but the bots (terrorists), frankly, cheat on any of the four difficulty levels. They spot the player three seconds before appearing, shoot, and kill through concrete objects. Ally behavior is a whole other story: sometimes they literally jump off high places, don't follow orders, and the one thing that could have been a major plus (AI) turns into a huge minus. Sometimes bots intentionally lose, stretching the gameplay with their dumb actions. And no matter how hard you try, killing bots with the local AWP or point-blank with a shotgun can be impossible - they shoot faster and aim 'better'. Plus, speaking about the bot cluster: on medium difficulty, for example, not all of them even become active. The sound design is pretty bad too: bot chatter, grenade bangs, and gunfire are really harsh on the ears. CS 1.6 had the same problem. The graphics are super lame and blocky, and the environment textures are blurry. With all the effects, sometimes it's totally unclear where to run, who to shoot, or if you even did any damage to the enemy. As for online play, there's almost none. Right now, you can't find full servers with lots of players. Sure, everyone hangs out in 1.6, Source, or CS2, but why didn't they just make Condition Zero purely a story-driven game, without taking up extra hard drive space, and actually work on Steam Cloud and achievements? Undoubtedly, CS Condition Zero is the weirdest game in the Counter-Strike lineup. While it offers something new, it doesn't improve the gameplay either visually or technically. This game might only be of interest if you never played CS 1.6 back in the day. If you're a sane person, a couple of hours with Condition Zero will leave you genuinely annoyed and kill any desire to play the older Counter-Strike games (except maybe Source and CS2). https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3612049014 [h3] P. The twist is: You're playing CS, but your teammates are bots who all share **one brain cell** and it's on cooldown. --- ### Pros: * It's Counter-Strike… kind of. Condition Zero is kind of the "forgotten cousin" of the Counter-Strike series, but honestly, I had a lot of fun with it. The big difference here is the single-player campaign (Tour of Duty), which lets you lead your own CT squad through different missions. It's cool being able to experiment with weapons you don't normally touch in multiplayer, and the objective-based gameplay keeps things interesting. That said, the AI can be a pain. Early on, it feels balanced enough, but later missions get brutal. Enemies will snap onto your head the instant you peek, and sometimes it feels completely down to luck whether you survive or not. On top of that, you end up fighting your own teammates for kills just to complete challenges, which kind of kills the whole "teamwork" vibe. Still, I loved the idea of organizing a squad - it really makes me wish Valve had fleshed this out more. Imagine a modern version where your squad gains experience and you can actually issue tactical commands. That would be amazing. Then there's Deleted Scenes, which is basically a full single-player CS campaign. It's goofy, over the top, and the voice acting is hilariously cheesy, but it's also super fun. Honestly, it deserves a remake on Source or something, because there's nothing else like it. Sure, the graphics are old, and yeah, the game can be buggy or frustrating at times. But underneath all that, there's a really unique Counter-Strike experience here. Multiplayer is basically classic CS and community servers have kept it alive even today. Condition Zero isn't perfect, but it's definitely not the "bad" game people used to make it out to be. It tried something new, and while it didn't fully land back then, it's still a hidden gem that I'd recommend if you're a fan of old-school FPS games. I really love the original Counter-Strike 1.6 it's a timeless classic but Condition Zero holds a special place in my heart. It has a unique atmosphere that sets it apart. The graphical overhaul, the addition of new maps, and especially the two distinct campaign modes gave the game something truly special. Both campaigns are excellent in their own ways, offering a refreshing single-player experience that the series rarely explored. I never understood why Condition Zero received so much hate at launch. To me, it was a step forward in many aspects. Even today, the game isn't dead - it still has a fair player base and a dedicated community that keeps it alive. Now with Counter-Strike 2, the series has gone full competitive, leaving behind some of the charm that made earlier entries so memorable. There's no story, no agents with character, no campaigns - not even the classic online mode missions like Assassination, where we had to escort the VIP. These elements were forgotten, and I truly miss them. Condition Zero may not be perfect, but for those who appreciate both competitive and immersive content, it's a gem that still shines today.

Counter-Strike: Condition Zero on Steam presents a compelling evolution of the classic tactical shooter franchise, blending refined gameplay mechanics with a variety of game modes that cater to both new players and seasoned veterans. Building upon the foundation established by the original Counter-Strike, Condition Zero introduces a more polished experience, featuring improved graphics, enhanced AI, and a broader range of missions and multiplayer options. The game's visual design, while not pushing the boundaries of contemporary graphics, effectively captures the gritty, military-inspired aesthetic that has become synonymous with the series. The environments are detailed enough to immerse players in intense combat scenarios, and the sound design-ranging from weapon effects to ambient noises-adds a layer of realism that enhances the tactical gameplay experience. The core gameplay of Condition Zero remains faithful to the classic Counter-Strike formula: team-based combat where strategy, communication, and precise shooting are vital. The game offers a variety of modes, including the traditional bomb defusal, hostage rescue, and a single-player campaign that serves as both a tutorial and a story-driven experience. The single-player missions are well-designed, providing structured objectives that challenge players to employ different tactics and adapt to various scenarios. The AI opponents are notably smarter than in some earlier entries, making single-player and cooperative modes more engaging and less predictable. Multiplayer remains the heart of Counter-Strike: Condition Zero, with a robust community and a wide array of community-hosted servers offering custom maps, mods, and gameplay rules, ensuring longevity and replayability. One of the most significant upgrades in Condition Zero is the introduction of the "Deleted Scenes" campaign, which features a series of missions designed to showcase improved AI and more complex objectives. While some purists prefer the simplicity and rawness of the original Counter-Strike, the campaign provides a more structured and cinematic experience, with a narrative that ties the missions together. The game's mechanics-ranging from weapon recoil, movement, and economy management-are all finely tuned, providing a realistic yet accessible shooting experience. The controls are responsive, and the game strikes a good balance between arcade-style fun and tactical depth. The matchmaking and server browsing systems are straightforward, although at times they can suffer from latency issues or server availability, which is common in multiplayer-focused shooters of this era. The game's community support and modding scene have also played a significant role in maintaining its appeal. Players have created custom maps, skins, and game modes that keep the experience fresh long after the initial release. Additionally, the game's longevity is partly due to the enduring popularity of Counter-Strike's core gameplay loop-teamwork, map knowledge, and precise aiming. However, some players may find the game's graphics and interface somewhat dated, especially when compared to more modern shooters, which can slightly detract from the overall immersion. Still, the gameplay mechanics remain solid and reliable, making it a worthwhile experience for those who appreciate tactical shooters rooted in skill and strategy. Overall, Counter-Strike: Condition Zero on Steam is a worthy entry in the series that offers a blend of refined single-player content and the timeless appeal of competitive multiplayer. While it may not revolutionize the franchise, it successfully modernizes and polishes the classic formula, providing a balanced experience for fans of tactical shooters. Its emphasis on teamwork, map control, and precise shooting continues to resonate, and its community-driven content ensures that it remains relevant long after its initial release. For players seeking a game that combines strategic depth with fast-paced action in a multiplayer setting, Counter-Strike: Condition Zero remains a solid choice, especially for those interested in experiencing a more narrative-driven take on the foundational gameplay of Counter-Strike. I remember the first time I got headshot by a bot named "Steve" on de_aztec. 2004. The family computer smelled like overheating capacitors and broken dreams. Then I realized the terrorists had better tactics than my squad. The tragedy of Condition Zero isn't that it's bad. It's that it's the FPS equivalent of a participation trophy. The way bots would announce their presence with perfect accuracy "Enemy spotted!" (immediately headshots you through smoke) The way the "updated" models looked like action figures dipped in Vaseline The way the entire game felt like a mod that got promoted beyond its pay grade And the multiplayer? That wasn't Counter-Strike. That was a ghost town where the only players left were either: 12-year-olds who didn't know this wasn't the real CS Bots pretending to be 12-year-olds Now? 2024. I don't play Condition Zero anymore. But sometimes, when I close my eyes, I still hear it: "Terrorists win." And I whisper back: "No shit."

Condition Zero is an artifact and not even worth collecting... This is an old entry in the Counter-Strike series. It has bot matches and a single-player campaign. When I tried to play online, all I found were chaotic and noisy servers. There was a lot of toxic behaviour, and it was hard to have a normal game. For those who might say this is just a "skill issue," I want to be clear: I have no trouble adapting to older shooters, and my feedback is about the experience itself, not personal performance. Because of this, I spent most of my time in single player. The single-player mode has missions, team assignments, and specific challenges for each level. There were a few moments that stood out, like having to guide hostages to safety, which did give me a good laugh. The AI in the game was inconsistent. Sometimes the bots would help, but other times they got in the way or made things more frustrating. The game's mechanics and controls are simple and feel old. Weapons work, but there is nothing special or modern about how they feel. The progression in single player is straightforward, but it does not make the game feel new or exciting. This review is based only on what I experienced while playing the game as it is available now. I did not notice anything about the visuals or audio that stood out enough to mention. Unless you are curious about Counter-Strike's single player or want to revisit it for nostalgia, I do not recommend this game in 2025. For most players, Condition Zero is just a piece of history and not worth picking up today. Final Rating: 4/10 Barely worth a look, even for die-hard fans.

I'll be clear immediately: I'm a very casual fan of this series. I really don't care for Counter-Strike 2, how it outright replaced CSGO, how it essentially killed CSGO's casual content (all custom and most official), and its seemingly even further hardlined esports direction. I don't exactly enjoy the playerbase """communication""" in this series either, so there's basically no incentive for me to bother at this point. So then, somehow, Condition Zero has stood the test of time even though infamously nobody cared about it. It stands up just because it simply has by far the best singleplayer offerings in the series. This is the only entry to have an Unreal Tournament style singleplayer (Tour of Duty) where you'll be given a checklist of normal bot matches with multiple challenges to complete in order to win per match. The bots could be better (it should be noted though the bots use "voice chat" to communicate what they're doing and planning, which you can also use chat commands to somewhat influence them too) but this mode turned out to be a very respectable way of keeping the series alive for me. There's a bunch of mission pack mods to extend the playtime of Tour of Duty too, so it massively adds value to Condition Zero. Bizarrely too it contains a proper traditional singleplayer campaign via a series of singleplayer missions via "Deleted Scenes"; mildly comparable to Half-Life (only because Deleted Scenes plays much more like as if it's just another Half-Life expansion pack, rather than being true Counter-Strike). I'm not even going to pretend your time isn't probably much better spent on just playing the entire Half-Life collection or the Tour of Duty mode instead, but it does exist. Of course there's multiplayer too, but nobody's playing it. It does seem to have benefited from HL1's anniversary update, so it doesn't look like it would take much to run a server for friends at least. I recommend this one just for the fact it's the most reasonable game for singleplayer in the series, even if you don't care about Deleted Scenes.

Huge respect to Valve for trying something new with the franchise at the time. The missions were engaging for what they were, and the concept of completing objectives with AI teammates brought a unique flavor to the series. It's not the kind of game I'd replay endlessly like 1.6 or Global Offensive, but it didn't need to be. For me, it served a different purpose. Condition Zero might be a one-time experience, but it was the game that made me realize Counter-Strike could be more than just online matches - and for that, it will always have a place in my heart.

Considering this game comes bundled with CS 1.6, I'm not really gonna talk about the multiplayer, I'm gonna talk about the single-player Campaign, Deleted Scenes. Deleted Scenes is comprised of multiple missions, each one being a different scenario where you play as a Counter-Terrorist Operator from one of the many CT factions depending on the mission's context. The best way to describe the level design is that it's sort of a hybrid between Medal of Honor and Half-Life. You'll be doing a lot of crawling through vents and tight areas like Half-Life, and there's a lot of corridor-style shooting with the game spawning enemies in areas you have to backtrack through after completing an objective like Medal of Honor. You're commonly doing 1-man infiltration missions, with a few sequences here and there with friendly NPCs. There's unfortunately no squad management type of gameplay like Rainbow Six, which in my opinion is a missed opportunity since they should've drawn more inspiration from it instead of Medal of Honor. The game still uses Counter-Strike's shooting mechanics, and the enemies seem to have the health of an armored opponent in the normal PvP (example being that M4 takes 2 headshots to kill while the AK takes 1). The game's setpieces are nice, and it's overall a fun older 2000s shooter that feels similar to Medal of Honor, while also having the blood and gibbing effects of Half-Life. This game was dropped and picked back up by a couple of different developers which is probably why it's as basic as it is. I honestly think they should drop an update for this game that merges it with the normal Condition Zero executable, and just sidelines that crappy bot "Campaign" the base game has. Overall it's worth playing to experience the novelty of a single-player CS game that has a similar charm to those community made Half-Life mods, but in the context of a neat Counter-Terrorism game. This sort of shooter genre needs to come back, because Rainbow Six is basically a shadow of its former self these days. I should also mention that the Campaign doesn't play through every mission, so it's worth checking out the World Map for the couple of missions it doesn't play.

A Nostalgic Journey with Some Hidden Gems Alright, let's talk about Counter-Strike: Condition Zero. I'm sure a lot of you probably know it's the "odd one out" in the Counter-Strike series, sandwiched between the original and Source. And yeah, it's got its flaws, but I can't help but feel a sense of nostalgia whenever I load it up. First off, this game has that classic Counter-Strike feel. If you've played 1.6, you'll instantly feel at home. The core mechanics are there: team-based, tactical gameplay, bomb planting, hostage rescues, all that good stuff. There's a reason CS became a staple in the FPS world, and Condition Zero carries that legacy well, even though it wasn't as big as its predecessors. Now, here's the thing about Condition Zero-it introduced a single-player component that was actually kind of fun. You get these little AI matches where you can practice your skills or just mess around. Sure, the bots aren't the brightest, but they do provide a decent challenge if you're looking to warm up or just want to play at your own pace without the pressure of online matches. The real hidden gem here, though, is the Deleted Scenes campaign. It's not perfect, but it was an interesting attempt to give Condition Zero a single-player story mode (something the franchise didn't have before). You go through different missions that range from stealthy approaches to all-out gunfights. The voice acting is... well, let's just say it's not going to win any awards, but it's got that goofy charm you can appreciate if you're into retro FPS campaigns. I won't lie, the AI is a little clunky, and the missions can get repetitive, but there's something oddly satisfying about taking on terrorists in a more structured way than the usual match-based chaos. For people who loved CS but wanted something different, Deleted Scenes was kind of an underappreciated bonus. Now, let's be real for a second. Condition Zero doesn't hold up to Counter-Strike: Source or Global Offensive. It's got that weird in-between vibe, where it's not as polished or fluid as Source, and the graphics-while decent for its time-look pretty dated now. The bots can be hilarious (in a bad way), and the online community was smaller than in the CS 1.6 days, which made it tough to get a full, active match going. Also, it had this weird mix of being too "arcade" for the hardcore competitive scene but not casual enough to be a proper "fun" game for people who just want to jump in and shoot stuff. It's like Condition Zero didn't really know what it wanted to be, and as a result, it kinda fell into this awkward middle ground that wasn't as well-received by the wider community. For me, though, Condition Zero is still a solid pick if you're a fan of Counter-Strike. It may not be the top dog in the series, but it's got that old-school charm. The maps feel classic, and the gunplay still holds up, even if it doesn't have the same polish as its successors. Plus, if you're into the history of Counter-Strike, this game is like a weird little snapshot of where the series was trying to go before Source changed everything. If you're into retro FPS games and enjoy diving deep into older titles that didn't quite make it, Condition Zero is worth checking out. Just don't expect it to dethrone CS 1.6 or Source.

[h1]Recommended - A Short, Focused Half-Life Side Story That Still Holds Up[/h1] [i]Played and completed multiple times (first in 2022, revisited on Linux in 2026).[/i] Half-Life: Blue Shift is often labeled the "weakest" Half-Life entry, but that reputation mostly comes from unfair comparisons. This expansion was never designed to rival Half-Life or Opposing Force in scope. What it offers instead is a compact, grounded retelling of the Black Mesa incident from a different perspective - and judged on those terms, it succeeds. [hr][/hr] [h2]What Blue Shift Actually Is[/h2] Blue Shift was originally developed as part of a cancelled Dreamcast port of Half-Life and later released as a standalone expansion in 2001. That development history matters when judging its size and ambition. You don't play a super-soldier. You don't get experimental weapons. You don't reshape the universe. You play Barney Calhoun - a security guard - trying to survive and escape. The smaller scope is intentional. The game focuses on: [list] [*]Environmental storytelling [*]Scripted sequences instead of cutscenes [*]Puzzles integrated into believable facility spaces [*]A more human-scale view of the Black Mesa disaster [/list] If you expect Opposing Force 2.0, you will be disappointed. If you expect a focused Half-Life side story, it works well. [hr][/hr] [h2]Gameplay & Design[/h2] Mechanically, this is classic GoldSrc Half-Life: [list] [*]Tight first-person shooting [*]Logical physics-based puzzles [*]Continuous narrative flow without hard scene cuts [*]Escort mechanics used sparingly [/list] Yes, the campaign is short (around 3 hours). Yes, there are no new weapons. Yes, there is no boss fight. Those are valid criticisms, but they do not make the game bad - they define its scale. The pacing benefits from that size, and the game does not overstay its welcome. [hr][/hr] [h2]Technical Performance (Linux / Wine)[/h2] This playthrough was completed entirely on Linux using Wine, with excellent results. [b]System configuration:[/b] [list] [*]OS: Ubuntu Server 25.10 [*]Desktop: XFCE [*]Display server: X11 (Xorg) [*]CPU: Intel Core i7-6850K @ 3.6 GHz (6 cores / 12 threads) [*]GPU: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2070 SUPER [*]RAM: 16 GB [*]Storage: SSD [*]Resolution: 1920x1080 [*]Wine: 11.0 Staging [/list] [b]Observed performance:[/b] [list] [*]Average FPS: ~72 [*]1% low: ~62 FPS [*]Frame pacing: Stable, no stutter [*]Load times: ~1 second [*]GPU usage: ~7% (expected - engine is CPU-bound) [*]VRAM usage: ~1.4 GB [*]Extended play session without crashes or degradation [/list] Once raw mouse input was configured correctly, input was flawless. No OpenGL errors, no freezes, and no stability issues during this revisit. [hr][/hr] [h2]Story & Atmosphere[/h2] Blue Shift's strongest point is perspective. Seeing Black Mesa through the eyes of a security guard adds grounding to familiar events. The interactions with scientists, the evacuation effort, and the final escape work because they stay small and believable. The ending is deliberately low-key. That fits the character. Not every story needs a final boss. [hr][/hr] [h2]Final Verdict[/h2] Half-Life: Blue Shift is: [list] [*]Short [*]Focused [*]Mechanically solid [*]Historically relevant to the Half-Life timeline [/list] It is not a replacement for Half-Life. It is not as ambitious as Opposing Force. But it is a worthwhile piece of the series - especially at its usual low price - and it runs exceptionally well on modern Linux systems. If you are a Half-Life fan, this is worth playing at least once. If you want a different angle on Black Mesa, it adds value. If you expect a large expansion with new systems, adjust expectations. [b]Recommended - with proper context.[/b]

That amount of time was nothing to scoff at back then, you could make a top-tier Zelda in half that time if you reuse the right amount of assets. No new guns, no new enemies, no new gameplay mechanics. Any notable characters in the second half are 60% water, 40% technobabble. The levels we get here are fun at first, until the story requires you to backtrack through cascading hallways and blood-stricken stairs, all enemies already dealt with, clanking boots echoing throughout mundane spaces. It doesn't expand. It doesn't compellingly work as another layer on the Black Mesa incident. It's just mindless muck coasting off the admittedly great intro portion. Half Life Blue Shift is small, but it is important. It shows the Black Mesa incident from a different pair of eyes, and that alone makes it worth playing. You are not Gordon Freeman. You are Barney Calhoun. Not a hero, not a scientist, just a security guard trying to survive a disaster that is far bigger than him. That perspective changes everything. You are not moving forward to fix things. You are just trying to get out alive. Blue Shift feels more personal. You see familiar places from new angles. Hallways you once rushed through now feel dangerous. Places that felt controlled before now feel fragile. Black Mesa is falling apart, and you are stuck inside it. The game does not try to be bigger than Half Life. It does not try to top it. It stays focused. Short, tight, and grounded. There is no saving the world here. There is only escape. Combat feels more desperate because you have less power. You are not chosen. You are lucky. Every fight feels like something you barely survive instead of something you dominate. What Blue Shift really adds is context. It reminds you that Gordon was not alone. While one person was pushing forward, others were just trying to survive the same nightmare in different corners of the facility. Blue Shift ends quietly. No big resolution. No victory. Just relief. And somehow, that fits perfectly. It is not an expansion you remember for scale. You remember it for perspective. If you are waiting for Half-Life 3... Prepare for unforeseen consequences!

The Dreamcast controller wasn't conducive to first-person shooters, so Gearbox made the levels much easier than the original, at least in terms of combat. Plus, it doesn't include any of the extra weapons or enemies from Opposing Force, which I liked. It plays more like the original game than Opposing Force, but it does not really build on the original in terms of gameplay.
