Das ist a very short extension pack for the original Half-Life game. I'm not sure how it would go as a separate game. Meanwhile Opposing Force brought new weapons, aliens, and mechanics besides showing events in Black Mesa from another perspective, Blue Shift only shows the perspective of a new character and brings Gordon Freeman as a cameo in some moments. Maybe this game's length influenced Gearbox Software to make it so. However, it's worth your time since it's still a funny first-person shooter; the developers have also brought new puzzles, so you won't get bored. Additionally, optimization is just great here(even better than in some modern games) - Half-Life: Blue Shift works extremely well on my computer and I don't have to install dozens of mods or change something in the app's settings; for whole time I've played with it(13 hours) I remember having had this game crashed only once, which is pretty good for a 24-year-old game. [h2]GAMEPLAY[/h2] Even though Gearbox hasn't brought any new mechanics, which is seen well by the absence of a unique Training Room, they still have given us new puzzles. This' the only difference between the previous 2 games, I guess. Game still makes you think with your own head, like in the chapter of Duty Calls when you're reluctant to find your way through a big crushing mechanism yourself. Or there's another good example in the Power Struggle chapter - the wire to dynamite is broken and electricity can't go through it; therefore you must find something that can conduct electric current(Physics class from school apparently became useful in real life). Besides adding puzzles they've cut off some content. At first, they brought back the crowbar and the whole set of guns is just a cut copy of one from the original game. Plus, now you can't replenish your suit's health since it's not an electric super technological device anymore and just a simple bulletproof vest which can be replaced by a new one if the old one is broken. It sucks because HEV stations are still on locations which confuses me. I know that it was mentioned in the Training Room and they left it so that it wouldn't look bizarre, like I'm in a different universe, but it still confuses me. [h2]PLOT[/h2] Like I said, we've got a new protagonist here; it's a Black Mesa's security guard: Barney Calhoun. He begins his usual day at work, but while he's on his way Resonance Cascade happens. Then Barney is reluctant to fight his way through aliens and HECU personnel to escape. There is nothing new among enemies Calhoun is dealing with - the same soldiers and monsters from Half-Life. The protagonist meets one scientist who tells him to find Dr. Rosenberg who can save himself and Barney. Having been found, Rosenberg sends Calhoun to a few missions to set up their device which can help them escape Black Mesa. Then they escape and the game is finished. Like I said, the game is very short and 2-3 hours is completely enough for it. But the greatest difference between Blue Shift and what was before in the series is that there is no last boss fight. Maybe the developers were lazy to create a new enemy with its 3D model, textures, and animations; having the absence of anything new in the lists of enemies and weapons, I can guess it was so. Anyway, a new perspective is worth it if you're a crazy Half-Life fan; otherwise there is a different reason why I can recommend this game. [h2]GRAPHICS[/h2] No, if you're aroused only by high texture resolution and billions of polygons on an enemy's teeth which you'll never see, then get the hell out of here! This' a game from 2001 and it obviously has an outlook that can tense your eyes. But I like old games for making their own atmospheres; BS isn't an exception. Its style isn't far from Half-Life and Half-Life: Opposing Force. It looks pretty formal in Black Mesa and very curious in Xen. Sometimes the aliens' world looks like a tale, in a good way. But Xen also can cause claustrophobia via its long tunnels; it especially will do so with its tortuous tunnel maze. All in all, this facet of the game isn't terrible, and the authors give updates occasionally so that I can play with my native resolution. [h2]MUSIC[/h2] There isn't much to say about the soundtrack. It's still good and puts energy into the moments when I'm supposed to cosplay Rambo. But sometimes it screws up and plays a bit earlier than it should; for instance, when I'm coming out of a tunnel in Xen to the place where I must do a few actions before I leave, a track begins playing, as though there's about to be a hard gunfire in a few seconds. But I do what I need to, and only then, after the song stopped, aliens come. Such moments look weird to me. Anyway, this game's track list is suitable, which is obviously great! [h2]CONCLUSION[/h2] This' a great addition to the main storyline. It shows a different point of view during the Cascade Resonance. Besides having brought new lore to the series Half-Life: Blue Shift has gotten a dynamic gameplay. I recommend playing it if you're a Half-Life fan, or want to learn a bit more about the Half-Life universe, or just like destroying dozens of enemies on your way with a shotgun.

Blue Shift is yet another stand-alone expansion for Half-Life. Unfortunately, this time with less content than Opposing Force and much, much shorter. This time you slip into the role of a security officer Barney on Black Mesa and, driven by the same events as Gorden Freeman, fight your way through the research facility and find your way out. No really new enemy types or weapons have been integrated into this add-on, it's more or less the same experience as Half-Life. To be more precise, there are even fewer weapons, as all the alien weapons or experimental weapons are not available to Barney. That's a shame, because I would have liked to have seen some of the typical weapons that you normally see on security guards. This would be an opportunity to swap the crowbar for a baton. Certain things are still different. Since Barney doesn't have an HEV suit, he can't use charging stations. However, for immersion reasons, these are located throughout the research facility, which is cool and feels that Black Mesa is a lively place. Also, during the course of the game you open up an old locked complex of the facility and then suddenly have older models of the health recharging stations, which adds a nice touch to the atmosphere. Like this facility is really a long forgotten part of the complex where they use old tech and such. One point in addition to the last statement I have to make, which was already brilliantly done in Opposing Force, was the world building. Here you experience the Resoance Cascade from a different perspective and, as in the main game, you have the opportunity to explore the first passages of the game, talk to every NPC or simply listen to conversations, which is very well done. Later in the game, scenes also offer a certain insight into what the other characters are doing at the time, because the paths cross with the protagonist from time to time or certain events are mentioned by NPCs. It gives you the feeling that the incident is an event that has complex effects and it is exciting to see this from different perspectives. In addition, an HD model pack was included at the time that provided better models for NPCs and weapons, which could also be used in the main game and Opposing Force. But now this is already integrated into the games anyway, so you wouldn't necessarily have to buy Blue Shift for it. I liked the original models more anyway. But that doesn't mean it's bad. So basically it's more levels that offer more puzzles and more Half-Life experience, and they're well done for that. Plus, seeing the Black Mesaa incident from another perspective is a must. So if you can't get enough of Half-Life, this short game is also a good choice. And in the sale, the game only costs a few cents.

Half-Life: Blue Shift is a short but solid expansion to the original Half-Life, putting players in the shoes of security guard Barney Calhoun. While it doesn't introduce groundbreaking gameplay changes, it offers a fresh perspective on the Black Mesa incident. [H3] Blue Shift is painfully lacking in originality and fun.[/H3] In the original Half-Life, Gordon Freeman's role as a scientist has a clear thematic influence on the gameplay. He solves logic and physics puzzles through his intelligence, referencing his degree in theoretical physics degree, and operates complex scientific equipment through his role as a Research Associate at Black Mesa. In Opposing Force, Adrian Shephard is a US Marine which translates to a greater familiarity with weaponry, and thus a more varied arsenal to fit the combat-focused gameplay. Blue Shift's focus on Barney the security guard also shapes the game's direction, as you spend roughly three hours wandering through empty corridors and supply rooms, while occasionally opening doors. Gone are the fun test chambers, dams and comically placed shark tanks from the original Half-Life, or the topside war zones of Opposing Force, and instead Blue Shift focuses on the dull procurement and operational backrooms of Black Mesa. No Half-Life player was clammering for more water treatment plants to swim through, and they [i] certainly[/i] weren't asking for more Xen levels. In this sense, Blue Shift doubles down on some of the dullest elements of Half-Life. It's not all negative, however. Blue Shift revisits some of the cooler moments of the original Half-Life, including reprising the signature opening tram segment. Yet, there's a feeling that it's more of an anxious retread rather than a genuine nod. Barney isn't a scientist, and so when he begins dimension-hopping like Gordon, it feels less thematically relevant and almost ham-fisted. Blue Shift does have a few ideas up its sleeve, such as a horror-inspired elevator malfunction (complete with lights flickering on and off) as each Black Mesa member is picked off by the aliens. Yet, the setpiece feels hastily put together; NPCs clip through the floor during the descent, and the views outside the lift feature a few other security guards running down corridors in an otherwise empty room. Blue Shift also clocks in at a much shorter three hours, compared to Opposing Force's eight. This should be an opportunity to cram as many ideas as possible into a short space of time, cutting all the fat. Except the game struggles to fill out even that reduced run-time. The HD models that come with the package provide a fresh coat of paint to the original game's assets, as if trying to sweeten the deal, but the focus on more realistic models has inevitably aged worse over time than the original interpretations. Blue Shift is worth the pennies that Steam asks for, but whether it's worth your time is another question. If you're looking to experience the Half-Life story in its entirety, sure. However, if your purpose is to tick off classics from an exhaustive list of FPS canon, you wouldn't lose much by skipping this one.

🎮 Personal Review Tiers 1 - Exceptional | 2 - Great | 3 - Good | 4 - Average | 5 - Bad Half-Life 2 Review Tier: 1 - Exceptional 📌 Disclaimers This review reflects my experience playing exclusively on Steam Deck. I've already played this game to exhaustion on Xbox 360 via The Orange Box-hundreds of hours, somewhere between 8-10 full playthroughs-and I've long considered it the best video game ever made. Now that I'm new to Steam, replaying it here felt like a rite of passage. At the time of writing, I'm mid-way through a 100% completion run, but I know the game inside out, so ignore the deceptively low playtime on my profile. ✅ Pros Visual fidelity This game simply refuses to age. Even after 22 years, the art direction and environmental detail remain astonishing. City 17 still feels oppressive, lived‑in, and hauntingly beautiful-one of the most iconic and fully realised game worlds ever built. It genuinely looks like a late‑PS3/360 title despite launching in 2004. The original immersive story-game Plenty of games experimented with in-world storytelling before, but Half-Life and Half-Life 2 perfected it. No cinematic cutscenes, no camera yanking you away-just you, in the moment, witnessing every major event as Gordon Freeman. It still feels revolutionary. Gameplay that prioritises creativity and fun Physics puzzles, environmental improvisation, frantic firefights-the game constantly rewards curiosity and experimentation. And the Gravity Gun remains the greatest weapon in video game history. It turns every object into a tool, a projectile, or a puzzle solution. It's pure design brilliance. A memorable journey through City 17 and beyond At its core, it's a simple "get from point A to point B" adventure, but every chapter is crafted with such care that each location feels distinct, purposeful, and dripping with atmosphere. Impeccable pacing Action, exploration, and puzzles flow together effortlessly. No chapter drags, no encounter overstays its welcome. Every level feels substantial, offering just the right amount of combat without ever becoming exhausting. A story that's engaging without being convoluted It's mysterious, intriguing, and filled with iconic moments. The narrative is efficient and direct, yet strange in ways that perfectly complement the world's tone-never bloated, never confusing for the sake of it. Characters that feel real From major allies to nameless rebels, every character is memorable, well‑acted, and written with restraint. Even brief NPC interactions carry personality and charm. Meaningful difficulty options The game respects both newcomers and veterans. Easy still requires attention, while Hard offers a genuinely demanding challenge. It's balanced, thoughtful, and fair. Steam Deck performance Flawless. Smooth, stable, visually gorgeous, and with excellent battery life even at high settings. It feels made for handheld play. ❌ Cons Enemy variety My only real criticism-both then and now-is that Combine soldiers and zombies could use more variation. There are only a few types of each, and most boss encounters are vehicular. The combat is so strong that this ends up being more of a nitpick than a real flaw, but it's still noticeable. It ends on a cliffhanger… and that cliffhanger will never be resolved Valve has largely stepped away from video game development, leaving one of the greatest games ever made frozen at a cliff-hanger. Poetic. Thanks, Gabe. 🎯 Final Thoughts Ahead of its time, endlessly fun, visually striking, and overflowing with atmosphere, Half-Life 2 remains-at least to me-the pinnacle of video game design. There's nothing it doesn't excel at. The heartbreak of the series never receiving a proper conclusion is a bitter pill, but perhaps a necessary one for the masterpiece we did get. It is what it is-and it's worth experiencing. Again, and again, and again.

These are my thoughts for Half Life 2 as a whole. Half-Life 2 as a whole is excellent. A benchmark, a standard for what games should strive to surpass. It is, in many cases, rarely surpassed. It is something that every gamer who can should play. The story is excellent, intriguing, and gripping. It often caught me off guard at some turns, and left me satisfied at others. I was genuinely knocked flat at the ending of episode 2. Half-Life as a whole story-wise, really shows the true feeling of people rising up against an oppressive force. Gordon is a one-man army, don't get me wrong, but the unity and feeling of the resistance is really well executed. The gameplay is top notch, it genuinely trusts you to perform to the best of your abilities most of the time. The gunplay is smooth, the flow of combat is great, rewarding you for playing well. The respites between combat encounters feel refreshing, being allowed to stock up on what you need, but the slight worry of if it'll be enough. And the puzzles are near perfect. Sometimes a bit obtuse, but the majority of the time it feels excellent to solve the various puzzles before you. The level design is great, going from an oppressive city where you can feel the weight of the Combine pressing down onto the residents, to ravenholm where you can see the destruction first-hand of what the combine can and does do. I will admit, possibly cause I'm not the brightest, there were a few times where I got caught up and couldn't figure out where to go. Whether it's due to my own inablity or the game's design, well, the jury is still out on that. The world itself is great, you can really tell the impact that the combine have had, Ravenholm as an example again, I think the idea of the Combine using headcrabs deposited from launched carriers to infect people is genius. The way they're always on you, rarely giving you a proper moment to breathe. How they monitor the people closely, how little havens of resistance communicate and survive together. It all comes together to make an amazingly believable, engaging world with a very sympathetic plight for the people under the Combine that makes you want to fight. All in all, Half-Life 2, as a whole, as I said, everyone who can play it should. It's a terrific experience, and really shows what games should strive to surpass or at the very least, surpass. Most of all, it's just really really damn fun. And man, I can't wait for episode 3, wonder when it's coming out?

Half-Life 2 is a first-person action game about Gordon Freeman, who joins a resistance effort to liberate Earth from the alien Combine empire. This is one of the games that I wanted my girlfriend to play for so long, just because it's a piece of my gamer childhood when I rented a game called The Orange Box for the PS3, which has this alongside Episode 1 and 2. There's only one problem, though: it's single-player. So I got a mod called Synergy, where we can play multiplayer together for all three of the games, and revisiting this game made me realize that not only did it not become one of my favorite video games, even though I still enjoyed it, but it's one of the worst games that my girlfriend has played. My girlfriend doesn't like science fiction at all, but I was hoping this would be an exception, since it's more grounded, but this didn't change her mind. She found the AI to be absolutely abysmal that was just getting in her way, and she couldn't really connect with the story and genuinely got a little confused about what was going on. She didn't mind G-Man at first, but then she got progressively annoyed with him because of his vagueness in the way he speaks that's giving her no close answers to what he's doing or what type of person he is and why. The platforming wasn't doing anything for her but to irritate her, and she was just not having fun; the only reason we managed to beat it was that she was with me in the game. She would've rage-quit the game herself. As for me, though, I find the story to be super engaging, so you start pulling the pieces together of what's going on through the journey. Especially with the beginning, where it puts you into City 17, which is run by Dr. Wallace Breen, which makes the place feel like a fascist place to live in. The gameplay, when it comes to running, action, and driving, is so smooth that I'm surprised it flows this well for a 2004 game. Although I will say that driving the boat can feel too smooth or slippery that can get a little annoying, and that definitely got my girlfriend completely pissed off. The graphics still look great to this day, and the gravity mechanics when it comes to using the Gravity Gun are just perfect, so that you can launch a lot of items to faraway places that we can't go. The soundtrack is a lot of fun to listen to, and the set-pieces can get tense, even on the easiest difficulty and on the multiplayer mod. My favorite part of the game is the Ravenholm stage. It's genuinely well designed with the look and atmosphere, which was the one saving grace that my girlfriend had with this game. I find the runtime to be very long, but well-deserved, which took us to so many memorable levels. The characters have such layers to them that I find it fascinating to look into these characters and figure them out as it goes. Half-Life 2 is kind of a fantastic game that has tons of variety to have fun with, which is why people have this as one of the best video games ever. 9/10

Half-Life 2 is a near-perfect amalgamation of incredible storytelling, engaging level design and innovative combat. Combine (heh!) that with an incredible level of ongoing support, most recently with the 20th Anniversary Update, and you get a game that does not feel like it was originally released all the way back in 2004. The first chunk of Half-Life 2 is one of my favourite singleplayer experiences of all time. The atmospheric, environmental worldbuilding that starts as soon as you arrive in City 17 - carrying on all through your journey into Ravenholm and the coast - is magnificent, with the context of events since the Black Mesa Incident slowly flowing in as you experience a world much unlike the one you left behind in the original game. Steadily exploring the dystopian metropolis, piloting the airboat through the abandoned canals, experiencing the shock of the destroyed Ravenholm and driving the scenic coastal route is such a vibe as you take in the apocalyptic world for yourself. The additional episodes provide a welcome addition to the ongoing story, with Episode 2's forest environment setting the scene for the better of the two expansions. But then once the sad realisation dawns on you that this iconic series is at its end, you can only live in hope that one day we will be reflecting on the events of the mythic third episode.

Technologically impressive even 20+ years after release. THIS is what you call a revolutionary masterpiece. Half-Life 2 re-defined the FPS genre and its influence can be felt to this very day. Graphically it holds up unfathomably well, and Half-Life 2's world is far more interactable than most video-games coming out nowadays. Very few games can even begin to rival Half-Life 2's physics, which are still really fun to play around with. Most importantly of all though, Half-Life 2 treats you like an intelligent human being. It expects you to explore and look for the details. Wish more modern games didn't hand-hold you as much. SPEAKING OF TRUSTING THE PLAYER'S INTELLIGENCE! The story and ESPECIALLY the lore are really well thought out (even if a bit contradictory and very retcon-y in some places, especially if we count the episodes). But seriously, if you love vague story-telling that focuses more on world-building than dialogue, then you'll LOVE delving deep into Half-Life's lore. That isn't to say that the main story along with its dialogue has been neglected though, quite the contrary in fact. If all the overwhelmingly positive reviews, and Half-Life's significance to the gaming industry as a whole isn't enough to convince you to buy and play it, then I don't know what will. Seriously, this is a must-play experience for anyone that plays video-games.

You know a game is amazing when you go to play it simply because you wanted to kill an hour, and it ends up turning almost 5 hours later. I kept wanting to put it down, waiting to finish a segment to save, but each time the new area, or narrative push kept me going, "just a bit further and i'll stop". This game absolutely holds up in 2026. Its one of those games that either has its own unique style that makes it never feel dated, or fits into one of those timeless styles that already exists, stuff like Metroid Prime, fixed camera tank-control games, Zelda, 2d platformers, Dead by Daylight, DMC etc, all games that are so rich and polished in mechanics or having such lively worlds that they never feel dated, aside from benefiting from QOL changes and updates. What is Half-life 2? Its a narrative driven fps. Campaign structure wise it plays like games like The Last Of Us, you go from point A to B to point C fighting enemies, viewing cutscenes, meeting npcs and solving puzzles/obstacles. Similar to TLOU remake(which is actually a remaster) everything happens in real time, so all cutscenes and dialogue happens in-game. Tonally it's not just a fps, it has some strong horror elements on occasions, in terms of occasional atmosphere, setting, music, enemy encounter and jump scares. You don't play the game scared like RE, but the game does manage to surprise with a scare here and there and some moments and can be a little tension driven. But for the most part is a fun, interesting sci fi adventure. Gameplay. If you love Metroid Prime, you'll feel at home here. Very similar gameplay loop, of going through area, dispatching enemies and solving puzzles/obstacles and getting important items to progress. The key differences is this game is 1) linear, 2) less focused on item hunting/key progression, 3) no enemy respawns and 4) more narrative driven. The game also plays like a boomer shooter, so if you love that genre you might feel at home here. In terms of the gameplay mechanics and feel, its alot closer to boomer shooters than standard fps flair like Dying Light, Halo, Metro, Borderlands and the like. You have the familiar walk and runs speeds(although this game has stamina), the familiar movement of the camera, the familiar jankiness of the aim, the physics of the jumps etc. The key difference is this game has a bigger focus on exploration, narrative and obstacle/puzzle solving and needing to constantly switch your weapons or use the best type isn't that encouraged. There are moments where you fight waves of enemies where you absolutely need to keep switching guns because reloading is slow and you risk getting hit, and those moments shine the most but for the most part you can strategically move around, shoot with one or two weapons and kill the enemies creatively with the environment or traps. Similar to Metroid Prime, puzzle/obstacle solving absolutely shines. Similar to that series, this game doesnt hold your hand and leaves absolutely to your vices to figure out a solution or how to progress. And unlike Metroid Prime or games like Silent Hill, where you can get stuck use a guide and the game doesn't lose any fun factor, Half-Life 2 absolutely wants you to figure it out on your own, because the problems it presents aren't difficult or even mathematical, they are just very creative and require observation. Using a guide absolutely robs the game of its problem solving charm, as almost EVERY single time you feel so good, so accomplished and so happy you didn't use a guide because you got to witness the genius unfold of how that obstacle was solved. The game rewards not only creativity but also experimentation, Ive solved 3 obstacles so far absolutely in a way that the game didn't intend, whether it was abusing the physics to stack up items to reach an area, that needed a key or alternate route, or finding a different solution to the problem that worked similar to the actual solution. For example my dumbass didn't know you can knock down a bridge in the game, so I could cross, so instead I built my own bridge and walked across. Dont get me started on the ways you can dispose of enemies. Lastly graphics. This game got a light remaster not too long ago. The game stills looks pretty even by todays standards, mostly what looks good is the visuals effects, like shadows, lighting particles, and physics. Some environments look good especially from afar, the world has decently size scope so there is viewing distance. The only thing that really hurts this game is the textures, its the one area that really doesn't hold up and if youre a modern gamer can def hurt the immersion quite a bit, characters could benefit from updating buts its not a big deal like the textures, they have a good enough style to have charm and they animate well enough. If the recent RTX remaster was more compatible with lower end hardware, or this game got another remaster that found a middle ground between this remaster and the RTX remaster in terms of graphics, this game would feel 100% modern and give any new game today a run for its money. Crazy how some games absolutely deserve the hype and live up to it.

I'm gonna ramble, but this game is THE standard. Twenty years later, it genuinely deserves every bit of praise it gets. Seriously, go play it. Half-Life 2 gave me the gravity gun, and now every FPS feels weak because you can't throw anything. you cannot interact with the enviroment and puzzle solve the same way this game does it. A 20 year old game ran so modern shooters could barely crawl. It's honestly insane how far ahead of its time this game was. Even the original is responsible for creating counter-strike. The gunplay is the only thing that's aged poorly, and even then it's the SMG and pistol being pea shooters. But honestly, why are you even using those? Play Ravenholm. Get the gravity gun only achievement. That level is a love letter to the game's level design and physics engine, and it changes how you approach the game almost permanently. It scared the shit out of me as a kid. Now it's one of my favourite levels to revisit. I can't remember who said it or where I heard it, but Valve are masters of "show, don't tell." By interacting with the world and exploring, you piece together what happened without the game stopping to explain itself. Even as a kid, I remember getting lost exploring Highway 17, just trying to understand what had happened there. then finding that building with the binoculars and seeing that they had been spying on the rebels the whole time. The real time eye tracking still blows my mind. A game released in 2004 had that. For comparison, San Andreas and MGS3 came out around the same time. now those games are goated, im not calling them bad. It still blows me away that Cutscenes are done entirely in engine, not CGI. This game is THAT good. If you haven't played it, you have to. You need to understand why we need Half-Life 3. It Deserves Game of the Decade. It deserves more. valve pls =(

I remember playing the first Half Life many years ago back on the Playstation 2. I've played the game religiously even when Half Life 2 finally released and played that on the original Xbox/Xbox 360. But now that I took off the nostalgia glasses I realized that this game is not the masterpiece that I thought it was ever since I had my revelation months ago. I will start with the gameplay then the story to explain why I came to this conclusion. First off, Half Life 2 gameplay is mediocre because it focuses on being a boomer shooter type of game where you run around with a huge arsenal of weapons the further you progress in the game which quickly stripes the ability to utilize the environment to a players advantage. Because of this decision from the developers it makes each scenario easy, dull, and predictable. I haven't forgotten about those long winded boat and car riding segments. I also could not stand sitting through the un-skippable cutscenes that use passive ways to give the player the ILLUSION that you are part of the story in Half Life 2 which got old real quick. The puzzles in Half Life 2 are creative despite being terrible which Valve used to brag about their physics engine but also in attempt to hide the fact that their gameplay is mediocre. A few games came out before Half life 2 which did a better job with their physics engine that didn't detract from the gameplay but actually enhanced it. The expected scripted events which happens at every awakening avenue in Half Life 2 makes the game lack depth and variety about how to go about each encounter. Not to mention the fact that EVERY single enemy in Half Life 2 have the same attack patterns especially from the combine enemies. The original Halo trilogy is the best example when it comes to a great FPS because it has unscripted events many times where enemies spawn in different locations on every level and have a hierarchy chain. Once the hierarchy is disrupted the enemies react to it depending on the enemy type. The higher the difficulty you play in Halo the more amplified the difficulty and tactics mixed with unscripted events makes every encounter unique/fun. Half Life 2 does not have any of these and the combine just stand out of cover like a swore thumb in both scripted and non scripted events through out the WHOLE GAME! I would argue for certain that if Half Life had a weapon limit like Halo it would have been VERY fun gameplay wise with strategy tactics in every encounter like Half Life 1 did despite the first game having the huge weapon arsenal also. Lastly, why are the Half Life 1 weapons completely discarded when they were the most fun and creative than any of the boring weapons in Half Life 2? Wasted potential to not reintroduce them especially Opposing Force ones! Secondly, Half Life 2 ruined the continuity of the story from Half Life 1 because Marc Laidlaw never considered the Gearbox content of Blue Shift and Opposing Force content canon by Gearbox. Barney Calhoun was one of those characters from the Blue Shift content that Gearbox created that they denied as canon but used him as a retcon in their own writing to make the story sound more "appealing" to the fans in Half Life 2. I cant even forget about General Adrian Shepard who was completely kicked to the curb also including Race X. Lets not forget Dr Kleiner and Eli Vance who were NEVER named in the ORIGINAL HALF LIFE because Valve is too arrogant thinking they created a good franchise while plagiarizing everyone else's hard work. The major plot hole that makes Half Life 2 a terrible story is the fact that G-man is an omnipotent being that can freeze time, change the past, etc. Why bother with a story like Half Life when their is no agency to anything that Gordon accomplishes by the player? G-man at any moment can terminate Gordon if he wanted to or Alyx on a whim since he SAVED Gordon INVOLUNTARILY at the end of Half Life 1 then threatened him with death if he refused to work for him. All of this "show don't tell" tactic in Valves story writing is ultimately what lead to the downfall of the franchise. Prepare for Unforeseen Consequences when you release Half Life 3, Valve... Not to mention how Gordon does not speak or express through any type of body language about how he feels about ANYTHING since the the first game. Not to mention the fact that Alyx and Elie objectify Gordon by forcing the idea of procreation on him. I will be amused with fanboys attempting to justify this by using passive aggressive tactics in order to objectify Gordon Freeman to go right along with it all. In conclusion, I am glad that I took off the nostalgia glasses and see the game for what it truly is. I hope Gordon takes off his and see that he truly is not a "Freeman" when being objectified left and right even by the people he considers allies. The game aged poorly and is not a game worth all of the praise that it deserves especially since Valve literally relies on fans of their community to make this game more interesting since Valve doesn't care about their own universe and will take other peoples well thought lore in attempt to make their game more coherently sound. Valve... "You have destroyed so much. What is it, exactly, that you have created? Can you name even one thing? I thought not."

The story is perfect for keeping you on the rails, you'll always have a reasonable reason to be where you are. Speaking of where you are, I played the original Half-life as well, and I'll tell you, the sequel is vastly superior, in story telling, mechanics, and polish, we're not even talking graphics! Valve clearly learnt a lot from the original half-life and it shows, the controls are almost perfect, MOST enemies feel like the fight is fair and well balanced (fuck striders, they suck), and for playing in 2025-2026, the settings are as modern as you really need them to be and the game runs without a hitch. All in all, I've rambled for a fair bit, but as I said at the start, just go buy the game, it's really good, and you'll get plenty of enjoyment out of it... It has been sitting in my library for ages, but only now, in 2026, did I finally commit to a full playthrough. I bought the game over 12 years ago, and yet the experience today feels just as relevant as it is timeless. Half-Life 2 feels genuinely authentic. The carefully crafted sound design, strong world-building, and dense, memorable atmosphere come together perfectly with a compelling story that spans both the base game and its episodes. What an absolute powerhouse this must have been when it launched back in 2004. It's no surprise that it still ranks among the highest-rated games on Metacritic. Despite its age, the game holds up remarkably well and runs flawlessly on modern systems. There's a natural momentum that constantly pushes you forward, making you want to follow the world, its characters, and the story as it slowly unfolds. I even ended up creating my own little side quest: hunting down all the hidden Half-Life symbols scattered throughout the game. Only later did I realize it was actually an achievement… one I unfortunately didn't manage to fully complete in the end. I've previously played Half-Life along with its expansions Blue Shift and Opposing Force, and compared to those, Half-Life 2 feels like a massive leap forward. The graphical upgrade is obvious, but even more impressive is the overall scope and ambition of the game. Everything feels more alive, more immersive, and more engaging. Recently I played through Half-Life 2, and I have some reflection on the experience. This is not the first time I've tried to play through Half-Life 2. My first attempt would have been circa 2010, via the Orange Box for the PS3. Arguably, the worst way you can experience the game (maybe beat by the OG Xbox version). I managed to complete the game on the PS3. I always chalked it up to the terrible port (which was inexplicably made by EA). A few sequences stuck in my mind, the boat section. The car section. Now, as we crossed into a new year, I figured it was time to give it another shot. I wanted to have the most optimal experience I could, I looked up which mods enhance the experience intended by Valve. It led me to MMod. It was simple enough to get up and running. My first thought is that the game looks pretty decent for a 2004 game. I am running the 2024 anniversary edition which apparently did some work to get it running on modern machines, and I can confirm it runs great, even without any mods. My second thought was "the game really just started, huh". You get like 2 lines of dialogue from G-Man and you're off to the races. "I'm sure there'll be more context and setup for the story" I thought, now in hindsight, foolishly. I'll cut to the chase. I think Half-Life 2 has aged poorly. The core gunplay is as good as it can be, I know the Source engine was and is a fantastic engine for shooters. But what surprised me is how much this game relies on the novelty of physics. Yes, it can be quite neat, even to a 2026 human. But man, does the novelty wear off quickly. What surprised me even more, however, is the story. I'd say the story is bad, but here's the thing. The game barely has a narrative. There's little to no context of what you're doing. 90% of Half-Life 2 is you going from A to B to C to D, usually with the mundane task of "rescue X" or "go to Y". There's no worldbuilding, no lore, no nothing. Dialogue is all matter of fact "I'm going to open this door" and "I'll catch up with you later". Okay. Cool. The lack of narrative, combined with some truly dull sections - yes I'm looking at you the vehicle sections (I knew there was a reason these parts stayed top of mind) - makes playing through HL2 a slog. Just a few hours in, I didn't want to play any more. I was done. But I was determined I would see it through to the end. I persevered. Despite being absolutely bored out of my mind. All I needed was a nugget of a narrative. A morsel of motivation. But despite my belly rumbling for some narrative sustenance, I was left to starve. You get nothing. In a fit of story-famished delirium I turned on god mode and just ran through the levels. I finally reached the credits. The game was finished. What greeted me in the end, were no answered questions to what little the game had set up. [spoiler] A few nonsensical lines from G-man; no great reveal, no pulled curtain. [/spoiler] This may very well be one of the worst narratives I've ever experienced (from a big budget game), and certainly the worst resolution to a narrative in video game history. I am excited to get started with Episode 1 & 2, I have heard they have more of a narrative. But at this point, I can't say that the world of Half-Life 2 is more to me than a time capsule showing gratitude that Valve does not make single-player games anymore.

Ah, Half-Life 2. While it doesn't hold as quite a special place in my heart as the original game, there's no denying the sequel's impact on first-person shooters-and video games in general-over the years. I only wish it had a satisfying conclusion.

🎮 Personal Review Tiers 1 - Exceptional | 2 - Great | 3 - Good | 4 - Average | 5 - Bad Half-Life 2 Review Tier: 1 - Exceptional 📌 Disclaimers This review reflects my experience playing exclusively on Steam Deck. I've already played this game to exhaustion on Xbox 360 via The Orange Box-hundreds of hours, somewhere between 8-10 full playthroughs-and I've long considered it the best video game ever made. Now that I'm new to Steam, replaying it here felt like a rite of passage. At the time of writing, I'm mid-way through a 100% completion run, but I know the game inside out, so ignore the deceptively low playtime on my profile. ✅ Pros Visual fidelity This game simply refuses to age. Even after 22 years, the art direction and environmental detail remain astonishing. City 17 still feels oppressive, lived‑in, and hauntingly beautiful-one of the most iconic and fully realised game worlds ever built. It genuinely looks like a late‑PS3/360 title despite launching in 2004. The original immersive story-game Plenty of games experimented with in-world storytelling before, but Half-Life and Half-Life 2 perfected it. No cinematic cutscenes, no camera yanking you away-just you, in the moment, witnessing every major event as Gordon Freeman. It still feels revolutionary. Gameplay that prioritises creativity and fun Physics puzzles, environmental improvisation, frantic firefights-the game constantly rewards curiosity and experimentation. And the Gravity Gun remains the greatest weapon in video game history. It turns every object into a tool, a projectile, or a puzzle solution. It's pure design brilliance. A memorable journey through City 17 and beyond At its core, it's a simple "get from point A to point B" adventure, but every chapter is crafted with such care that each location feels distinct, purposeful, and dripping with atmosphere. Impeccable pacing Action, exploration, and puzzles flow together effortlessly. No chapter drags, no encounter overstays its welcome. Every level feels substantial, offering just the right amount of combat without ever becoming exhausting. A story that's engaging without being convoluted It's mysterious, intriguing, and filled with iconic moments. The narrative is efficient and direct, yet strange in ways that perfectly complement the world's tone-never bloated, never confusing for the sake of it. Characters that feel real From major allies to nameless rebels, every character is memorable, well‑acted, and written with restraint. Even brief NPC interactions carry personality and charm. Meaningful difficulty options The game respects both newcomers and veterans. Easy still requires attention, while Hard offers a genuinely demanding challenge. It's balanced, thoughtful, and fair. Steam Deck performance Flawless. Smooth, stable, visually gorgeous, and with excellent battery life even at high settings. It feels made for handheld play. ❌ Cons Enemy variety My only real criticism-both then and now-is that Combine soldiers and zombies could use more variation. There are only a few types of each, and most boss encounters are vehicular. The combat is so strong that this ends up being more of a nitpick than a real flaw, but it's still noticeable. These are my thoughts for Half Life 2 as a whole. Half-Life 2 as a whole is excellent. A benchmark, a standard for what games should strive to surpass. It is, in many cases, rarely surpassed. It is something that every gamer who can should play. The story is excellent, intriguing, and gripping. It often caught me off guard at some turns, and left me satisfied at others. I was genuinely knocked flat at the ending of episode 2. Half-Life as a whole story-wise, really shows the true feeling of people rising up against an oppressive force. Gordon is a one-man army, don't get me wrong, but the unity and feeling of the resistance is really well executed. The gameplay is top notch, it genuinely trusts you to perform to the best of your abilities most of the time. The gunplay is smooth, the flow of combat is great, rewarding you for playing well. The respites between combat encounters feel refreshing, being allowed to stock up on what you need, but the slight worry of if it'll be enough. And the puzzles are near perfect. Sometimes a bit obtuse, but the majority of the time it feels excellent to solve the various puzzles before you. The level design is great, going from an oppressive city where you can feel the weight of the Combine pressing down onto the residents, to ravenholm where you can see the destruction first-hand of what the combine can and does do. I will admit, possibly cause I'm not the brightest, there were a few times where I got caught up and couldn't figure out where to go. Whether it's due to my own inablity or the game's design, well, the jury is still out on that. The world itself is great, you can really tell the impact that the combine have had, Ravenholm as an example again, I think the idea of the Combine using headcrabs deposited from launched carriers to infect people is genius. The way they're always on you, rarely giving you a proper moment to breathe. How they monitor the people closely, how little havens of resistance communicate and survive together. It all comes together to make an amazingly believable, engaging world with a very sympathetic plight for the people under the Combine that makes you want to fight. All in all, Half-Life 2, as a whole, as I said, everyone who can play it should. It's a terrific experience, and really shows what games should strive to surpass or at the very least, surpass. Most of all, it's just really really damn fun. And man, I can't wait for episode 3, wonder when it's coming out?

Half-Life 2 is a first-person action game about Gordon Freeman, who joins a resistance effort to liberate Earth from the alien Combine empire. This is one of the games that I wanted my girlfriend to play for so long, just because it's a piece of my gamer childhood when I rented a game called The Orange Box for the PS3, which has this alongside Episode 1 and 2. There's only one problem, though: it's single-player. So I got a mod called Synergy, where we can play multiplayer together for all three of the games, and revisiting this game made me realize that not only did it not become one of my favorite video games, even though I still enjoyed it, but it's one of the worst games that my girlfriend has played. My girlfriend doesn't like science fiction at all, but I was hoping this would be an exception, since it's more grounded, but this didn't change her mind. She found the AI to be absolutely abysmal that was just getting in her way, and she couldn't really connect with the story and genuinely got a little confused about what was going on. She didn't mind G-Man at first, but then she got progressively annoyed with him because of his vagueness in the way he speaks that's giving her no close answers to what he's doing or what type of person he is and why. The platforming wasn't doing anything for her but to irritate her, and she was just not having fun; the only reason we managed to beat it was that she was with me in the game. She would've rage-quit the game herself. As for me, though, I find the story to be super engaging, so you start pulling the pieces together of what's going on through the journey. Especially with the beginning, where it puts you into City 17, which is run by Dr. Wallace Breen, which makes the place feel like a fascist place to live in. The gameplay, when it comes to running, action, and driving, is so smooth that I'm surprised it flows this well for a 2004 game. Although I will say that driving the boat can feel too smooth or slippery that can get a little annoying, and that definitely got my girlfriend completely pissed off. The graphics still look great to this day, and the gravity mechanics when it comes to using the Gravity Gun are just perfect, so that you can launch a lot of items to faraway places that we can't go. The soundtrack is a lot of fun to listen to, and the set-pieces can get tense, even on the easiest difficulty and on the multiplayer mod. My favorite part of the game is the Ravenholm stage. It's genuinely well designed with the look and atmosphere, which was the one saving grace that my girlfriend had with this game. I find the runtime to be very long, but well-deserved, which took us to so many memorable levels. The characters have such layers to them that I find it fascinating to look into these characters and figure them out as it goes. Half-Life 2 is kind of a fantastic game that has tons of variety to have fun with, which is why people have this as one of the best video games ever. 9/10

Half-Life 2 is a near-perfect amalgamation of incredible storytelling, engaging level design and innovative combat. Combine (heh!) that with an incredible level of ongoing support, most recently with the 20th Anniversary Update, and you get a game that does not feel like it was originally released all the way back in 2004. The first chunk of Half-Life 2 is one of my favourite singleplayer experiences of all time. The atmospheric, environmental worldbuilding that starts as soon as you arrive in City 17 - carrying on all through your journey into Ravenholm and the coast - is magnificent, with the context of events since the Black Mesa Incident slowly flowing in as you experience a world much unlike the one you left behind in the original game. Steadily exploring the dystopian metropolis, piloting the airboat through the abandoned canals, experiencing the shock of the destroyed Ravenholm and driving the scenic coastal route is such a vibe as you take in the apocalyptic world for yourself. The additional episodes provide a welcome addition to the ongoing story, with Episode 2's forest environment setting the scene for the better of the two expansions. But then once the sad realisation dawns on you that this iconic series is at its end, you can only live in hope that one day we will be reflecting on the events of the mythic third episode.

Technologically impressive even 20+ years after release. THIS is what you call a revolutionary masterpiece. Half-Life 2 re-defined the FPS genre and its influence can be felt to this very day. Graphically it holds up unfathomably well, and Half-Life 2's world is far more interactable than most video-games coming out nowadays. Very few games can even begin to rival Half-Life 2's physics, which are still really fun to play around with. Most importantly of all though, Half-Life 2 treats you like an intelligent human being. It expects you to explore and look for the details. Wish more modern games didn't hand-hold you as much. SPEAKING OF TRUSTING THE PLAYER'S INTELLIGENCE! The story and ESPECIALLY the lore are really well thought out (even if a bit contradictory and very retcon-y in some places, especially if we count the episodes). But seriously, if you love vague story-telling that focuses more on world-building than dialogue, then you'll LOVE delving deep into Half-Life's lore. That isn't to say that the main story along with its dialogue has been neglected though, quite the contrary in fact. If all the overwhelmingly positive reviews, and Half-Life's significance to the gaming industry as a whole isn't enough to convince you to buy and play it, then I don't know what will. Seriously, this is a must-play experience for anyone that plays video-games.

You know a game is amazing when you go to play it simply because you wanted to kill an hour, and it ends up turning almost 5 hours later. I kept wanting to put it down, waiting to finish a segment to save, but each time the new area, or narrative push kept me going, "just a bit further and i'll stop". This game absolutely holds up in 2026. Its one of those games that either has its own unique style that makes it never feel dated, or fits into one of those timeless styles that already exists, stuff like Metroid Prime, fixed camera tank-control games, Zelda, 2d platformers, Dead by Daylight, DMC etc, all games that are so rich and polished in mechanics or having such lively worlds that they never feel dated, aside from benefiting from QOL changes and updates. What is Half-life 2? Its a narrative driven fps. Campaign structure wise it plays like games like The Last Of Us, you go from point A to B to point C fighting enemies, viewing cutscenes, meeting npcs and solving puzzles/obstacles. Similar to TLOU remake(which is actually a remaster) everything happens in real time, so all cutscenes and dialogue happens in-game. Tonally it's not just a fps, it has some strong horror elements on occasions, in terms of occasional atmosphere, setting, music, enemy encounter and jump scares. You don't play the game scared like RE, but the game does manage to surprise with a scare here and there and some moments and can be a little tension driven. But for the most part is a fun, interesting sci fi adventure. Gameplay. If you love Metroid Prime, you'll feel at home here. Very similar gameplay loop, of going through area, dispatching enemies and solving puzzles/obstacles and getting important items to progress. The key differences is this game is 1) linear, 2) less focused on item hunting/key progression, 3) no enemy respawns and 4) more narrative driven. The game also plays like a boomer shooter, so if you love that genre you might feel at home here. In terms of the gameplay mechanics and feel, its alot closer to boomer shooters than standard fps flair like Dying Light, Halo, Metro, Borderlands and the like. You have the familiar walk and runs speeds(although this game has stamina), the familiar movement of the camera, the familiar jankiness of the aim, the physics of the jumps etc. The key difference is this game has a bigger focus on exploration, narrative and obstacle/puzzle solving and needing to constantly switch your weapons or use the best type isn't that encouraged. There are moments where you fight waves of enemies where you absolutely need to keep switching guns because reloading is slow and you risk getting hit, and those moments shine the most but for the most part you can strategically move around, shoot with one or two weapons and kill the enemies creatively with the environment or traps. Similar to Metroid Prime, puzzle/obstacle solving absolutely shines. Similar to that series, this game doesnt hold your hand and leaves absolutely to your vices to figure out a solution or how to progress. And unlike Metroid Prime or games like Silent Hill, where you can get stuck use a guide and the game doesn't lose any fun factor, Half-Life 2 absolutely wants you to figure it out on your own, because the problems it presents aren't difficult or even mathematical, they are just very creative and require observation. Using a guide absolutely robs the game of its problem solving charm, as almost EVERY single time you feel so good, so accomplished and so happy you didn't use a guide because you got to witness the genius unfold of how that obstacle was solved. The game rewards not only creativity but also experimentation, Ive solved 3 obstacles so far absolutely in a way that the game didn't intend, whether it was abusing the physics to stack up items to reach an area, that needed a key or alternate route, or finding a different solution to the problem that worked similar to the actual solution. For example my dumbass didn't know you can knock down a bridge in the game, so I could cross, so instead I built my own bridge and walked across. Dont get me started on the ways you can dispose of enemies. Lastly graphics. This game got a light remaster not too long ago. The game stills looks pretty even by todays standards, mostly what looks good is the visuals effects, like shadows, lighting particles, and physics. Some environments look good especially from afar, the world has decently size scope so there is viewing distance. The only thing that really hurts this game is the textures, its the one area that really doesn't hold up and if youre a modern gamer can def hurt the immersion quite a bit, characters could benefit from updating buts its not a big deal like the textures, they have a good enough style to have charm and they animate well enough. If the recent RTX remaster was more compatible with lower end hardware, or this game got another remaster that found a middle ground between this remaster and the RTX remaster in terms of graphics, this game would feel 100% modern and give any new game today a run for its money. Crazy how some games absolutely deserve the hype and live up to it.

I'm gonna ramble, but this game is THE standard. Twenty years later, it genuinely deserves every bit of praise it gets. Seriously, go play it. Half-Life 2 gave me the gravity gun, and now every FPS feels weak because you can't throw anything. you cannot interact with the enviroment and puzzle solve the same way this game does it. A 20 year old game ran so modern shooters could barely crawl. It's honestly insane how far ahead of its time this game was. Even the original is responsible for creating counter-strike. The gunplay is the only thing that's aged poorly, and even then it's the SMG and pistol being pea shooters. But honestly, why are you even using those? Play Ravenholm. Get the gravity gun only achievement. That level is a love letter to the game's level design and physics engine, and it changes how you approach the game almost permanently. It scared the shit out of me as a kid. Now it's one of my favourite levels to revisit. I can't remember who said it or where I heard it, but Valve are masters of "show, don't tell." By interacting with the world and exploring, you piece together what happened without the game stopping to explain itself. Even as a kid, I remember getting lost exploring Highway 17, just trying to understand what had happened there. then finding that building with the binoculars and seeing that they had been spying on the rebels the whole time. The real time eye tracking still blows my mind. A game released in 2004 had that. For comparison, San Andreas and MGS3 came out around the same time. now those games are goated, im not calling them bad. It still blows me away that Cutscenes are done entirely in engine, not CGI. This game is THAT good. If you haven't played it, you have to. You need to understand why we need Half-Life 3. It Deserves Game of the Decade. It deserves more. valve pls =(

I remember playing the first Half Life many years ago back on the Playstation 2. I've played the game religiously even when Half Life 2 finally released and played that on the original Xbox/Xbox 360. But now that I took off the nostalgia glasses I realized that this game is not the masterpiece that I thought it was ever since I had my revelation months ago. I will start with the gameplay then the story to explain why I came to this conclusion. First off, Half Life 2 gameplay is mediocre because it focuses on being a boomer shooter type of game where you run around with a huge arsenal of weapons the further you progress in the game which quickly stripes the ability to utilize the environment to a players advantage. Because of this decision from the developers it makes each scenario easy, dull, and predictable. I haven't forgotten about those long winded boat and car riding segments. I also could not stand sitting through the un-skippable cutscenes that use passive ways to give the player the ILLUSION that you are part of the story in Half Life 2 which got old real quick. The puzzles in Half Life 2 are creative despite being terrible which Valve used to brag about their physics engine but also in attempt to hide the fact that their gameplay is mediocre. A few games came out before Half life 2 which did a better job with their physics engine that didn't detract from the gameplay but actually enhanced it. The expected scripted events which happens at every awakening avenue in Half Life 2 makes the game lack depth and variety about how to go about each encounter. Not to mention the fact that EVERY single enemy in Half Life 2 have the same attack patterns especially from the combine enemies. The original Halo trilogy is the best example when it comes to a great FPS because it has unscripted events many times where enemies spawn in different locations on every level and have a hierarchy chain. Once the hierarchy is disrupted the enemies react to it depending on the enemy type. The higher the difficulty you play in Halo the more amplified the difficulty and tactics mixed with unscripted events makes every encounter unique/fun. Half Life 2 does not have any of these and the combine just stand out of cover like a swore thumb in both scripted and non scripted events through out the WHOLE GAME! I would argue for certain that if Half Life had a weapon limit like Halo it would have been VERY fun gameplay wise with strategy tactics in every encounter like Half Life 1 did despite the first game having the huge weapon arsenal also. Lastly, why are the Half Life 1 weapons completely discarded when they were the most fun and creative than any of the boring weapons in Half Life 2? Wasted potential to not reintroduce them especially Opposing Force ones! Secondly, Half Life 2 ruined the continuity of the story from Half Life 1 because Marc Laidlaw never considered the Gearbox content of Blue Shift and Opposing Force content canon by Gearbox. Barney Calhoun was one of those characters from the Blue Shift content that Gearbox created that they denied as canon but used him as a retcon in their own writing to make the story sound more "appealing" to the fans in Half Life 2. I cant even forget about General Adrian Shepard who was completely kicked to the curb also including Race X. Lets not forget Dr Kleiner and Eli Vance who were NEVER named in the ORIGINAL HALF LIFE because Valve is too arrogant thinking they created a good franchise while plagiarizing everyone else's hard work. The major plot hole that makes Half Life 2 a terrible story is the fact that G-man is an omnipotent being that can freeze time, change the past, etc. Why bother with a story like Half Life when their is no agency to anything that Gordon accomplishes by the player? G-man at any moment can terminate Gordon if he wanted to or Alyx on a whim since he SAVED Gordon INVOLUNTARILY at the end of Half Life 1 then threatened him with death if he refused to work for him. All of this "show don't tell" tactic in Valves story writing is ultimately what lead to the downfall of the franchise. Prepare for Unforeseen Consequences when you release Half Life 3, Valve... Not to mention how Gordon does not speak or express through any type of body language about how he feels about ANYTHING since the the first game. Not to mention the fact that Alyx and Elie objectify Gordon by forcing the idea of procreation on him. I will be amused with fanboys attempting to justify this by using passive aggressive tactics in order to objectify Gordon Freeman to go right along with it all. In conclusion, I am glad that I took off the nostalgia glasses and see the game for what it truly is. I hope Gordon takes off his and see that he truly is not a "Freeman" when being objectified left and right even by the people he considers allies. The game aged poorly and is not a game worth all of the praise that it deserves especially since Valve literally relies on fans of their community to make this game more interesting since Valve doesn't care about their own universe and will take other peoples well thought lore in attempt to make their game more coherently sound. Valve... "You have destroyed so much. What is it, exactly, that you have created? Can you name even one thing? I thought not."

Let's be real, just go play it. If Valve hasn't already given it away to you by some miracle, then even if it's NOT on sale, it's still going to cost less than a night out and you'll have a hell of a fun time. Half-life 2 was a genre changer, and to many, one of the greatest single-player story FPS they've played! So what do I, over 20 years late to the party, have to think about it? Plain and simple, it was a blast! Valve never let the mechanics get stale, you'll be playing with a new mechanic every level, and before it gets boring, you'll be on to the next one. Legitimately, some games struggle with that even today. I won't tell you the story is perfect, it's definitely got it's cliches and you can often see the plot twists coming from a mile away, but this was 2004, it probably created many of the cliches, so you've got to let it off. The story is perfect for keeping you on the rails, you'll always have a reasonable reason to be where you are. Speaking of where you are, I played the original Half-life as well, and I'll tell you, the sequel is vastly superior, in story telling, mechanics, and polish, we're not even talking graphics! Valve clearly learnt a lot from the original half-life and it shows, the controls are almost perfect, MOST enemies feel like the fight is fair and well balanced (fuck striders, they suck), and for playing in 2025-2026, the settings are as modern as you really need them to be and the game runs without a hitch. All in all, I've rambled for a fair bit, but as I said at the start, just go buy the game, it's really good, and you'll get plenty of enjoyment out of it... And you'll still be in time for Half-life 3 (Valve please I beg you, the story needs to go on).

At long last, it was time to properly dive into Half-Life 2. I've waited far too many years to play this game the way it deserves. It has been sitting in my library for ages, but only now, in 2026, did I finally commit to a full playthrough. I bought the game over 12 years ago, and yet the experience today feels just as relevant as it is timeless. Half-Life 2 feels genuinely authentic. The carefully crafted sound design, strong world-building, and dense, memorable atmosphere come together perfectly with a compelling story that spans both the base game and its episodes. What an absolute powerhouse this must have been when it launched back in 2004. It's no surprise that it still ranks among the highest-rated games on Metacritic. Despite its age, the game holds up remarkably well and runs flawlessly on modern systems. There's a natural momentum that constantly pushes you forward, making you want to follow the world, its characters, and the story as it slowly unfolds. I even ended up creating my own little side quest: hunting down all the hidden Half-Life symbols scattered throughout the game. Only later did I realize it was actually an achievement… one I unfortunately didn't manage to fully complete in the end. I've previously played Half-Life along with its expansions Blue Shift and Opposing Force, and compared to those, Half-Life 2 feels like a massive leap forward. The graphical upgrade is obvious, but even more impressive is the overall scope and ambition of the game. Everything feels more alive, more immersive, and more engaging. It's clear that Valve poured an incredible amount of care and quality into every detail, which is why I can confidently say this is one of the greatest games ever made. ✅ Pros ✅ Timeless atmosphere and world-building ✅ Exceptional sound design ✅ Strong storytelling across the base game and episodes ✅ Still plays perfectly on modern systems ✅ Immersive, living world that constantly drives you forward ❌ Cons ❌ Some achievements can be easy to miss without prior knowledge ❌ May feel slow-paced for players used to modern shooters

Recently I played through Half-Life 2, and I have some reflection on the experience. This is not the first time I've tried to play through Half-Life 2. My first attempt would have been circa 2010, via the Orange Box for the PS3. Arguably, the worst way you can experience the game (maybe beat by the OG Xbox version). I managed to complete the game on the PS3. I always chalked it up to the terrible port (which was inexplicably made by EA). A few sequences stuck in my mind, the boat section. The car section. Now, as we crossed into a new year, I figured it was time to give it another shot. I wanted to have the most optimal experience I could, I looked up which mods enhance the experience intended by Valve. It led me to MMod. It was simple enough to get up and running. My first thought is that the game looks pretty decent for a 2004 game. I am running the 2024 anniversary edition which apparently did some work to get it running on modern machines, and I can confirm it runs great, even without any mods. My second thought was "the game really just started, huh". You get like 2 lines of dialogue from G-Man and you're off to the races. "I'm sure there'll be more context and setup for the story" I thought, now in hindsight, foolishly. I'll cut to the chase. I think Half-Life 2 has aged poorly. The core gunplay is as good as it can be, I know the Source engine was and is a fantastic engine for shooters. But what surprised me is how much this game relies on the novelty of physics. Yes, it can be quite neat, even to a 2026 human. But man, does the novelty wear off quickly. What surprised me even more, however, is the story. I'd say the story is bad, but here's the thing. The game barely has a narrative. There's little to no context of what you're doing. 90% of Half-Life 2 is you going from A to B to C to D, usually with the mundane task of "rescue X" or "go to Y". There's no worldbuilding, no lore, no nothing. Dialogue is all matter of fact "I'm going to open this door" and "I'll catch up with you later". Okay. Cool. The lack of narrative, combined with some truly dull sections - yes I'm looking at you the vehicle sections (I knew there was a reason these parts stayed top of mind) - makes playing through HL2 a slog. Just a few hours in, I didn't want to play any more. I was done. But I was determined I would see it through to the end. I persevered. Despite being absolutely bored out of my mind. All I needed was a nugget of a narrative. A morsel of motivation. But despite my belly rumbling for some narrative sustenance, I was left to starve. You get nothing. In a fit of story-famished delirium I turned on god mode and just ran through the levels. I finally reached the credits. The game was finished. What greeted me in the end, were no answered questions to what little the game had set up. [spoiler] A few nonsensical lines from G-man; no great reveal, no pulled curtain. [/spoiler] This may very well be one of the worst narratives I've ever experienced (from a big budget game), and certainly the worst resolution to a narrative in video game history. I am excited to get started with Episode 1 & 2, I have heard they have more of a narrative. But at this point, I can't say that the world of Half-Life 2 is more to me than a time capsule showing gratitude that Valve does not make single-player games anymore.

This sleek remaster of the original Counter-Strike which ran on the GoldSource engine is truly the definitive way to experience Counter-Strike. I'm not a big fan of multiplayer-only games, and Counter-Strike is hardly my go-to shooter series, but there's no denying this product is maybe the competitive-shooting genre at its best. It's mostly bots playing online, but this still allows for some authentic enjoyment (at least for the most part). The bots are very irritatingly prone to camping, glitching out on doors or ladders, or worst, when they nail a headshot on you with a single bullet the millisecond you step into view. If playing with the smatterings of other real human players still isn't your thing, playing offline in bot versus bot matches are still actually quite fun - at least, as is the case with most multiplayer games, it's only fun if you're winning. Spectating the other players goofing around just because you happened to get killed at the start of the match is supremely boring, but this is maybe just because I grew up on Call Of Duty games. If playing offline, be sure to set the bot count to the max and you can have a full platoon on your side going to war with the opposing team, and it's sort of fun. The peculiar thing about Counter-Strike Source is the little similarities to Half-Life - some maps remind me of Black Mesa, or Highway 17, or Nova Prospekt. The game actually uses the same footsteps sound from the first Half-Life (and by extension, the original Counter-Strike) though this feels just a little too out of place. The gunplay is all fine but hitting enemy players can still feel somehow hollow and not very satisfying. If you like competitive first-person-shooters, and the newer Counter-Strike 2 just isn't your thing, this Source remaster will be sure to impress.

This was the game that made me quit Counter-Strike. Coming from Counter-Strike 1.6, Source never felt like an upgrade, just a departure from everything that made CS special. The gunplay felt floaty, movement lacked precision, and the tight, disciplined mechanics I loved were replaced with awkward physics and inconsistent hit registration. The Source engine looked better on paper, but visually smoother didn't mean mechanically better. Recoil felt off, spraying felt unreliable, and the overall flow of matches lost the sharp, tactical edge that defined 1.6. It felt like the game was fighting me instead of rewarding mastery. The physics, especially ragdolls, pulled focus away from competitive play and made the experience feel less serious. What once was about skill, timing, and positioning now felt softer, messier, and less demanding. When the community started shifting from 1.6 to Source, I didn't follow. I didn't want to relearn a version of Counter-Strike that no longer felt like Counter-Strike to me. So instead of adapting, I walked away. If Source was your entry point, you might love it. But for players who grew up on 1.6, this felt like the moment Counter-Strike lost its soul, and that's why I stopped playing.

Counter Strike: Source is one of my favorite childhood games to play. Source is exceptionally good from my experience. I can tell that from playing for so many times on my uncle's desktop before. Source is really fun to play especially with friends, of course. Collecting the achievements are fun to collect, but a few of them might require some skill and it is pretty difficult to achieve in some ways, in my opinion. Source is unique in its own way. Source introduced me into action/shooter games and showed me how fun and challenging it can be at first. The way how you play the game and how you master it is heavily depend on you. Choosing and buying a weapon that is suitable for you and does not make you look like a fool using it is also a part that you need to understand on how they work and all. Other than that, Source's community are very creative with map-making, weapons, characters and etc. It is funny how a serious shooter game can turned into some goofy ass effects in your game. But hey, it is for your own fun in the end anyway. But all in all, Source has a special place in my heart for one of the Valve games. I would really recommend Source to my friends, even though it is an old game, but it is still gold for me.

It's alright, it's age shows. Day Of Defeat is I assume Valve's answer to early Call Of Duty. I think it would have sufficed back in 2005, but 20 years later, the game's systems are quite tedious, and I don't think this game really benefits from a port to the Source engine (although I will admit I never played the original) I think Stamina and class restrictions are my main issue, this game wants to be a military simulator so bad, but can't shake it's arcade shooter roots of Half-Life. Some guns have really forgiving recoil, and some guns have to be mounted because their recoil is the most unforgiving. This mimics the weapons of then, sure, but it doesn't help that movement is super slippery, and that I don't think most people are going to playing this today seeking realism. The maps feel like they force teams into a stalemate, which is great for the 24/7 servers of today, but not the best if you actually want a goal to achieve when playing. The game still has that Valve touch though, the sound design is on point, soundtrack is great and the game does reap the rewards of still looking serviceable today due to being on Source. This is also one of the only multiplayer games I have played as well with this much of an active voice chat. Sure, it's probably fathers who have been playing for 20 years, but I sure do get a laugh when I play this game. I do recommend, if you get the Valve Complete Pack, but unless that's the case, you would probably find your money better spent elsewhere, but it's still a very chill shooter to just zone out in. 7/10.

Day of Defeat: Source is an updated release built on Valve's Source engine, bringing improved visuals and technical changes. I played the original version before this, so I can make a basic comparison between the two. The newer engine improves map detail, lighting, and character models, and even today the visuals still look acceptable without major issues. I played this version after spending time with the original Day of Defeat, which made the changes easier to notice. The setting is based on World War II, which stands out more now since many shooters focus on modern or future themes. The gameplay is the strongest part, with several classes that fit the setting well and serve clear roles. Combat is responsive and consistent, but the game does not offer a large variety of modes or maps. There is still an active multiplayer community, so finding matches is usually possible. In conclusion, Day of Defeat: Source remains a focused and well-made multiplayer shooter that shows its age but still works as intended. It may not match newer titles in scope or content, but its core mechanics and setting keep it relevant for players looking for a classic based experience.
