Day of Defeat (DoD) is a solid old skool squad Shooter that is probably on its way out at no fault of its own. It is still semi-active and has a fairly strong community of dedicated long time players. There is also bots and they are good. I feel bad for putting this game one on the way side. Placed in exchange for more modern shooters emerging at the time. Mainly leaving for online competitive leader boards. Day of Defeat was a very competitive shooter in its time and it still holds it titles up today. You don't lose your championship belt when you retire. No different than what R6 or CS is today. We aim trained, we practiced, we farmed. It was the start of what became hardcore titles. I remember back in 2020 a group of friends and I where playing. Many games were getting remade around this time and the hard core genre was being defined. We talked about why DoD was not getting any meaningful updates or even a full remake, like the other games of the time. The conclusion we came to was that Day of Defeat does not need a remake. "Don't fix what aint broke" There is nothing wrong with this classic shooter, not even today. So do your self a favor. Put down the competitive shooter of 2025 and have some fun instead. Todays shooter will be as dead as Day of Defeat in ten years anyway. Take a moment to enjoy what you have while its there. Because before you know it, the fun has passed while you were too busy taking things seriously and you end up missing all the actual fun to be had. Please don't make the same mistake I did. Play the games you love to play, not just what everyone else is playing. Because eventually there will be no more players and no more servers for the game you actually enjoy. Instead you wasted that chance trying to force your self to stay in the competitive zone. Grab some buds and a couple copies of the game on sale. "This is where the fun begins!" To the guys who stayed with Day of Defeat I say this: You hold Solace in knowing you made the right choice. I commend you for your dedication. "hold the line."

Day of Defeat: Source is a team-based multiplayer first-person shooter developed by Valve Corporation, released in 2005 as a reimagining of the original Day of Defeat, built on the Source engine. Set during World War II, the game pits Axis and Allied forces against each other in objective-based maps inspired by real European locations. While it shares some DNA with Counter-Strike: Source, the game's emphasis on squad tactics, class-based roles, and historical authenticity gives it a distinct flavor that still resonates with a dedicated, if niche, community nearly two decades after its release. At its core, Day of Defeat: Source is a tightly designed multiplayer experience focused on small-scale infantry battles. Unlike many shooters that emphasize individual kill counts or wide-open maps, this game revolves around coordinated control of choke points, precise timing, and class synergy. Each player chooses a class with a specific role-rifleman, support, assault, sniper, machine gunner, or rocket troop-each with distinct weapons and movement limitations. The gameplay is fast-paced but also unforgiving, with a low time-to-kill and an emphasis on positioning and map knowledge. This encourages slower, more tactical play rather than the run-and-gun chaos seen in more arcade-style shooters. One of the game's standout features is its weapon feel and historical realism, especially for its time. The audio-visual presentation is simple by today's standards, but it holds up remarkably well due to its attention to detail. Weapons like the Kar98k, Thompson, and BAR each have unique recoil patterns, sound design, and reload animations that give them personality and weight. There's a rawness to the combat that feels satisfying without being overly cinematic. Even small touches, like the slight delay when deploying a machine gun bipod or the arc of a thrown grenade, add to the immersion and reinforce the importance of preparation and awareness. The maps in Day of Defeat: Source deserve special mention. Though relatively few in number, each is meticulously designed with balanced sight lines, multiple approach routes, and critical control zones. Maps like dod_donner and dod_avalanche are icons in their own right, offering complex layered terrain that rewards players who understand the flow of battle. The gameplay loop of capturing and holding flags-a simple mechanic-is elevated by this map design, making every round a tug-of-war where frontlines are in constant flux. It's a model of how good level design can elevate objective-based multiplayer games. While the game shines in its design and mechanics, its longevity is both a testament to and a limitation of its legacy. Valve has not updated Day of Defeat: Source in any meaningful way in many years, and while the core mechanics remain strong, the game lacks modern features like matchmaking, progression systems, or even basic quality-of-life options like robust stat tracking. This creates a steep barrier to entry for new players who may be used to contemporary shooter conveniences. Servers are player-hosted, often modded, and the remaining community is small but loyal, which can result in inconsistent experiences depending on where and when you play. Still, for those willing to invest the time to learn its systems and tolerate its aging infrastructure, Day of Defeat: Source offers an incredibly rewarding experience. It's a game that thrives on precision, teamwork, and situational awareness rather than reflexes alone. In many ways, it serves as a fascinating snapshot of multiplayer shooter design before the dominance of persistent unlocks and microtransactions. It's both a relic and a reminder of a more focused era in PC gaming, where gameplay balance and depth were often prioritized over spectacle. In conclusion, Day of Defeat: Source is a deeply satisfying tactical shooter that still holds up in many areas due to its deliberate design, well-balanced classes, and masterfully crafted maps. It is not a game for everyone-it lacks modern polish and caters to a specific playstyle-but for fans of classic WWII shooters and tight competitive experiences, it's a hidden gem worth revisiting or discovering for the first time. Even in 2025, its blend of authenticity and mechanical depth stands as a testament to thoughtful game design, and it remains one of Valve's most underrated offerings. Rating: 9/10

Instead of twitchy teens and team strategy, you're met with the soothing sound of middle-aged wheezing, the clack of mechanical keyboards, and arguments about whether Metamucil counts as cheating. It's less "Call of Duty" and more "Call a Nurse." Each match now feels like an awkward reunion at a weird dive bar where everyone kinda knows each other but forgot how. Picture this: You sprint across a bombed-out street, only to get shot by a guy named "Darryl_1959" who immediately types, "Nice try, dipshit." Seconds later, he follows up with, "BRB changing my pants."you think it's a joke. It's not. The gameplay? Still OG. The gunplay? Surprisingly crisp. The map design? Classic. But the vibe… the vibe is somewhere between "aging punk rock show" and "digital assisted living facility." You're not flanking Germans,m you're flanking grandpas with arthritis and an unhealthy obsession with the Garand ping. If you're gonna spend $10, you might as well grab an overpriced coffee at Starbucks... Day of Defeat: Source is a class-based World War II multiplayer shooter released in 2005. It runs on the Source engine and includes six preset classes with distinct weapons and roles. Matches are objective-based, with fast respawns and a very short time-to-kill. Most weapons kill in one or two hits. The core mechanics include solid movement, responsive gunplay, and high punishment for poor aim or positioning. There is no progression system, unlocks, or customization. Every player has the same access to weapons and abilities from the start. The only way to improve is through map knowledge and mechanical skill. The game still has an active player base in 2025, with full servers and quick matchmaking. However, voice chat is unreliable. Most players do not communicate, and those who do often make the experience worse. There is no global mute option. Each player must be muted individually. Map rotation is limited and repetitive. Many community servers loop the same few maps for hours. Gun recoil is strong on some automatic weapons, making them harder to control. There are no tutorials or onboarding systems. New players are expected to learn through trial and error. There are no rewards, no unlocks, and no long-term objectives. Matches feel disconnected and repetitive once the core mechanics are understood. The game is still functional and balanced for what it is, but it lacks modern design features that most shooters now consider standard. In 2005, this was probably a banger. In 2025, it feels outdated and overpriced. Final Score: 5/10 Technically sound, but lacks depth, variety, and value for its current price.

I played Day of Defeat: Source for the first time right after my grandfather passed. He was a World War II veteran, and I grew up listening to his stories of combat. He wasn't a man of many words, but when he talked about the war, you could hear the weight of every battle, every life lost. I wasn't sure I could even handle playing a game set in World War II. But something about the historical setting, the gritty realism, drew me in. Each round, I thought about my grandfather. How he'd probably scoff at the idea of a "game" about war, but also how he would have been proud of the level of detail. As I fought in the trenches, I thought about him. He'd lived through real combat, and here I was, standing in his shoes, even if only for a little while. Day of Defeat: Source wasn't just about fighting. It was about understanding the sacrifices made, the lives forever changed by war, and trying to honor that history.

Day of Defeat: Source is an underrated gem in Valve's lineup, delivering a tight, tactical, and immersive World War II multiplayer experience. Built on the Source engine, it modernized the original Day of Defeat with improved visuals, physics, and gunplay, while still retaining the fast-paced, teamwork-driven gameplay that made the original great. The class-based system is one of the game's strengths. Each role-whether it's a rifleman, machine gunner, sniper, or support class-feels distinct and essential. There's no lone-wolfing here; success depends on coordinating with teammates, holding key positions, and executing well-timed pushes to capture objectives. The game's momentum-based gameplay makes every battle feel dynamic and strategic. Gunplay is crisp and satisfying, with weapons that feel powerful and accurate. Rifles like the M1 Garand and Kar98k reward skill with deadly precision, while automatic weapons like the Thompson and MP40 excel in close-quarters combat. Machine gunners can set up suppressive fire, and snipers can lock down lanes, creating a balanced, tactical experience that rewards positioning and teamwork over run-and-gun chaos. The map design is another standout. Classic WWII battlefields like Donner, Avalanche, and Flash offer well-balanced chokepoints and flanking routes, ensuring that matches feel fair, intense, and strategic. The objective-based gameplay, where teams must capture and hold key points, adds a layer of tactical depth beyond standard team deathmatch modes. Visually, Day of Defeat: Source may not be cutting-edge today, but the Source engine's physics and lighting effects still hold up well, giving battles a gritty, immersive feel. The sound design-with authentic weapon sounds, explosive artillery, and tense battlefield chatter-adds even more realism to the experience. While it never reached the mainstream popularity of Counter-Strike, Day of Defeat: Source remains one of the best WWII multiplayer shooters ever made. Half-Life 2: Deathmatch wasn't just a game for me. It was my introduction to the "online" world. It was the game that taught me how "just one more round" could accidentally turn into 5:00 AM, realizing the sun was coming up and I should have been in bed hours ago. The memories I have of this game are pure, high-speed insanity. It was non-stop run-and-gun fun where the physics engine was the star of the show. One minute you're launched across the room by a stray explosion, the next you're successfully "decapitating" someone with a wooden chair launched from your Gravity Gun. And nothing, absolutely nothing hit quite like the sound of a steaming hot crossbow bolt pinning you to a wall. I tried booting it up again recently, but it just didn't hit the same. It's not that the game is bad. It's that as an adult, the "time tax" feels heavier. Looking at my massive backlog of unplayed titles, I found myself thinking, "I should probably be playing something else." My time is limited now, and the frantic, twitchy energy required for HL2DM feels like a young man's game. To me at least. I've decided that I likely won't ever boot this up again. Not just to save time or brain cells, but because I want to preserve the version of the game that lives in my head. I want to remember it as the peak of online chaos, not as a ghost town of empty servers or a reminder that my reflexes aren't what they used to be.

Half-Life Deathmatch: Source, developed and published by Valve, is a reimagined version of the original Half-Life's multiplayer mode, rebuilt using the more advanced Source engine. Released in 2006, it serves both as a technical update and a nostalgic preservation of one of the earliest and most influential deathmatch experiences in first-person shooter history. It doesn't attempt to modernize or expand upon the formula; instead, it faithfully recreates the fast-paced, no-frills combat of the late 1990s in a more stable and visually refined framework. For longtime Half-Life fans, it's a trip back to a simpler era of multiplayer gaming, while for newcomers, it's a curious artifact that demonstrates how far the genre has evolved since its inception. The core of Half-Life Deathmatch: Source remains almost identical to the original. Players are dropped into confined, interconnected maps designed around verticality, chokepoints, and weapon placement. The objective is straightforward: rack up as many kills as possible before time runs out or the score limit is reached. There are no objectives, classes, or progression systems-just pure, chaotic competition. The familiar arsenal returns, including the iconic crowbar, MP5 submachine gun with grenade launcher, shotgun, revolver, and crossbow. Each weapon has its own rhythm, damage output, and range considerations, demanding players to adapt quickly to their environment and available tools. The combat flow is fast but methodical, emphasizing map knowledge and movement as much as shooting accuracy. Every spawn point, ammo crate, and health station matters, and victory often depends on who controls the best weapon spawns or navigates the map most efficiently. What distinguishes this Source version from the original GoldSrc engine iteration is its improved technical foundation. Valve's Source engine introduces cleaner physics, smoother animations, and more responsive hit detection. Movement feels slightly more fluid, and firefights benefit from improved netcode, which reduces latency and the inconsistencies that plagued earlier online matches. Graphically, the game sits somewhere between Half-Life 1 and Half-Life 2 in fidelity. Textures are sharper, lighting is more dynamic, and the environments have a faint polish that makes them easier on the eyes without altering their fundamental layouts. Environmental props now respond to physics, adding a layer of visual dynamism as explosions send barrels and debris tumbling across the floor. Despite these updates, it's clear that the developers opted for authenticity over reinvention-this isn't a complete remake, but rather a cleaner, more stable re-release of a classic experience. Unfortunately, this dedication to preserving the original's feel also means that Half-Life Deathmatch: Source lacks the complexity and depth that modern multiplayer shooters offer. There are no customization options, no ranking systems, and no progression mechanics to encourage long-term investment. Matches rely entirely on the raw fun of quick respawns, fast movement, and tight gunplay. For players raised on games like Counter-Strike: Global Offensive, Apex Legends, or Call of Duty, this stripped-down simplicity might feel outdated or even empty. However, that simplicity is precisely what gives it its charm. It captures an era when multiplayer games were defined by skill and map control rather than unlocks or cosmetic incentives. Every death feels fair, every victory earned, and the sense of personal improvement comes purely from practice rather than in-game rewards. One of the game's most notable issues is its lack of an active community. While Half-Life Deathmatch: Source maintains a modest following, finding full lobbies can be challenging. Most active servers are community-run, often populated by long-time fans or nostalgia seekers rather than newcomers. As a result, the experience of playing can vary greatly depending on when and where you log in. Some matches are lively and competitive, filled with players who remember every corner of maps like Crossfire and Stalkyard, while others are eerily quiet or sparsely populated. This fluctuating activity underscores the game's role more as a historical remnant than a thriving multiplayer hub. For most players, the real value of the game today lies in its preservation of early first-person shooter design rather than in its online activity. Despite its dated structure, there's an undeniable sense of purity to Half-Life Deathmatch: Source that's rare in modern multiplayer gaming. It's a reminder of a time when technical skill, reflexes, and map knowledge were the sole determinants of success. There are no microtransactions, battle passes, or artificial progression systems-just an even playing field where every player starts with the same tools and must rely on instinct and experience to win. The game's design encourages constant movement and improvisation, rewarding players who understand momentum and spatial control. While the learning curve can be steep for beginners, those who persevere often find an addictive rhythm in its straightforward design. It's this focus on skill-based gameplay that continues to attract a small but passionate group of players nearly two decades after its release. Visually and atmospherically, the game holds up surprisingly well for its age. While the maps are simple by modern standards, their design is both functional and memorable. Each one is built with clear visual language-distinct textures, strong lighting, and clever use of vertical space-that aids orientation and supports fast-paced combat. The Source engine's lighting effects breathe new life into these familiar settings, and while it doesn't push the boundaries of what the engine can do, it successfully modernizes them enough to feel comfortable on contemporary hardware. Sound design, too, remains excellent, with crisp weapon effects and the nostalgic clatter of footsteps echoing through metallic corridors, evoking the tension and pace that defined late-'90s multiplayer shooters. Ultimately, Half-Life Deathmatch: Source is less a reinvention and more a preservation effort-a time capsule that showcases the simplicity and intensity of old-school competitive design. It is a product of an era when multiplayer shooters prioritized raw mechanics over progression systems, where success depended on practice rather than persistence. While it can no longer compete with the spectacle or player counts of modern online games, it still offers something valuable: an unfiltered, skill-driven experience that rewards reflex, awareness, and mastery. For players who grew up with Half-Life, it's a nostalgic trip back to the LAN parties and early online matches that helped shape the genre. For newcomers, it's a glimpse into the roots of modern multiplayer shooters-a reminder of where it all began, and why that foundation still matters. Rating: 7/10

The Last Stand of a Classic Half-Life's multiplayer component represents both the charm and challenges of retro online gaming. While the community has dwindled significantly since its heyday, what remains offers a unique glimpse into FPS multiplayer history. Community and Atmosphere The Half-Life deathmatch community exemplifies old-school gaming culture at its best. Veteran players, many with years of experience, create a welcoming environment for newcomers despite the steep skill gap. This mentorship approach - where seasoned players offer genuine advice rather than toxicity - feels refreshingly rare in modern gaming. During its more active periods (around 2013), the game maintained 5-6 populated servers, with Crossfire dominating as the map of choice. Custom maps, many ported from HL2DM, provided variety for those seeking alternatives to the standard rotation. Technical State The various iterations of Half-Life multiplayer exist in different states of health: Classic HLDM remains the most stable, with dedicated servers still findable for those willing to search HL2DM has seen recent updates and maintains both competitive and mapping scenes Half-Life Deathmatch: Source (HLDMS) suffers from significant technical issues, including entity duplication glitches and problems inherited from engine updates Current Reality Today's landscape is sparse. HLDMS struggles with barely two populated servers, while classic HLDM maintains a small but dedicated following. The community has largely migrated to other titles or moved on entirely. Bottom Line Half-Life's multiplayer serves as a time capsule of early online FPS gaming - complete with tight-knit communities and technical quirks. While not viable for sustained modern play, it offers valuable historical perspective and occasional nostalgic fun. What makes Portal quite unique from other puzzle games is its use of the "Portal Gun", a mechanism developed by Aperture Science that allows the holder to make 2 portals from A to B, expanding the horizons of what types of puzzles the game can put you through. Portal is truly a mind boggling game. It's one of the best puzzle games out there with a rich story. It only took me 3 hours to complete the story. Honestly, I first played Portal 2 then Portal with RTX and then Portal. I must say, I would highly recommend playing Portal before RTX (if you choose to) because when I played RTX, not only was I confused from the gameplay.. but I was having constant problems regarding low FPS and crashes. If you're into Valve games in general, DEFINETLY give all of these games a try. Starting from Portal, to RTX, to Portal 2. I am really impressed at seeing every Valve game.. considering the amount of employees they have (~400) It's truly amazing. OH and there WILL be cake, trust me ;) Enjoy while being "Still Alive".

What Portal taught me is that Valve really is a big deal like everyone always says. Being the first game i completed on Steam, Portal already holds a very special place in my heart and i couldn't be happier with my choice! Every aspect of this is honestly perfect (i just wish it was a bit longer, maybe 3 or 4 more test chambers), the main mechanic of the portals is obviously the selling point and it will mesmerize you from start to finish, it's so inovative and works so well! If you played it before or at least seen some gameplay, im sure you at least thought of placing one portal above you and one underneath just to create an infinite loop, it's so silly. Each chamber is so unique and provides incredibles puzzles, giving you that amazing feeling of accomplishment when you solve a hard room. The chambers and escape sessions all share the same atmosphere and sound design that honestly creeped me out a lot, i was so scared when playing, i get scared easily of course, but it encapsulates the feeling of being watched so well, and until you start your escape and reach the boss room, you have no idea of how Glados looks and what exactly she wants to do to you, it's so frightening and interesting. Please play Portal if you can, i got it for less then a dollar on a Steam sale! But don't forget... *the cake is a lie*

Portal feels simple at first. Clean rooms, white walls, calm music, a friendly voice guiding you forward. It does not look threatening. That is exactly why it works. The game teaches you without explaining. You learn by doing. Every puzzle feels logical, but never obvious. When you solve something, it feels earned. Not because the game told you what to do, but because you understood it. GLaDOS is always there. Calm, polite, and unsettling. She talks to you like everything is normal, even when it clearly is not. Her voice slowly becomes part of the atmosphere. You start listening closely, not just to follow instructions, but to understand what kind of place you are in. Portal never rushes. It builds tension quietly. Rooms start to feel wrong. Promises feel empty. Humor becomes darker. You begin to question everything you are told. What makes Portal special is how it mixes intelligence and emotion. The puzzles engage your brain, but the world engages your instincts. The isolation, the control, the lack of human presence all sink in without needing a single explanation. Then the game breaks its own rules. The moment you are not supposed to survive is the moment Portal truly begins. From there on, the game shows its real identity. Clever, cruel, and unforgettable. Portal is short, but it leaves a mark. It trusts the player. It respects intelligence. And it proves that silence can be just as powerful as action. This is not just a puzzle game. It is a perfectly controlled experience. Nearly two decades since its 2007 release, Portal remains a masterclass in elegant, revolutionary game design. What began as a experimental project has become a permanent pillar of the medium. The "portal" mechanic is as perfect today as it was then, a simple concept of spatial connectivity that completely rewires how you perceive your environment. It turns the first-person perspective into a tool for physics-defying logic rather than just a way to aim a gun. This innovation is wrapped in a thick layer of some of the best writing in gaming history. The dark, deadpan humor and the promises of "cake" set a tone that is simultaneously hilarious and deeply unsettling. At the center of it all is GLaDOS, one of the greatest villains ever put on screen. Her passive-aggressive taunts and clinical, detached sociopathy provide a motivation far more compelling than any traditional antagonist. Though the game is famously short, completable in a single afternoon, it leaves a lasting impression that most 100-hour epics fail to achieve. While the first Portal feels like a flawless proof of concept, Portal 2 took those same bones and built a full-fledged, epic masterpiece. Well after 500 hours, I think I can write up a review on this gem. I was first introduced to TF2 from the plethora of content on it. Whether that be the dumb 2008 SFM's or well thought out video essays on the intricacies on certain weapons, the content hooked me and honestly, feels like the heart of this game. After around a week of seeing people sing the praises about this game, I decided enough was enough and eventually just installed it. I instantly fell in love. Well besides having to watch a video to fix the god awful default settings (no seriously they really suck), I was having the time of my life. I find it surprising I chose to main scout in the biggening , the "run and gun" but thinking about it some more I can understand why since he was the easiest class to learn, at least for me. Running around, shooting people and moving around at lightspeed was so addictive, however I wanted to see what the rest of the game offered. I loved the movement and damage output of the soldier, the chaotic mess of keeping your buildings up as engineer and keeping you team mates alive as medic. The simple yet also complex skill ceiling of pyro and heavy. The satisfaction of sniper and spy. It all seemed to click with me so early on in my TF2 journey that I can confidently say I've never had more fun with a game so quickly. But ultimately, I decided to main demoman due to the high skill ceiling, the raw damage, and the movement. Even though demo is my favorite, I would be lying if I said all the other classes weren't a lot of fun too. Their are so many playstyles that you are bound to find the one that suits you and I feel like that is what keeps me playing. The thought of improvement and experimentation between hundreds of loadouts is why I find this game so fun. The variety of matchups with other classes, the amazing maps (although their are waay too many maps in the game so I happen to only select less than half of them due to the map quality being very bloated). 500 hours and 9 months later, I think its safe to say that TF2 is my favorite game of all time and I now understand why so many keep retuning to this old yet somehow fresh masterpiece.

You can play this game without paying a single dime, it costs absolutely nothing to download and play normally without voice chat, text chat, anything like that. All you have to do is buy any one item in TF2, some costing as little as a dollar, and you'll gain access to voice chat and be able to communicate with other players. I'd encourage any players who want to get good at the game to either buy some weapons they want to try out or grind the achievements and unlock a few weapons that way. The main thing about TF2 is that there are multiple ways you can play. What I mean is that there are 9 characters, or "classes" you can play as. I recommend trying them all out and seeing which ones you like playing the best. Me personally, I think that the Engineer, Spy, and Soldier are my three favorite classes to play. However, other players might like to play other classes like Scout, Demoman, Medic, or Heavy. It all really depends on YOUR playstyle what classes suit you best, So here's what I recommend to people just looking at this game and reading the reviews before downloading: Spend some time (preferably equal amounts) on each class and find out what playstyle you like best. There are stock weapons for each class, but I'd recommend trying out some weapons in the shop (There's a free trial option for those who aren't sure about a weapon they want to try that gives a 25% discount on them during the trial that you can do once a week) to try to optimize your playstyle. My default spy loadout, for example, has the "Deadringer" watch, the "Your Eternal Reward" knife, and the "L'etranger" pistol because they work so well together when going behind enemy lines and killing off the enemy team wile staying hidden. TLDR: Try everything. Throw shit at the wall and see what sticks. Learn your playstyle. Once you do what you love, you'll love what you do. That's what makes TF2 so fun in the end.

I've been playing multiplayer FPS games since the end of the 90s and I have to say that this one is at the top of my list. Now i really love this game so this review is by definition very subjective. Here are my reasons : Positives : - The artwork, graphics, lore and general atmosphere are just fantastic - The characters are hilarious and unique in their own steriotypical way - The gameplay is solid and teamwork is crucial - a solid team which knows how to work together will almost always win over individual skill - The overall balance is relatively good given the amount of builds and weapons available today (which will always be a cause of balancing issues). - Communication is needed but no mic is essential thanks to a good number of voice commands - A good variety of maps and different game mods - Quality updates throughout the years (while the game is still supported properly) - Music, voice acting and sound effects are quality ! Negatives (most have to do with the current situation) : - No more updates - Perhaps too many weapons and items which are borderline useless with most older or vanilla builds still being the most effective ones (just my opinion) - Bots being present on multiple servers (a long lasting issue, not sure how much of it was fixed though) - Not many servers rolling old time popular maps (GoldRush, Badwater are almost impossible to find today) - Overload of cosmetics and flare which takes away from the original art theme (once again, more of a personal one for me) Now, i am rating the game based on all of the time i've spent on it, not just its current state. I think it is safe to say that the game is not at its best and has some major issues, but to be fair, it has been running on fumes for some time now. Some updates were amazing, some less so but it was always new and refreshing even though some aspects were not for everyone. I find myself a bit nostalgic about the past state of this game and i do play it less today. However, i still come back to it from time to time for a quick game on a public server even after 1700+ hours. To sum up, an amazing experience which i would recommend to anyone who enjoys Class Based Team vs Team shooters with various objectives. P.S.: I have briefly tried mods which attempt to bring the "genuine" TF2 experience back to the game such as TF2 Classic and TF2 Gold Rush. I do recommend everyone who is a fan of this game to try them out. Even though both have a rather subjective take on what TF2 originally should be like, they do make me feel like i am going back to a more simpler time without the overload of cosmetics). I think newer players should check them out as well (more for the feel rather than the mechanics and balance which do not resemble the past reality).

This game is (almost) a gold standard of balance that can hold both the test of time and extreme conditions. Community tinkering and experience have pushed this game so far and the depth of the game means that almost 18 (!) years later the playerbase is still kicking and rabid as ever. There's not much that can be said about this game that hasn't been discussed at least 3 times over, however I will still point out one of the flaws that strikes the hardest to me, that being the weapon balance. The stock classes themselves are fine and show a lot of tweaking and thought into their designs, however some items that were added after initial release do not show this consideration, such as the Homewrecker for Pyro, the Vaccinator for Medic and also some of the weaker weapons like Sun on a Stick for Scout, Red Tape Recorder for Spy or the Eviction Notice for Heavy. I'm reviewing this primarily to review every game in my steam library. So this will have limited value. But I'll do my best. TF2 is the foundation of many people's entire selves. It is a game that is fundamentally tied to the fans that have supported it for years on end. It sparked creativity in so many people and has led to some incredible fan works. Some of which being as long and complex as feature films. So how does the game compare to its effects? It's pretty alright. TF2 is a fun class shooter game that was the early foundation for modern entries like Overwatch, Marvel Rivals, and the like. It is goofy and ridiculous while also being a competent game on top of that. There's a lot of value in creating team comp strats that win you games in fun, niche ways. There are jokes to be had and friends to make throughout your experience playing. It's sort of old feeling, but not so much so that you feel like you're playing a game from the late 2000's. I'm sort of glazing the game because truthfully, it's not entirely my cup of tea. It doesn't need to be though and I respect the hell out of it. For new players, I don't know how much I can really recommend this game. It's good fun, but it's got it's issues. The bot issue was made better, but idk if that held since I last heard about it. The player base isn't wholly the same as it once was. You'll get an experience by playing it, but that'll be what you make of it. Just don't expect things to go super ultra smoothly like you're picking up a modern version of this concept. Definitely check it out though. For the price of absolutely free, I can't really say no to giving it a shot. Also, the worst that can happen is you hate it and uninstall. This is the foundation for a lot of different things, and if you recognize the game at all or are a returning fan, then you'll have a good time here.

Left 4 Dead - 8/10 - A Classic Co-Op Zombie Shooter That Still Delivers the Thrills Left 4 Dead is the kind of game that's stood the test of time-not because it's revolutionary in terms of mechanics, but because it nails the core elements of what makes a zombie shooter so much fun. From the tense, heart-pounding co-op action to the endless hours of chaos and teamwork, Left 4 Dead remains a fantastic experience for anyone who loves fast-paced, cooperative gameplay. At its heart, Left 4 Dead is a co-op zombie shooter where you and up to three friends must fight your way through various levels, battling hordes of the undead while trying to reach an evacuation point. The game is simple, but that simplicity is one of its strengths. You don't need to worry about complex mechanics or intricate systems; it's all about shooting, running, and surviving with your team. The pacing is spot-on, with constant waves of zombies keeping you on your toes, and the occasional special infected throwing a wrench in your plans. What really makes Left 4 Dead shine is its focus on teamwork. The AI is decent enough if you're playing solo, but the game truly comes to life when you're playing with friends. Communication and cooperation are key to surviving the relentless zombie onslaughts, and the tension of trying to keep your teammates alive while fending off an overwhelming horde creates an experience that's as chaotic as it is thrilling. The special infected, like the Boomer, Smoker, and Tank, each bring their own unique challenge to the table, and their unpredictable appearances keep you on edge the entire time. The game's AI Director is another standout feature. It dynamically adjusts the intensity of the game depending on your progress, making sure that no two runs are exactly the same. If your team is doing well, the game will throw more challenges your way; if you're struggling, it'll ease up a bit, allowing you to catch your breath. This system keeps the game feeling fresh and ensures that every session is unpredictable and exciting. Visually, Left 4 Dead holds up decently for a game that's over a decade old. The environments are well-designed, with eerie, dilapidated towns, dark forests, and crumbling buildings adding to the sense of danger. The sound design is also top-notch, with the terrifying shrieks of zombies and the thundering footsteps of a Tank always adding to the tension. That being said, Left 4 Dead does have its limitations. The campaign levels can feel a bit repetitive after a while, and the lack of variety in terms of maps and game modes can lead to burnout if you play for too long. The AI teammates, while functional, aren't perfect-sometimes they'll get stuck or fail to help you when you need them most. And while the game's simplistic mechanics are part of its charm, it can also feel a bit shallow compared to more modern shooters that offer more depth in terms of customization or character progression. 8/10 - A Thrilling Co-Op Classic That Still Delivers Left 4 Dead remains a fantastic co-op experience that's fun and exhilarating, especially with friends. It may not have the most complex mechanics or the widest variety of content, but it delivers where it counts: tense, fast-paced action, and a real sense of teamwork. While the game may feel a little dated compared to newer zombie shooters, it still holds up as one of the best co-op games of its time. If you're into zombie mayhem and love playing with friends, Left 4 Dead is still worth jumping into.

Quick clarification up front - because I'm consistent about this: I only review games I have beaten. Campaigns completed. Credits rolled. Sometimes four people are all that's left between chaos and silence. I played Left 4 Dead mostly on Xbox 360 back when it launched - not by choice, but because at the time I didn't have a working computer. Even then, the game left a permanent mark on me. Years later, out of respect and genuine love for Valve and this game, I bought it again on PC. And it was worth it. Left 4 Dead is built on one simple idea executed perfectly: co-op survival driven by tension and unpredictability. The AI Director ensures that no two runs feel the same, pacing encounters in a way that keeps everyone on edge. One moment you're calm and coordinating - the next, everything collapses. The gunplay is straightforward, but that simplicity is intentional. The real challenge isn't aiming - it's positioning, communication, and knowing when to move together or hold your ground. Special Infected punish mistakes instantly, and teamwork isn't optional - it's survival. What makes the game timeless is how well it reads players. Difficulty adapts, encounters shift, and the experience responds to how well (or poorly) your team is doing. It's not scripted spectacle - it's emergent chaos, and that's why the game still holds up. Even today, the atmosphere, sound design, and pacing remain unmatched. The music cues alone are enough to spike your heart rate. Does it show its age visually? Sure. Does it matter? Not even a little. Pros: Legendary co-op design AI Director keeps runs fresh Strong pacing and atmosphere Still incredibly fun with friends Cons: Limited weapon variety Best experienced with a coordinated group Shows its age visually Verdict: A completed classic that helped define cooperative shooters. Whether on Xbox 360 back then or PC now, Left 4 Dead remains a masterclass in tension, teamwork, and design - and absolutely worth owning again.

Left 4 Dead is undeniably a landmark in co‑op zombie shooters, but looking back at it today-especially with Left 4 Dead 2 available-it's hard to see it as anything other than the rough draft of a much better game. L4D1 laid the foundation, but almost every part of that foundation was rebuilt, expanded, and polished in its sequel. L4D1 introduced the core formula: four survivors, AI Director, frantic co‑op, and iconic infected types. But the problem is simple-Left 4 Dead 2 includes every campaign, mode, and infected type from L4D1, plus more. Valve literally ported the entire L4D1 campaign lineup into L4D2, meaning nothing is exclusive to the first game anymore. So when you compare them side‑by‑side, L4D1 ends up feeling like a stripped‑down version of what the series eventually became. Even at release, L4D1's visuals were serviceable but not impressive. Today, they look noticeably dated: - Lower texture quality - Simpler lighting - Less environmental detail - More static, less reactive world design L4D2's graphics aren't radically different stylistically, but they're objectively more detailed, more dynamic, and more atmospheric, especially with its improved lighting and weather effects. When you revisit L4D1 after playing L4D2, the downgrade is obvious. This is where the gap becomes massive. L4D2 adds: - More weapons - More melee options - More infected types - More campaigns - More mutations - More environmental hazards - More map variety And again, it includes all of L4D1's content on top of that. L4D1 simply can't compete with the sheer amount of stuff L4D2 offers. Left 4 Dead is historically important, but Left 4 Dead 2 completely replaces it. The sequel has: - Better graphics - More content - More variety - Better pacing - All of L4D1's campaigns included That leaves L4D1 feeling like a prototype-interesting as a piece of gaming history, but unquestionably a worse version of L4D2 in every practical way. If someone wants the "true" Left 4 Dead experience today, there's no reason to play the first game except nostalgia.

I first played L4D through my cousin's Xbox and would play for hours into the night fighting through hordes of zombies and special infected. I remember playing slow, careful, and deliberate as we navigated to the safe room injured and limping. Playing it years later it brings back a strong sense of nostalgia playing as Zoey, Bill, Louis, and Francis, because I have gotten to know the characters through the dialogue that occurs naturally as you play. Zoey, the only female survivor of the group, retains what little hope is left in a world that is now unrecognizable. Francis, a biker, has a rugged appearance, but everyone know he has got their back when it matters most (think Daryl Dixon from The Walking Dead). Louis is an office worker who is at times timid, but lifts up the spirits of the rest from time to time. And Bill is the veteran and leader of the group with the most experience who keeps the group together. Playing it now, many years later, it doesn't feel like the horror game it once was and is quite a breeze to go through if you know a few tricks. Still, to me, this is a horror game above all else and I try to keep that feeling by playing on low brightness and different aspect ratios and resolutions to darken the game further. And despite what other players might tell you, there is no "right" way to play. Just do you and have fun.

Left 4 Dead is a first-person shooter in which the player takes control of one of four survivors; if human players are not available, the remaining survivors are filled by AI-controlled bots. They play through campaigns fighting off the infected-living humans who have been infected with a rabies-like virus that causes psychosis.[2][3] The overarching goal is not to clear infected, but only to reach the next safe area alive. This is compounded by the presence of an "AI Director", who tracks each player's current situation, and will add or remove items and infected in response; with the goal of maintaining constant tension and creating a new experience with each playthrough. Left 4 Dead received praise for its replay value, focus on cooperative play, and cinematic feel, although some criticized its limited level selection and lack of narrative. Considered one of the greatest video games ever made, the game won several publication awards

Released back in 2008, it set the standard for team-based zombie shooters and became an instant classic. You, your friends, guns, and endless waves of the infected - it was the perfect formula then, and it still works now. Even today, the game feels surprisingly modern. The lighting, the dark corridors, the flashlights cutting through smoke and chaos - it's pure atmosphere. The story is simple: four immune survivors fighting their way through zombie-infested cities to reach safety. But the real story isn't in the plot - it's in teamwork, support, and shared panic when everything goes wrong. Left 4 Dead isn't just a shooter. It's a social experience - a memory of late-night sessions filled with yelling, laughter, and chaos. ✅ Pros: ✔ Fast-paced, intense gameplay with constant action. ✔ Strong survival atmosphere and teamwork focus. ✔ Great lighting and visuals that still hold up. ✔ Memorable special infected (Hunter, Smoker, Boomer, Tank). ✔ Legendary 4-player co-op experience. ✔ Playable even solo with surprisingly capable bots. ❌ Cons: ➖ The story is basic - more action than narrative. ➖ Without friends, the experience loses some magic. ➖ Campaigns are short and can be completed quickly. ➖ Some mechanics feel a bit dated now. ➖ Less content compared to Left 4 Dead 2. 📝 Conclusion Left 4 Dead is a co-op classic that defined a generation. You don't play it for the story - you play it for the chaos, the teamwork, and the adrenaline rush of surviving together. Even years later, it's just as fun to jump in and fight through hordes of infected. 👉 Rating: 8/10. Old but gold - fast, intense, atmospheric, and still alive after all these years. 🎮 Fun Facts: • Developed by Turtle Rock Studios and published by Valve, the creators of Half-Life and Portal. • The soundtrack was composed by Mike Morasky, who also worked on Portal 2 and Team Fortress 2. • Built on Valve's Source Engine. • Inspired countless co-op shooters like Killing Floor, World War Z, and Back 4 Blood. • Features an adaptive AI Director system that dynamically changes enemy placement and pacing for each playthrough. • The infected behavior was inspired by films like 28 Days Later and Dawn of the Dead.

Valve took a simple idea - four survivors against endless hordes of zombies - and turned it into one of the most iconic co-op games ever made. Every campaign feels like a mini action-horror movie, where teamwork is the only way to survive. The AI Director is pure genius: it changes enemy spawns, item locations, and pacing, so each run is unpredictable and intense. One moment you're clearing a hallway together, the next you're ambushed by a Smoker dragging your friend into the dark. The special infected (Hunter, Boomer, Smoker, Tank, Witch) add so much personality and strategy - they're not just enemies, they're obstacles that force cooperation. And when the Tank theme kicks in… pure adrenaline. Playing with friends is where the game truly shines. The panic, the laughter, the moments where someone sacrifices themselves so the team can escape - it all creates unforgettable memories. Even playing with bots, the game still has that sharp, tense atmosphere. Pros: ✔️ Timeless co-op gameplay ✔️ AI Director keeps things fresh every time ✔️ Unique and memorable special infected ✔️ Excellent map design, feels like horror/action movies ✔️ Pure adrenaline in every campaign Cons: - Shorter than modern games (but endlessly replayable) - Bots aren't great compared to real players Verdict: Even after all these years, Left 4 Dead holds up as one of the best co-op shooters ever made. It's fast, chaotic, scary, and fun in a way very few games have matched. If you love co-op, this is essential. 10/10 - still the gold standard of zombie survival.

satisfying medium-to-fast-paced shooter. it's easy to see why it spawned a microgenre. impressively, the game manages to have a distinctive aesthetic identity in spite of the muddy gray-and-brown color palette that was in vogue for shooters of its time. there are 14 campaigns, which might take an hour or two each. more, if you have the difficulty up and/or are playing one of the harder campaigns. you might have heard buzz about this game having a unique "AI director"; this is a marketing gimmick referring to the game's adaptive difficulty, where enemies and items are distributed proportionally to challenge players when they dominate and assist players when they struggle. over the years, the workshop has been filled with enough custom content that there is no reasonable chance of exhausting the game's replayability. arguably, the expansiveness of the workshop is a selling point in its own right. there are plenty of gameplay mutators to change up gameplay and offer a new challenge. the selection of zombies to blast and weapons to blast said zombies with is a little on the leaner side, but what there is is balanced pretty well. the special infected (elite enemies that spawn every 20 seconds or so) can create emergent interactions with each other that jeopardize your progress without feeling unfair. some weapons are better than others, but enough are viable that you'll be willing to experiment with the loot you find while you're holding out for your favorites. the game can be played solo. it's a good way to kill an afternoon. if you can convince your friends to download your furry playermodels of choice, co-op can be a great time and you'll absolutely hate each other by the end. legends speak of a third mode called "versus", but those brave souls who venture into its depths recount an experience not unlike hitchhiking through afghanistan wearing a pride flag as a hijab. this game frequently goes on sale at a steep discount, but it's worth the full price, if you're okay with that. don't bother with the first game, even if you insist on playing games as originally intended. you can play the first game's maps, with the first game's mechanics, in left 4 dead 2. some cosmetic changes have been made, but they can also be rolled back via workshop mods. for the fullest experience, find a chronological list of all campaigns, and trawl the workshop for the cut campaign "dam it" and the "redemption 2" campaign adapting the left 4 dead comic.

Been playing this game since 2011 (on the Xbox) and still this game is amazing. It's an iconic zombie game that other games try and fail at replicating (looking at you Back 4 Blood). The perfect intro game to zombie games in my opinion. The maps stay the same, but the item and infected spawns change every game, so it keeps the game interesting after you've done all the maps before. Quite a lot of weapons to choose what to explode a zombie's head with, fun gadgets to use against zombies, and the game is very forgiving when you're injured by giving you lots of health items (in easy or normal mode). A bit of horror, but not too much since you're too busy trying to survive or save your teammates. Biggest jump scare is opening a door and finding a tank already ready to send your body across the map. The computer for the special infected zombies are also smart: they are aware of your position, so they'll hide behind corridor walls, cars, or any other object till you pass by to attack you. This way you must be aware of your surroundings either by eye or ear (since all the specials have different sounds WHICH IS SO SMART). This game is very much about learning how to position yourself and your team. You cannot run, have limited amount of times you can melee zombies off you, and there is friendly fire that cannot be turned off. Because of this, positioning is key. You standing in the front of your team? Crouch so they can shoot over you and they don't shoot your head off. Horde is coming cuz you got blinded by vomit? Can't run your way out of that, so find a safe corner where your team can defend you. Once you understand positioning and the game movement, the game is breeze. You can speed run your way through the game all you want once you understand it. Love the game, will never stop playing it.

Timeless co-op shooter built on teamwork Left 4 Dead 2 is a cooperative first-person shooter centered on four-player teamwork against waves of infected. Rather than relying on progression systems or loot, the game focuses on coordination, positioning, and moment-to-moment decision-making. Pros: Co-op Design: Teamwork is essential; success depends on communication and awareness. AI Director: Enemy spawns, pacing, and item placement adapt dynamically, keeping matches unpredictable. Replayability: Multiple modes and varied campaigns give the game long-term value. Special Infected: Each enemy type forces specific tactical responses. Mod Support: Extensive community mods extend the game's lifespan significantly. Cons: Aging Visuals: Graphics are dated by modern standards. Limited Progression: No deep unlock systems, which may not appeal to progression-focused players. Toxic Public Lobbies: Playing with randoms can be hit or miss. Repetition Solo: The game is far stronger with friends than alone. Verdict: Do I recommend it? Absolutely. Left 4 Dead 2 remains one of the strongest co-op shooters ever made. With friends, it delivers tense, fast-paced, and endlessly replayable sessions even years after release. Rating: 9/10 ⭐

Left 4 Dead 2 - 8/10 - A Co-Op Zombie Shooter That Perfects the Formula Left 4 Dead 2 is the definitive version of the co-op zombie shooter. It builds on the foundation laid by its predecessor, Left 4 Dead, and expands the experience in every meaningful way. While the original game introduced the core mechanics of fast-paced, cooperative zombie survival, Left 4 Dead 2 takes everything to the next level, making it bigger, better, and more chaotic. If you loved the first game, this one is an easy upgrade, and it adds so much more to keep players hooked. The core gameplay in Left 4 Dead 2 is familiar: you and up to three friends battle through hordes of zombies across various campaigns, working together to survive and reach safe zones. What makes Left 4 Dead 2 stand out, though, is the sheer amount of variety it brings to the table. The first game had its moments of brilliance, but here, you get a wider range of weapons, new special infected, and more varied environments that really spice things up. The inclusion of melee weapons like the chainsaw, axe, and (of course) the frying pan, offers new ways to tackle hordes that make combat feel more diverse and satisfying. In the original game, weapons were largely limited to firearms, so these additions bring an exciting new element of fun, especially in close-quarter situations. The new special infected are also a huge step up. While the first game had memorable ones like the Boomer, Smoker, and Hunter, Left 4 Dead 2 adds the Charger, Spitter, and Jockey, each with their own unique abilities to mess with your strategy. These new enemies force you to rethink your approach to combat, and that unpredictability keeps the gameplay feeling fresh and engaging. The game's AI Director also returns and works even better this time, dynamically adjusting the intensity of the action based on your progress. Whether you're breezing through a level or struggling to stay alive, the AI Director keeps things tense and unpredictable. Visually, Left 4 Dead 2 is a noticeable upgrade. While the original game had solid environments, Left 4 Dead 2 feels more polished, with detailed locations that range from swampy Louisiana to urban decay in Savannah. The world feels more varied, and there's a stronger sense of place. The sound design also stands out more, with zombie sounds, environmental noises, and character interactions helping to build a more immersive atmosphere. One area where the first game had an edge was in its simplicity. Left 4 Dead was straightforward in its design, with no complicated systems getting in the way of the action. Left 4 Dead 2 adds more mechanics-like the new special infected and the extra weaponry-which enhances the depth of gameplay but can also lead to a bit more complexity in handling situations. While most players will love these additions, the pace can feel slightly less streamlined compared to the original. The first game, with its slightly more pared-down mechanics, felt like a pure rollercoaster of action, whereas the sequel, with its extra features, can feel a bit busier at times. However, this is a minor quibble, and most players will find the additional content to be a welcome upgrade. 8/10 - A Must-Play for Co-Op Zombie Fans In many ways, Left 4 Dead 2 refines and expands the formula of the first game, making it the superior experience for anyone who loves fast-paced, chaotic co-op action. The variety of weapons, new enemies, and polished environments all make for a more engaging and unpredictable game. It doesn't stray too far from what made the first game so great, but it enhances the experience in nearly every way. While some of the simplicity of the first game is lost, Left 4 Dead 2 makes up for it with even more thrilling, frantic action and a deeper sense of variety. If you're a fan of Left 4 Dead or just love co-op zombie shooters, this game is an essential play.

Under all of the memery, it's just a "typical" sequel, but not a good one. Where Portal didn't overstay it's welcome, Portal 2 can't say the same. Too much "dead time" that isn't puzzle solving detracts from the element everyone actually came for. A story that's...neat...I guess, but it just drags on and on. When you really look it over, there's so much that just doesn't need to be here. I don't even know how you do that, have bloat on a puzzle game, but here it is. It's the Die Hard 2: Die Harder or The Matrix: Reloaded of video games. Everything you liked from the original? Yeah it's here...but MORE!!!! Deedleleedleeedlee!!! Rwooww!111! More gimmicks. More puzzles. More murderbots! More wacky, zany songs! But, man, I just wanted more puzzles...the other 50% of this game could just go and nothing would be lost except some memerific lines. But this was around the "peak Borderlands" era of video game comedy, so if the writers came up with a funny idea you were GOING to hear it, a lot... Oh...Glados is insulting me? Can't wait to hear this for an hour. Oh! The facility has funny messages for the apocalypse, can't wait to hear this for an hour. Oh...there was a director of this facility decades ago? Can't wait to hear him for an hour... Every joke and gag beaten to death, all to make the game bigger and flashier for the executives. But, for real, I just wanted more puzzles... And then the...I don't know..."exploration" segments, but exploration really needs to have an order of magnitude more quotation marks. Instead of solve a puzzle, you solve how to pull up a youtube walkthrough to show you what little smidgeon of portalable surface you overlooked or other foible of game design that valve had no business being incompetent at. You like it? That's fine, I get it...but you can just look up that flaming lemons rant on Youtube, bro. Stop playing around that this is transcendent because of that...

The story, although it includes more comedic dialogue than the first, removing less of the eerie atmosphere, is greater and adds a load of lore to the characters (not as much Chel though) and in general. There's just much more polish in this one compared to the other, with a clearly larger budget and the new modes included. This [puzzle] game is great, please get it!

Portal 2 is an absolute masterpiece. The creative and innovative puzzling the series is now known for is fun of course but where Portal 2 really excels is in the amazingly crafted environments, writing and voice acting. Portal 2 builds upon its predecessor's foundations by vastly expanding the scope and history of the Aperture Science facility. After revisiting the wrecked and dilapidated test chambers, events move down below into the abandoned Cave Johnson-era silos framed by a much-deeper narrative twist. The atmosphere across each act of Portal 2's singleplayer campaign is exceptional while the expert pacing means no environment overstays its welcome. Portal 2 has aged superbly and remains an essential PC title even as we approach its 15-year anniversary. It remains one of my most beloved and favourite games of all time.

Back in school, people were always talking about how iconic it was, and everyone recommended starting with the second one - they said it's bigger, more complex, more fun than the first, and it even has co-op. At some point, I just launched Portal 2 without overthinking it, and pretty quickly I understood why it gets so much praise. Once I started playing, Portal 2 immediately felt different. Every puzzle made me think, try different approaches, and experiment with the portals. At first, it seemed like just physics challenges, but over time I realized how cleverly the game ties together space, story, and humor. Co-op adds another layer of fun: solving puzzles with a friend was hilarious and sometimes chaotic, and every perfectly timed combo gave a real sense of accomplishment. Portal 2 left an amazing impression on me. It's smart, engaging, and never makes you feel stupid - everything makes sense, but can still surprise you. The story, the atmosphere, and the puzzles make a playthrough memorable. And the memories of the fun times I had in co-op with a friend will stick with me forever. Personally, I'd recommend picking it up without hesitation - it's absolutely worth it. 8/10

Counter-Strike 2 is supposed to be a new chapter in the legendary series, but the truth is that it's more like CS:GO after a solid facelift than a full-fledged revolution. Valve came in with the Source 2 engine, better smoke, nicer maps, and a sub-tick system... and said, "Look, it's more modern." And okay - the game looks better, the lighting does its job, the smoke is awesome (you can finally disperse it with a grenade), and the animations are smoother. Shooting? Still top notch. Gunplay in CS2 is still one of the best in FPS games - the satisfaction of a headshot is still as addictive as nicotine. But... that's just it. CS2 can also be annoying. Optimization? It can be a disaster. On one patch it runs smoothly, on another the frames drop like morale after 5 consecutive losses. Matchmaking? Still a lottery. Either you get normal people, or you get a team consisting of a guy with no mic, a kid screaming in Russian, and a guy who's been AFK since the third round. Cheaters? Yes, they still exist. VAC continues to pretend to do something, and the player continues to wonder if they just lost to a pro or a moron with a wallhack. The biggest problem with CS2 is that the game still thrives more on habit than innovation. We play because we played 10 years ago. Because we know the maps. Because the skins are worth crazy money. Because CS is CS. Valve knows you'll come back anyway - even if you leave pissed off and say, "Fuck this game." To sum up: CS2 is a great, infuriating, addictive, and at times unpolished game. [h2] What is CS2? [/h2] Counter Strike 2 is a disappointing reimagining of Counter-Strike: Global Offensive on the Source 2 engine, featuring the removal of Global Offensive's identity as well as fewer gamemodes, maps and overall content originally in GO or added throughout its lifetime. The developers decided to remove the core theme that characterized Global Offensive (based on CTUs vs Terrorists), in favour of a more bland and uninspired "Esports-competitive" one. All CS2 has is just the Counter Strike brand, but has nothing to do with Global Offensive. [hr][/hr] [h2] CS2's gameplay [/h2] The gameplay is still the classic Counter Strike fun, just without the soul nor quality. The game feels sluggish, slow and not as responsive as GO. Typical examples being movement, animations and shooting. The latter, in particular, just doesn't feel responsive regardless of the ping. [hr][/hr] [h2] CS2's visual problems [/h2] With the change in theme to a more "Esports" one, the game features remakes of GO's maps with bright, washed out colours that ultimately becomes tiresome to look at. The new graphics, along with their new lighting system, look distracting during gameplay. Everything seems to blend together and overall looks cluttered and "noisy"; the elements on screen do not look as sharp as in GO. CS:GO's graphics offered more clarity in visuals also thanks to its simplicity that made it easier and faster to notice the most important elements on the screen. The clarity was further reinforced by the lighting that, while not being colourful, was easier to look at and didn't strain the eyes as in 2. [hr][/hr] [h2] CS2's lack of map based factions [/h2] It should also be noted that the clarity was aided by the presence of map-based factions (not present in CS2) that not only enforced the game's counter terrorism theme, but also fit in the scenario they were located. On some occasions, it was also possible to identify individual players (friend or foe) based on the playermodel they were assigned. CS2 features only 2 of the 14 original factions. Of these two, they utilise a single playermodel for all players on the respective team. No matter the map the same voicelines play over and over again. Factions made the game more interesting to play and spectate, but without them every match feels repetitive. [hr][/hr] [h2] CS2's cluttered HUD [/h2] CS2's HUD is flashy and cartoony, with the bottom part being cluttered in useless information and decorations. Each kill is represented in the lower-middle part of the screen via cards that appear with flashy animations. A good QoL change could be to bring back the original HUD that was more minimalistic (thus less distracting) and serious looking, and make it an option to choose either of these. [hr][/hr] [h2] CS2's OST [/h2] The game's soundtrack was also changed: with the drastic change in core theme, shifting from serious counter terrorism to a competitive esports one, the OST was changed from a more cinematic sounding one, to a more "techno" sounding one. No matter if you're in the main menu, at the start of the round or planting/defusing, the tracks that play all sound identical and overall noisy. Unfortunately there is no way to obtain CS:GO's score following its delisting. [hr][/hr] [h2] CS2's lack of hardware accessibility [/h2] CS:GO was well optimized: most low-end PCs could run it at a good framerate, something that can't be said about CS2. CS2's graphics don't even look good enough to justify its existence. Despite the lacklustre graphics, the game still alienates a portion of people who play on low-end devices that could run CSGO without any issues. [hr][/hr] [h2] CS2's lack of content updates and casual downgrades [/h2] Regarding maps, the last official remade map was added on the 13th of November 2024. So far, the devs only added community maps and reskins of already existing maps soaked in rain. This means that now, in early 2026 (at the time of this review), after an entire year, no new maps that were originally present in 2013 or Legacy GO have been added. CS2 features only 3 maps for the non-competitive gamemodes. As far as gamemodes are concerned, the classic "demolition" mode (present since GO's launch) and others that were added during GO's lifecycle have yet to be added. No effort has been put in the casual aspect of the game, unlike its original counterpart. Offline BOTs mode also has taken a hit. While the game still features a vs BOTs mode, the devs removed the difficulty slider, a basic QoL feature present in every Counter Strike game. To change it, the user will be forced to use the console. CS:GO's bots, while not as challenging as Source's, were still fun to play with and could provide a neat challenge at times. Bots also don't seem to have received any improvements, as a matter of fact, they seem less responsive than ever before. [hr][/hr] [h2] CS2's Premier problems [/h2] Premier is a slog to play through without being bored to death. As I see it, the current voting system ruins the game mode as players, most often than not, vote the same maps - rendering the mode stale. I believe the game would benefit from a map selection system akin to the one from Rainbow Six Siege: out of a randomized assortment of 5 maps, both teams vote to remove 1 map and then the game randomly picks one of the 3 remaining maps. This would make the game more interesting to play and force players to adapt and form new strategies in maps they'd otherwise not choose. [hr][/hr] [h2] CS2's reveal set the direction of the game [/h2] Even the reveal of the game seems scuffed: it seems rushed and lazily made, much like the game itself. GO had a literal animation created for it that presented the core themes of the game. How was CS2 revealed? With a pseudo-documentary boasting about Counter Strike's importance in Esports and how great it is and the addition of interactable smoke grenades and whatever "subtick" is. "Subtick", which was supposed to make "what you see, what you get", fails to deliver on its promise. [hr][/hr] [h2] Lack of developer transparency or communication [/h2] Ultimately, the game suffers from severe lack of content and transparency by the developers, whose only means of communicating with the community are with "memes" or "emojis" on social media usually posted before an update that, more than likely, will add new ways to drain money out of people's wallets with new gambling schemes and microtransactions. [hr][/hr] [h2] Conclusions (and what remains of CSGO) [/h2] This game is just disappointing. It could've been its own standalone thing for people who are willing to be unpaid QA testers in the development of whatever Valve's idea for Counter Strike's future is. Instead, they force-deleted a polished and complete game and replaced it with an inferior one. What's concerning is that CS:GO used to be paid for up until December 2018 and now is less accessible to anyone who still wants to play it alone or with friends. When accessing CS:GO Legacy, the user will be greeted by a text advising them not to play GO but to switch to CS2 since the version being played is outdated. If I installed Legacy (that's hidden in the betas), that means I intend to play it; why insist? If you want to play original CS:GO (be it 2013 or Legacy), Steam forces you to install CS2 along with it, requiring 60GB of free space in order to download 6GB / 30GB of the actual GO games. Valve could've done what they did with CS:Condition Zero and Condition Zero Deleted Scenes, where if you added one game to library, you would receive the other standalone. This would've preserved GO's achievements as well, which are yet another feature that was removed. In one swift move, CS2 removed 167 achievements and replaced them with a single one that simply requires to start the game - that's it. What an embarassing, sorry excuse for a game.

Red Orchestra: Ostfront 41-45, developed and published by Tripwire Interactive, is a unique and unflinchingly realistic World War II first-person shooter that challenges conventional FPS expectations in favor of gritty authenticity and tactical depth. Originally born from a mod for Unreal Tournament 2004, Ostfront 41-45 matured into a full standalone title that centers on the brutal Eastern Front conflict between Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union. Released in 2006, it marked a departure from the Hollywood-style presentation of World War II common at the time, instead opting for immersion grounded in realism, and an unforgiving level of difficulty that demanded teamwork, patience, and situational awareness. Even nearly two decades later, it remains a cult classic and a milestone in tactical multiplayer gaming. What immediately sets Red Orchestra apart is its uncompromising commitment to realism. Weapons handle with noticeable weight and recoil, and there's no crosshair in the center of your screen-aiming is done through iron sights, and shooting from the hip is both imprecise and often suicidal. Ballistics are modeled with bullet drop, penetration, and real-world damage models. Getting hit in Red Orchestra doesn't just wound-it incapacitates or kills in one or two shots. There are no regenerating health bars, no arcade-style killstreaks, and no handholding. This results in a steep learning curve that initially frustrates but ultimately rewards players who are willing to adapt and learn the nuances of positioning, timing, and teamwork. The maps are sprawling, atmospheric, and meticulously crafted to reflect historical locations from battles like Stalingrad, Kursk, and Arad. Urban combat and open-field warfare are both represented, with many maps offering combined arms scenarios-infantry fighting alongside tanks, each with their own roles. Vehicles are not afterthoughts here; they require multiple crew members and demand coordination. Tank combat is fully realized, with interior views, manual reloading, and armor penetration modeled realistically. You can play as a tank commander, gunner, driver, or infantryman, and each role feels essential. The game pushes you to play your part rather than go off on individualistic kill sprees, which is rare in the genre. Another standout feature is the reliance on communication and coordination. Teamwork is not just encouraged but necessary. Without a solid squad, attacking objectives or holding positions becomes nearly impossible. The command system allows for structured teamwork, with squad leaders and commanders issuing orders and calling in artillery strikes-features that laid the groundwork for later games like Squad and Hell Let Loose. The minimalist HUD and lack of conventional kill confirmations keep you in constant doubt, intensifying the sense of uncertainty and paranoia on the battlefield. Every shot fired could mean survival or instant death, and the stakes always feel high. Despite its age, Ostfront 41-45 still holds a certain appeal thanks to its solid core mechanics and the unique atmosphere it cultivates. The audio design, while not modern by today's standards, is raw and impactful. Weapon fire echoes across battlefields, mortars crash down with unsettling force, and the sound of a distant tank's engine can send chills down your spine. Visually, the game is certainly dated, with blocky character models and lower-resolution textures. However, the art direction and map design compensate by creating believable environments where the historical context shines through. Tripwire's focus wasn't on visual flash-it was on crafting a battlefield that felt lived in and lethal. Community support was crucial to Red Orchestra's longevity. Mods, custom maps, and organized multiplayer events extended the game's lifespan far beyond what might have been expected. It was never a mainstream hit, but it carved out a dedicated niche of players who appreciated its authenticity. In many ways, the game acted as a blueprint for later hardcore shooters. Titles like Red Orchestra 2, Rising Storm, Post Scriptum, and even Arma owe some design heritage to what Ostfront 41-45 pioneered. It proved that there was a market for military shooters that emphasized historical accuracy and tactical realism over speed and spectacle. That said, the game isn't without its flaws. Its accessibility is a major barrier-new players are often thrown into the deep end with little in the way of onboarding or tutorials. The harsh pace and lack of instant gratification make it a tough sell for players more accustomed to fast-paced modern shooters. The AI in offline mode is rudimentary, and the lack of a strong single-player component means its value is almost entirely dependent on active multiplayer communities. While these existed robustly in its prime, finding populated servers today can be hit or miss, though dedicated fan-run servers still keep the game alive in a limited capacity. Ultimately, Red Orchestra: Ostfront 41-45 is a game for players who crave authenticity and a deeper connection to the historical realities of war. It doesn't romanticize conflict-it depicts it with a rawness that still stands out in a market crowded with stylized violence and cinematic set-pieces. It's a title that respects its subject matter, demands respect from its players, and delivers a sense of tension and immersion few shooters ever achieve. It may be rough around the edges, but its bold design philosophy and tactical depth ensure that it still deserves recognition as one of the most influential hardcore shooters of its era. For those willing to embrace its challenges, it offers a deeply satisfying and memorable experience that remains unmatched in its genre. Rating: 8/10
