I boot up my PC. It's evening. The cold wind is howling behind my window, it's minus 15 outside but I don't care. I fetch an old dusty bottle of whiskey and pour it in a small shot glass, I grab a crumpled pack of Luckies unfiltered and light up one with my Zippo lighter. I click on Red Orchestra: Ostfront 41-45 and… Suddenly I'm clad in Soviet winter uniform, all bundled up, I stiffly hold onto my PPSH-41, my both hands are a little shaky from cold wind but I don't pay much attention to it. Our commissar with a morose countenance tells us that the German push attack is expected to start in approximately 30 minutes. His words are sharp, they make me excited and a bit scared. We're inside of a steel factory called 'Krasniy Oktyabr', our mission is to defend it at all costs… At least what is left of it after weeks of heavy bombings. It's raining again. Everyone is in position. Silence. I only hear the raindrops… They fall from gritty dark skies and bump against the damp ground. Red bricks of once a great thriving factory get soaked. Everyone is not daring to utter a single word. There's no time for words now, everything was already said a long time ago. Now the guns will talk and we will hear their harrowing dialogues. It'll happen soon… any minute now. I catch the loud yell of our commissar "The attack has started! No retreat! For our Motherland, stand your ground, comrades!". Bullets are flying all at once, to and fro, ricocheting off soaked ruins of walls and ceilings, penetrating poor souls who happened to stand in their way, eagerly taking their lives with them. My comrades, they swear and curse "f**ing Nazi scum, you'll pay for everything, pigs" while firing their rifles. Germans shout and fire back, I hear their incensed cries of anger and distant grumble. I aim my PPSH and fire in small bursts, I see them running around with their grey uniforms but I don't care. I'm angry, hungry, cold… I will kill. I kill. Burst after burst, one down, another one down.. and another one gone. I grab a grenade, pull the pin and fling it with all my force… Screams. All these screams around me. I'm truly in Hell. I think to myself "What a dismal day to die… If only I gave a f**k". They're inside the factory, just across the workshop facility. They are shooting at us and we are shooting back. A bullet flies past me, ripping a little part of my ear off. It's painful but I'll make it. I have no permission to bleed out, I'll fight and kill every f**ing Nazi that came here burning and destroying our lands. Blood is everywhere, explosions… Echoes of pain. It starts to seem like we've been fighting for hours. The attack fades away. They're retreating… For now. Corpses of Germans and Soviets are all around the factory building and its outskirts. I'm tired, I feel dried sticky blood on my face, my hands and all my clothes are dirty as well. The air is filled with the aroma of petrichor mixed with the smell of gunpowder and freshly murdered human bodies, almost creating a fine line between life and death. I sit down on a damp stone floor. I reach for my cigarettes. Fumbling around a little I get them, then I get an old box of matches. The lit match creates a lot of bright sparkles and gives life to the flame. It flickers, licking at my crumpled cigarette, creating some kind of an almost peaceful atmosphere. I take a long puff of my lit cigarette. My lungs are filling with thick rich tobacco smoke… I don't pay attention to my hurting ear anymore. I'm relaxed. I think to myself "well, it's not so bad after all, there will be more attacks, I'll probably be dead by the next week. But I'm here and I'll fight" It's twilight. it's still raining. My hands are trembling from cold. I'm sitting against the cold wall, hugging my PPSH and slowly smoking, enjoying every puff I take. I think about my hometown… my parents… "How are they?" The past barely feels real anymore… It feels like a dream. Everything is gritty, nippy and wet and only the tip of my cigarette, smoldering in complete darkness, makes my poor rugged soul warm.

The streets of London are currently being overrun by "Zeds" which are basically science experiments gone horribly wrong that now want to turn your vital organs into a light snack. You are part of a ragtag group of survivors ranging from riot police to disgruntled office workers who have decided that the best way to handle a biological apocalypse is with a massive amount of high-caliber firepower. It is a dark and claustrophobic wave-based shooter where the air is thick with smoke and the floor is permanently stained a deep shade of crimson. The gameplay is a tense cycle of frantic combat and desperate shopping trips during the short breaks between waves of enemies. You have to choose a "Perk" like the Sharpshooter or the Medic which gives you specific bonuses and determines which of the massive arsenal of weapons you should be carrying. I found the Zed Time mechanic to be the absolute star of the show because everything suddenly shifts into slow motion when someone pulls off a particularly impressive kill allowing you to watch the physics-defying carnage in glorious detail. The atmosphere is pure industrial horror with a heavy metal soundtrack that kicks into high gear the moment the sirens wail and the specimen doors open. It is a game that rewards tight teamwork and careful ammo management because once you get cornered by a chainsaw-wielding Fleshpound your chances of survival drop to zero almost instantly. It is unpolished and gritty and feels like a cult classic horror movie that you stumbled upon late at night and realized was actually a masterpiece. 9 out of 10. It is a brutal and satisfying co-op experience that proves you do not need a complicated plot when you have a double-barrel shotgun and a hallway full of monsters. Stick together during the waves and weld the doors you do not want to be flanked by and remember: if you hear a woman screaming in the dark it is definitely time to start running in the opposite direction.

I am rather half and half to whether I like the game. The horde slaying I enjoy, but the niche features of the game diminish the game by game experience for me. + Slaying Hordes The gameplay is tense and fast paced. Enemies rush after you and if you do not gun them down quickly enough you will either be pinned or die rapidly. Mowing them down with an assault rifle, or blowing them up with the shotgun, or setting them all on fire, is very gratifying. / Semi-Realism * No Crosshair All weapons must be fired by aiming or hip firing without a crosshair. * Magazines When reloading, the game reloads through magazines. Meaning if you shoot 2 bullets in an assault rifle and want to reload, you will have wasted one of your limited magazines, wasting the remainder of the last one. - The Store * OBNOXIOUS Gun Vendor I have never dealt with a more frustrating personality in a game than this game's gun vendor. If you want to browse weapons to buy before you have the cash, or want to swap your main gun, the vendor will non-stop belittle you like a child saying, "You don't have the money for that sweetie!" or, "Money doesn't grow on trees babe!" Every. Single. Time. You click on a weapon you cannot buy yet or do not the have the carrying capacity for. If I could, I would blow up the gun shop and steal what I needed... * Very narrow time window Once a round is complete, you get around a minute or perhaps a minute and a half on lower difficulties, to rush to the shop and buy what you need. When you are across the map, you barely get any time left over to see what you might want. You are intended to rush to the gun shop before the round ends by killing all the zeds. If timed correctly this issue is avoided, but still a frustrating experience none the less. - Lack of Sight Customization There is no freedom in modifying weapons to have different sights. Almost all of the sharpshooter weapons lack any digital sights. Aiming under the fast paced pressure of game paired with sights that block most of your view is very frustrating. - Tripwire In 2022 there are a selection of off-topic reviews. During this period the game was being review bombed because Tripwire had fired the CEO of tripwire, one of the founders of the OG killing floor, for publicly, and independently, expressing their stance on being anti-abortion. He did this because the majority of game developers during this period were expressing their support for abortion, whereas there were nearly no developers representing their stance against abortion. Following this the developer was fired from Tripwire. The top review of the off-topics review period includes a link and quotation of the CEO's stance on the issue if you want to research this further. If you are familiar with gaming, you know there are two kings of co-op survival shooters. There is Left 4 Dead 2 and Killing Floor. As I've grown up, I didn't liked zombie games as I liked them in childhood. A few days ago I felt bored and decided to give it a try, becouse it was a long time after the last time I played. I gotta tell you, I had a really good time playing it again. No, I didn't mean it becouse of nostalgia or something like that. I really enjoy it as a game. The athmosphere still hits even tho the graphics are outdated, even for 2009. It's dark, nasty, sometimes scary, with a good old piss filter on it. Too many maps have dark places without lights. Sometimes you need to switch to a gun to get lights on. Yeah, not every weapon has a flashlight. Gunplay mauls every other shooter I ever played. It's heavy and powerful. You feel the weight of shotguns, the recoil of assault rifles, the speed of SMGs. Just go and play one wave with duel wielding golden Desert Eagles. Then you can know what I'm yapping about. Zombies called zeds here. It matters too much (doesnt). Enemies are fun. They are strong. Even weak starting zeds are bigger treat on late game or on highter difficulity. For example, Clot, most basic wave 1 zed, can grab you and lock you in one place. It's nothing special. But in wave 8 or 9 one suprise Clot can wipe out half of team. I'm not joking. But even if enemies are powerful, balanced perks make it even. Perks grow power as you play. You skill grows and your game difficulity can higher up. It's good progression system to be honest. Music is on another level. zYnthetic, the guy who wrote most of the OST, is genius. Some people compare Killing Floor music to DOOM 2016 music but if you have even played one full game you will know it has absolutely different feeling. As a co-op survival of course need good core. Perks (classes) are balanced. Even Medic is fun to play, sometimes broken tho. Every class has only pros, not negative side. As I said perks are balanced and can play whatever your team needs to be played without being chained to something you dont want to play. Most of maps are claustrophobic, but also they are huge most of time. It's more like tactical game too, becouse most of time you need find place to hold and make fast moving up if something getting out of a hand, and it always happens on highter difficulities. It's masterpiece in every way. Yes, it's clunky and buggy, but it's 2009 game so of course it is. I read few negative reviews. All people complain about is this game is dead, which is absolutely not true. It still have decent amount of people playing. Also there was some people who was saying game is clunky. Well, yes, it's 2009 game, of course it will be clunky, but if you get used to it, it's charm to be honest. I'm huge 00's gaming fan. I have tried Killing Floor 2, I invest nearly 100 hours into it, but after I uninstall game, I never wanted to go back. Don't get me wrong, Killing Floor 2 is solid game and I like it so much. But it have some flaws which makes me lost interest soon. I'm not even talking about Killing Floor 3 becouse there is not Killing Floor 3. In future we can see. In the other hand Killing Floor 1 has not real flaws for 2009 game which makes me drop it after 16 years. Try it out. [h1]Killing Floor 1 - A Classic That Laid the Foundation[/h1] Killing Floor 1 is undeniably a great game for its time. The atmosphere is gritty, the soundtrack goes hard, and the co-op gameplay loop is still fun and intense even today. It really nailed that desperate survival horror vibe and built a strong foundation for what the series would become. You can feel the passion and creativity that went into it, and it's easy to appreciate why it became such a cult classic. That said, it [i]is[/i] dated - everything from animations to movement and overall game feel definitely shows its age now. Because of that, if I'm going to boot up Killing Floor, I'd much rather play Killing Floor 2. KF2 takes everything the first game did well and modernizes it with smoother mechanics, better visuals, and way more polish. Still, Killing Floor 1 is a solid experience and deserves respect - it's just more of a nostalgic classic at this point than my go-to version to actually play today.

What is there to say? Wave based zombie shooter. It was the first game I got on Steam, considering I saw my friend from Xfire playing it (Thank you Hobocannibal for introducing me to Steam). The only issue I have with this game is that the leveling is extremely awful, with only 6 levels for each perk, you have the most drawn out leveling system in any game. KF2 is much better when it comes to leveling, as max level isn't an insane grind. For instance, the support class requires not only doing shotgun damage, but welding door health. The first few levels are fine, but once you get to a point where you have to weld a million total door health, it becomes an insane grind, as welding doors isn't a very common thing, and on top of that, it's such a small number compared to what you have to reach. In KF2, you just get a basic XP bar, where anything you do related to the class is what gives you XP and you get to level 25 by just using class weapons. But this is the start of the best zombie wave shooters. People look at CoD: WaW and remember fondly of the nazi zombies mode, but I was over here playing KF instead. I had a friend that sat me down to play WaW zombies with him, and all I could think about was "Wow, this is like Killing Floor. I want to play more Killing Floor." Though the community is a bit... words to describe someone who have a mental disability. I remember back in 2012, my friend Kris and I were playing on a community server with just the two of us, and the owner was typing to us through the server console, claiming Medics aren't allowed to fight, only heal. Killing Floor is a cooperative first-person shooter developed and published by Tripwire Interactive, originally released in 2009. While its roots trace back to a popular Unreal Tournament 2004 mod, the standalone release established itself as a cult classic in the realm of co-op zombie shooters. The game places players in the boots of military operatives and civilians attempting to survive waves of horrific biological specimens-referred to as "specimens" rather than zombies-across various maps set in a dystopian version of the UK. Over time, Killing Floor carved out a loyal fanbase due to its satisfying gameplay mechanics, eerie atmosphere, and distinct tone. The core gameplay loop is deceptively simple yet endlessly engaging: survive multiple waves of increasingly difficult enemies, earn money, and spend that money on better weapons, armor, and ammo between rounds at a randomized trader location. What elevates this otherwise familiar concept is the synergy between team roles, enemy diversity, and sheer brutality of combat. The game heavily rewards cooperative play; lone wolves will quickly find themselves overwhelmed, particularly on higher difficulty levels. Classes-referred to as "Perks"-such as the Sharpshooter, Support Specialist, and Medic each have their own strengths, weaknesses, and weapon preferences, offering meaningful gameplay variation and encouraging players to complement one another. Graphically, Killing Floor was never a technical powerhouse, even by 2009 standards. Its visuals are utilitarian, occasionally bordering on outdated, but the art direction and overall atmosphere compensate where polygon counts fall short. The gritty, industrial environments-abandoned hospitals, burning cities, and blood-soaked labs-are dripping with tension. The sound design, particularly the chilling enemy audio cues and the adrenaline-pumping metal soundtrack, adds to the game's immersive horror tone. Enemy design is another highlight: the grotesque specimens are unsettling, especially the invisible stalkers and the menacing Fleshpounds, which ramp up the difficulty and panic when they appear. What truly sets Killing Floor apart from other co-op shooters of its time is its sense of identity. The British setting and dry, dark humor lend it a unique charm. Character voice lines range from grim to ridiculous, providing moments of levity amidst the carnage. The persistent perk progression system gives players a reason to return, as leveling up a perk not only boosts its effectiveness but also unlocks new tactical possibilities. Mods and community maps further extend the game's lifespan; Tripwire wisely supported modding from the beginning, and the Steam Workshop became a haven for creative fan content, from weapons to entirely new game modes. That said, the game is not without its faults. The learning curve for new players can be steep, particularly on higher difficulties where a lack of coordination leads to quick defeats. The user interface, especially the trader menu, is clunky and dated. Additionally, while perk progression adds longevity, it can feel grindy, and power disparity between new and veteran players can create balance issues in public games. Still, these shortcomings are relatively minor compared to the overall experience. Once players find their rhythm with a good team, the game becomes a thrilling blend of strategy, reflex, and chaos. In retrospect, Killing Floor has aged remarkably well for a game with modest ambitions and technical limitations. It doesn't rely on flashy gimmicks or cinematic spectacle; instead, it offers raw, visceral, team-oriented gameplay that remains compelling years after its release. It's a title that rewards teamwork, planning, and precise execution-and punishes complacency with brutal, unrelenting violence. For fans of survival shooters or those seeking a hardcore co-op challenge, Killing Floor remains a hauntingly memorable experience that deserves its place in the pantheon of cult FPS hits. Rating: 9/10

One of the first games I got on steam all those years ago and it still has a community that is currently playing, even with its sequels that are out now. When it comes to coop zombie survival games, Killing Floor holds a special place. I used to compare it to other popular titles like Left 4 Dead and Zombie Army, forming what many would call the big three of the genre. Over time, more contenders have emerged, giving fans plenty of options but Killing Floor still stands out. Visually it captures a dark and eerie atmosphere that perfectly sets the stage for intense gameplay. And it's in the gameplay that Killing Floor truly shines. The experience is incredibly fun and addictive, pulling players into relentless action against endless hordes of zombies. Taking down enemies, watching the slow motion effects, and feeling that adrenaline rush with each kill is immensely satisfying. I found myself fully immersed throughout my time with the game, with little to complain about. Killing Floor knows exactly what it is pure rampage and relentless zombie slaughter. It doesn't try to be everything to everyone, which is refreshing in a gaming world where many titles overreach. While it may not have as much coop variety as Left 4 Dead or Zombie Army, it carves its own niche with fast paced combat and intense action. As for the current player population, I'm unsure due to the existence of the sequel, but my experience left a lasting impression. For any fan of coop zombie survival games, Killing Floor delivers exactly what it promises.

[h1]A Brutal, Fun, and Dated Co-Op Classic That Refuses to Die[/h1] [i]6-player co-op survival horror at its finest! Free updates, free special events and a ridiculous amount of fun![/i] [h2]Story[/h2] The story is very minimal. A biotech company called Horzine conducted genetic and cloning experiments in the UK. Things went horribly wrong when an experiment led to the creation of genetically modified mutants, also known as "specimens" or "Zeds". These creatures escaped containment and overran parts of London and southern England. A government cleanup operation fails, and chaos spreads. The cities fall, and the military struggles to contain the outbreak. [h2]Gameplay[/h2] Killing Floor is a co-op survival horror FPS game. You play as part of a small group of survivors-mercenaries, ex-soldiers, and civilians-banding together to fight wave after wave of horrific monsters called Zeds, struggling to survive. After the final wave you fight a boss. You earn money (Dosh) by killing enemies, which you spend at a trader between waves to buy weapons and armor. You can weld doors shut to keep the Zeds out, but they can destroy the doors. A cool feature in the game is Zed-Time. A slow-motion effect that adds dramatic flair when scoring kills, especially headshots. It's very satisfying to shoot headshots in this game. There are 6 core Perks. Each Perk provides passive bonuses and weapon discounts, and levels up through in-game actions. Perks level up through specific tracked stats (e.g., headshots for Sharpshooter). Max level is 6. You choose your Perk at the start of a match, but can switch between waves. Each one is tied to a specific weapon class or role: [b]Berserker[/b] - Melee tank and crowd control. [b]Sharpshooter[/b] - Precision long-range killer. [b]Commando[/b] - Assault rifle expert and cloaked Zed spotter. [b]Medic[/b] - Team support and survivability. [b]Support Specialist[/b] - Shotgun powerhouse and a better door welder. [b]Firebug[/b] - Area denial and fire damage. The game is designed for 6-player co-op but also playable solo. Way more fun to play with your friends than solo though. [h2]Enemies & Bosses[/h2] All Zeds scale with difficulty and player count, becoming more aggressive and numerous. They can spawn from different directions, encouraging constant movement and awareness. There are 9 different Zeds and 1 Boss: [list][*][b]Clot[/b] - The basic Zed, can grab you and immobilize you. Dangerous in numbers. [*][b]Gorfast[/b] - A faster melee attacker with a cleaver-arm. Stronger than Clots and hits harder. [*][b]Bloat[/b] - A fat, slow disgusting Zed that will vomit acid on you, and explodes in bile on death. [*][b]Husk[/b] - A ranged Zed that is equipped with a powerful flame cannon. It fires a flammable ranged attack that pierces armor and deals continuous damage to those hit by it. [*][b]Stalker[/b] - A cloaked and stealthy Zed. Dangerous in numbers. [*][b]Crawler[/b] - A fast spider-like Zed that moves on all fours. Jumps and lunges at the player. Dangerous in numbers. [*][b]Siren[/b] - A screaming psychic Zed. Emits a deadly sonic scream that damages players through walls and destroys grenades mid-air. Don't let her get close, especially if there are many. [*][b]Scrake[/b] - A mini-boss type Zed with a chainsaw. Calm and walk until provoked (takes a certain amount of damage) and then enrages and sprints at the player. Teamwork can be key to surviving this enemy. [*][b]Fleshpound[/b] - A mini-boss and the most dangerous Zed with a glowing chest and massive bladed arms. Enrages when taking too much damage too quickly or on sight of players. Deals devastating melee attacks. Requires strong coordination to bring down. [*][b]The Patriarch[/b] - The final boss after all waves are done. Can cloak. Has a chain gun and rocket launcher. Heals himself up to 3 times by running away. Spawns additional Zeds during battle. Strategy involves coordinated damage to prevent healing. Trap him, then burst him down.[/list] [h2]Environment[/h2] The maps are dark, gritty, and often claustrophobic, and vary widely in layout, style, and tactical challenges. There are different variations of maps such as industrial/facility maps, urban/street maps, outdoor/forested maps, and experimental/custom maps from the modding community. Every map has weldable doors where you can seal off paths to control Zed flow or protect chokepoints. Some maps encourage kiting (running and shooting in circles), while others favor holding tight chokepoints. Zeds appear from dark corners, broken walls, or sewer grates. Knowing these helps plan defenses. [h2]Visual Design & Sound Design[/h2] The visuals are good for a game from 2009, and the Zeds look scary and disturbing. It looks dated playing it in 2025 though. Some maps can often be very dark where flashlights and muzzle flashes are your main light sources. The sound design is good. Some sound cues are vital. Hearing a Siren scream or a Scrake rev his chainsaw gives players a chance to prepare. The soundtracks, heavy metal, kick in during combat and pumps you up for the action. [h2]Constructive Criticism[/h2] Killing Floor is clearly designed for co-op, playing solo is less fun. There are no bots available to fill the empty slots either. Playing solo as a Medic or Support Specialist is basically useless and impossible to survive as. So there are some balance issues, even in co-op, where some Perks are far stronger than others, especially at high levels, where Sharpshooter and Support dominate, while Firebug struggles. The UI is an outdated interface with a confusing Perk system. Making max level at 6 is a bit weird as well. The trader menus are slow and a bit awkward to navigate under time pressure, especially for new players. No real progression system or cosmetic unlocks either, except leveling your Perks. Movement is slow and weighty, especially compared to modern FPS games. You have no sprint and jumping is very clunky where It feels like you should be able to jump up on for example a box, but the character doesn't jump high enough. Feels like you just jump up 10 centimeters from the ground. [h2]The Verdict[/h2] Despite the flaws, it's a very fun co-op game that I had a lot of fun with back in the day. This is a good game, but Killing Floor 2 is much better. [h2]Rating: 7.5/10[/h2]

Killing Floor 1 is almost timeless. The atmosphere, the look of the game, the amazing maps and the great weapon models, the weapon animations and sounds. The biggest issue with the game and the part that holds it back from being the best horde shooter ever is the hitboxes. There are plenty of videos on the internet that show that the hitboxes are completely broken, making headshots impossible unless you've studied the jank of this game and achieved a PhD in where the hitbox should be in X scenario. If you can't feel solid feedback from when you shoot, it leads to frustration. The only reason I am recommending this game is because of the ScRN balance patch which fixes the hitboxes. If you are going to play this game, only play it using the ScRN mod or preferably find a server hosting the ScRN mod since it stores your progress. It adds in new weapons, more classes, and makes the game into the timeless masterpiece that it should have been on launch. The only issue with this method is that the balance patch is not 'whitelisted' meaning that any levels you gain when using it are locked behind either the server you're playing on or on your machine. Also, if you buy this game, I can't recommend getting the full edition with all the DLC enough. When the game goes on sale, that full edition drops to around 13 dollars which is a fair enough price for such a great game.

Killing Floor: A Business Model I Can Respect When I first loaded up Killing Floor, I felt a familiar rush-the thrill of total control. You and your team of well-armed professionals take out endless waves of mindless, expendable creatures, all while stockpiling cash and resources for the long haul. It's basically a Wall Street investment strategy, but with more chainsaws and flamethrowers. The game throws you into abandoned city streets, creepy underground labs, and desolate industrial complexes-places where nobody hears the screaming. The environment reminded me of my private real estate holdings, minus the luxurious carpeting and VIP clientele. The sense of isolation? Authentic. Now, let's talk mechanics. The money system is brilliant. Each round, you earn cash for kills, reinforcing the golden rule: the more bodies that pile up, the richer you get. Just like real life, you can loan out your wealth to "associates," but they'll always be in your debt. I respect a game that understands how power truly works. The enemies are a standout. The Clots are weak-minded, easy to herd, and easily controlled-I know a thing or two about that. The Sirens? Loud, shrieking nuisances that need to be silenced immediately. And the Patriarch? A wealthy, well-connected individual who mysteriously vanishes, only to return stronger than before. Now that's storytelling I can relate to. That said, I have some complaints. The prison-like environments hit a little too close to home. The AI teammates are unreliable-kind of like certain high-profile friends who "never met me" the moment things got hot. And worst of all? There's no way to buy your way out of the final round. In reality, there's always a way out-unless someone makes sure there isn't. Final Verdict? 10/10. The only thing missing is a panic button when the authorities start asking questions.

Sin Episodes is a tragic look into what could have been a very good sequel. It's short and significantly closer to Half-Life 2 than its predecessor (even down to using the same engine). I'm conflicted on whether to recommend it to fans of the franchise... Gameplay-wise, I think it's almost excellent. I love the weapons, the game does a very good job of giving them unique roles and the abilities they all have are a cool addition. It gives you enough ammo to use what you need and I'd say that the toolkit is well-rounded for the 2 hours of gameplay the first episode has. There isn't much enemy variety however. For most the game you'll be shooting bad-guys that look the same (as you can see from the pics). The tougher Soldiers are okay but they lack variance. There's only one boss which is fought twice, I think the game did a good job of making the two fights stand out and I think the boss fights themselves were fun. The music is great and the game has one of the best main menu tracks I have ever had the pleasure of listening to. Level design is excellent, straight-forward whilst still leaving room for navigation and some mobility. Surprisingly, Blade can be very mobile in this game, though it may just be the animaitons making it look more pronounced than in the first game. There are a couple secrets scattered about each level but it's nothing like the first game, just some extra ammo. Sadly, the game took a more action-focused approach, which means the neat little side objectives from the original do not make an appearence. You can't make any choices or give yourself boosts. The health and healing systems are very well done. I also enjoyed the UI. The game does a neat little thing where it tracks your actions and has charts, showing what weapons you use, how you proceeded, other stats, etc. It even gives you little titles based on it! I loved it, would have made for an excellent addition if it was longer. The dynamic difficulty system is excellent, I love it is a shame we didn't get to see more of it. The new character and companion, Jessica is okay. She's got a good role in the game and shows potential but sadly, we'll never see more as the gmae didn't get any follow-up episodes. As a companion in combat, she's not that useful. She just has a rifle and shoot, no grenades, no special abilities, no voice-lines in combat and no aid beyond the shooting. She's also invulnerable to damage. Trying to talk outside of scripted sequences leads to a generic "We can't stop here" voice line, which is sad. The new villain is meh, he feels rather rushed. Most of the characters are underwhelming in fact. Blade has no voice-lines, no quips or one-liners. I don't think he makes for a good silent protagonist, especially not when considering his role in the first game. JC, your buddy from the first game makes an appereance but it feels underwhelming. The game extra dialogue at certain sections that you have to press Tab to hear, I don't think that's a good design choice as those can easily be missed. The game ends on a cliff-hanger that feels unsatisfying and a lot of the questions it poses are left unanswered, almost all of them in fact. Overall, it's disappointing. I wouldn't call the combat that intense, nor is there much if any vehicle combat at play. Performance-wise, the games runs very smoothly. Do be aware that on higher resolutions, the text elements of the menus, as well as the subtitles, will be extremely small, almost unreadable. Overall... 8.5/10 for what is there. It was still surprisingly fun to play for its duration and would have made for a good set-up for the rest of the Episodes. The only notable issue with the game, if you can tolerate the short length, is the story which is left incomplete.

I suppose they were trying to make it more serious and contemporary for 2006? The game is in constant first-person mode with in-game cutscenes. It clashes harshly stylistically from the original game. While still being good, it should have done a little bit more to distance itself from Half-Life. The latter half of the game feels more epic and aesthetically similar to the original game. Unfortunately it ended right when it was getting interesting. * Also, the main menu soundtrack is awesome. SiN Episodes: Emergence, developed and published by Ritual Entertainment, represents both a fascinating experiment and a lost opportunity in the evolution of first-person shooters. Released in 2006 as the first installment of a planned episodic series, it sought to revive the late-1990s SiN franchise with modern technology, tighter pacing, and a new narrative arc. Built on Valve's Source engine, it was intended to demonstrate how serialized gaming could deliver cinematic action in digestible chapters. What emerged instead was a game that blended ambition with inconsistency-a solid, stylish shooter that hinted at a grander vision but was ultimately left stranded after a single episode. The story picks up years after the events of the original SiN, with the player once again stepping into the boots of Colonel John R. Blade, the hardened but human commander of HardCORPS. Freeport City, a grimy, neon-lit metropolis, is under siege from a new bio-mutagenic threat known as U4. The chemical's effects-ranging from monstrous mutations to psychotic aggression-are being exploited by corrupt corporate factions, including the ever-manipulative scientist Elexis Sinclaire. Early in the game, Blade is injected with an unknown variant of U4, giving the narrative an urgent personal dimension as he struggles to understand what is happening to his body while attempting to stop the city's collapse. The plot unfolds through radio chatter, in-game conversations, and short cutscenes, relying on environmental storytelling rather than lengthy exposition. Though the writing is uneven and occasionally pulpy, it conveys the right blend of corporate conspiracy and comic-book melodrama that defines the series' tone. Where SiN Episodes finds its greatest strength is in its presentation and pacing. Powered by the Source engine, the game boasts detailed environments and fluid physics that were impressive for their time. Freeport's decaying skyscrapers, industrial docks, and corporate facilities feel tangible, filled with interactive elements that highlight the game's emphasis on immersion. Doors can be breached with explosives, objects react believably to impacts, and enemies collapse with ragdoll physics that add cinematic flair to the combat. The lighting and color palette give the world a striking personality-gritty but vibrant, futuristic yet familiar. The techno-industrial soundtrack complements the visuals perfectly, driving the pace of battle while echoing the cyberpunk overtones of the setting. Combat is the backbone of SiN Episodes, and while its core mechanics are solid, they occasionally struggle to stand out. The arsenal includes standard fare-pistol, shotgun, submachine gun, rifle-each with alternate fire modes, providing tactical flexibility but limited long-term variety. Firefights are brisk and violent, emphasizing headshots and environmental destruction, with enemies exhibiting decent aggression and use of cover. The standout feature is the Personal Challenge System, Ritual's attempt at dynamic difficulty balancing. This system constantly monitors player performance-tracking accuracy, damage taken, and reaction times-and adjusts enemy numbers and resilience accordingly. The idea was to create a fluid difficulty curve that adapts to individual skill levels. When it works, it keeps encounters tense and engaging. When it doesn't, it can turn fights into punishing slogs, particularly when the system misreads player intent or reacts too drastically. Nevertheless, it was a forward-thinking mechanic that anticipated features later seen in modern shooters. Level design in Emergence is both varied and uneven. Early chapters shine with strong environmental storytelling-gunfights in flooded warehouses, escapes through burning corridors, and rooftop chases that make use of the game's verticality. The pacing is brisk, alternating between claustrophobic interiors and open arenas that let the player flex their combat strategies. Unfortunately, the latter half of the game leans heavily on more linear corridor sequences, with repetitive enemy spawns and predictable ambush triggers that undercut the initial excitement. There are flashes of creativity, such as the inclusion of vehicle sections and multi-stage set pieces, but the repetition of combat scenarios begins to dull their impact. Even so, the overall design reflects the studio's deep understanding of classic FPS principles-momentum, rhythm, and the balance between movement and precision. The cast adds personality to the experience, though the characterization is thinly spread. Blade, the gruff protagonist, has evolved since his original 1998 incarnation; here, he is quieter, more introspective, and less overtly quippy, though still steeped in that old-school hero archetype. His new partner, Jessica Cannon, offers capable support but lacks much depth beyond being the voice in his ear. Elexis Sinclaire returns as the seductive, manipulative villainess, her motivations again tied to genetic manipulation and control. While the voice acting captures the pulpy charm of the material, it sometimes feels mismatched with the tone the game tries to maintain-a mix of self-aware camp and gritty sci-fi drama. Nonetheless, the chemistry between Blade and his allies gives the story enough energy to propel it through its brief runtime. Despite its strengths, SiN Episodes: Emergence is ultimately defined by its incompleteness. Ritual's plan was to release nine episodes over three arcs, each continuing the story and expanding Freeport's world. The first entry ends abruptly, teasing future developments that never arrived. Shortly after release, the studio was acquired by MumboJumbo, which shifted its focus to casual games, leaving the SiN saga unfinished. This abrupt halt casts a shadow over Emergence, transforming it from a bold new beginning into a fascinating relic of mid-2000s experimentation. What might have evolved into an expansive narrative-driven FPS series remains a single, tantalizing glimpse of what could have been. Looking back, SiN Episodes: Emergence feels like a bridge between eras-between the cinematic bombast of Half-Life 2 and the modular storytelling ambitions of modern episodic games. It captures the confidence of early Source engine titles, offering visceral combat, environmental interactivity, and flashes of narrative ambition, yet it also reveals the growing pains of an industry still learning how to deliver games in smaller, serialized formats. Its gunplay may not rival the polish of its contemporaries, and its story stops just when it starts to intrigue, but there's a raw enthusiasm in its design that makes it hard to dismiss. In the end, SiN Episodes: Emergence stands as both a testament to Ritual Entertainment's technical talent and a monument to the unfulfilled promise of episodic gaming. It delivers a polished, energetic shooter experience packed with personality and cinematic flair, even as its brevity and structural flaws limit its impact. For fans of classic FPS design-tight combat, striking visuals, and unapologetically pulpy storytelling-it remains a fascinating time capsule, an ambitious first chapter that never got to finish its sentence. Rating: 8/10

Simple, but quite entertaining action flick, build on solid foundation and occasionally showing glimpses of serious potential. Imo the running and gunning here feels better than in Half Life 2 :) Hey hey hey! Before you start throwing stones at me - I'm not saying HL2 is a trash game (just a bit overrated);p SiN's guns feel more powerful, and the pacing of combat is better - game is more condensed, and it doesn't drag you through miles of copy pasted corridor-y locations like HL2 likes to do ;p Good ragdolls, great headshots, familiar Source visual style and physics - all that works in the game's favor. It gets good right from the early game, when you get your first pistol and find out it isn't some weak last-resort junk, but absolutely lethal gun that lets you go on serious power trips, scoring whole series of headshots while firing from the hip. Then you get the shotgun and SMG with grenade launcher - only 3 weapons may be a bit disappointing, but all 3 are powerful, and have useful alt-fire modes :) Most of the time you fight masked mercs, dressed in yellow combat suits. Some of them have helmets that need to be shoot-off before they can taste your lead. Their AI isn't very sophisticated, but does the job. Hey - sometimes they can even kick some random barrel in your direction, and that's already above my expectations for a simple shooter :) Later on, you will also face mercs with jetpacks, fortunately they aren't very annoying or bulletspongy, and they even have dedicated death animation sequences when you break their jetpacks - very nice :) The game also throws some mutants at you. Bigger mutants rush at you trying to hurt you up-close, while smaller ones jump around throwing projectiles. Nothing too deep, but their pathfinding works pretty well, and before you get bored of them game reasonably switches back to shooting yellow mercs. Few times I saw some mercs vs mutants in-fighting, which is absolutely a positive surprise :) There is even one boss. Big mutated gorilla, with few attack patterns, can even destroy some environment assets :D You have to fight him twice XD I guess that's one of the necessary budget cuts, but if they really had to do it, to pump more cash into character models - fair enough :) From the moment I saw Elexis Sinclaire I understood it all. The game has only 3 weapons, bc it's very hard to make them with one hand! Game cuts corners with level design and sends you through the same locations twice - back and forth, bc the team was so laser-focused on making her 3D model, there was barely any time or budget for anything else! But what a nice model it is :D For sure more famous than the game itself. Your ally, Jessica, while also well rounded, doesn't have any cutscenes in the water, and I think it's the saddest thing about this whole game. There is also a story, game starts a few threads, but doesn't elaborate on any of them, I guess they planned to do the pay-off in later episodes, but they finally never came out. Overall, it's nothing groundbreaking, but it has enough going for it to keep you interested for 3 hours :)

[h1]SiN Episodes: Emergence[/h1] Meh, I do not know how to review this game… A few years after the release of the original [i]SiN[/i] and its addon [i]Wages of Sin[/i], [i]Ritual Entertainment[/i] decided to continue the franchise by making a series of nine episodic games called [i]SiN Episodes[/i]. The first episode - [i]Emergence[/i] - was supposed to gather money for the development of the second one or find a publisher to fund the project. Nonetheless, despite pretty high sales for a 3-hour-long game, less than a year since the release of [i]Emergence[/i], [i]Ritual Entertainment[/i] was fully bought by a publisher of casual games that immediately cancelled [i]SiN: Episodes[/i] and all potential [i]SiN[/i] sequels and sent the developers to work on casual for-all-ages family-friendly games. With the death of [i]Ritual Entertainment[/i], the [i]SiN[/i] franchise was dead too. So, basically, here we only have the first episode - a chunk of what was planned to be a long 30-40-hour game consisting of nine episodes. If you came to this page accidently, there is absolutely no reason to buy [i]SiN Episodes: Emergence[/i] now. Go look for other [i]Source[/i] games or just play the original [i]SiN[/i] and its expansion pack. However, if you are a SiN fan, who came here to read some reviews… Well, let's imagine that [i]Emergence[/i] has just been released and we do not know about the fate of [i]SiN Episodes[/i], and try to rate this game via this [i]thought experiment[/i]… [b]Story[/b]. Unfortunately, the game barely expands the story and explains what happened after [i]Wages of Sin[/i]. Why Elexis is alive? Why SinTEK is still operating? What Blade was doing all these years? Who's Radek and why he hasn't met Mancini's fate yet? None of these questions will be answered in [i]Emergence[/i]. Of course, there will be more episodes in the future but it is still a pretty weak start for a game… [b]Music and Sounds[/b]. Music was one of the strongest points of the original [i]SiN[/i] and created the atmosphere, yet here… It is almost absent except for the combat sequences and does not stay in your memory at all. Moreover, the biggest crime the developers committed is turning John R. Blade into Gordon Freeman №2! In the original, the witty dialogues between Blade and JC made a good deal of fun in the game but now all of this is entirely absent. As for the sounds and sound effects - they are fine. Guns sound like guns, explosions sound like explosions, etc. [b]Gameplay[/b]. Another failure too. Emergence has nothing for what [i]SiN[/i] fans fell in love with the franchise. The complex armor system went to a dumpster and now we just have a default health bar. There are objectives system, no alternative routes, no actions that affect the playthrough. The levels are linear as a stick with the exception for a few secrets. Of course, it is just the first episode but what was the problem of adding at least some basic alternatives. Like, if you save a character at the start of the episode, they assist you at the end? Or if you blow up some pipes on the current level, an area will be flooded on the next one which will make it easier or harder to complete? It was not difficult to implement but it would show what makes the [i]SiN[/i] franchise unique. As for the shooting itself, there are only 3 guns, each with an alt-fire mode, plus grenades. Even though the game is just 2-4 hours long depending on the difficulty and how meticulously you will look for secrets, it still feels lacking. The alt fire modes, as well as the HUD, are far from intuitive, and for the first half of the game I did not use them at all along with the grenades, the latter one because I simply thought I haven't unlocked them yet. There are only 5 types of enemies: regular soldiers, heavy chaingun soldiers, flying regular soliders, turrets and drones + mutants that are only present on one mission. Again, even though the game is just 2-4 hours long, it still feels lacking. As for the shooting and impact… it's weird… Like, the guns behave and sound like guns, enemies react to shots and even try to act tactically but… you still don't enjoy the shooting process. Last but not least, there is also an arena mode with 7 maps where you need to survive as long as you can and… I really don't understand why this was made. You have a limited budget but instead of spending it on developing and adding another weapon or an enemy type you waste it on a survival mode that barely anybody will play for more than an hour? For what? [i]End of the thought experiment[/i]. Well, even though I am still very disappointed that the [i]SiN[/i] franchise died like that, I kinda understand why [i]Emergence[/i] never managed to sell high enough to keep [i]Ritual Entertainment[/i] afloat. It has nothing in common with the original game and what made it unique and memorable. Honestly, it just feels like a fan made [i]Half-Life 2 SiN[/i] mod rather than an official game in the series. Maybe all of the aforementioned problems would be fixed in the subsequent episodes and the absent mechanics added but as the first episode, [i]Emergence[/i] is a mediocre game by itself and a bad game in the [i]SiN[/i] series. Not that it matters now anyway… P.S. If you still desire to play [i]SiN Episodes: Emergence[/i] yourself, I wrote an [url=https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3488778516]all-secrets-guide[/url] for it, so I would really appreciate if you check it out too. [h1]SiN: The Movie[/h1] As a bonus, I will also leave my thoughts on [i]SiN: The Movie[/i] here. Initially, it was supposed to come out along with the original game to fuel the hype, however, due to the troubled production, it was only released in 2000. The movie is weird… It is neither a sequel, nor a prequel, nor a spin-off, it is just a reworked story of the original game set in a more cyberpunk-ish universe with more characters and more detailed backstories. While the animation is pretty good and there is a good amount of blood and gore, the movie is just 60 minutes long, so it just becomes a kaleidoscope of rapidly changing scenes. I doubt that those who have not played the original game will be able to grasp the plot. As for the story changes, they are very questionable (spoilers ahead): [spoiler]JC is killed in the first 5 minutes, Blade is either totally unemotional or hyper hysterical, he also now has some shady backstory being a part of the mafia and having some Elexis's mutagen in his body as the result of augmentation[/spoiler]. And let me remind you that all of this is stuffed into one hour of footage. Maybe if the movie was at least an hour and a half long or better split into a TV series of 8 episodes, 20 min each, there would be time to unravel the characters and these ideas could work but as a 60-minute-long film, they don't. Is [i]SiN: The Movie[/i] terrible? No, but it is also very far from good. If you are a [i]SiN[/i] fan, you can give it a try but don't expect too much.

SiN: Gold is an ambitious remaster of a late 1990s shooter that captures the essence of an experimental era in first-person gaming. Developed originally by Ritual Entertainment and later enhanced and reissued by Nightdive Studios, this version stands as both a preservation and a modernization effort. It restores the original SiN along with its expansion, Wages of SiN, while introducing important technical upgrades that make it accessible to contemporary audiences. Nightdive Studios, known for its careful approach to reviving classics, ensures that this version maintains the fast-paced gunplay and gritty cyberpunk tone of the original while addressing compatibility and stability issues that have long plagued older PC titles. The result is a product that feels both nostalgic and newly alive, keeping the chaotic charm and daring design of the 1998 release intact. At its core, SiN: Gold delivers the familiar mechanics of a classic shooter but with a flair that set it apart in its time. Built on the Quake II engine, the game showcases impressive interactivity for its era, offering multiple paths through missions, destructible objects, and an arsenal that feels powerful and responsive. One of its most interesting mechanics is the ability to disarm enemies by shooting weapons out of their hands, an uncommon feature among its contemporaries that adds tactical depth. The levels mix urban warfare, industrial complexes, and high-tech laboratories in a way that emphasizes exploration and problem-solving rather than simple linear progression. The game's pacing, however, occasionally suffers from inconsistency. Some missions stretch too long, with maze-like layouts that can frustrate players unaccustomed to the less guided design sensibilities of the 1990s. Yet, beneath these rough edges lies an undeniable charm-the sense that the developers were attempting to create something bigger, smarter, and more ambitious than the straightforward shooters that dominated the time. Visually, SiN's aesthetic has aged into something of a stylized relic. The blocky character models and stiff animations are unmistakably products of their era, but the world itself-bathed in neon glow and corporate grime-retains a distinct cyberpunk identity. Nightdive Studios' restoration work helps elevate the presentation, enabling widescreen resolutions, stable frame rates, and cleaned-up textures while preserving the game's visual personality. The moody lighting and destructible environments lend the world a tactile quality that still resonates, particularly in comparison to some sterile modern designs. Despite these improvements, SiN: Gold cannot fully mask its age; its geometry is simple, its animations jerky, and some environmental details lack cohesion. But in this case, the roughness is part of its authenticity-it's a time capsule that captures what "cutting edge" looked like in 1998, now rendered playable without the headaches of retro hardware tinkering. From a narrative standpoint, SiN embraces pulp excess with unapologetic gusto. The story follows John Blade, a gruff law enforcer battling against Elexis Sinclaire, a scientist and corporate mogul bent on reshaping humanity through genetic manipulation. The plot is filled with conspiracies, bioengineered monsters, and a tone that oscillates between noir grit and comic-book camp. Voice acting is exaggerated, dialogue borders on absurd, and the humor often feels unintentional-yet these qualities give the game a distinct personality. It's a self-serious story that never quite realizes how over-the-top it is, and that paradox makes it fun. The blend of corporate satire, grotesque science, and one-liners evokes a mixture of Robocop and Saturday-morning cartoons filtered through a violent late-90s lens. While the writing can be clumsy, its unfiltered enthusiasm feels refreshing in an era when shooters are often polished to a fault. Nightdive's enhancements go beyond cosmetics. Under the hood, the re-release corrects numerous technical problems: crashes tied to cinematic sequences, broken networking protocols, and outdated memory management routines have all been replaced or optimized. Multiplayer support now works through modern systems, though the community is niche. The inclusion of the Wages of SiN expansion extends the experience significantly, adding more missions and weapons while polishing the gunplay. The re-release also benefits from improved performance on modern operating systems, with players reporting far fewer crashes or input issues than older digital editions. Still, minor quirks persist-mouse acceleration inconsistencies, sensitivity problems, and occasional rendering bugs remind players that this is, at its heart, a twenty-seven-year-old engine dressed in new code. As a game experience, SiN: Gold holds an awkward but admirable position. It is not as elegant as Half-Life nor as tight as Quake II, but it offers a broader sense of freedom and interactivity that feels ahead of its time. Levels can branch in subtle ways, choices sometimes affect mission order, and the world's reactive elements encourage replay. Yet this ambition occasionally overwhelms the pacing; not all mechanics feel refined, and some systems, such as the enemy AI, fluctuate between clever and broken. The gunplay remains the highlight-visceral, weighty, and loud, with each weapon offering satisfying impact. The arsenal ranges from traditional ballistic weapons to high-tech explosives and energy arms, each suiting different styles of engagement. Even when repetition sets in, the combat loop maintains a gritty satisfaction. For modern players, SiN: Gold functions as both a historical artifact and a genuinely enjoyable shooter. It demonstrates how developers in the late 1990s were beginning to experiment with player agency and narrative branching before the genre's consolidation under cinematic realism. The Nightdive restoration succeeds not because it transforms the game into something modern, but because it allows it to exist on today's hardware without compromise. SiN's imperfections-its dated visuals, clunky dialogue, and uneven design-are also its identity. They remind players of a time when games took bold risks and often stumbled, but did so with creativity and conviction. For veterans of the era, this reissue is a nostalgic revival. For newcomers, it's a chance to experience a piece of shooter history that helped bridge the gap between the raw chaos of Doom and the narrative ambition of Half-Life. In every sense, SiN: Gold stands as a restored fragment of gaming's rebellious adolescence-rough, flawed, but unmistakably alive. Rating: 7/10

Sin Gold is a masterpiece of a game... as long as you are willing to download and install a quick fix. The game does not properly support high resolutions, menus and text are not scaled, which can be fixed by installing the game's source port Dominatrix, made by Rohit. https://github.com/rohit-n/dominatrix/releases/tag/v1.2 It's pretty easy to install, link is attached. You choose the version apt for operating system you have (mingw is for Windows), download it, unpack it and move the files to your game directory, overwriting any that are needed. Lastly, you delete the game's executable and rename the dominatrix.exe file to sin.exe in order to have steam boot-up the port by default. Onto the game itself, I'm in love with it. It's pretty close to Deus Ex, being almost an immersive sim at times. It has got two charming characters, side quests, a great selection of weapons. And it comes packaged with its expansion pack Wages of Sin that serves as an excellent expansion! The shooting is a bit rough however, the guns don't feel sufficiently impactful at times and the lack of a weapon wheel or properly ordered weapons means it can be a hassle to switch them, however Dominatrix provides you with a weapon wheel that simplifies the process. You do have to bind it yourself if you're on PC, by opening the console and typing "bind KEY +radial_weapons" without the quatation marks and replacing "KEY" with the key you want it to be bound to. On the bright side, the game offers you all of the armor, health and ammo pickups you could need to get through its levels and the overall difficulty is more than enjoyable. More importantly, there isn't much weapon fall-off, the first weapons you get, the SMG and Pistol remain relevant even into the final levels (barring, of course, using them against the mini-boss enemies). Sin Gold features numerous secrets and bonus objectives, which is a very cool design choice. These require you to focus more on the environment and complement the narrative. These can give you boosts, change aspects of upcoming missions or just give you a reason to pay more attention while playing. On a similar topic, the game does a good balance with its hand-holding, you do get a tab with your objectives listed and characters explain where you need to go but the dialogue is not repeated. It will inform you of changes and new goals if needed. The level design is solid. That said, there are multiple sections that are too dark, to the point where even on max brightness you cannot see where you are going and there is next to nothing you can do about it. The voice acting itself is very good. The underwater sections, of which the game has several, can be rather maze-like but they serve as a neat break from the usual format I suppose. The main game does fall-off near its ending in my opinion. The last 5 levels are significantly shorter and more straight-forward with little dialogue. The final level is just a boss fight whose design is ring-around-the-rosie against a behemoth with a massive amount of HP, culminating in a few seconds of wondering if the mission bugged out before a fade to grey and a cutscene that doesn't work that well on modern hardware (visual lag). It's a little sad because most of the game is a real gem. The "Femme Fatale", overly sexualized antagonist is... very hit or miss. It feels like a case of the Authors-Not-At-All-Disguised-Fetish. On the technical side of things, I've suffered no crashes, FPS drops or anything else of the sort while playing, which is a very big plus. However, it's worth noting the game doesn't have sufficient auto-saving and doesn't seem to have Cloud Saves either, so make sure you save frequently. As for Wages of Sin, it's made by 2015 and has the expected standard of quality. It's smoother, introduces new mechanics, fixes faults of the original and is generally of a more consistent quality. Though keep in mind it's an expansion, not a full-game. The two provide good, complementary takes on Sin's gameplay I'd say. Except for the boss fights. Wages of Sin's Bullet Sponge Bosses are not fun. Overall, it's very competently made and has aged pretty well. I wholeheartedly recommend it. 9/10

At its frequent discount prices, it's definitely worth picking up. Just go in expecting a product of its time, not a modern shooter. Valve was probably CIA-funded to overshadow it.

[i]Honestly, I do not know how to write this review… I've spent so much time and effort on SiN that I just want to be finished with this game and forget about it even despite my deep appreciation. So, I think… I will just tell you how it started…[/i] Recently I've been playing a lot of boomer shooters and, after taking a little break for some indie games, I suddenly remembered about [i]SiN[/i]. I actually heard about this game a long time ago but because there was so little info on it on the internet, I always postponed playing it. Now, I've decided the time has come. I started [i]SiN[/i] without much expectations, thinking it would be a mediocre late 90's FPS but with some story added… and fell straight down into a deep rabbit hole I couldn't expect… [b]Story[/b]. I wish there was more of it, honestly. I know it was written in a comical way with jokes, oversexualized villainess, and a badass protagonist saving the world but considering the complexity of the game (we will talk about it later), it feels really underdeveloped. Moreover, back in the day when [i]SiN[/i] still tried to rival with [i]Half-Life[/i], the developers and publishers themselves emphasized who important the story would be. The game really gives off [i]Deus Ex[/i]-ish immersive sim kind of vibes and I just wish there was more to explore and learn in terms of the story. [b]Music and Atmosphere[/b]. Pretty solid. The game starts as a regular "badass-cop" movie with a bank heist, but the farther you go and the more info you get - the deeper the rabbit hole goes. You begin to visit more unique locations and meet more unusual enemies. The music is mostly a mix of techno and ambient. While this is not very original and many shooters utilized that style of soundtrack back in the day, it is still made pretty well. Moreover, almost every level has its own track which gives it its own unique vibe. I almost never care about the soundtracks of the FPS games I've played but [i]SiN[/i]'s music is something I've been relistening from time to time for the past few weeks, and it definitely goes to my personal collection of appreciated atmospheric scores. [b]Gameplay[/b]. Shooting - pretty good; complexity - amazing. The game has a good variety of weapons: some of them are more classical like assault rifle and rocket launcher, some are more interesting like spider mines or quantum destabilizer. The enemy diversity is pretty solid too: from regular soldiers with pistols and rifles to augmented melee or rocket launcher mutants. Even though by the last quarter the game almost stops presenting new types of foes, the story still makes you keep going until the end. The shooting itself feels quite solid: guns have their own impacts and the enemies react to the shots. They even seem to try to act tactically by retreating or going around you, yet, unfortunately, AI is far from perfect and often they just get stuck or run around not attacking you trying to pathfind the retreating route. My main complaint, though, is that the max difficulty - HardCorps - is quite unbalanced. Enemies take many more shots to die, while you receive much higher damage, yet the quantity of ammo, health and armor on the level remains the same. In the end, the situations when you are with no armor, 20 health, only pistol ammo, and there are rocket and chaingun soldiers waiting for you behind the door are not rare on that difficulty. Nonetheless, the real deal and charm of [i]SiN[/i] is its complexity. Some levels have two starting points depending on how you finish the previous one; some missions have two exits to two different missions - and these are not just secret levels to complete and return but full-fledged separate routes to continue the story; failing some of the primary objectives does not cause instant "game over" but instead gives access to new areas and changes the story; actions done on one mission can affect the layout of another one much later in the game; the levels are also very coherent and you can frequently see a glimpse of a part of the next levels from the current one. Overall, I will just give you one example: you can collect coins on missions 3-5, use them to buy a candy bar on mission 6, and that candy bar will become extremely useful on mission 18. The biggest problem of all this complexity, however, is that all those alternative routes and secrets are really obscure and unobvious, and most players will simply play the game one time as a mediocre shooter, and will never see even half of the content it can actually provide. [b][i]Wages of Sin[/i][/b]. This is the only expansion that [i]SiN [/i]received about 3 months after its original release. It continues the story with 16 new missions, adds new interesting weapons and items, and retains the depth of the original game. Even though it's pretty solid and if you liked the original [i]SiN[/i], you also definitely should play the addon, the main problem remains the same. The complexity is again very obscure and unobvious and most players will never know that there is an alternative story route which changes the order of missions, their objectives and conditions. Conclusion. So, after all of my praising in this review, you may want to ask a question: is [i]SiN[/i] a masterpiece? Actually, no. The game does have its weak points and I totally understand why it's lost in competition with [i]Half-Life[/i] in the end. Yet, is [i]SiN[/i] an unfairly forgotten gem? Definitely, yes! I am simply amazed how much details and features the developers put into the game, and it really hurts me that there is so little information about it online and that many players will simply play it once as a mediocre shooter of the 90s. Who would I recommend [i]SiN[/i] to? If you like classic FPS, like to explore games yourself and dive deep into them - [i]SiN[/i] is definitely for you. If you want a nice shooter with an okay story for a few evenings - you may appreciate [i]SiN[/i] too. However, if you want a deep story-based game which will directly explain you what choices you have and how they will result - then [i]SiN[/i] is likely not for you. If after my long review you decided to give [i]SiN[/i] a try, I highly recommend playing on the [url=https://rohit.itch.io/dominatrix][i]Dominatrix [/i]source port[/url], as it properly scales the HUD for modern resolutions, adds a few extra options in the settings, and allows you to rebind all buttons via the config file. I've also wrote two guides on all secrets, objectives and bonus mission for both [url=https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3464637763][i]SiN[/i][/url] and [url=https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3475752422][i]Wages of Sin[/i][/url], so I will highly appreciate if you check them out too. I really hope that you, if not love, at least appreciate the complexity and the depth of this game!

Darwinia, developed and published by Introversion Software, stands as one of the most creative and distinct independent games ever made. It merges the structure of a real-time strategy game with elements of action, puzzle solving, and digital simulation, wrapped in a visual style that feels like a living homage to the early days of computing. The story unfolds within a massive virtual theme park known as Darwinia-a digital world created to simulate the evolution of artificial life. When a viral infection spreads through this artificial ecosystem, the player is tasked with helping the Darwinians, tiny pixelated inhabitants of the world, fight for survival and rebuild their fragile society. What makes the experience special is how it blends nostalgic computer aesthetics with an emotional sense of discovery and preservation, turning what could have been an abstract idea into something surprisingly moving. The world of Darwinia is striking from the very first moment. Everything is presented in a stylized, low-poly visual design reminiscent of classic vector graphics, but with a vibrant color palette and dynamic lighting that breathe energy into its simplicity. Each area feels like a digital diorama, filled with geometric landscapes, abstract structures, and glowing lines that represent circuits and code. Despite the minimalist presentation, the world feels alive and beautiful, constantly humming with movement and light. The visual style isn't just for show-it reinforces the concept of entering a simulated environment, a computer world that feels both familiar and alien. It's a rare case where the art direction defines the tone so completely that it becomes inseparable from the game's identity. Combined with a subtle, ambient soundtrack that hums like a machine at work, the atmosphere is hypnotic and strangely serene even amid chaos. Gameplay in Darwinia is an intricate blend of strategy and direct control. Players interact with the environment by deploying "programs" such as squads, engineers, and officers-each represented by simple but functional polygons. Squads serve as your combat units, clearing out viral infections and defending the Darwinians. Engineers recover digital souls from fallen creatures and repair key infrastructure, while officers help organize the movement of the population. The game cleverly balances high-level management with hands-on control, allowing you to switch between overseeing the battlefield and directly steering units in real-time combat. This hybrid system gives the game a unique rhythm: one moment you're managing population logistics and production, and the next you're personally fighting off a swarm of enemies with laser fire. It captures the thrill of action while retaining the cerebral satisfaction of strategy. As the campaign progresses, the depth of Darwinia's design becomes apparent. Each level introduces new challenges-whether it's reclaiming infected territory, guiding survivors across dangerous terrain, or reconstructing the virtual world's systems. There's a gentle learning curve that rewards experimentation and persistence, and every victory feels earned. The sense of progress doesn't come from unlocking flashy upgrades but from watching the digital world come back to life. The more you save the Darwinians and rebuild their environment, the more vibrant and self-sustaining the world becomes. This creates a powerful emotional loop where your actions have tangible, visible results. Despite the abstract visuals, the game manages to evoke genuine empathy for its tiny inhabitants, making their survival feel meaningful. The story of Darwinia is minimalist yet profound. It doesn't rely on cutscenes or heavy exposition, instead using environmental storytelling and the natural evolution of gameplay to communicate its ideas. The premise-that you are helping a creator restore a broken digital ecosystem-is simple but layered with thematic resonance. It explores ideas about artificial intelligence, creation, digital decay, and the ethics of intervention in a simulated world. The Darwinians, though made of polygons and simple animations, become symbols of resilience and adaptation. The narrative's subtlety invites interpretation, and players often find themselves reflecting on the nature of life and technology as they guide these artificial beings toward a new future. Darwinia's one notable limitation lies in its brevity and learning curve. The campaign is relatively short, and while its pacing feels tight, some players may wish it lasted longer or offered more complex scenarios. The gesture-based interface for summoning units can also feel cumbersome at first, though it becomes second nature with practice. Yet these imperfections are part of what gives the game its charm-it feels handcrafted and experimental, the product of vision rather than formula. Its concise length means it never overstays its welcome, and the sense of wonder remains intact from beginning to end. Even years after its release, Darwinia remains an exceptional achievement in independent game design. It's both a technical experiment and an artistic statement, proving that innovation doesn't require massive budgets or photorealistic graphics. Introversion Software succeeded in creating a world that feels alive, mysterious, and deeply personal-a digital space where strategy meets empathy. Its blend of retro aesthetics, clever mechanics, and emotional subtlety makes it a timeless experience that still feels original today. For players seeking something different, something that feels like a cross between an old-school computer dream and a modern meditation on creation, Darwinia is a journey worth taking-strange, beautiful, and unforgettable. Rating: 7/10

Darwinia is a nice little RTS which reminded me a lot of the movie TRON. It is not an overly long game, and you could probably beat it in around 10 hours, less if you try to get through as speedily as possible. The writing is decent. The gameplay is decent. The soundtrack is okay. It should be noted that the game is single-player only, unlike most well-known RTS games. You can tell that a lot of care went into this game. It runs well, did not have any noticeable bugs, and also includes some nice extras like a map editor. I really appreciated the work that went into the game's startup screens, which are all very nice and fun to watch. Some of them even reveal background information about the game's story. The number of different startup screens really surprised me. I finished the game over many sessions, and I had already finished just over half the game before I saw a startup screen repeated. It is certainly unusual to see so much effort put into something that most people would probably consider an extremely minor part of a game these days. I have no more to say on the graphics, writing, soundtrack, etc. They are nothing too remarkable, but they are all decent. The gameplay is where my main concern is. Darwinia's gameplay is, honestly, pretty slow-paced. There were a lot of times when I was waiting for my units to get from one place to another. This issue is exacerbated by the fact that this game has the lowest unit cap I have ever seen in an RTS, three units! This is upgradable to five. That's it. Sure, the Darwinians don't count towards that cap, but they are not very useful except for manning fortifications and objectives, which they are required for. The upshot is that building units other than Darwinians is instant and takes no resources, so if you lose a unit you can instantly reconstitute it at the nearest spawn point. Another complaint I have is that the tutorial does not seem complete. Sure, you get walked through a few things, but some very important basic mechanics are omitted from the tutorial. In particular, the transmission dishes which serve as bridges between parts of levels were not explained to me by the game, and I ended up only finding out about them when they were mentioned by another player. This is a central mechanic that exists on every map and is essential for the later missions! I am not sure why something so critical is not in the tutorial, especially considering that there is such a bridge in the tutorial level, though using it is not required to finish that level or the other early levels. This would not be quite so bad were it not for the fact that this mechanic is non-obvious, as the transmission dishes appear to be part of the level as opposed to something you can control. There are some other, less critical omissions as well, like how to switch a squad's weapons. The game does have a well-executed Linux port, which I very much appreciate. The game runs natively on Linux, and it runs well. It is refreshing to see a native Linux port which works just fine and has no issues that I noticed. If you like single-player RTS and computer-themed stuff, this is a good pick.
