Uplink, developed and published by Introversion Software, is one of the most distinctive simulation games ever made, offering players an immersive experience in the world of cyber espionage and digital intrusion. Originally released in 2001 and later brought to Steam, it places you in the role of a freelance hacker, an anonymous agent for hire who takes on covert assignments from corporations, governments, and secret organizations. Instead of flashy action or cinematic sequences, the game unfolds entirely through a minimalist computer interface, creating the illusion that you're operating inside a clandestine digital world. It's a concept that feels remarkably ahead of its time, blending role-playing elements, economic management, and puzzle-solving into a unique hacking simulator that still resonates with players today. At the start of the game, you sign a contract with the mysterious Uplink Corporation, which provides you with access to a "gateway" computer. From this base of operations, you begin performing low-level jobs: breaking into public servers, deleting records, and stealing simple files for small amounts of money. Each successful job earns credits that can be spent on upgrading your system-faster processors, better modems, additional memory, or advanced hacking tools. These upgrades are crucial, as each mission increases in difficulty and complexity. Before long, you'll find yourself infiltrating corporate networks protected by proxy servers, firewalls, and security traces, forcing you to juggle multiple tools while racing against time to avoid detection. The game's tension lies in that constant countdown: the flashing "Trace In Progress" warning, the slow climb of the trace percentage, and the desperate scramble to cover your digital footprints before you're caught. Few games have ever captured the thrill of high-stakes hacking as effectively or as convincingly. Uplink's minimalist interface is a masterstroke of design. The entire experience takes place through a simulated operating system-a dark blue desktop filled with pop-up windows, status monitors, and email clients. You don't control a character; instead, you control a system, and it's the player's intellect, rather than reflexes, that drives progress. The aesthetic feels simultaneously sterile and atmospheric, with its abstract sound effects, low-key electronic soundtrack, and the steady hum of data streams underscoring every move. The sparse presentation encourages imagination, letting you fill in the blanks of the world beyond the screen. When you see a connection chain trace back through multiple servers or hear the subtle ping of a firewall being bypassed, it feels like you're part of a larger, shadowy network where every keystroke carries weight. This immersion is something modern games often struggle to achieve even with far more complex visuals, yet Uplink accomplishes it through restraint and suggestion. What makes Uplink stand out, even decades after its release, is its commitment to player freedom and emergent storytelling. Though there is a central plot involving two rival corporations-Arunmor and ARC-fighting over the fate of the internet via powerful viruses called Faith and Revelation, the game allows players to decide whether to get involved or simply pursue their own career. You can remain a neutral contractor, align with one side, or even double-cross your employers for personal gain. The missions themselves range from simple data thefts to framing innocent users, altering academic records, or stealing classified research. Each task can be approached in different ways depending on your setup, and the game encourages experimentation. There's no scripted handholding; success comes from learning how each system works and from gradually developing the instincts of a professional hacker. It's a rare design philosophy that rewards curiosity and persistence rather than spoon-feeding solutions. The difficulty curve, however, can be steep. New players are likely to fail their first few missions, either by being traced or by forgetting to erase evidence on the servers they infiltrate. The game's refusal to hold your hand may seem harsh, but it's also part of what gives it authenticity. Every mistake carries consequences, and the sense of risk makes every victory feel meaningful. The higher-level missions, especially those involving corporate networks and LANs, can feel daunting at first, demanding multitasking and precision timing. Yet this challenge is exactly what keeps Uplink engaging. You're constantly balancing speed, planning, and resource management, and even after dozens of missions, the thrill of narrowly escaping a trace never loses its intensity. Beneath its austere interface lies a surprisingly rich simulation of hacker culture. Uplink presents a world where information is currency, corporations are untrustworthy, and morality is flexible. The game doesn't moralize your choices; it simply lets you act and then face the consequences. This gives it an emergent narrative quality-your story as a hacker is shaped by your actions rather than dictated by cutscenes. You might spend an entire playthrough building a legitimate reputation as a reliable contractor, or you might turn rogue, spreading chaos for your own amusement. Either way, the result feels personal. The slow accumulation of wealth, the satisfaction of upgrading your hardware, and the growing confidence in tackling high-risk jobs all contribute to a strong sense of progression rarely achieved through traditional storytelling. Uplink's longevity owes much to its design simplicity and moddable structure. Its interface may look dated by modern standards, but its mechanics remain remarkably intact. Fans have created mods, new skins, and expanded missions that keep the game alive long after its release. Even without modifications, it remains endlessly replayable thanks to procedural generation and open-ended goals. The combination of tension, freedom, and atmosphere ensures that each playthrough feels unique. It's a game that doesn't rely on graphics or spectacle but instead on imagination and immersion, allowing players to step into a world of clandestine operations where intellect is your greatest weapon. Two decades on, Uplink still feels like a blueprint for immersive simulation design. It doesn't try to simplify or glamorize hacking-it distills it into something abstract yet believable, where strategy and timing matter more than spectacle. Its flaws-repetitive mission types, occasional interface confusion, and a lack of accessibility features-are outweighed by its sense of identity and purpose. There's a hypnotic rhythm to the gameplay loop: accepting a contract, tracing connections, bypassing systems, cleaning logs, and vanishing without a trace. Each completed mission reinforces that feeling of being part of a secret world, invisible but powerful. Uplink remains one of the most iconic independent titles of its generation-a cult classic that captures the fantasy of the hacker archetype without resorting to clichés or exaggeration. Its blend of tension, atmosphere, and open-ended design still feels remarkably fresh, proving that immersion doesn't require realism so much as conviction. It's a quiet, cerebral experience that rewards patience and cleverness, a game that turns a simple interface into a window into an invisible digital war. For those willing to embrace its minimalist presentation and steep learning curve, Uplink offers one of the most authentic and satisfying cyberpunk experiences ever created-a simulation of solitude, intellect, and danger inside the infinite expanse of the virtual world. Rating: 8/10

A thriller, text-based game released in 2001. This game is one of the earliest hacker simulators that still holds up to this day, featuring a mix of casual point-and-click gameplay and analytical skills required to become an elite hacker. You play as [u] [Yourself][/u], a freelance anonymous hacker who decided to work in Uplink, a corporation that offers hacker services in the black market. Uplink provides you with a remote terminal, as well as internal services such as news, software/hardware market, and a job bulletin board. As a hacker, you are expected to breach into terminals around the world to perform these jobs and get money, and the game as a good variety of jobs to select for, based on your hacker rank: Copy/delete files, edit academic scores, delete criminal records, track monetary transactions, exposing other hackers, sending and executing sabotage programs, and more. The gameplay flow is simple: You set up interwoven remote connections across various terminals around the world map, and then you select your victim to hack. Once connected, you have to hack your way inside the terminal and perform the job you have assigned, triggering a connection trace to stop you. And finally, delete all traces of your doing and disconnect before getting caught. The real deal of the gameplay is that the entire game world has consistent rules. This means you can hack everything, even Uplink servers, if you are really good, and get away with it. But it also means that any dumb slip can end in your demise, and the consequences of your deeds are not apparent at first. For example: If you are a noob and delete all admin access logs and disconnect before getting caught, you are leaving behind a disconnection log, which is going to be used to track you down (why there is a disconnection log if no initial connection log is present? This must be a hacker who wiped all the log files!). You must be careful to leave consistent information to cover your tracks successfully. In extreme cases, you are also required to hack across various terminals in a short amount of time to avoid a game over, like when you are robbing a bank, so you have to cover the money transfer. You can also affect the outcome of various NPCs of the game, like leaking personal data of your fellow hackers to the public, which will result in their deaths if you check the Social Security network. This is what makes this game special; it's almost like a sandbox. Although I don't like the "[i]press X to start hacking![/i]" gameplay, and the "roguelike" mechanics (if you get caught, you have to start all over again), this attention to detail is what makes up for it. Surprisingly, the game also has a story mode, presented to you once you advance your hacker rank. One of Uplink hacker members died, and an email was sent to all Uplink agents, including you, requesting an investigation into a company called Arc. You can ignore this email and remain a freelance hacker forever, but if you want to go with it, you will find a hidden corporate war that could end the Internet as you know it, depending on your choices. The final bit of the story was really intense. The bad thing is that, since this game is really old, there are many problems regarding screen resolution and current-day keyboard shortcuts. For example, F12 will shut down the game, and any big resolution will break the placement of pretty much every element. You could add a mod called UplinkOS, which fixes these issues, but I like the old style the most.

DEFCON, developed and published by Introversion Software, is a distinctive real-time strategy game that places players in the chilling role of a commander overseeing global thermonuclear warfare. Released in 2006, it stands out for its minimalistic design and its powerful ability to evoke the tension and dread of Cold War-era nuclear brinkmanship. Unlike many strategy games that emphasize complex graphics or detailed unit management, DEFCON uses a simple, stylized interface with muted colors and clean lines, which paradoxically intensifies the cold, mechanical nature of nuclear conflict and highlights the devastating human cost beneath the strategic calculations. The gameplay centers around managing your country's military assets-including missile silos, submarines, air forces, and radar installations-and coordinating attacks against enemy territories while defending your own. The game is divided into distinct phases, each progressively ramping up the tension: early rounds focus on positioning your forces discreetly across the globe, mid-game revolves around launching strikes and defending against incoming attacks, and the final phases are about damage assessment and survival. The strategic depth comes from carefully balancing offense and defense, bluffing to mislead opponents, and timing your nuclear launches to maximize enemy casualties while attempting to preserve your own population. What truly sets DEFCON apart is its haunting atmosphere and the psychological intensity it fosters. The minimalist visuals, dominated by glowing outlines on a dark world map, create a feeling of detachment that mirrors the real-world abstraction of nuclear war: a cold calculation with catastrophic human consequences. The ambient soundtrack, with its sparse, ominous tones, further heightens this sense of dread and inevitability. The game's "death toll" counter, which continuously updates as cities and populations are destroyed, serves as a grim reminder that this is not just a tactical contest but a scenario of mass human tragedy. This moral undertone encourages players to reflect on the real horrors of nuclear conflict, beyond the game mechanics. DEFCON's multiplayer mode elevates the experience by introducing elements of diplomacy, betrayal, and alliance-building. Players must navigate a delicate balance of cooperation and self-interest, forging temporary partnerships to eliminate common threats before turning on each other in a desperate scramble for survival. The tension this creates is palpable, as trust can be broken at any moment, mirroring the fragile nature of Cold War alliances. This social layer adds a rich complexity to the game that rewards both strategic foresight and psychological savvy, making every match feel unique and emotionally charged. While DEFCON has been praised for its innovative design and thematic depth, it is not without its drawbacks. The game's deliberate pacing and lack of traditional action-oriented combat may feel slow or sparse to some players, particularly those used to faster-paced strategy or war games. The minimalistic graphics, while thematically fitting, might not appeal to players seeking visual spectacle. Additionally, the learning curve can be steep for newcomers unfamiliar with strategic planning in a global context, especially when playing against more experienced opponents. Overall, DEFCON is a thought-provoking and immersive strategy game that challenges players to engage with the chilling realities of nuclear war on both a tactical and emotional level. Its minimalist approach strips away distractions to focus on the essential horror of mass destruction, creating a uniquely somber and reflective experience. For those interested in strategy games that go beyond mere conquest to explore ethical dilemmas and the human cost of conflict, DEFCON remains a compelling and memorable title that continues to resonate years after its release. Rating: 8/10

Multiwinia, developed and published by Introversion Software, is a fast-paced, minimalist real-time strategy game that reimagines large-scale combat as a vibrant digital playground of chaos and color. Set within the same virtual universe as the studio's earlier cult hit Darwinia, it trades the introspective tone of its predecessor for a more competitive, arcade-like energy. The premise is simple but effective: the once peaceful digital inhabitants known as Darwinians have splintered into factions, now waging endless wars for dominance across surreal landscapes inside a computer simulation. The game abandons traditional base-building and resource management mechanics, instead focusing entirely on the movement, coordination, and survival of massive pixelated armies. This streamlined approach gives Multiwinia a distinct rhythm that feels both refreshingly immediate and deceptively strategic. Visually, Multiwinia carries Introversion's signature aesthetic-abstract, geometric environments and vast swarms of tiny, glowing stick figures moving in synchronized chaos. The landscapes resemble low-poly sculptures painted in bright, otherworldly hues, while explosions, laser fire, and particle effects create a constant sense of kinetic motion. Each battle resembles an abstract painting in motion, and though simple in appearance, the visual design perfectly complements the game's underlying theme of digital warfare. The interface is clean and minimalistic, allowing players to focus on the ebb and flow of their armies rather than micromanaging menus. This purity of design is one of Multiwinia's great strengths; it captures the essence of large-scale strategy without clutter or overcomplication, maintaining an aesthetic charm that remains recognizable even years after release. Gameplay is divided into several distinct modes, each emphasizing different aspects of control and tactical improvisation. These include Domination, King of the Hill, Assault, Rocket Riot, and Capture the Statue, among others. Each mode takes a familiar concept-holding territories, escorting objects, or launching rockets-and reimagines it within Multiwinia's swarm-based framework. Players command hundreds of tiny units, directing them to capture spawn points, secure objectives, and overwhelm enemy positions. The core appeal lies in managing chaos rather than constructing order; with limited tools, you must adapt on the fly as reinforcements arrive, terrain shifts, and unpredictable power-ups drop across the battlefield. Matches are typically short and intense, lasting around fifteen minutes, which makes the game highly replayable and ideal for quick sessions. Beneath the surface simplicity, there is a surprising amount of tactical nuance in positioning, timing, and reading the flow of battle. The multiplayer component represents the heart of the experience, offering both online and local play. Matches against human opponents showcase the game's brilliance-its unpredictable skirmishes, sudden reversals, and emergent moments of humor or desperation. Power-up crates can turn the tide in seconds, introducing temporary advantages like airstrikes, teleportation, or the ability to summon devastating weapons. These elements ensure that no two battles feel alike, yet they also inject an element of randomness that can occasionally frustrate players seeking pure strategy. Still, this unpredictability is part of Multiwinia's charm. It's not about perfect control but about thriving in disorder, adapting to shifting conditions, and embracing the absurdity of digital warfare. The artificial intelligence is competent enough to provide a challenge in single-player matches, but the game clearly shines brightest when humans clash over its colorful arenas. While Multiwinia's design philosophy emphasizes accessibility and instant action, it also limits the game's long-term depth. Without a traditional single-player campaign or progression system, the experience can feel transient once the novelty of its modes wears off. Players looking for a narrative-driven strategy game or complex economic systems will find little of that here. The structure is more akin to a competitive playground than a full-fledged grand strategy experience. Yet within this simplicity lies a purity of design that few games achieve-the mechanics are tight, the pacing brisk, and every match tells its own improvised story of triumph and annihilation. The game's brevity and unpredictability ensure that it never overstays its welcome, but they also mean that Multiwinia functions best as a short-burst experience rather than a long-term obsession. Technically, the game remains smooth and responsive even during massive battles involving hundreds of units, a testament to Introversion's careful optimization. The soundtrack enhances the digital atmosphere with electronic rhythms that pulse beneath the chaos, while the minimalist sound effects-crackling lasers, distant explosions, the rhythmic march of pixel soldiers-reinforce the sensation of being inside a simulated world. The presentation is cohesive in every respect, immersing players in a stylized digital war zone that feels both alien and oddly endearing. There is an unmistakable charm in watching countless tiny figures charge heroically into battle, only to dissolve into glowing fragments moments later, as if the game itself is celebrating the beauty of organized disorder. In the end, Multiwinia stands as an unusual but captivating entry in the real-time strategy genre. It distills the complexity of warfare into a kinetic, visually striking, and immediately playable experience that thrives on spontaneity. While it lacks the narrative and systemic depth of traditional RTS games, its speed, accessibility, and distinctive art direction give it a unique identity that few contemporaries share. For players who appreciate fast, chaotic strategy games that value creativity over control, Multiwinia delivers a satisfying blend of competition and spectacle. It may not satisfy those looking for intricate long-term strategy, but as a snapshot of Introversion Software's experimental spirit, it remains a memorable and refreshingly original title-one that celebrates both the simplicity of play and the unpredictability of digital life. Dangerous Waters is a demanding and uncompromising military simulation that remains one of the most detailed portrayals of modern naval combat ever released on PC. Developed by Sonalysts and published by Strategy First, the game was never designed to appeal to a broad audience. Instead, it targets players who crave realism, procedural depth, and a genuine understanding of how modern naval warfare actually functions. From the moment you step into your first mission, it is clear that Dangerous Waters prioritizes authenticity over accessibility, asking players to think like real-world naval officers rather than arcade pilots or action heroes. The gameplay revolves around commanding a wide range of naval platforms drawn from contemporary military arsenals, including nuclear-powered submarines, diesel-electric submarines, surface combatants, maritime patrol aircraft, and helicopters. Each platform can be controlled at multiple stations, allowing players to jump between sonar, navigation, fire control, radar, and command roles as needed. Rather than simplifying these systems, the game models them with remarkable fidelity, forcing players to interpret sonar contacts, manage sensor noise, plot intercept courses, and carefully plan weapon deployments. Combat is rarely immediate or flashy; instead, it unfolds slowly, often over long stretches of tense silence punctuated by moments of sudden, decisive action. Submarine warfare is where Dangerous Waters truly distinguishes itself. The game places enormous emphasis on acoustic stealth, positioning, and patience, making undersea combat feel like a high-stakes chess match played in near darkness. Players must constantly balance speed against noise, depth against detection risk, and aggression against survivability. Identifying a contact is rarely straightforward, as sonar returns can be ambiguous or misleading, demanding careful analysis and cross-referencing. This creates a level of psychological tension that few games manage to replicate, where victory often comes from outthinking the enemy rather than overpowering them. Surface and air warfare add further layers of complexity. Managing a surface ship requires attention to radar coverage, missile defense, and coordination with allied units, while aircraft operations introduce entirely different tactical considerations such as search patterns, fuel management, and sensor range. The game encourages players to think holistically, combining assets rather than relying on a single platform. Success often depends on information superiority - knowing where the enemy is before they know where you are - reinforcing the game's core theme that modern naval combat is as much about data and detection as it is about firepower. The structure of Dangerous Waters supports long-term engagement through campaigns, standalone missions, and a powerful mission editor. Campaigns place players within broader geopolitical conflicts, lending narrative context and strategic continuity to individual encounters. The mission editor, meanwhile, has played a major role in the game's longevity, enabling a dedicated community to create and share custom scenarios that expand the experience far beyond the original content. This community-driven ecosystem has helped keep the game relevant years after its release, especially among hardcore simulation enthusiasts. Presentation is utilitarian and reflects the game's age, but it serves its purpose effectively. Visuals focus on clarity rather than spectacle, with much of the action conveyed through tactical displays, sonar waterfalls, and radar screens rather than cinematic views. While the 3D graphics and interface feel dated by modern standards, they remain functional and readable. Sound design plays a critical role, particularly in submarine operations, where subtle audio cues can mean the difference between remaining hidden and being detected. The inclusion of voice command support further reinforces the simulation mindset, allowing players to interact with systems in a way that feels surprisingly immersive. The most significant barrier to entry is the game's learning curve. Dangerous Waters demands time, study, and patience, often requiring players to consult manuals or community resources to fully understand its systems. Tutorials are limited, and the game assumes a level of prior knowledge that can be intimidating for newcomers. However, for those willing to invest the effort, this complexity becomes one of its greatest strengths, offering a sense of mastery that few modern games attempt to deliver. Ultimately, Dangerous Waters stands as a benchmark for realism-driven naval simulations. It is not flashy, forgiving, or easy to approach, but it offers an unparalleled depth of tactical and procedural gameplay that continues to reward serious players. While casual gamers may find it overwhelming or outdated, those with an interest in military simulation, naval strategy, or submarine warfare will discover an experience that remains intellectually engaging and deeply satisfying even years after its original release. There's something deeply absorbing about diving into a turn-based 4X strategy game where the galaxy unfolds not in explosions, but in spreadsheets, diplomacy tables, and tech trees that go on for light-years. Space Empires IV Deluxe is a love letter to an era when complexity wasn't a bug-it was the feature. It's not a game for the faint of heart, but for those who enjoy managing empires with the finesse of a galactic accountant and the foresight of an admiral, it offers a unique blend of strategy that's rarely matched even today. What It Does Well The scope is nothing short of staggering. You don't just pick a race and expand-you design it from the DNA up. Want a species that breathes methane and lives on molten rock? Go for it. You can customize ships down to individual systems, creating fleets that reflect not only strategic choices but personal playstyle. The freedom is intoxicating. The tech tree is vast-so vast that your first dozen games will feel like tutorials. But once the rhythm kicks in, the discovery becomes part of the satisfaction. Finding obscure techs that shift your strategy or developing doomsday weapons that tip interstellar balance keeps each campaign fresh. Diplomacy, colonization, and warfare are all layered with complexity that rewards long-term planning over impulse decisions. Multiplayer, while a bit dated in terms of interface, adds a chess-like depth when played against equally obsessive opponents. Battles feel earned, not triggered by luck or rushed aggression. When you win in Space Empires IV Deluxe, it's because you out-thought the enemy-not just out-gunned them. Where It Stumbles Let's get it out of the way: the interface is brutally outdated. The UI feels like it was lifted from a DOS-era spreadsheet program, and navigating menus is often a lesson in patience. Even with the Deluxe version, which irons out a few bugs and adds quality-of-life tweaks, there's a persistent clunkiness that no patch has quite polished away. Graphics are purely functional, bordering on ugly by modern standards. If you need flash and flair to stay engaged, this won't hold your gaze for long. The tactical battles, while satisfying in theory, play out more like detailed math problems than cinematic spectacles. You have to squint hard to find the drama. AI, though serviceable, often behaves in ways that break immersion-sending ships into suicide runs or making bizarre trade offers that feel more like random number generation than intelligent negotiation. And while modding can extend the game's lifespan, setting it up can be an intimidating wall of text and folders. Verdict Space Empires IV Deluxe is an acquired taste-but one that can be deeply rewarding for those who enjoy methodical planning over flashy execution. It's not a game that welcomes newcomers with a warm hug; it's more like being dropped into the control room of a star empire with a stack of unread manuals. But for those willing to embrace its depth, the payoff is immense. It's a strategy sandbox that lets you write your own spacefaring saga in excruciating-but satisfying-detail. Pros: Immense customization of races and ships Vast, complex tech tree with meaningful progression Deep strategic layers across diplomacy, colonization, and warfare Hugely replayable with different strategies and setups Satisfying for long-term thinkers and micromanagers Cons: Outdated UI and clunky interface Poor graphics and minimal visual feedback AI inconsistencies in both combat and diplomacy Steep learning curve with little in-game guidance Tactical battles feel dry and overly abstract Final Score: 7.5 / 10 This is not a polished blockbuster, but a dense and rich strategy gem buried beneath an avalanche of text and data. For the right kind of player, it's a galaxy worth ruling. Disciples II: Rise of the Elves, developed and published by Strategy First, stands as both an expansion and a reintroduction to one of the most distinctive turn-based strategy titles of its era. While the base game already offered a dark, gothic-infused take on high fantasy, this edition expands the world of Nevendaar with the long-awaited Elven Alliance as a fully playable faction. Rise of the Elves bundles the original content together with a substantial new campaign and new scenarios, creating what is effectively a definitive version for anyone interested in exploring the series' moody, stylized universe. It marks a milestone not only because it adds new narrative layers, but because it enriches the strategic landscape with a faction that plays unlike any of the existing races. From the moment you start a campaign, the game's signature aesthetic takes hold. Disciples II has always been renowned for its haunting hand-drawn artwork, somber color palettes, and richly atmospheric world design. Rise of the Elves continues this direction, presenting forests twisted by ancient magic, ethereal landscapes, sacred groves, and grim wartime ruins that frame the Elven storyline. The new race feels at home in this artistic vision: their units evoke myth and mysticism rather than brute force, and their allegiance to nature gives them a thematic identity that contrasts meaningfully with the corruption of the Undead Hordes, the demonic ambition of the Legions of the Damned, the stoic Mountain Clans, and the holy human Empire. This shift in tone introduces welcome variety, especially for returning players familiar with the harsher aesthetics of the previous factions. Strategically, Rise of the Elves maintains the core mechanics that define Disciples II: small squad-based armies, tight unit progression paths, resource-driven territory control, and a world map where every move carries weight. What sets the Elven faction apart is their flexibility: their units branch into two philosophies - the Noble Elves, who favor discipline and traditional magical affinity, and the Wild Elves, who lean into primal ferocity. Each side offers its own upgrade trees and combat roles, allowing players to tailor strategies toward healing, summoning, ranged dominance, or aggressive frontline damage. This duality ensures the Elves do not merely feel like a reskin of existing factions but instead present new tactical rhythms and decision points. The campaign itself enriches the lore of Nevendaar with a story steeped in ancient grudges, betrayal, the burden of tradition, and the Elves' struggle to protect their forests from encroaching enemies. Like the other Disciples campaigns, it is written with a sense of mythic gravitas, framing battles not just as map objectives but as steps in a larger spiritual and political conflict. Missions often demand careful army preservation, deliberate movement, and long-term planning rather than reckless expansion. The game's pace, slow by modern standards, emphasizes the weight of each encounter. When a single unit falls, its loss is felt acutely, reinforcing that this is a strategy game built on hero-like squads rather than expendable armies. At the same time, the expansion inherits the limitations of the underlying system. While the strategic layer can be engaging, combat itself is relatively constrained. Each squad has a fixed formation, and battles unfold in a predictable turn-based exchange with limited tactical input beyond targeting and managing unit roles. The satisfaction comes from building a strong lineup and nurturing units along upgrade paths, but this can also make combat repetitive once your goals are clear. Spells, too, rarely reach the dramatic impact that one might expect from a world steeped in powerful magic. They offer utility and support but seldom transform battles the way more complex strategy systems allow. Exploration rewards, while present, are similarly modest. Venturing off the beaten path often yields small bonuses rather than game-changing artifacts or narrative revelations. This can make the world feel less dynamic than its beautiful artwork suggests, particularly for players accustomed to more interactive or richly rewarding exploration mechanics. Yet the subdued rewards do align with the series' philosophy: Disciples has always been a strategy game defined by long-term incremental growth, careful territory management, and slow but steady escalation rather than explosive breakthroughs. Despite these shortcomings, Rise of the Elves succeeds at broadening the game's scope and deepening its thematic resonance. The new faction adds longevity to the gameplay loop, offering fresh tactical possibilities and a campaign that stands apart from the base game's arcs. The expansion also reaffirms what makes Disciples II special: its atmosphere, its unique visual identity, and its blend of strategy and light RPG progression that rewards patience and planning. The sense of commanding a small but meaningful force - and watching it evolve throughout a campaign - remains compelling even decades after its release. For players who appreciate classic dark fantasy strategy games, where narrative weight, mood, and careful unit development matter more than complex battles or high-speed play, Disciples II: Rise of the Elves remains a rewarding experience. Its flaws are noticeable, yet its strengths - especially its art direction, faction diversity, and mythic storytelling - give it an enduring appeal. It's a game best approached slowly, with an appreciation for atmosphere and worldbuilding, and for players willing to embrace its deliberate pace, it offers a rich and distinct journey through the shadowed realms of Nevendaar. Rating: 8/10

It's 2003. My older brother and I are home after school, booting up our windows XP PC, blowing out dust on the Disciples 2 disk before running it and getting sucked into the sacred grimdark lands of Nevendaar. Disciples 2 was a foundational fantasy strategy game experience up there with titles like age of empires, warcraft and starcraft and we chocked up thousands of hours beating every campaign and scenario multiple times. The Mountain Clans faction in Disciples 2 was my first exposure to badass dwarfs and my ingress into dwarfceldom. If you think dwarfs in warhammer and DnD are based, wait till you check out how incredibly stocky and fearsome the children of Wotan are. The Mountain Clans are the thickest and most bearded dwarfs who fight alongside terrifying looking giants wielding massive weapons or wielding elements of magic to bring untold destruction to their foes. The central plotline about kingdoms on the brink of ruin and facing down rising tides of demons and undead is quintessential fantasy storytelling. The devs' passion for roleplaying manifests in many RP-flavored interactions. If you attack an abandoned brewery haunted by zombies, some of your dwarf warriors request that the party linger after the battle to quaff on some pristine and unspoiled barrels of ale. The only criticism from a gameplay standpoint is the somewhat limited roster of units available to each faction compared to modern titles. This shortcoming is shored by a decent range of customizable hero characters that you can deck out with artifacts, banners and boots. The game also features an interesting magic system in the overworld map. You can tap into the winds oof magic to buff units, debuff enemies and nuke them with a plethora of hex and sorcery in your spell arsenal. The sound design is top notch pure fantasy vibes with a chilling undercurrent of horror and devastation. Nevendaar is a realm past its golden years of prosperity. Horror and death await you at every corner, past every knoll and abandoned farmstead, a brutal land teeming with merciless beasts blocking the way. The sound design communicates this imagery very effectively. Years later, I find myself returning to this old timey classic and remembering how fun it was to play video games 20 years ago. With a lot of modern games, I find that there is some anxiety in trying to complete the game or getting through some difficult sections. Disciples 2 brings my adult self right back to my childhood days of carefree gaming and getting immersed in an amazing fantasy world of axe, sword and magic. The game runs smoothly with no crashes. The default hotkeys are super intuitive for a 2003 game and make replaying decades later a pleasant experience. If you like turn based strategy RPG titles set in fantasy, Disciples 2 is an unrivaled and timeless experience and there is nothing quite like it especially in today's gaming market.

Disciples II: Gallean's Return is a comprehensive re-release of the acclaimed turn-based strategy game Disciples II: Dark Prophecy, bundled with its two expansion packs, Guardians of the Light and Servants of the Dark. Developed by Strategy First, this title represents one of the most distinct entries in the strategy genre, combining deep tactical combat with strong RPG elements and a dark, atmospheric fantasy setting. First released in the early 2000s, Gallean's Return remains a compelling experience for players who enjoy deliberate pacing, persistent unit progression, and stylized art that still stands out today. At the heart of the game is a traditional hex-grid strategy formula with a twist. Players control one of four distinct factions-the Empire, the Mountain Clans, the Legions of the Damned, or the Undead Hordes-each with its own units, storyline, and combat philosophy. Rather than controlling massive armies, players lead small, focused squads consisting of a hero and a handful of units that level up over time. This design choice makes each decision in battle matter immensely, as the loss of an experienced unit can be devastating and often unrecoverable. Unlike many turn-based strategy games that emphasize quantity and large-scale encounters, Disciples II rewards long-term planning, precise unit development, and careful positioning. Each faction plays quite differently, not just in terms of unit design and aesthetics but also in how their tech trees, spells, and upgrade paths function. For example, the Empire is a balanced human faction with strong healing abilities and knights, while the Undead Hordes specialize in curses, debuffs, and resilient undead minions. The Mountain Clans focus on defense and earth-based magic, while the demonic Legions lean heavily into brute force and destruction. This asymmetry, coupled with detailed upgrade options, creates significant replay value and encourages players to explore the unique strengths of each race. The structure of the game unfolds through long-form campaigns and custom scenarios. Campaign missions are narrative-driven and often include scripted events, branching objectives, and story developments that immerse the player in a dark, brooding world full of political intrigue, fallen gods, and doomed civilizations. The writing, while sometimes overwrought, carries a distinct tone that fits the game's gothic art direction. The hand-drawn character portraits, ominous landscapes, and richly detailed unit animations contribute to a visual identity that remains iconic. Few strategy games of its era-or even today-look quite like Disciples II, with its blend of dark fantasy and painterly visual design. Combat, while turn-based, is more rigid than some might expect. Units do not move on a battlefield grid during combat-instead, they remain in their formation, and turn order, attack type, and spell use determine the flow of battle. This simplified approach emphasizes preparation over improvisation. Knowing when to level up a unit into a support healer or a frontline damage dealer can decide the outcome of later battles. There is a deliberate rhythm to the game: exploration, city upgrading, hero training, and calculated skirmishes slowly build toward eventual map domination. It can feel slower than more action-oriented strategy titles, but it rewards patience and a methodical approach. Another strength of Gallean's Return lies in its strategic layer. Players control territory by capturing cities and mana nodes, which fuel spellcasting and research. Defending these points becomes critical as enemy factions grow stronger over time. The balance between offense and defense is tense and often forces hard decisions. Spells play a major role in turning the tide of battle or fortifying a position. Everything in the game, from hero abilities to resource collection, contributes to a tightly woven system that demands long-term thinking and risk assessment. Mistakes early on can snowball, which makes each campaign feel weighty and consequential. Despite its many strengths, the game is not without flaws. The user interface feels clunky by modern standards, and the lack of quality-of-life features like auto-resolving battles or streamlined unit management can be frustrating. Pathfinding is occasionally awkward, and some campaign missions can feel overly punishing due to difficulty spikes or poorly telegraphed enemy movements. New players may also find the initial learning curve steep, as the game provides minimal hand-holding. However, these issues are often outweighed by the game's charm, depth, and satisfying sense of progression. Disciples II: Gallean's Return stands as a classic in the genre-one that successfully blends turn-based tactical gameplay with rich lore and atmospheric world-building. It's a game that values strategic foresight and unit loyalty over mindless conquest. For players willing to invest the time to master its systems, it offers a rewarding and memorable experience that holds up remarkably well despite its age. Its legacy as one of the most visually distinct and thoughtfully designed strategy titles of its era is well-earned, and for those seeking a dark, challenging, and narratively immersive tactical experience, Gallean's Return remains a gem worth revisiting. Rating: 8/10

It might be the nostalgia talking because I first played this when it was new, but there's a lot of little mechanics here that I don't see in newer games. Passing exp rewards to surviving party members rather than "You joined this fight with 4, so each unit gets 1/4 of the reward even though only 2 survived/stayed." Movement over different terrain varies, so noting if a nearby enemy is flying or whatever and if you're next to trees can really make a difference. The different factions work similarly enough to learn how to play with any of them, yet differ enough to easily have a preference. When advancing to another mission, you get to choose one leader and 5 items to take with you. Can be gear, potions, or treasure, so keeping something to sell for early gold on the next map is a valid tactic and you don't have to keep a warrior leader if you had more fun leveling up the mage. You could even leave them all behind if you feel like it. One of my favorite mechanics is transferring units between leaders. Use a scout to ensure that Dread Lord gets into the city to heal and replace it with a Fighter so you don't need to pay the huge revival cost and the party can keep going. There's so many little things I love regardless that it's a 20+ year old game.

Your imagination is the limit.

Creepy, hollow droning noises in the dungeons make you keep your weapon drawn; the ratmen made me jump more than once. Hitting the teleport back to the main area feels relieving, because that oppressive atmosphere gives way to hopeful, heavenly synthwork and sparse but lively NPC activity. Sure, some of it may seem outdated, janky or even unfinished compared to what we play today. But take a chance and see the game for what it is. Something so densely packed with nuanced, interlocking mechanics and gameplay (especially for a closed-loop game that's only about 40+ hours long) that a modern publisher would probably start sweating about "risk" and "market viability" lol Super-clean, crisp, adequate combat system. NPC dialogue is very charming and the AI still holds up in places. The inventory system is more sophisticated and sometimes requires more deliberation than Elder Scrolls games. The mix of free-look and stationary point-and-click is blissful.

Unfortunately, it's just a dull game. Its core mechanics work decently enough: - Combat is simple but functional. - Casting spells by drawing runes with the mouse, the game's distinctive feature, is gimmicky but not annoying. - Visually it's still pleasant. - With Arx Libertatis, I encountered no bugs or weird behavior. The issues I have with the game have more to do with its content: - The pace is extremely slow. The protagonist moves painfully slow, yet you have to walk around a lot. It's so exasperating that you still feel it even after getting fast travel and a speed-up spell. A sprint button outside of combat would have greatly helped. This is further aggravated by the next points. - Story progression is confusing. More often than not, you lack a clear direction and are left to wander around for a solution. This also caused me to do several things ahead of time. The game leaves you free to explore, but then behaves as if you had to do things in a specific order. It doesn't make much sense, as the game is not an open world and has only a handful of quests outside the main one. They should have streamlined the progression more. - Most levels are mazes, with corridors that all look the same. It seems like they took inspiration from old dungeon crawlers, but it doesn't work as well here. - Enemies are uninteresting and not challenging (you fight rats way too often). There is a single exception that instead represents a big difficulty spike and likely needs to be cheesed. - Quests are boring. Even when knowing what to do and where to go, there isn't much excitement. - Some puzzles, or tasks required to proceed, are excessively cryptic. Completing this game without a walkthrough is unlikely unless you enjoy being stuck for hours. Keys and levers don't make clear what they open or activate, you just have to try or look around for changes, adding to the confusion. - The premise of the lore, as narrated in the opening movie, had me hooked. Unfortunately, it all devolves into the most generic fantasy setting, where races fight one another while some powerful demon tries to conquer the world. The sun shutting down and the world becoming an ice wasteland, with only a dedicated guild of travellers moving between underground fortresses, was a cool premise. Unfortunately, it has zero weight on the events of the game. - The plot is just bad. It starts off with the "protagonist with amnesia" trope, forces events, then dives into lengthy expositions. Events and interactions feel disconnected, and we don't have much say in how they unfold. - All characters, including the hero, are bland. - The world feels fake. Arx is one of the most artificial, lifeless cities I've seen in gaming, and the rest of the world follows suit. - Inventory management is puzzling. A feature on which the game seems to have an identity crisis. The inventory is fairly limited, and there is a hunger mechanic. You would expect the player to make critical decisions about how much precious space to give up for food. Nope. The game always provides an insanely high amount of food, and hunger decreases at an incredibly slow rate, making the whole system pointless. Then the game undermines it further by doubling the inventory fairly early on. - The stat system is unbalanced. This is one of those games that shoot themselves in the foot by having stats distribution just for the sake of being more like an RPG. It causes the usual problems for player satisfaction, where depending on your build you will have to give up one of: opening appealing chests, wielding strong weapons, or casting interesting spells. Investing points into non-fighting skills is risky, as not being able to open a chest will never stop your story progression, but not being able to win fights will. I think this also contributes to enemies being pushovers. Beyond that, some skills simply aren't worth it (like stealth, which barely has a place in the game at all). The implementation also leaves a lot to be desired, as you have to reach a certain threshold (e.g., 14 Strength or 50 Object Knowledge) before seeing any tangible result, making every point before that feel wasteful. - Jumping is outright bad: it's laggy and gets stuck all the time. Fortunately, it's barely needed. - There is practically no music, just short ambient loops that get old fast. I didn't hate the game; it's playable, but I got really bored and would have rather played something else.

Arkane rarely misses and even their first game, Arx Fatalis turned out to be a pleasant surprise despite its rough edges. The gesture-based magic system is genuinely unique and fun once you get the hang of it (use the Arx Libertatis mod to make it more bearable on modern computers), making spellcasting feel more involved than your typical RPG. What really stands out is the atmosphere, spending the entire game in a labyrinthic world. The level design is solid, with each area feeling appropriately distinct. There is some jank, still, if you can look past the jank, it's absolutely worth experiencing for anyone interested in immersive sims or unconventional RPGs.

Arx Fatalis is a deeply atmospheric first-person RPG that remains one of Arkane Studios' most distinctive early accomplishments, a game that simultaneously pays homage to the legacy of immersive sims like Ultima Underworld while carving out its own identity. Released in 2002, it embraces a subterranean fantasy world where the sun has died and all surviving civilizations have retreated underground. This premise alone gives the game a uniquely oppressive tone: every corridor, tunnel, and cavern reflects a world forced into shadow, clinging to survival. You begin the journey as an amnesiac prisoner, thrust into a society of humans, goblins, trolls, snake-like nobles, and mysterious religious factions, all of whom exist in uneasy proximity under the threat of an ancient god's return. It is a setting drenched in tension, mystery, and a sense of inevitability, and Arx Fatalis uses that atmosphere to draw the player deeper into its labyrinthine plot. What defines Arx Fatalis more than anything is its commitment to immersive interactivity. Nearly every object in the environment-food, weapons, runes, ingredients, notes, torches-can be manipulated, combined, or used in meaningful ways. You can bake bread by mixing flour and water and placing the dough at a fire. You can lure enemies with noise, extinguish light sources to create darkness for stealth, and interact with NPCs in a range of quests that favor player agency over scripted sequences. This systemic approach builds a world that feels tactile and reactive, giving the player the impression that they're navigating a living underground ecosystem. Arkane Studios would later refine this design philosophy in games like Dishonored and Prey, but the seeds of that creative vision are unmistakably planted here. The magic system stands as Arx Fatalis's most innovative feature. Instead of selecting spells from a traditional menu, the game requires players to draw runes manually with their mouse to cast spells. This system turns spellcasting into a skill-based action rather than a passive choice and adds a tactile sensation to every magical gesture. When enemies rush you and adrenaline rises, attempting to quickly sketch the shape of a rune to summon a fireball or cloak yourself in invisibility becomes an exhilarating gamble. The spellbook expands with discoveries, allowing creative combinations once you master the runic strokes. Few RPGs before or since have implemented spellcasting in a way that so directly ties the player's physical input to the magic they wield. The underground world is built with a careful mix of handcrafted detail and naturalistic design. The hub city of Arx serves as a connective center, populated with merchants, priests, nobles, and craftsmen who each contribute to the political and economic tapestry of the setting. Surrounding layers of caverns, temples, crypts, mines, and ruins provide a wide variety of challenges, traps, hidden passages, and environmental puzzles. Exploration is constantly rewarded: secret rooms contain rare loot or shortcuts, and venturing off established paths often reveals optional quests or narrative fragments that enhance the world's lore. Unlike many modern RPGs, Arx Fatalis avoids waypoint-driven progression, trusting the player to observe, remember, and piece together clues. This creates a feeling of old-school discovery-and occasionally old-school frustration. Combat is likely where the game's age shows most clearly. The melee system has weight and intent, requiring timed swings and positional awareness, but it can feel stiff compared to contemporary standards. Enemies hit hard, and careless players can be overwhelmed quickly. As the game progresses, magic becomes increasingly powerful to the point of overshadowing melee and stealth-focused builds. Stealth can be satisfying when executed properly-slinking through darkness, slitting throats, or bypassing patrols-but enemy detection can be inconsistent. Still, these mechanical imperfections don't undermine the overall structure; instead, they reinforce the game's emphasis on creative solutions, careful resource management, and adaptable strategy. Arx Fatalis also embraces a darker tone than many fantasy RPGs. Rituals, curses, ancient cults, cannibals, and demonic conspiracies form the backbone of its narrative. NPCs often behave with a grounded pragmatism shaped by hardship and fear, and the world's history is told through fragmented journals, ruined temples, forgotten gods, and whispered legends. This writing style enhances the oppressive subterranean setting, giving the world a feeling of long-faded grandeur buried under decay. The soundtrack, though sparingly used, amplifies this mood with haunting melodies and ambient echoes that make the tunnels feel alive. The game's weaknesses-occasionally awkward controls, a confusing map system, lack of modern conveniences, and a difficulty curve that sometimes punishes experimentation-are real, but they stem from its ambition rather than lack of vision. Arx Fatalis wants players to engage deeply, to think, to try unusual solutions, to feel their way through the dark instead of being led by the hand. In that sense, it is a spiritual bridge between role-playing's past and the immersive sims Arkane would later perfect. Ultimately, Arx Fatalis stands as an uncompromising, atmospheric, and deeply immersive RPG experience. It captures the feeling of being lost in a hostile world while empowering you to shape your own path through cleverness, magic, stealth, or brute force. Its underground kingdoms, interactive systems, and signature rune-casting mechanic create an adventure that feels personal and distinctive, even decades after its release. For players who appreciate immersive sims, atmospheric dungeon crawlers, or richly reactive game worlds, Arx Fatalis remains a remarkable and influential achievement-one that rewards patience, curiosity, and imagination. Rating: 8/10

Arx Fatalis is long, complex, and unapologetically difficult. It throws you into a harsh underground world where survival depends on your choices, your wits, and your willingness to experiment. The sheer amount of freedom on offer is impressive you can approach situations in multiple ways, interact with nearly every object in the environment, and uncover hidden passages and secrets that reward curiosity. The level design constantly encourages exploration, and the interconnected areas feel like a living, breathing labyrinth. You're never guided too directly, which can be overwhelming at first, but it also makes discovery that much more rewarding. The magic system in particular, with its rune-based spell casting, is both challenging and satisfying once mastered. What really stands out, though, is how immersive the world feels. The oppressive atmosphere, dark dungeons, and ever-present sense of danger keep you on edge, and it's easy to lose yourself for hours in its winding tunnels. It's not a game that holds your hand, but for players willing to adapt to its difficulty and complexity, Arx Fatalis offers a unique and unforgettable RPG experience.

This is a toughie. There's a lot to like about Arx Fatalis, and the price is right. However, the things I loved most about the game in the first half really fell away, and the things that were most frustrating about the game really increased in the second half. As an immersive sim, this feels a bit like a prototype. There are a few open-ended puzzles (moreso in the early half), but there aren't that many options and there isn't that many interactions in the game's sub-systems. That said, the sense of exploration and finding your own way is really strong... until the plot just falls off the rails. After about the halfway point the game just feels sort of unfinished. The plot is half-baked and not well-articulated. And, I get that fans of this genre don't like to have their hands held, but it gets to the point where there's only one obscure, nonsensical solution for you to basically just guess at. I stopped playing when I had to re-explore the entire map in search of anything slightly that might have changed, and what I found was a plot nonsequitur that had nothing to do with player agency or open-ended design. The quests are increasingly like that as you progress, the difficulty spikes without warning, exploration becomes less and less worthwhile, many of the things you probably should have been able to explore are gated off for plot reasons, and most of the content is actually just hack and slash rather than immersive sim. Not to mention it gets progressively glitchier the longer you play. Arx had a lot of potential, but didn't follow through. I don't regret buying it per se, and it was interesting as a retrospective, but forced too choose between 'recommend' or 'non,' I'm afraid I have to say that most people won't find this very fun for very long, even if you like immersive sims.

I already want to do more play throughs to see how stealth changes the outcome of a few things and one with a strength build to see the effect it has on a few mechanics. Arx Fatalis is a unique dungeon crawler known for its innovative spell-casting system, where players manually draw rune combinations to cast spells. Additionally, its immersive setting and engaging story, combined with a focus on exploration and puzzle-solving, set it apart from other games of its time. The game features a rune-based magic system where players draw runes on the screen to cast spells. This manual drawing adds a layer of interactivity but can be clunky, as players must accurately replicate rune shapes, which can lead to frustration, especially in fast-paced situations. It is recommended to use a patch to make it smoother. Almost every object in the game can be interacted with, allowing players to combine items to create tools, weapons, and potions, enhancing immersion. And that was pretty amazing for it's time. I recommend this RPG wholeheartedly

There's a lot to love here and there are some glaring flaws, but it's neither the things Arx Fatalis does well, nor those that it doesn't, that ate at me while playing and continued to eat at me once done. What I CANNOT stop thinking about are the things the game doesn't do at all. The reason it's [i]so close[/i] to being an all-time masterpiece, and why I think it's beloved to this day, is the [i]potential[/i] on display around every corner. There's SO MUCH here but none of it is ever quite enough. It all just feels a bit half-baked, like a tech demo the developers inexplicably abandoned. Arx Fatalis is fascinating in the way P.T. is fascinating, only much longer and in a completely different genre. I could give numerous examples of the [i]incompleteness[/i] of Arx Fatalis - everything from the story, to the factions, to the world's overarching lore feels incomplete, while its caves feel empty - but the thing that really gets my goat is how the developers created this intricate magical system and clearly intended for you to use it, yet failed to integrate it into the game. Here's what I mean: there are TWENTY magical runes to 40 published spells. That's a bad ratio to begin with, made worse by most of those spells being utterly useless. For example: [list] [*]There's a spell for FEED despite food being [i]everywhere[/i]. [*]There's a spell for TELEKINESIS but only one [i]optional[/i] opportunity to use it and you'll find a scroll long before the runes required to cast the spell. [*]There are spells for LEVITATE, REVEAL, and DISPEL FIELD, but only one necessary opportunity to use any, and all can be accomplished by scroll or other means. [*]There are spells to RAISE DEAD and SUMMON demons, but they only attack you--they ignore NPCs and NPCs ignore them and they provide 0XP to kill. [*]You can DETECT and DISARM traps . . . or just tank every trap in the game and walk it off. Also, why are these distinct from REVEAL and DISPEL? [*]There are spells to create fire fields and ice fields, and spells to project fire, ice, poison, and lightning, but enemies are agnostic to elemental type so it's all cosmetic in the end. [/list] The point is, it's a magical system that's over-developed, under-utilized, and often circumvented by other means, rendering much of it superfluous. You WILL use magic, and in fact you should prioritize magic during your first play through or you'll have a very difficult (if not impossible) time, but only THREE spells are truly useful (literally. And one of those is purely a QoL upgrade) while 2-3 others could be considered handy but aren't necessary. I [i]want[/i] magic to be necessary. I [i]want[/i] to use telekinesis to reach out-of-the-way loot. I [i]want[/i] to use levitate to discover secret areas. I [i]want[/i] a reason to reveal enchantments and dispel them, but I don't want separate spells to do the same thing for traps. I [i]want[/i] reasons to cast poison instead of fire instead of lightning. I [i]want[/i] a magical system deeply integrated into this fascinating world with countless opportunities to use it, but Arx, as it is, doesn't provide. Arx Fatalis is the rough draft for a truly great game, if not a series of games. It's completely original IP, which is harder and harder to find these days, and the setting - a frozen world, a dead sun, survivors of varying races living in disconnected, labyrinthine underground cave systems filled with secrets and mysteries and terrors - is an untapped wellspring of story ideas and areas to explore. How is Arkane sitting on THIS goldmine while churning out garbage like Redfall and Deathloop? Arkane, what are you [i]doing[/i]??

Arx Fatalis dumps you in a dungeon with no map, no markers, and absolutely no hand-holding. It's the kind of game where figuring things out is the game. Early on, it's a blast. It's immersive, strange, and oddly charming. But after a few hours, the fun starts to fade into endless lever puzzles and wandering in circles. Combat takes a back seat to key hunts and cryptic quests. It's not a bad game - just a very specific kind of old-school. If you love Ultima Underworld-style dungeon crawls, you'll probably dig it. Everyone else? Maybe bring a guide… or a strong tolerance for confusion.

Very good RPG with a lot of Looking Glass Studios energy. The whole map is a big underground dungeon, and it's very interesting to explore, full of secrets and intriguing worldbuilding details. It's incredibly atmospheric with great sound design, graphics, map details, etc and is made with a lot of care to really pull you into the unique setting. You're given a lot of freedom to explore the world at your own pace and even affect it in significant ways, like being able to kill anybody and get unique reactions and alternate quest endings. There's no handholding in Arx. You're given little quest updates, but beyond that, it's up to you to remember things and figure out where you want to go and how to progress. Alongside that, the mechanics are really fun. Melee combat is good but isn't anything to write home about, but the magic is amazing. Having to draw spells out is a little cumbersome but adds a layer of strategy with the real time and memorization elements. Spells can be crazy powerful and only get more powerful as you level up. I also really loved the inventory system and how you're able to combine things and freely place and move around objects in the world. What really shines about the mechanics is the discovery element. Just like how you've gotta explore the world to find secrets, you frequently have to experiment with the mechanics to figure out what works, like what item combinations do or how they can help you or what secret spells there are through memorizing symbol meanings and experimenting with them. Even after you already know most of this stuff, it's just really engaging how intertwined it all feels. It's hard to fully describe the appeal of everything, but Arx Fatalis is a really satisfying RPG to make your way through with a fantastic setting that only helps to draw you in. Highly recommended, just remember to grab Arx Libertatis so it runs fine on modern computers.

However, the world building, exploration, and the story are really good. In fact, I think the only Arcane Studios game with a better storytelling is Prey.

[b] [h1] The review contains minor spoilers! [/h1] [/b] [b] I'm a huge Arkane Studios fan - EVERY one of their games that I've played was an absolute banger. I came into Arx Fatalis expecting really good and immersive experience, but nothing groundbreaking, and it absolutely exceeded all of my expectations. I got absolutely obsessed with the game for few days (i've beaten it in 40h over one week), wanting to discover every single detail, open every door, every chest, read every note and so on. It got to the point that when I was going to sleep I only thought about tomorrow's game session. I haven't felt like it for who knows how long. Arx Fatalis is an underrated masterpiece for me and one of my favorite Arkane Studios games out of all I've played so far (and I've only got Dark Messiah and Deathloop left). Arx Fatalis kinda feels like a mix of Morrowind and Thief but in an insanely unique setting. Game's world and lore is one of the most unique I've seen in an rpg game. I loved every piece of it, every detail (it has a lot of small, immersive details and secrets) and had a blast while exploring the game's map and discovering all secrets I could. The story isn't anything groundbreaking, but doesn't feel bad at all. The game doesn't hold your hand, you HAVE to experiment, explore and often figure things out on your own. Puzzles are clever, often requiring thinking outside the box. There are many hidden activities you can do, like for example crafting a fishing rod, making bread, forging a sword out of seemingly useless blades. The game rewards you for experimenting with items. The map is pretty big, but not oversized. You have 8 different floors of the mine, each one with it's unique atmosphere, design, enemies, secrets and surprises. And the deeper you go, the more dark and eerie it gets. You have a feeling like one more step and you'll awaken some freaking Cthulhu or something. The last 2 floors and the crypt are ESPECIALLY atmospheric and overwhelming, especially with game's insanely immersive sound design. Fight system is very old-school rpg like, but feels really satisfying in the end. You have melee, archery and magic and I'm gonna say that the magic system is probably BEST I've ever seen in ANY rpg game. You don't just click the button, you literally DRAW unique runes to cast spells. There are 20 runes and over 40 different, amazing spells, even hidden ones. It's next level immersion. It has some issues of course, especially considering it's age. I'm easily getting used to old games since I'm huge enthusiast of them, but getting really used to Arx took me a few hours. It's really archaic, even for it's time. The game's UI isn't the best, controls are pretty clunky and voice acting sometimes gets a bit weak. The graphics are obviously very 00's like, but for me it's more of a pro than a con. Most of those issues can be fixed or at least improved with an amazing Arx Libertatis mod that I'd even say is a must have. It improves optimization, controls, resolution and many other stuff without changing anything from the actual gameplay. I can't recommend Arx Fatalis enough. It's an overlooked masterpiece and a MUST PLAY for all old game lovers or Arkane fans. I am obsessed with this game and I'm definitely going to replay it at some point, maybe even try some other mods.[i] Just buy it. [/i] [/b]

The controls take some getting used to, but once you got the hang of it they feel so natural and perfect for a game like this. Think System Shock, but better. The tech (graphics, sound, speech,...) still holds up fine and has not lost any of it's charme. The load times between areas are usually only two seconds. Using Arx Libertatis I had no issues with graphics, crashes or spell casting not working. It is a must have to enjoy Arx Fatalis to the fullest! Ignore my 61 minutes, the Arx Libertalis patch makes the game not show up on steam. This game is fantastic, oozing in atmosphere and has one of the few truly unique worlds in a fantasy setting. The post apocalyptic setting makes it feel like a first person fallout 1 with fantasy elements. The world is really fun to explore and you'll occasionally come upon things that make you think, "Hmm I wonder how I can get there" leading you to experiment with different things. Its controls hold up fairly well for how much it tries to do and it strikes a perfect balance between classic DOS RPGs that let you manipulate the environment and a more modern action RPG with hacking and slashing. The magic system is a little rough, but it's uniqueness makes it a treat to interact with and expands magic into a skill based class instead of just relying on mashing a "cast spell" button over and over again. The story is told well and broken up by wonderfully illustrated scenes instead of relying on in-engine graphics for cut scenes and boy it just works. Everything about this game just works. I cannot recommend it enough to those looking to dip their toes into older RPGs or Immersive Sims, and I think this entry is far more approachable than a game like Deus Ex.

DISCLAIMER: I did receive the game for free for pre-ordering Dishonored, but if you enjoyed Dark Messiah of Might & Magic or enjoy old-school RPGs in general, Arx is a unique gem that is 100% worth the $5. The predecessor of Arkane's next greatest hit, Dark Messiah of Might & Magic. This is regarded by many to be a "hypergem" or "supergem" by many fans because the exact genre it embodies is just so rare, and has been made even rarer because the RPG formula has been streamlined so much that many of the systems that are implemented are now considered vestigial and archaic. This unique blend of Old-School RPG, immersive sim, runic magic system, puzzles, dark atmosphere, kicking and object physics systems come together in such a way that's extremely difficult to nail down. On top of all this, it even has its own cooking, crafting and stealth system and is fully voice-acted. This all may seem a bit overwhelming at first, but most of these systems (besides magic) are fairly intuitive and should be fairly digestible. While many players may struggle with progression through the story if they don't pay attention to every detail, the world itself is extremely rich, responsive, and varied, despite having such a dark atmosphere. My Recommendation: Play through as much as you can without a guide, and finally read a guide when you get frustrated to wit's end. I guarantee that most players will probably spend hours in the interesting world of Arx, and quite possibly play it more than once after they learn the most optimal route in completing the game's objectives. Also, make sure to use Arx Libertatis, as it is the modern open-source port of Arx Fatalis, aimed at fixing bugs, compatibility, and QoL issues. tl;dr Unique Old-School RPG immersive sim game, that not only stood the test of time, but remains a true classic gem that has yet to meet its match in modern times.

This is an *extremely* good game for its time period and genre. I really enjoyed it, and put in a lot of hours just messing around. I got it during the Chinese New Year festival sales, and I feel like I got every last dime of my money's worth from it. I give it 9/10 stars and would highly recommend. Pros: If you like a story-based quest progression game in a swords&sorcery genre, then this fits the bill. It's not mind-numbingly expansive like Skyrim or Witcher3, and it's not truly open-world (areas are restricted until you progress the main quest), but it's loads of fun and decent exploration. I searched through every last nook and cranny of the game world, finding hidden treasures or the occasional easter egg. The game is relatively easy to learn, and the combat is pretty simple if you're into combat. It's nowhere near Dark Souls difficulty, and you could probably run this game on a well rigged potato. Having said that, you WILL want to download the community "patch" (Arx Liberatis) to make the game playable on modern systems (it was almost entirely unplayable until I did so because modern mouse sensitivity kinda destroys the magic system and you *must* have *some* magic on your character to make the game work...ish). In 136 hours, I had no lag or stutter, and not a single crash or "have to reload" bug....not one. I only dropped through the world geometry requiring a reload (I never enabled the console) *once*, and I was really trying very hard to get somewhere players were clearly not meant to go at the time. ;) The economy is great (I never struggled for cash, but you have to manage some resources like torches mid-to-end game), and most of the loot makes sense (you get a couple pieces a wee tad too late for my tastes, but I'm greedy). I only did a very minimum amount of savescum grinding out of a personal desire to max out my character for kicks and theft. You're not buying this for sandboxing or jaw dropping graphics, you're buying this to tell/reveal/experience a single main story and save the world. Again...this isn't Skyrim and you can't "live" in this world long-term. Think of it more like decent-length digital one-shot solo D&D campaign. My one complaint is that the absolute end scenes after *everything* was done and/or defeated felt a wee bit . . . underwhelming. I guess I wanted accolades of some sort. I'd love to see the company revisit and reboot this title someday...expand some side quests, add some content (I really wanna be able to talk to the king about a certain letter I found....). Still, I've loved everything I've ever played from Arkane, and this is another great title.
