Two Worlds: Epic Edition is one of those RPGs whose ambition is immediately visible, even before its flaws come into focus. Developed by Reality Pump Studios and published by Topware Interactive, it attempts to deliver a sprawling open-world fantasy adventure on a scale rivaling larger-budget contemporaries. The story follows a mercenary searching for his kidnapped sister, a setup that begins simply but quickly widens into political conspiracies, ancient prophecies, and escalating conflicts across the war-torn land of Antaloor. While the narrative does not reinvent the genre, it provides a serviceable backbone for exploration, and its willingness to let players wander freely rather than pushing them down a tightly scripted narrative path is one of its defining qualities. The world feels lived-in, not because of impressive storytelling, but because of how much of it exists outside the player's direct involvement. The real draw of Two Worlds lies in its sense of freedom. From the earliest moments, players can ignore the main quest entirely and instead traverse plains, mountains, forests, ruins, villages, and monster-infested roads, picking up quests, loot, or simply appreciating the changing landscapes. Progression is flexible-skills, weapons, magic, and attributes allow for a hybridized build system rather than forcing players into rigid classes. Melee fighters can learn spells, archers can dabble in alchemy, and mages can wield swords without penalty. This design philosophy encourages experimentation, and its modular spellcrafting system, where magic scrolls can be combined into increasingly absurd effects, offers glimpses of mechanical creativity that many larger RPGs never attempt. The crafting system, which lets players stack identical equipment pieces to improve their stats, rewards obsessive looting and feels surprisingly satisfying despite its simplicity. However, the game's enormity exposes its rough edges. Combat is responsive enough to be enjoyable but lacks the precision and weight expected from modern action-RPGs. Enemy encounters sometimes rely more on stats than tactics, leading to occasional difficulty spikes or anticlimactic victories. Character animations, AI behavior, environmental interaction, and physics can feel stiff or unpredictable, reminding players of the game's mid-2000s budget limitations. Dialogue and voice acting have earned notoriety for their theatrical awkwardness, occasionally turning serious moments into unintentional comedy. These quirks can frustrate players seeking polish, but for others, they add a strangely endearing charm. Two Worlds feels earnest, unfiltered, and unconcerned with refinement, which gives it an identity-however uneven-that distinguishes it from more sanitized entries in the genre. The presentation reinforces this mixture of ambition and uneven execution. The environments are vast and varied, with sweeping vistas, bustling towns, and isolated wilderness areas that invite exploration, but textures, lighting, and character models reveal their age despite the enhancements included in the Epic Edition. The soundtrack, on the other hand, remains a highlight-melancholic, adventurous, and atmospheric in ways that elevate the world beyond its visual limitations. Technical performance varies depending on hardware, but the PC version is generally smoother and more stable than its console counterparts, benefiting from community patches and years of post-launch updates. This edition also bundles the expansions, extending the adventure with new locations, quests, enemies, and gear, making it the most complete and convenient way to experience the game. Two Worlds is also shaped heavily by pacing. It is not a fast RPG, nor does it attempt to create constant forward momentum. Instead, it thrives when players approach it like a wandering traveler-talking to NPCs without urgency, clearing roadside bandit camps, exploring ancient ruins, gathering alchemical ingredients, and stumbling into small stories tucked away from the main narrative. It rewards patience far more than efficiency, and its best moments appear organically rather than through scripted spectacle. For players raised on tightly guided, cinematic RPGs, this looseness may feel directionless. But for those who miss the open-ended structure of older PC role-playing games, it offers a rare sense of autonomy. Ultimately, Two Worlds: Epic Edition is a game best understood through expectations. It is not polished, balanced, or narratively elegant, nor does it attempt to compete with modern giants in the genre. Instead, it is a relic of a transitional era in RPG design-ambitious, messy, creative, uneven, memorable, and earnest. It is a game made for players who find joy in exploring flawed but fascinating worlds, who can overlook technical missteps in exchange for freedom, discovery, and experimentation. For those willing to embrace its imperfections, Two Worlds offers dozens of hours of wandering through a fantasy landscape that feels handcrafted rather than manufactured. It may never reach the heights it aimed for, but its willingness to try-boldly and without restraint-is what makes it endure. Rating: 7/10

Polish developer Reality Pump boldly attempts to challenge Oblivion's dominance in the open-world RPG space with Two Worlds, but while the ambition is admirable, the execution falls short of its lofty goals. The Good Two Worlds nails the fundamentals of an open-world RPG. The game offers vast terrain, bustling cities, and countless side quests for exploration enthusiasts. Unlike Oblivion's controversial level scaling, enemies here maintain fixed difficulty levels, creating genuine progression satisfaction as you grow from weakling to powerhouse. The main quest structure is refreshingly open-ended, requiring reputation building through side missions rather than simple map-following. This creates meaningful consequences for your actions and makes the world feel more interconnected. The Bad Unfortunately, technical issues plague nearly every aspect of the game. Animations are awkward, objects pop in randomly, and collision detection is broken. Expect NPCs walking through walls regularly. Performance stutters during combat, independent of world-loading pauses. The horseback combat, while conceptually appealing, suffers from atrocious controls. Horses have minds of their own, often traveling in opposite directions from your input. Combat glitches cause enemies to teleport unpredictably, breaking immersion entirely. Voice acting is embarrassingly poor. Imagine monotone delivery at a Renaissance fair, and the dialogue relies heavily on tired fantasy clichés. Multiplayer Caveat Co-op play exists but requires separate characters and smaller maps. It's functional with dedicated friends but lacks the seamless integration many expect. Bottom Line Two Worlds demonstrates solid game design concepts buried under layers of technical incompetence. While RPG enthusiasts might find enjoyment despite the flaws, the numerous bugs and polish issues prevent it from achieving mainstream appeal. A case study in how poor execution can undermine good ideas. Recommendation: Wait for patches or consider alternatives unless you're desperate for open-world RPG content.

I remember the day this game came out on Xbox360 so clearly. I had heard about it randomly somewhere, and followed it through to release date. It's broken, but a fun, playable, quirky kind of broken that isn't seen very often. I think it has to be broken given how ambitious this seems to be to have been released in 2007. I cannot imagine how many hours it took to develop this at the time, and I appreciate that as I play the game in 2025 - people are still booting this game up, for that hit of nostalgia, 18 years after it was released. That has to be worth something ! A game like this was destined to be lost to time; taken over by releases with better story lines, better game mechanics and better marketing teams, but I think it has a place in gaming history, and I'm sure it helped in the development path to where we are today.

Right off the bat, Two Worlds is pretty jank. It's got corny writing, corny voice acting, and this particular version of the game has some issues with performance for some reason. However, pushing that aside, there is a charming game, with a lot of big ideas with some that unfortunately just aren't implemented well. The combat is an interesting back and forth. You run in, swing a few times, and back out. Almost every single enemy has a few different attacks with obvious tells that you can then dodge immediately with an invincible backdash. That backdash can be cancelled into from ANYTHING. So even though your attacks lock you into a swinging animation, you can still fluidly move around an encounter and skilfully take on enemies. However, most of this goes out the window when you are surrounded by multiple enemies, which you will encounter many times, especially with wolf, orc, and bandit packs that consist of 5+ enemies at times, and you'll be running in circles, waiting for an opening to attack once, back out and try not to die And you will die, because even basic enemies deal absurd amounts of damage. Outside that, every hit feels chunky and good, and each weapon has its own combo string that looks visually cool, and have different properties that are good for different situations. However death isn't a big deal since you'll respawn shortly after at a nearby checkpoint, and you can simply run back and try again. This lessens the impact of death, and eases the frustration of the unfortunately overtuned enemies. There are many interesting RPG elements, however the main character is billed as a certain archetype and starts with a handful of skills which you are encouraged to follow. Other skills can be trained for a cost at various NPCs in different cities. They are unforunately hard to find though, and the cost is quite high at low levels. On level up, you can also dump points into HP, Dexterity, Strength, and Willpower. All of them are quite important for you build, but HP and Dex are the ones that you'll find you may need the most for melee early, due to the high damage, and dex helping you keep up your damage and defense values. Dex unfortunately is required because every level up ticks down those damage and defense values. Quests are generally simple, requiring you to either kill monsters, talk to people or go into dungeons to collect items. Nothing special, but they all are voice acted which is nice. The world itself is vast, but mostly sparse, but the weather effects and different environments are varied enough it sets the tone well enough. Items are generally pretty simple, upping damage and defense values, and you'll occasionally find something with a bunch of stat increases on it which is cool. What I found most interesting is you can mash items together to upgrade them and merge stats. Helps decrease clutter, and you're never upset to find a duplicate. The music is pretty good. No real notes, but it sets the tone very well. Finally, the main quest is quite short if you beeline it, but it's worth it to maybe take your time. I enjoyed my time with this game, and while it's not a perfect game, or even a good game, it's certainly not a bad game, and I don't regret playing. Its sincerity is refreshing, and for that I think it elevates itself above many RPGS of the time

It's painful to play, this old, polygonal pc clunker -- if you're not already so [i]steeped[/i] in it that the rose-tinted goggles do all the heavy lifting. Released at a time when physics were a new and wondrous thing in games, you'll spend most of your Battle Time kicking guys off cliffs and throwing omnipresent barrels and crates (and not very well at that) . . . because what, after all, is the most powerful weapon in Ashan? Is it the [b]Sword of the Dragonclaw[/b]? Try again! Is it the [b]Skull of Shadows[/b] perhaps? No, no, no! It's a heavy chunk of wood, lobbed by a maniac with apparent [i]gorilla strength[/i]! Watch 'em rag-doll, Sareth, then it's your time to strike, because you sure can't hit them very well with your sword if they're moving at all! Sure, it's fun to play around with the kicking and the Crates of Death in the first level or so, but that only goes so far in the face of all that's wrong. And the game (if you can even get it to run in the current year) is held together by bubble gum and Dollar General duct tape, so it [i]will[/i] fly apart under the pressure of a strong look. Ah, dammit! The door won't open again! Guess I've got to load . . . again. (I've heard a lot of folks actually have to uninstall and reinstall the thing to get past these points, and it's [i]certainly[/i] not worth that kind of trouble.) I suppose if you want to relive some of your past gaming glories, it might be okay. I never played it back in 2006, but freely admit that I might have gone through it several times for the sheer novelty, if I had. In 2026, however, I just can't get over the long, tangled dungeon levels where you keep getting stuck on the geometry (or the ropes), or what's even [i]worse[/i]: the [b]darkness[/b] of absolutely everything. Yes, if you're not standing in the bright sunlight, things are just too dark to see . . . [i]unless[/i] you turn on your Paris Hilton nightvision, which means you [i]have[/i] to use it. A lot. So I hope you like your games in really ugly, washed-out monochrome, because that's how you'll see so very much of this one. I [i]do[/i] understand what they were trying to accomplish here, and wIth limited processing power, but it's just not much fun to play now, if it even works. Autistically awkward swordplay (let's see you make a thrust connect with [i]anything[/i]!), nastily necessary night vision, glitchy landscapes, various door-locking bugs, and a sub-generic fantasy story vastly outweigh the fun you'll have from making guys go [i]floppy-flop[/i] with the power of Donkey Kong. Do I like anything about it? I certainly like the [b]idea[/b] of [i]Dark Messiah[/i]; there should be games made every month that do what this one [I]set out[/I] to, but there aren't, admittedly. I also like Sareth's voice! He reminds me of David Naughton, star of the short-lived 1970s sitcom [i]Makin' It[/i], a Doctor Pepper commercial or two, and my [b]favorite[/b] B-horror film, [i]The Sleeping Car[/i]!

I got the game after multiple YouTubers showcased it as an obscure RPG like [i]Elder Scrolls but with physics[/i], throwing stuff at your enemies, and ability to kick them off ledges. E.g. your skill tree fits in the corner of the screen but [b]skill choices open interesting and unique combat options[/b]. I highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys high fantasy RPGs. It has stood the test of time and holds up well 20 years later in 2026. Dark Messiah features linear levels and progression unlike a lot of the other games in its niche, but still offers an interesting amount of choice in the endings you choose to go with. The combat feels weighty and satisfying, from the bow, to the sword, to magic spells, it all feels impactful. Enemies visually recoil and let out grunts in response to each hit, you can kick them to push them off a cliff, smash them into spikes, drop barrels on them, you name it. I've never seen a game involve physics so deeply into its combat and execute it this well. Combat does not disappoint, but neither does the adventure. The moment to moment gameplay of exploring the different fantasy environments and taking in the scenery is amazing and it's a powerful motivator. It has just enough retro charm in its graphics to not look dated. Story is your typical epic fantasy quest on the surface but actually goes pretty deep if you choose to read the various collectable books and manuscripts. What hasn't aged so well is the state of playing the game on a modern PC and the somewhat janky movement. You without a doubt will need to be able to do some mild tinkering to get this game to not crash, and even then there will be parts where you seemingly just crash for no reason, but reloading a save fixes it 99% of the time. The thing that can't be easily fixed is the parkour and movement system. Sometimes it works, sometimes it barely even registers inputs. Sometimes you don't notice it, sometimes it makes you want to blow your head off. Quick save before putting down any ropes or attempting to make risky jumps, because more often than not the system will NOT function as you think it will. Dark Messiah has a lot of charm and charisma and will not disappoint anyone who is willing to put forth the effort (and patience) to deal with its quirks. I strongly recommend picking it up if you are that type.

Dark Messiah of Might and Magic is a first-person action game with both magic and melee combat that was programmed in the source engine. So needless to say it was extremely messy and unpolished. But in spite of that, I had a fun time and the game had enough unique elements that I kinda wish there was more stuff like it that just had a bit more refinement. It's not something I would outright recommend to people, but I would say it's worth giving a shot for the novelty if nothing else. -------------------------------------------------------- A lot of the gameplay foundations seem like what you would expect for a fantasy RPG. You have a few melee weapons to fight enemies close up, a bow for ranged, and magic spells with a variety of effects. None of these options are great in retrospect with each weapon doing relatively little damage and enemies who can tank a lot of hits and stuns while dealing a lot of damage to you in the meantime. And the fact that everything is in first person can make combat quite chaotic as enemies will maneuver around you in groups while the reach of your weapons is deceptively short. If you play this like a conventional first person action game then you're not gonna have a great time. And yet despite that, the gameplay ends up being the best part thanks to the focus on physics. As a source engine game, Dark Messiah uses the physics effects as essentially the main method of combat. Rocks, boxes, and other inanimate objects scattered around the map can be picked up and thrown at enemies, kicked into their chest, knocked down stairs, and so much more. You'll quickly learn that a sword might be necessary in a pinch, but if you can surprise your enemy by lobbing a rock at their face then they'll be stunned far more than a few sword swings can ever hope for. These items have an immediate effect in terms of damage and stuns, but they really excel when used in conjunction with environmental hazards. Knocking an enemy off a ledge so they fall to death, shoving them into a spiked wall or fireplace, luring them into a staircase or alleyway where you have a trap prepared, and plenty of other possibilities are all a fun time. While fun on its own, you won't always have what you want to pull off the kinds of tricks and traps you want. And that's where magic comes into play. You have some generic spells that are more damage focused, but the best are those with additional physics effects. Fire will ignite oil, electricity will shock anything in water, and the best of all is ice which will cause enemies running along its surface to slip and fall. The former two are useful when the situation allows it and you can make some fun combos (like lighting an enemy on fire, then kicking them into a group of their comrades to burn them as well), but the ice is going to be your best friend in any physics related shenanigans. I can't tell you how many times I lured an enemy through a doorway, spread some ice around the corner, and watched them slip off a cliff or into a fire. Rather than a typical fantasy hero, Dark Messiah makes you feel more like Kevin McCallister has gone on the offensive. ---------------------------------------------------------- The effect would be much better if the physics were actually consistent though. As to be expected given the game's age and engine, objects can be very unwieldy at times. The physics of each object can just feel wrong at times with the arcs they go through the sky or how quickly they reach their target, rendering precise setups a non-starter without a huge amount of trial and error. Collisions can feel weird with objects often clipping through each other, the ground, or the characters in a way that can have unpredictable effects (including a few deaths thanks to weird collision physics, both enemies and myself). And finally there's just a great deal of inconsistency with a lot of the environmental effects. Sometimes fire just won't light oil and enemies will run over ice without missing a step. It all leaves a system that feels very chaotic, sometimes in a good way when the chaos of the battlefield is a result of your own hijinks and enemy ai and other times in a frustrating way when a plan falls apart because the engine decided not to cooperate with your plans. ---------------------------------------------------- Beyond the gameplay itself, a large part of the experience is driven by the level design. They're all littered with objects, traps, and plenty of opportunities for your chaotic plans to take effect, though their success at doing so varies quite significantly. The early portions of the game were the most fun with open maps and dumb enemies that offered lots of opportunities for messing around. But as the game progresses, levels start feeling more restrictive either with very clearly telegraphed opportunities for you to mess around or with few enough options that some amount of normal combat becomes necessary. Levels become more enclosed as you move on and enemies start having ranged attacks that they can use instead of chasing you. I dont know whether its their ai being smarter or just everything else being unconducive to the tricks that used to be staples of my playstyle, but the last few levels felt like a real bore that required far more fighting and far fewer tricks than the great levels of the early and mid-game. ----------------------------------------------------- And there isn't much else worth mentioning besides that. The story is fine, not particularly engaging but enough to provide context for what you're doing in each level. The visuals are pretty good, especially at highlighting what items you can interact with and what's just for show, and just being a solid dark-ish fantasy setting all around. And the sound, music, voices and other elements are just fine. There's nothing bad enough to take you out of the experience but I don't think anything besides the gameplay will stick around in my mind for very long. -------------------------------------------------------- Dark Messiah was a pretty fun game overall. It's one of those experiences that's deeply flawed and undoubtedly suffers from some age-related issues but still has plenty going for it. I can safely say that I've never played anything else like it, but really wish that I could. A lot of the core ideas are good and a game that is fully committed to them would probably be a blast if some of the rough edges of the system here could be patched up. But as it stands right now, I have to admit that for all the fun I had while playing this game the flaws are way too hard to ignore and really bring the experience down. This is really a case of a game which does one thing particularly well and everything else is serviceable enough not to cause an issue most of the time. Mixed feelings on this one, think I'd enjoy it as a kid when it was new but playing it for the first time now I have way too many issues with it. First the combat. The game has a massive focus on getting environmental kills primarily through kicking enemies, for example kicking an enemy off a cliff, into convenient wall spikes, or campfires, all will instantly kill an enemy. There is a lesser focus on trying to knock enemies down (kicking them down stairs, blasting with fireball, slipping with ice) so you can then "execute" them (not guaranteed to kill). There's other environmental effects that some kill, some don't, like dropping barrels on them or a swinging rock. While I appreciate the creativity with the environmental kills, the game has wayyy too heavy a focus on them, which causes a problem where your regular attacks/spells do trash damage and when you're being swarmed by dudes it's better to lure them to areas you can get instant kills. So the combat becomes you constantly trying to kite enemies to death zones, which gets exhausting after several hours of this because it never changes. The game also has some weird hitboxes/animations: goblins will swing and hit you when their club was three club lengths away from your body while you can't hit them from the same spot, someone will swing and miss and then you walk in to take advantage and you somehow take damage (they didn't swing again, idk if it's an invisible animation or if their first swing just lingers), the kick is usually reliable but sometimes will pass through the enemies or send them in the wrong direction. Game crashed on me maybe 5 times, so not horrendous but still annoying. Story was super forgettable (maybe better if you're really into Might and Magic). Other random issues: Your weapon and especially your spells takes up way too much of your screen, if you're trying to aim off an edge at someone with a fireball it's difficult to see anything. The visibility issue gets way worse with the lighting because a lot of the levels are super dark, so you activate your free night vision spell but because there are some torches in parts of the room those become way too bright so again it's hard to see (not to mention your magic weapons/spells glow like the goddang sun in night vision). The levels drag on, I think this game would've been much better if it was half the length, you will be fighting the same enemies in the same environments for 1-2 hours a level, it gets tiring. Like the spider temple, instead of making me gather 3 gems fighting a bunch of zombies the entire time in a dark crypt how about I just get one gem and kick 30 zombies into spikes instead of 90? There's too many crypt style levels also, the highlights of the game were definitely the outside areas because they actually were interesting looking (the boat, the desert, the city). For some reason I usually hear this game come up when talking about Bethesda-likes and if you look at "more like this" down below you will see a lot of large adventure games listed, so just to be clear this is absolutely nothing like those games and is much more like Wolfenstein or Doom being very linear with the occasional secret area with items.

Dark Messiah of Might & Magic, developed by Arkane Studios and published by Ubisoft in 2006, stands as a distinctive entry in the realm of first-person fantasy action games. Drawing upon the robust Source Engine, the game delivers a visceral combat experience that emphasizes player agency and environmental interaction. Set within the expansive Might & Magic universe, it introduces players to a narrative centered around the battle between light and darkness, with the protagonist, Sareth, caught in the ensuing conflict. One of the game's most lauded features is its dynamic melee combat system. Players can execute a variety of attacks, including slashes, thrusts, and powerful kicks, each offering different tactical advantages. The environment plays a crucial role in combat; for instance, enemies can be kicked into hazards like spikes or off ledges, leading to satisfying and often brutal outcomes. This emphasis on environmental interactions is further complemented by a diverse array of magical abilities, ranging from elemental spells to stealth techniques, allowing for varied combat strategies. The game's level design is another standout aspect. Each environment is meticulously crafted, offering multiple pathways and hidden areas that encourage exploration. This design not only enhances replayability but also ensures that players can approach challenges in diverse ways, whether through brute force, stealth, or magical prowess. However, some critics have pointed out that certain levels can feel repetitive, with similar environmental puzzles and enemy types reappearing throughout the game. Narratively, Dark Messiah of Might & Magic presents a straightforward tale of good versus evil, with Sareth's journey serving as the central narrative thread. While the story may not break new ground, it effectively supports the game's action-oriented gameplay, providing context and motivation for the player's actions. Character development is somewhat limited, with Sareth remaining largely silent throughout the game, leaving much of the storytelling to the environment and supporting characters. On the technical side, the game showcases the capabilities of the Source Engine, delivering impressive visuals for its time. The detailed character models, realistic physics, and atmospheric lighting contribute to an immersive experience. However, some players have reported performance issues, particularly on older hardware, and occasional bugs that can disrupt gameplay. Despite these technical hiccups, the game's overall presentation remains commendable. In conclusion, Dark Messiah of Might & Magic offers a unique blend of first-person combat and fantasy elements, set against a richly detailed world. While it may not have achieved widespread commercial success, it has garnered a dedicated fanbase and is often cited as a cult classic among action RPG enthusiasts. For those seeking a game that emphasizes player choice, environmental interaction, and dynamic combat, Dark Messiah of Might & Magic remains a noteworthy title in the genre. Rating: 9/10

Dark Messiah of Might and Magic combines Source engine physics with a first-person action RPG formula, allowing players to creatively dispatch enemies in entertaining ways. You play as Sareth, a disciple of a mage, on a quest to find the Skull of Shadows. While the game offers engaging combat and a role-playing system for upgrading skills, the single-player campaign suffers from pacing issues and a lackluster narrative. Gameplay: The game features a variety of combat options, including melee attacks, magical spells, and environmental interactions. Players can kick enemies into spikes or fire, creating a "wow" factor, but this can make traditional combat feel less relevant. The gameplay becomes repetitive as the campaign progresses, and the lack of advanced stealth mechanics limits tactical options. Boss encounters, while visually impressive, often disappoint in execution. The multiplayer mode is where the game shines, offering class-based gameplay with unique abilities and strategies. Modes like Deathmatch and Crusade provide a more satisfying experience, emphasizing skill over environmental kills. Visuals and Sound: Dark Messiah boasts impressive graphics with detailed character models and environments, though some textures are lower resolution. The character perspective adds immersion, but the sound design is hit-or-miss, with average voice acting and decent music. Technical Issues: Unfortunately, the game is plagued by technical problems, including frequent crashes and bugs that can disrupt gameplay, particularly in multiplayer. Conclusion: While Dark Messiah of Might and Magic offers a visually appealing and innovative combat experience, its single-player campaign is marred by pacing issues and technical problems. The multiplayer mode provides a more enjoyable experience, making it a mixed bag overall.

[h1]Immersive sim with revolutionary ideas, great combat and a ton of jank.[/h1] [hr][/hr] I just finished [i]Dark Messiah [/i]after originally starting it in April. Took a bit of an unplanned break about two-thirds through, but I'm glad I came back to finish what I started. This is one of those rare games that feels unpolished and chaotic, yet still completely worth playing if you're into immersive sims or physics-driven gameplay. I went with a mostly melee-focused build, but unlocked most of the utility spells as well. I didn't care much for the flashy stuff, I was here to mess sh*t up. Settings ice traps around tight corners, baiting enemies into slipping, and watching them ragdoll of a cliff or into hazards was consistently hilarious and satisfying. The real MVP here is kicking, and it's [b]ABSURDLY[/b] powerful. This dude has the most overpowered lower body I have ever seen. You can kick enemies off cliffs, into fire, into very conveniently placed spike walls, into other enemies - Hell, you can kick barrels into them. The whole world feels like a trap waiting to be used, and the physics-driven combat makes every encounter feel dynamic and improvised. Stealth exists. Allegedly. And while I appreciated the light-level mechanic, it feels inconsistent. Enemies spot you a little too quickly, and there isn't much grace or nuance to how detection works. Good luck figuring out how close is too close. Still, there's a sense of tension when you hug the shadows and try to get the drop on someone with a surprise attack. Story also exists. Allegedly. You play as Sareth, a wizard's apprentice sent off on a [i]Very Important Quest™[/i] involving a prophecy, some ancient evil, and a glowing artifact called Skull of Shadows. Some twists and dramatic reveals but none of it really lands. There's also a really hot demon lady living rent-free in your head whispering questionable things, trying to seduce you throughout the entire game. So that's really cool I think. The writing and voice acting are... fine? They're not the reason you're here, you're here to find creative ways to ruin an orc's day. What really stands out is how ahead of its time this game was. In 2006, most games were still experimenting with physics like it was a tech demo. Meanwhile, [i]Dark Messiah [/i] built an entire combat system around it. Every room feels like a trap waiting to happen. The level design may be linear, but it's filled with tiny arenas that let you improvise. You're encouraged to think creatively, whether that means icing a slope at the right moment or weaponizing gravity like it's part of your toolkit. Hell, it might as well be. It's messy, experimental, wildly unbalanced, but never boring. Now for the rough part: the jank is real. Very much so. The game crashed often. Alt-tabbing? Good luck. Switching resolutions? Flip a coin. Saving frequently is necessary. Thank god Source Engine quicksaves make that painless. I cannot recommend [url=https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3378556750]this steam guide[/url] enough, I think it reduced my crashes drastically. That said, even with fixes, the game froze after the final cutscene lol. Didn't get to see the credits until removing my stability fixes. A true [i]Dark Messiah[/i] ending, honestly. I strongly recommend following the guide if you plan to play this. If you can't deal with jank, just skip this one. But here's the thing: I still loved it. Despite the bugs, the stiff animations, and the occasional crash% world-record speedrun, this is a gem of a game. If you enjoy immersive sims, physics-based combat, and don't mind chaos, [i]Dark Messiah's[/i] a forgotten classic that deserves more love than it gets. You'll kick stuff. You'll laugh. You'll reload a save because you accidentally kicked [b]yourself[/b] off a cliff. There's nothing else quite like it.

Remember the time, when Ubisoft was not a conveyor? Yeah, probably not, you, probably, were not even born yet or you were, but did not play such games yet. Dark Messiah was one of those games, that would not be made in modern Ubisoft, because it was an experiment. And from what I understand it was not that successful financially, but it did achieve some love from from gamers, so much love, that Ubisoft gave modders X-Box version of the game to make a remaster. God forbid them to do that themselves... But would it deserve a remaster? This one of the games, that I played back in the day, but for some reason did not finish. I think the biggest issue for me was performance and stability, because Source engine was very demanding back in the day (and still can be). It was a difficult game without that, too, but that was less of a problem for me, from what I remember. Ether way I decided to finish it properly and, I would say it probably could use a remake, rather than a remaster. Dark Messiah has pieces, that could have been made into amazing game, but most of them feel unpolished, now that I look at them after having more experience. Or, at least, they feel like that now, back in the day, perception would be different, of course. The game has lots of little annoyances in the gameplay. Shields can block half the screen, the lighting can be very uneven with some places being too dark (with night vision not making them more "visible"), and some places can have too much light (or sun shining through buildings somehow). The way you switch through gear is somewhat annoying after Skyrim, but understandable, at least. The most annoyance for me were physics, though. Worst case was jumping. There were cases when character seemed to stumble or slow down when doing a running jump, and the way I was not able to grab onto lots of ledges when I should have was very frustrating. Kicks seemed to have no effects on some small enemies (although could have a lot of effect on small goblins). Some objects got highlighted for telekinesis, but were not really interactable. But most importantly (although not the worst in terms of annoyance, of course), was effect on enemies when you hit them. Or rather the lack of it, unless you are doing an adrenaline kill. Most of the times hitting enemies felt like they are not getting any damage at all, and at some point it started feeling like I am clicking them to death. Not literally, because number of enemies and their general toughness does force you to dance around using your skills, but still. The most common scenario for me were those magicians, that seemed to sink in more damage than their fully armored counterparts. Since most weapons do not really provide any tangible feedback of successful attack, it felt like I was playing Morrowind with it's probability based combat on lower levels. This can be just skill issue, of course, and maybe I just need to git good. That won't help with the story, which could use a make-over. Conceptually it's interesting, there are still not that many games that even try to put you in shoes of a (potential) baddie. But it does not really lean that much into the concept. Some quests from The Elder Scrolls games and, dunno, Mass Effect's renegade choices probably give more flavor. The reason for that is... Characters are just flat, stupid and annoying. They seemed to be mostly an after-thought even to somehow "connect" several maps. Which are not bad, but are still bleak dungeon walls for like half the game. If the game was made today, then besides polishing the physicality of combat a bit more, it would be required to make the story more emotional, more "heavy", so that your choices matter more to the world around you, and so that it would be more difficult to make them. In the original game, it mostly affect what weapons you may be using in the last boss fight. Would I recommend this game now? That's a tough one. Definitely do not play it for the story, there is barely any. For combat and some level of freedom you have in it - maybe, but your experience can vary greatly depending on the playstyle you choose. I probably would not recommend playing as archer, because to me it felt really unsatisfying, although the bow itself was fine overall. Maybe wait till the modders finish the remaster? Maybe they will improve more than just looks and some some bugs? On the other hand, it's quite cheep in the first place, so maybe it's fine as is.

If you loved Dishonored, you will LOVE this. 9.5/10 The game is old yes, but it's aged well and is still very playable. The fighting and magic mechanics are very well made and well-balanced, with each weapon feeling unique and fluid for a different playstyle, each spell is fun to use and you can build your character however you want. The stealth system is also well-made and while it's not super impressive it get the job done well for a game that isn't built to be stealth-centered. The music is great, and besides some outdated graphics the game still looks very aesthetically appealing. I often feel like I'm playing a more RPG-themed version of Dishonored with a bigger weapon selection. Combat is fun,fluid, and difficult if you're careless but once your get the hang of things it becomes a very fun system to master. One thing people complain about is that it feels like your mana pool recovers too slowly, which I can understand but I felt like it was balanced fine even as a mage-focused player. Magic is powerful, but you can't rely solely on magic for every encounter, you need to use it wisely, which gives the game more charm. Where this game really shines is its level and mission design. Unlike many RPGs which just fill a room full of enemies and a trap or puzzle here and there, Dark Messiah really makes you feel like you're going on an adventure. EVERY level feels unique, and takes place in a different biome, and every single mission has a special activity you need to engage with in whatever way you choose. One level you're parkouring across city rooftops, the next level you're trying to outmaneuver a dragon in a maze, the next mission you're fighting a town of orcs in a dessert, the next level you're trying to infiltrate a ship on the beach without getting blasted on the shore by their canons, another level you're sneaking around trying to steal an artifact in a secret lair. EVERY. SINGLE. MISSION. Has soooooooo much variety and always keeps you guessing, you never are given the same task twice and nothing overstays its welcome. Every area has unique enemies with different movesets and fighting styles in a different biome with a different mission to complete. You really feel like a heroic adventurer going on an epic quest where there's never a dull moment; you're always left eagerly wondering what will happen next. The characters are very well written and develop very well. Every character serves a crucial role in the story and brings their own unique sense of suspense and intrigue. You always feel like you understand the motivations of each character while at the same time wondering if they're secretly hiding ulterior motives. Take my advice and give this one a try. It's hella cheap and takes up no space on your hard drive. They don't make 'em like this anymore. 9.5/10

I realized if there were only another 40-45 skill points left to earn, there was no way I could build a character strong enough to deal with endgame enemies. Dark Messiah demands that you specialize, so I abandoned my first character and started another. The first time I finished the game was with my second character, a dedicated mage build. It was fine. It wasn't bad, it wasn't great, it was just good. And boring. Good and boring. You never really feel a sense of progression as a mage. You don't become more powerful, you just gain more mana to crank out more of the same boring spells. Arkane's previous title, Arx Fatalis, suffered from too many spells and an overly complex casting system; here, they over-corrected and gave you too few spells, all available at the push of a button. The worst part about playing as a mage is that it feels like the developers don't want you to play as a mage--every secret area is stocked with scrolls you don't need and weapons you can't wield. Sure, you could put 1 skill each into Melee and Archery, and there are a few staffs that require Magic Affinity, but they are all thoroughly useless for most of the game. There's one powerful Dragon-class staff available to mages towards the end of the game, but it's [i]towards the end of the game[/i] so . . . thanks? My lust to use all of those cool weapons and shields encouraged me to create a third character and play as a warrior, and for f*cks sake I wish I hadn't. F*ck the melee combat in this game, and f*ck this game for making me think it was going to be epic. The melee combat in Dark Messiah is hot garbage that turns a boring but serviceable role playing adventure game into a tiresome and infuriating test of one's patience. NPC and PC melee combat are both broken in ways that punish you, the player. For starters, NPC melee attacks inflict damage at any point during their animation, beginning with Frame 1. This makes it impossible to time your own attacks without getting hit, because once you break parry all they have to do is twitch and you take damage. This includes when you shield bash, which is f*cking stupid. Enemies hit you from impossibly far distances. This is particularly true for goblin kick attacks, those short kings might as well be Mr. Fantastic. There's a dash attack that's supposed to stun your enemy, but it never actually stuns your enemy. Quite often it doesn't even execute properly and all you get is a standard power attack. You also have to be the exact distance away from your target and they have to be standing still through the entire animation. Too far away and you'll wiff empty air; too close and you'll blow past them and wiff empty air. If they move at all your first strike might land while your second wiffs empty air. If the enemy sees you and starts their attack animation, you take damage even if you're eight feet away because: see above. Honestly it's f*cking useless. You can impale a downed enemy to insta-kill them, except 50% of the time it refuses to enter the animation and you just end up striking them until they stand back up. When it does enter the animation, quite often it doesn't kill the target. I impaled one guy [i]four times[/i] and he got up and walked it off. Simple Black Knight, weakest enemies in the game, tanking a sword through the chest like a champ. Kicking an enemy should send them flying, giving you an opportunity to repeatedly fail to execute an insta-kill. Except, not always. For some inexplicable reason some enemies that should go flying refuse to do so. Go ahead and kick that b*astard until you're exhausted, he'll stand his ground like it's Florida. You cannot bash enemies with your shield to stagger/stun them if they've started their attack animation, they just ignore the hit and you'll take damage because of the Frame 1 attack glitch. To make matters worse, some of these issues aren't universal. One minute you'll rip through a room with five enemies like a whirlwind, the next you can't stagger one stupid guard for no god d*mned reason. Sometimes, the game behaves contrary to what you've been led to expect and what should be an easy and fun combat turns into a frustration of broken mechanics. And don't get me started on the puerile story and the ridiculous dialog from the obnoxiously horny demon inside your head. "Oh yes, I've 'known' your father" FFS barf.

I was pleasantly surprised by this game. Literally the only reason I have this game in my library is because I got it for just a few bucks in the Arkane Collection on Steam, and it just came with it. I had never heard of this game until I bought it with the collection, and I assumed it would be a boring game that I would play an hour or two of and end up never finishing, if I even played it at all. Instead, I'm so glad I decided to play it and I had no issue playing for hours at a time. It surely isn't the prettiest game in the world, but the combat has aged gracefully and was incredibly fun from start to finish. I also love the finishers once you build up enough adrenaline, it still feels so cool even though they're not exactly the best animations. The many ways you can defeat enemies using the environment also never gets old. I can't even begin the count the amount of times I would reposition myself so that I could kick enemies off a cliff or into a spike trap. Also, unlike many other games from this time and earlier, I had no issues personally with actually getting the game to run, which is fantastic. The music was also surprisingly good. However, despite as much fun as I had with this game, I did come across a few issues. The first was the plot. It wasn't necessarily an issue, but it just wasn't the most captivating story, and most the time I was just focused on killing things. I could see it being interesting for some, but it just wasn't for me. A real issue I had though was some of the weapons. For me, the bows felt absolutely useless, and spears just felt clunky. The only weapons I consistently used were swords and daggers. Even when I tried upgrading my archery, it still felt useless. Having to upgrade archery to the max to finally get a faster reload speed when enemies can move SO fast towards you kinda just made me feel that skill points would be better spent trying to upgrade weapons that are already better in the first place, but it could just be my playstyle. The ending also felt just okay to me. I didn't feel great about it but I also didn't feel terrible. Overall, this game truly feels like a hidden gem. I wish more people knew about this game, because I didn't. In fact, I wouldn't mind if Arkane ended up returning to this game, either in the form of a sequel or a remaster. I quite honestly think that this game would do extremely well as a remaster with modern graphics, reimagined areas, and some minor tweaks to the weapon balancing and the skill tree. I highly recommend people give this game a try. [b] 8/10 [/b]

[h3] Things I like about the game [/h3] - The physics based gameplay is as good as a cold glass of water on a boiling hot day. - A relative freedom of movement. There were many instances I've ended up in places I was not expected to go to just from using basic movement mechanics like sprint jumping and clamber. - The rope bow (very jank, but super fun to use). - The freeze spell, which gives you the ability to make enemies banana peel slip onto the ground, or down a flight of stairs, or off a cliff, or into a spiked wall. [h3] Things I don't like about the game [/h3] - This game is super old, and does not like being played on modern hardware. It is guaranteed to crash multiple times throughout the game, and if your graphics settings are high enough, you won't even be able to play the game past the tutorial. - The story starts off pretty good and then falls off a cliff around 1/4 through the game. It has a whole bunch of endings, and none of them are good. - Outside of the physics, combat in this game feels really lackluster. If there's an object like a barrel or a box around, you're gonna want to use that over any of the other weapons you can find in the game. - Most of the spells in the game are pretty boring to use other than freeze. For instance, the heal spell (which is an early game spell btw) has the ability to trivialize the entire game. Since the game force feeds you mana potions you just end up spamming heal and never have to worry about taking any damage or looking for healing items at all. Most of the other spells are just variations on "Do a whole bunch of damage" which is not great. I wish there were more spells in the game like freeze, that spell is actually the GOAT. - The difficulty in this game (no matter which one you select) is pretty much dependent on how much mana you have, although the difficulties do impact how the early-mid game plays out. On normal mode the game's difficulty is pretty balanced overall, I would recommend only playing this mode. The harder difficulties are not very well balanced at all. It takes a billion hits to kill something, but they can kill you in like 1-2 hits. But, once you get past the the brutal early-mid game and get enough mana, you've pretty much just got god mode for the rest of the game. - As I've said before, the rope bow is super jank. If you don't let the rope settle before you climb it, there is a very good chance that you'll end up clipping through a wall and get yourself stuck. If this happens, you're either gonna have to turn on cheats and noclip back into the map (which I do not recommend, it will make you sick) or reload your last save; either way, not fun. - Adding on top of the rope bow jank, jumping off ropes and chains in general feels pretty jank too. The distance you travel jumping off the rope is pretty much dependent on where you're looking, so there have been times where I'm looking on a weird angle to where I want to go and just end up falling without moving an inch. This isn't really that big of a deal to be honest, but it is a bit annoying. [h3] In conclusion [/h3] There is a lot of bad things about this game, but in my eyes the good of it hard carries the game. This is a high 6/10 game for me, but I also can't really recommend the game due to how much bad there is.

The game has a lot of fun mechanics and it tries a lot of cool things. The melee system is fun and different. The magic can actually impact your surroundings, as well as be used against your enemies in various ways. The systems-driven and physics-based emergent game-play is very rewarding and unique. The skill system actually offers a lot of useful and entertaining abilities. The loot system is fine, and although not amazing, it offers some interesting variations of equipment. However, as great as some of these ideas are, some of them feel a little rough. The melee and platforming can feel a little fiddly. You don't really get enough arrows for a proper ranger build. The stealth is unreliable and unpredictable. Skill points are a little too sparse for a regular play-through, and you will not become particularly powerful until late in the game. The story is generic and shallow. With a bit more polish and testing i think this game could have been a proper hit, and I would have loved to see another attempt at this game or a sequel from Arkane. This will likely never happen though, since Ubisoft own the rights to Might and Magic. But I guess Dishonored in a way is that complete and polished version of this game, and that game is a proper masterpiece. All in all, a fun experience with some flaws, but definitely a recommendation, and an interesting insight into Arkane's immersive-sim/action-rpg legacy.

Let's be honest Dark Messiah is what happens when someone took a traditional fantasy RPG and said, "Okay, but what if we added a physics engine and made kicking a core mechanic?" And it works. It shouldn't work this well, but it does. You play as a young warrior named Sareth, who is definitely not harboring a dark secret (he totally is). You've got a sword, a bow, some basic spells… and the most overpowered lower body in fantasy gaming history. The game gives you so many environmental traps spike walls, fire pits, rope bridges, ragdoll physics and then gives you one instruction: abuse it all. 🗡 Combat: This isn't your average "click to win" system. You have to actually aim, block, parry, and time your strikes. Melee feels crunchy and impactful, especially when you mix in the environment. Freeze the floor and watch enemies slip to their doom. Set them on fire. Kick them off cliffs like you're starring in "Lord of the Rings: Parkour Edition." 🎯 Stealth? You can sneak through levels, silently taking out guards. But why stab someone from behind when you can snipe a rope, drop a chandelier on their head, and then set the room on fire just to make a point? 🔥 Magic: The magic system is great fireballs, lightning, telekinesis… but the real spell is casting chaos in every room you enter. The fun isn't just in winning it's in making your enemies look dumb while you do it. 🗺 Level Design: It's linear, but each area feels thoughtfully designed for maximum destruction. You'll start looking at every spike wall like it's a personal invitation to ruin someone's day. 🧀 Story & Voice Acting: The plot? Classic "chosen one with a dark destiny" stuff. The voice acting? Cheesier than a goblin's birthday fondue, but in a loveable way. And let's not even start on Xana, your demonic companion who whispers things like she's narrating a fantasy soap opera. 🎮 Final Thoughts: Dark Messiah is an underrated gem. It's not perfect the AI has its moments, the inventory is a little 2006, and yes, sometimes the physics break in hilarious ways but none of that matters when you're slow-mo kicking a flaming orc off a balcony while laughing like a maniac.

This is an incredible gem that should be advertised more on Steam. This is a game I thought I didn't need or didn't care for, boy was I wrong. It is an old game that has a very positive review - for a very good reason. Although I strongly recommend purchasing this game (especially on sale), some machines may have an issue running the game at first and even possibly crash issues. It did crash a few times for me, but the saving system did come handy when it did happen. The [b]gameplay[/b] is outstanding. For a game made almost 20+ years ago it still holds true to every aspect that entertains the player. Notably, the physics engine plays a large part of that fun. There is nothing like a satisfying Sparta kick that sends an enemy flying through the air, and into a pit. Paired with a solid [b]story[/b], immersive RPG elements, smooth level design, and items/traps on the map provide for a very good [b]gameplay[/b] experience. Dark Messiah (DM) at first may seem like something from Skyrim or some other sort of hack and slash game, but it offers fun moment-to-moment experiences as Doom would. Weapons are various (from swords, axes, double knives to magical abilities of all sorts) and combinations to take down opponents depend on how the player would like to approach the situation. Traps are generally laid out in strategic places, but can sometimes feel like certain rooms were created with a little excitement in mind. Some traps include wall spikes, automatic traps (such as spikes or flames), overhead traps that may hold stones or barrels, firepits to knock or kick opponents into, cliffs (especially one level in particular), and a few more. This part of the game is the true draw to the fun, the ability to create chaos and take out multiple enemies at once. Pair that with variations of swings (with the sword, for example) with an ability to swing hard, in addition to a "finisher" type swing (adrenaline) the game is rock solid. The leveling up in the game occurs as the player completes missions and allows new unlockable items that the player may find on the way (or magical abilities, depending what path the player favours more). The variation in enemies was also another welcomed feature. The [b]visuals and graphics[/b] still hold up, again, 20+ years later. There was no significant drop in FPS at any point, levels were well designed which created an immersive atmosphere, and animations (although be it old) were still providing solid effects to the player's and level's actions. Magical effects look different and weapons certainly are distinctive to one another. There are also cutscenes in the game, and it certainly doesn't have a problem throwing the player right into the story. The [b]sounds and music[/b] were also another domain that was well done. Music flowed very nicely level to level and provided a certain amount of suspense when required. All sounds were included and were well picked. Nothing in this realm became annoying, rather empowering at times when being able to hear surroundings (and plan an attack). Overall, this is a rock solid game I would absolutely recommend to anyone. I bought it on sale for $2 and I can certainly say those two dollars were probably 100%, pound for pound, worth it. This is when games were fun, this is the era before all big developers ruined fun games. This is when the Ubisoft intro sound and visual actually had meaning. [b]+ Game physics:[/b] There is a lot of contextually destructible terrain (e.g., taking down pillars to drop debris on enemies). Otherwise, there are a number of set pieces where the level changes to some degree. For example, a house built on the side of a cliff falling apart because of your added weight. This reminded me of a moment in Max Payne where an entire wall came crumbling down (except for the door frame). There was no reason for this and no other instance of destructible terrain in the game. The developers just wanted to have fun. [b]+ Gameplay diversity:[/b] The magic systems are fun to play around (e.g., creating slippery patches of floor with the ice spell instead of freezing enemies). However, the amount of mana available in the beginning does not allow much experimentation. Melee builds are quite satisfying and the equipment has interesting effects (e.g., shock damage and stun on hit, life steal / mana drain, etc.) There is also a ranged build, but I've no idea why you'd bother. [b]+ Narrative:[/b] The game is experienced from the point of view of your character, not cut scenes. Even in the introduction of the game, you walk among people evacuating within the city walls, expecting an imminent attack. Additionally, you get presented with a talkative companion that does not directly contribute to combat, but instead comments on your actions. Unlike the one in Forespoken or the one in the VtM: Bloodlines 2 gameplay trailer from the Chinese Room, this one is not annoying as hell. Even more, the developers programmed multiple voice lines, adapting to your actions in certain situations, validation your agency. [b]+ Graphics:[/b] Excellent by 2006 standards. I was particularly blown away by some rondel windows in the first level. You can actually see the other side of the window, distorted based on the glass shape. Many games within the past 10 years would rather use some pre-rendered scenes with parallax effect instead. [b]+ Level design:[/b] There is a large variety of environments. Some more pleasant than others. The latter levels are more sprawling and labyrinthine while at the same time restricting your use of the rope arrow to navigate it vertically. The game was built with multiple play styles in mind, including a stealth alternative. Therefore, there are always two-three ways of navigating the larger, open section. [b]+ Enemy AI and design:[/b] The AI is probably better than in Star Wars: Outlaws. In one instance, I noticed a goblin running away to another room after taking a few hits, only for it to be waiting in ambush when I finally got around to looking for him. This behavior was replicated at least two more times, so I don't think it was a coincidence. Additionally, the enemies have elemental resistances depending on their race (e.g., orcs and goblins are resistant to fire but susceptible to lightning). [b]- Inventory management:[/b] This game is distinctive in that you don't get XP for killing enemies, but only for completing objectives. Similarly, the items and weapons you collect are for your use only. There is no in-game economy so if you gather armor pieces for an alternative build that you won't unlock, they'll just take up space. [b]- Clunky controls:[/b] In order to equip weapons or spell, they need to be bound to your action bar. Well what can I say about this game that hasn't already been discussed. It's a game made by the ImSim legends Arkane Studios in a time where they were still finding their own footing. The basic gameplay that's happening here is an experiment in creative melee/magic combat with a Might&Magic setting. It's not fully refined, but that's probably because this is 2006 and it had to be finished at some point. It makes sense then that this game for it's ideas and their implementation would end up a Cult Classic, albeit not very influential outside of it's own circle. A game very famous for it's kick and physics based fatalities that is hard to recommend without mentioning various caveats. So, let's go with a few goods and bads for simplicity's sake: The Good: 1)THE KICK - a tool that you start with and the game makes sure to teach you about when you encounter your first enemy. Arcane wanted the game to use a lot of the versatility of the Source engine and Havok physics to make a very unique combat system. This one tool makes the game endlessly creative and pushes the player, in a good way, to try to experiment on every combat encounter. How it works: You kick to stun an enemy. If that enemy is near: a ledge, spikes, fire or any insta-kill zone they will get comically ragdolled with speed toward that thing and killed instantly. Nothing quite like kicking an orc off a cliff. 2)The leveling system. As a deeply imsim inspired game, the story will award you skill points to be used in the skill tree after you complete various objectives. There are no levels per se in the game. There are a lot of builds that can be done. 3)The melee combat. Satisfying enough and the animations are great. You also get a cool Adrenaline mode with enough hits. And melee combat also includes picking up a barrel and throwing it into a guy to knock him out. 4)The frost and telekinesis spells. Absolute bangers to transform combat encounters into puzzles. 5)The rope bow. If any of you has played an open ended sandbox game with a grapling hook, Dishonored, Prey or THIEF, you know. Wish it was used in a more sandbox style instead of semi-scripted puzzles. 6)The story. It's pretty good and some choices do matter. 7)Xana 8)Xana The mediocre: 1)The spell system. Most spells are really boring outside of the above mentioned ones. This really is a Might and Magic game, haha. 2)Stealth. It's not really relevant ever, and a bit obtuse despite having an indicator in the middle of the screen. It's half-implemented. 3)Burglary. I love a skill that's only used for secrets and literally just gives me a lockpick. 4)THE JANK. As an early Arkane game, that is mid-2000s and in the source engine, one would expect a certain ammount of jank that is happening in this game. That is not even close to 5% of the sheer level of jank that is in this game. However, not once will you get softlocked or have annoying bugs happen to you, at most some questionable design. And it's excused since it was trying to punch way above what was possible at the time with it's ideas. Let's call it the funny and harmless type of jank. Vaulting and platforming are very jank. Jump to a ledge ->Mrghh, Mrghh, Mrghh, Mrghh-> DAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAARGH->Black Screen The Bad: 1-5)THE CRASHES. Oh boy, this game was not stable at release and unless we get a full source code distribution, it won't get better... or worse. There is one fix that would let the game use 4GB RAM instead of 2, but that reduces around 20% of the crashes. The game will crash and you will come to treat it as a normal occurence. It will crash if you try and softlock yourself, corrupting your last save(doesn't matter, you have quicksaves and the autosaves come very often). It will crash with any overlay. It will crash if the hour is 18:34 PM. It will crash if you ever visited Europe in june. It will crash in 5 colours at the same time. And... it will crash because it wants to. 6)Some Pseudo Boss-Fights are a bit obtuse and result in you being 1-2shot way too many times. THOSE DAMN GOBLINS........ GET AWAY FAST, FIND SOME PLACE TO HIDE NOW......... "Quest Updated: Kill The Pao Kai." All in all a fun experience, especially with the price you can get it at nowadays. It's almost free when it's on sale. Thoroughly recommended. Also Xana is best girl.

After finally playing it for the first time in 2025, I can say this classic arena shooter improves on Quake II in almost every way. The soundtrack is intense, the weapons are satisfying, and the maps are superbly designed. Visually and thematically, it's much closer to Quake I, which I prefer over the grimy, industrial style of Quake II. There's no real campaign, but you can run any map against bots, and the AI is remarkably advanced for its era. I was genuinely impressed by how well it performs. While the arsenal is good, I do miss some of the punchier weapons from Quake II, like the super shotgun, chaingun, and railgun. Because everything is geared toward multiplayer, a lot of the balancing issues from Quake II are largely absent, and the Quake III maps feel better thought-out. My only gripe is that on modern PCs the game displays in a square window on widescreen monitors, and sometimes your desktop remains stuck in that aspect ratio even after you quit (restarts don't always fix it), which can be annoying. There are a few other minor bugs, too. There are probably workarounds, but it's still annoying. Overall, a 9.5/10 experience, though the Steam version could use some technical polish.

In Quake 4 the human race mounts a second assault wave on the Strog homeworld following the success of Operation Alien Overlord (Quake 2). You play as Kane, a marine from the Rhino squad who became known for their accomplishments during the Earth Invasion (Enemy Territory Quake Wars). The game was built on the cutting edge Id Tech 4 engine (Doom 3) leveraging a lot of its strong points with moody dynamic light and shadows, incredible levels of geometric detail and textures, as well as an impressive amount of ambience and atmosphere with sounds going on everywhere. Raven also enhanced several key areas of the engine's capabilities, and one such area was the push for a much more complex friendly AI system. Quake 2 had you be a part of an invasion but act out the entire game in solo. In Quake 4 you actually feel like you are part of an invasion and Raven approached this in an excellent way that combined the grounded dark and methodical combat of Doom 3 with friendly units that you bump into which enhances the immersion and believability that you aren't alone during the invasion. You'll run into friendly units during the entire campaign and help them sort different objectives ranging from demolition jobs to escorting technicians. The AI is also capable of actually killing enemies, so it's not just set dressing even if they go down easily. At the time cod really had established the "no one fights alone" concept but with an extremely passive friendly AI ,so it was still refreshing to have friendly units who can actually kill enemies and help you outside of scripted events. The tone of the game is quite dark and gritty and I think the direction they took with Q4 SP was great. MP retained the sort of Q3 speed and feel which honor that while SP is very well paced for the most part. You don't run too fast either making it possible to really immerse yourself and take in the atmosphere just like in Doom 3, and you even having a dedicated walk-key! Had it had a few less cheesy one-liners and a little more emphasis on darkness and horror it could've been really eerie. However Strauss is a refreshing icebreaker that is well done in it's humor, but beyond that it just undermines the horrific Strog when AI jokes about it like nothing while everything else just shows all the horrors they are capable off were friendlies lay dead, dismembered or even kept alive half mutilated to serve some horrific purpose. The quality of the levels can be extremely impressive in terms of detail and mood but also quite uneven in certain areas, especially the outdoors which seems like a push to just satisfy drastically different gameplay that might have upset butthurt people in Doom 3, but at that point in time it was the weak points of both the visuals and gameplay, and more time could've been spent on the very impressive indoor missions instead. Combat is quite well balanced, both in pacing and difficulty but at times it feels like more could've been done to pressure the player in interesting ways, especially given the quite diverse range of enemies. The need for supplies is actually something you need to keep in mind, looking for medpacks, ammo or friendly support units, because while not extremely rare or anything, you ain't flooded with ammo either, especially on the hardest difficulty "GENERAL". Unfortunately the checkpoints can be quite weird in their placement at times which in combination with General difficulty makes that quite annoying for someone who doesn't want to save scum, so playing on LT if you want a challenge and a decent level of progress without saving scumming is to recommend. The game seem to run just fine on modern hardware, all you should do is create an autoexec.cfg file in the q4base directory. Then add these lines which ensure you get a good texture hud scale plus a proper resolution. Adjust resolution to yours, and if your aspect ratio isnt 16:9 you also need to switch that parameter to the proper value. seta gui_mediumFontLimit "0" seta gui_smallFontLimit "0" seta r_customWidth "2560" seta r_customHeight "1440" seta r_mode "-1" seta r_aspectRatio "1" seta r_renderer "best" If we ever get a return to the Strogg-version of Quake one could hope that it would keep going in the vein of Quake 4 and push that dark narrative and moody methodical combat in claustrophobic environments, however with recent Doom's and their success I think that it's unfortunately highly unlikely. If anything I think they would transform it into something way more similar to the modern Dooms than the D3,Q4 era which is sad, in that case they're way better of bringing that sort of gameplay to a Quake 1 reboot.

Being a Quake fan for a while, I had the impression that Quake 4 was not just a bad Quake game but also a bad game outright. After playing it I would say that there are several complaints I would levy towards it but it is not a bad shooter or even a poor addition to the Quake franchise. The gameplay in the campaign towards the start is rather un-Quake like: you have slow movement speed and acceleration, you take a lot of damage and rely more on cover than on movement to avoid attacks. However after the mid point (In which you gain access to new powers) the gameplay and array of weaponry becomes far more familiar to Quake and overall the game becomes more entertaining. I would agree that even by this point your base run speed is too slow but the strafe jumping in this game is enjoyable: it's slower to build momentum and requires more skill compared to previous titles but in those ways I somewhat prefer it to Quake II's. The sliding is also a fun mechanic which helps further differentiate this game from its predecessors and in a way that still meshes with Quake's identity. I have played multiplayer deathmatch using the SABOT mod. It preserves the familiar movement and weapon design of earlier titles while introducing a few unique weapons, a lower time to kill, and the aforementioned sliding, all of which help the multiplayer stand on its own compared to say Quake Live. The designs of weapons and the Strogg are reasonably faithful to the prior games but also with enough of their own identity. Most of the Strogg also behave and look cooler than their earlier counterparts with only a few exceptions. I also enjoyed the increased amount of clearly alien Strogg as in Quake II it's pretty difficult to discern which Strogg are assimilated humans vs another alien race. Though onto the issues this game suffers from: a dead multiplayer scene and a lack of bots to make up for it, poor optimisation on modern systems. As far as the campaign is concerned the worst offending elements are the vehicle and turret sections which are so distant from the core of Quake's gameplay and really quite jarring. I think Quake 4 has core gameplay with allot of potential but unfortunately the campaign doesn't really utilise all that potential and there are also very few mods to compensate for that. Overall I recommend Quake 4 to Quake fans especially fans of the Strogg-Human war.
