Quake 4 occupies a fascinating and often overlooked position in the long history of id Software's iconic shooter franchise. Developed by Raven Software in close collaboration with id, it attempts something no other Quake entry has seriously pursued: a direct narrative continuation. While Quake III Arena abandoned story entirely in favor of pure competitive multiplayer, Quake 4 returns to the grim industrial sci-fi setting of Quake II and continues the war against the Strogg as a full-scale military invasion of their homeworld. The result is a game that straddles two eras of FPS design - one defined by fast, uncompromising gunplay and another driven by scripted sequences, cinematic presentation, and narrative cohesion. This ambition brings both strengths and complications, giving Quake 4 a hybrid identity that remains divisive but undeniably intriguing. From the outset, the game immerses players in a massive planetary assault. You assume the role of Matthew Kane, a newly arrived Marine whose dropship is shot out of the sky minutes into deployment. The tone becomes one of gritty desperation as you regroup with scattered squads and push forward through trenches, bunkers, and technological corridors scarred by war. Quake 4's take on science fiction is dirty, mechanical, and oppressive - a world of flickering lights, metallic shrieks, and cold machinery integrated grotesquely with living flesh. The Strogg are not merely aliens; they are cybernetic abominations created through brutal forced augmentation, and that narrative thread is woven into nearly every environment and encounter. The campaign's pacing emphasizes the escalating brutality of the conflict, offering a sense of cohesion that earlier Quake titles never attempted. As a shooter, Quake 4 blends the speed and immediacy of id's heritage with a more grounded military structure. Weapons retain the punch and clarity expected from the franchise: the shotgun, machine gun, hyperblaster, and railgun all feel satisfyingly familiar, while Strogg-inspired tech broadens the arsenal with more experimental firepower. Unlike many shooters of its era, Quake 4 gives these weapons mid-campaign upgrades that subtly alter their utility - expanding magazines, increasing stability, or adding alternative functions. This progression helps keep the combat loop fresh without venturing into RPG territory. Encounters tend to emphasize forward momentum, funneling you through combat arenas, corridors, outposts, and industrial machinery as enemies swarm with increasingly aggressive patterns. Raven Software's level design frequently shifts between tight indoor battles and larger, more chaotic skirmishes, occasionally supplemented by vehicle sequences that punctuate the infantry-focused gunplay. The single most memorable moment of the campaign arrives at its midpoint: the infamous Stroggification sequence. Kane is captured and subjected to the Strogg's horrific conversion process, experiencing the surgery in a scripted first-person sequence that remains unsettling even today. It is a rare moment of vulnerability in a genre often defined by empowerment, and it fundamentally alters both the narrative and the gameplay. From that moment on, Kane is no longer fully human, gaining certain Strogg-like enhancements that subtly change how he navigates combat. Thematically, this transformation marks the game's shift from a grounded military shooter to something more disturbing and alien. It is also the emotional anchor of the story - a reminder of what the Strogg truly are and why the war feels so desperate. The atmosphere benefits greatly from id Tech 4, the same engine that powered Doom 3. Quake 4 uses its dynamic lighting, shadowing, and texturing to create an oppressive sense of place. Strogg environments pulse with organic machinery, while human military facilities buzz with dim fluorescent lights and scattered debris. The visual fidelity, while dated by modern standards, remains cohesive and serves the narrative well. The audio design enhances this effect: metallic shrieks, mechanical thumps, alien roars, and the constant hum of technological horror contribute to a dense sonic backdrop that defines the setting. While the single-player campaign is the heart of Quake 4, its multiplayer component carries forward the arena-style legacy of Quake III. The movement physics, however, are slightly altered - resulting in a feel that is similar but not identical to its predecessor. Some fans bristled at these differences, citing slower acceleration and altered jump mechanics. Nevertheless, with modes like Deathmatch, Team Deathmatch, and Capture the Flag, the competitive framework remains intact and enjoyable, especially when enhanced by community patches and mods such as Q4Max. The player base never achieved the enduring longevity of Quake III, but multiplayer still provides a fast, skill-based experience grounded in classic arena principles. Despite its successes, Quake 4 is not immune to criticism. Its pacing occasionally falters, especially during escort missions, vehicle sections, or corridor-like sequences that feel more like filler than meaningful progress. The narrative aims higher than previous Quake titles but rarely explores its themes beyond surface-level military urgency. Enemy variety, while adequate, can become repetitive in extended firefights. These shortcomings do not undermine the overall experience, but they prevent Quake 4 from achieving the iconic status of other entries in the series. Ultimately, Quake 4 stands as a rare example of a franchise taking a bold step toward narrative continuity without abandoning its core identity as a shooter. It offers intense firefights, a cohesive world, memorable set pieces, and one of the most iconic transformation moments in FPS history. It may not fully capture the purity of Quake III's multiplayer or the anarchic intensity of the original Quake, but it forges its own path - a blend of cinematic ambition, visceral action, and grim sci-fi worldbuilding. For players willing to embrace that mixture, Quake 4 remains an atmospheric and rewarding journey into the heart of Stroggos. Rating: 8/10

I've played Quake 1-3 for years, but somehow never touched Quake 4 until 2025. And honestly? This game is criminally underrated. Played on PC (RTX 3080 Ti, 4K upscaled, M+K) using these mods: Sikkmod Lite, Quake 4 Tweaker, Assorted Fixes, Quake 4 Hi-Def, Impacts & Injury. These mods modernize the game completely - uncapped FPS, better lighting/shaders, HD textures, fixed bugs, improved blood/decals, FOV slider, the whole package. 🔥 The Game Released in 2005, developed by Raven with id Software, running on the Doom 3 (id Tech 4) engine. And YES - it absolutely feels like Doom 3's cousin: the same moody lighting, heavy shadows, chunky sound design, and that dark sci-fi horror vibe. I love it. Combat is fast, fluid, old-school Quake goodness. Railgun is still god-tier. Dark Matter Gun literally fires a black hole. Movement has that classic "Quake/Doom glide" that modern shooters lost years ago. No health regen - you hunt for health kits and armor like real FPS gamers. Level design is mostly linear but fun, with lots of enemy variety. Some later battles let you bunny-hop around like a psycho, which feels amazing. 🧠 Story & Gore You play as Matthew Kane, invading the Strogg homeworld after Quake 2. Mid-game, you get captured and brutally Stroggified in one of the wildest sequences I've ever seen in an FPS. After that you move faster, hit harder, and look way more badass. This game isn't afraid to be dark, gruesome, and weird. Human bodies being harvested, chopped, wired into machines… peak early-2000s sci-fi horror. Modern AAA would never. 👎 Weak Points NPC allies get in your way Vehicle/turret missions are boring filler Some bosses are either too easy or cheap Scoped sensitivity feels weird even after console tweaks None of these are deal breakers, but worth noting. ⭐ FINAL SCORE: 4/5 Not as iconic as Quake 1 or 2, but way better than 99% of modern shooters. Amazing atmosphere, great weapons, creative ideas, old-school difficulty, and that unbeatable Doom-3-era vibe. Play it with the lights off. Play it with mods. Play it if you miss when FPS games actually had soul. HIGHLY underrated.

Quake 4's campaign is 5 out of 10. Here are observations in bulleted form: - There are only 3 environments: extremely brown and bland top-world (mostly where vehicle missions occur), home base (where there's a good amount of chatter among different soldier folk that's worth an eavesdrop), and dark metallic rooms (where you shoot your gun at not-humans and spend 80% of the game). That last environment starts to wear after a couple hours... - It's a shame you can't adjust character voice volume, because it's sometimes hard to hear what people are telling you on comms. - The game is aggressively not scary. Sure, it has a lot of pretty shadows, and there are low-polygon-counted soldiers in test tubes that sometimes make unwelcoming noises. There's also 3 or 4 minor setpieces where a not-dog runs in front of you while violins go shrill. But none of this is scary. Which feels like a shame because it seems that Quake 4 wants to be scary. - Quake 4 is kinda like a scuffed version of Half-Life. There are: disposable soldiers who fight alongside you for as long as they can survive. A set piece / boss with giant claws that poke at you. A judicious use of non-diagetic sound. A plot told (mostly) via first-person. Sneaky commando enemies with their own radio chatter. But, even though the game was released six years after Half-Life, it isn't nearly as engrossing, or interesting, or enjoyable to play. - You can no reg shots on commando enemies who are partially behind cover. Boo. - Quake 4 starts to feel repetitive after the first two hours. Nothing really changes in terms of your interaction with the game - you go through dark corridors, shoot at the same 8 enemies (most of whom are humanoid), hit "interact" on a touch screen, then return through the corridors you just came through. Like the game's story (what if the Borg were called Strog???) and dialogue (an unintentional parody of Aliens' military personnel), the combat and player options in Quake 4 are tolerable enough to sit through, but by no means memorable. - The dark matter gun is cool. Also cool: the "glow up" scene.

Quake 4 is one of those games that stayed with me long after I played it. I remember how, as a kid, I found peace in its intense and gritty sci-fi world. The cold, metallic environments, the heavy industrial sound design, and the overall oppressive atmosphere made the experience strangely calming for me. The part I'll never forget is when you're captured by the Strogg and forced through their terrifying conversion process. That sequence was unforgettable. It wasn't just a cool plot twist - it made the conflict feel personal and gave real weight to your character's journey. You literally become what you were fighting, and the game doesn't shy away from showing every disturbing step of that transformation. Graphically, it was impressive for its time. Built on the id Tech 4 engine, the same one used in Doom 3, it had some incredible lighting and shadow effects that helped sell the atmosphere. The single-player campaign was strong, with well-paced combat and a solid sense of progression. The squad-based moments with Thunder Squad added some nice variety too. Even though the multiplayer didn't quite reach the heights of Quake III Arena, it was still a fun addition for anyone who wanted that fast-paced arena-style action. Quake 4 might not be the most iconic entry in the series, but to me, it's one of the most memorable. If you enjoy dark sci-fi shooters with a strong narrative and intense action, this one is absolutely worth playing.

Quake 4 is desperately in need of a refresh. The PC gaming industry breathed new life into Quake 2 by upgrading it to ray tracing technology in order to demonstrate Nvidia's newest AI technology of the time. Quake 2, however, wasn't just a tech demonstrator - it was a genuinely solid game. A staple FPS of the 1990's. The first PC game I owned on my brand new Packard Bell Pentium 2. I initially owned Quake 4 as one of my first games on my shiny new XBOX 360. The game looked great for the time and played faster than Quake 2 with a multiplayer component slightly less focused than Quake 3 Arena. The real focus here was returning to the singleplayer campaign introduced by Quake 2. Mankind has launched a direct assault on the "Strogg" - a race of cybernetic organisms that use humans and any other race they encounter as flesh to marry their machinery to. In Quake 2, a lone marine was able to penetrate the Strogg defenses, deactivate the planetary anti-space weapons and kill the "Makron" (Strogg leader). Quake 4 opens with a continuation of the assault. You play as Matthew Kane, a regular soldier who is about to have a long, painful and violent adventure against the Strogg war machine and their new Makron. Graphics were not a strong suit for this engine in terms of ground topography, landscape, human skin or facial features, but metal and textile surfaces it did ok. The interiors of the installations and enemy characters look great, but most other things aren't very sharp. This game runs in 720p and hasn't gotten an update to 1080p, 1440p or 4K like Quake 2 has. I have a 34" curved Alienware monitor and can't run the game in widescreen even with an RTX 3090. Quake 4 does not support ultra wide resolutions. The available resolutions are 4:3, 640x480, 800x600, and 1024x768. However, on the Xbox app for PC, you can select 4K resolution for Quake 4 in the settings. Quake 4 did have clever use of fog, smoke and shadow, but it would absolutely benefit from an RTX update even at the expense of performance - just like Quake 2 RTX did. Quake 4 is genuinely a good game with a lot of good ideas. Midway through the game, you'll be captured and forced to watch in horror as your character is mutilated while simultaneously being upgraded for combat efficiency as the newest soldier in the Strogg army. You are rescued right before the mind control device can be activated and you'll fight for humanity as a newly created super soldier capable of using Strogg technology, reading their language and surviving their death traps. It would have been revolutionary if you were allowed to choose whether to fight for humanity or turn against it at this point, but the game keeps you moving forward on the side of mankind. You fight through the Strogg installations, kill the new Makron and then the game ends on a cliffhanger. We desperately need this game updated and we desperately need a final chapter to the Human-Strogg war.

The Quake games were designed to be something of an evolution to the ideals first presented in Wolfenstein 3D and Doom - FPS games that were just as much about traversing complex levels as they were about combat. Quake and Quake 2 were a step forward in that they introduced verticality to levels, allowing them to be multi-layered: they were properly 3D now. Gamers now could not only jump, but rocket-jump as well, breaking levels if they found key-fetching too difficult. But Quake III represented a radical departure for the series, in that it had no campaign and was all about multiplayer combat. Then there was Quake 4, which may have brought the single-player campaign back, but was such an aggressive swift from what the games once were that it feels Quake in name only - a mish-mash of ideas that were much more reflective of its time than its history. Gone are the minimalist story and maze-like levels, in favor of simpler levels, cutscenes and lots of dialogues. All of this makes - at least for me - Quake 4 a fascinating game to ponder about. A time capsule of its time, capturing the zeitgeist of the mid-2000's. But I'm not here to talk about it as a contextual relic: I'm here to talk about it as a video game to anyone who might be interested in it. Quake 4 is very much linear. There can be a lot of doors, but they're mostily locked: the path forward is the door that opens for you. There's a fair share of backtracking to be had, when you're ordered to return to a previous position, and some few levels feature multiple paths that can get a bit confusing (specially since the game doesn't hold your hand that much). But overall, the levels are straightforward enough for you to know where to go, with the occasional arenas where baddies are awaiting. There are no more secret areas, but rather side rooms that can reward you with supplies should you step out from the main path - when there are path deviations, that is. This linearity is clearly inspired by Half-Life, and that's ironic since Half-Life itself was heavily inspired by Quake. When you're required to backtrack, most likely you'll find new enemies on your way back, which once again was a motif of the time. Another clear inspiration for Q4 was Call of Duty: no longer you're this one man army, fighting multiple enemies on you own, but you're often assisted by fellow soldiers, each with their own names and ranks. In Half-Life tradition, medics will refill your health if you're weak, and also tech specialists will refill your armour. I have to say that they're much more helpful than fellow soldiers in CoD games, in that they actually assist in killing enemies. But they did some of those annoying things that NPC allies usually do, like blocking my fleeting path during combat, and getting into my line of fire (but I'm defaulted not to shoot at them). Once again following the trends of the time, there are turret gun and vehicular sections - but they're not as fun as I imagined. About the gameplay, your character is curiously slow at first, which may make combat clunky and force you into a more tactical gameplay (which the game wasn't really designed for). However, and I hope this is not much of a spoiler, later in the game you'll become faster, and this may make the combat a bit closer to the original games. You'll also be able to use these heart-like health stations that are all around the place: the game shows them at first when you can't use them, only for you to realise their propose later on. In fact, after the hoover tank session, the game does start to get better, in that you'll have a large variety of weapons and new enemies to use them against. The machine gun can double as something of a sniper rifle, taking enemies at a distance. The shotgun is surprisingly accurate, and you'll also get the good old grenade launcher, as well as a devastating nail gun, and so forth. A nice touch of the game is that every once in a while, you'll find tech specialists who will upgrade your weapons, improving them considerably. One sore point for the game is its checkpoints: Quake 4 is incredibly stingy with them. I'm habituated with constant auto-saves at every moment, so when I died only to know that I missed some considerable progress, that pissed me off. So I started to instinctively quick-save the game with F5, and it became almost second nature to hit that button after getting into a new room. The game also doesn't support Steam Overlay, but then again, it's not like I would have much use for it. In terms of presentation, the game wants to woo its players with its scripted scenes and Starship Troopers vibes. But in terms of graphics, the game is just bad. The scenarios are okay, but even at max settings, character textures look blurry as if they weren't rendered properly, and models look incredibly uncanny. Even back then you have games that looked better than this. On top of that, the game did crash on me a couple of times, and there were two moments with textures missing: at the end of the tank session, the place was all dark, and I was literally guided by the lights to reach the next level. Later on, I came across a pit that had bright pink placeholder textures. Quake 4 may not be essentially a Quake game, and I don't know if it will ever receive the Nightdive Studios treatment as Quake 1 and 2 received. But it would certainly deserve so, even as a way to correct its issues.

It's a pretty solid Quake 2 sequel, and i'm glad to see the Quake fan base has warmed up to it over the last twenty years. It is essentially Quake's equivalent of Doom 3 in that it's slightly slower paced with more of a "horror" element than the pure action of the previous titles, but it's certainly not a bad game.

Quake 4 has not aged very well. The levels are ugly and uninspired; the Strogg's facilities are not too dissimilar from the UAC base on Mars, but are way uglier than what you'd see in Doom 3. Navigating the levels is also a pain because of your slow moving speed and the sometimes confusing level design; not all doors are clearly marked as open or locked and there is a decent amount of backtracking. Not fun at all! The gunplay is also boring; the guns have no punch to them and are as uninspired as the levels. The basic pistol is perhaps the worst pistol I have ever used in a video game. The enemies are either pushovers or tanks and fighting them is not fun in the least. Despite being released close in time to such classics as Half-Life 2 and F.E.A.R, there is little to no impact on your environment from your battles. Corpses disappear after a few seconds, leaving bare and boring rooms behind. It's baffling how few developers understand the importance of leaving traces after your battles behind. There are some turret sections and scripted events that are supposed to be epicsauce, but they are not interesting or fun either. The graphics are fairly decent despite their age and the worldbuilding is nice; despite the backtracking being a hassle, they sometimes change it up by having soldiers arriving with equipment, taking care of the wounded and dead and inspecting Strogg machinery. You can also listen to them talk about stuff, which is great for immersion. I don't recommend playing Quake 4 unless you are able to deal with boring levels and boring gunplay.

If by any chance you are reading this review and have not played Quake 4, I should offer a content warning- Quake 4 is extremely gory, even in comparison to other games made on Id tech 4, and has some wince-worthy scenes that some folks might not want to see. I first received Quake 4 as a holiday gift years ago when it was new, and subsequently played the 360 version and purchased the id mega-pack to get the Steam version. It's one of my favorite games from that time (after the original F.E.A.R.) and, to me, emblematic of the quality you'd expect from Raven Software in the years prior to their sentencing to the Call of Duty mines. Games like Heretic, Jedi Knight II, Singularity, all good shooters. For those unfamiliar, Quake 4 is a direct sequel to Quake 2, and bears no direct connection to other titles in the series outside of Quake Wars and certain playable characters in Quake 3 and Champions. Quake 4 tells the continuing story of humanity's struggle to overcome the alien Strogg, an army of brutal, hack-job cyborgs with a decidely bloodier appearance then say, the Borg of Star Trek. After successfully repelling a Strogg invasion of Earth (as loosely depicted in Enemy Territory: Quake Wars), human forces launched a counteroffensive against their homeworld of Strogos. A lone marine (known only by the name of Bitterman) managed to penetrate the Strogg defenses, disable their primary orbital defense cannon, and even assassinate their leader, the Makron (as depicted in Quake 2), opening the way for large scale infantry and armor deployment- this is where you come in in Quake 4, as the mute Mathew Kane, "one certified badass", newly-minted recruit to Rhino Squad. A lot of people give this game a hard time, including Civvie, for things like its relatively slow player movement, linear campaign and a lack of interest in Quake 2 to begin with, preferring either the medieval, Lovecraftian environs of the first Quake or the multiplayer focus of Quake 3 to Quake 2's drab, twisting, and frankly, samey and confusing Strogg industrial complexes. That's fair, but I don't however share Civvie's pervasive and singular dislike for things like plot and dialogue in a videogame, or his insistence that "nobody cares about the Strogg". Though his theory that Quake 4 must have had a more complex weapon upgrading system prior to the decision to have NPCs simply hand them out to the player at specific points in the campaign I think holds weight. Quake 4, now 20 years old as of this writing, is an example of a 2000s shooter that isn't garbage, and that is, of course, a short list. You can carry every weapon, most of these are powerful and flashy (I found the nailgun to be a personal favorite), and enemies come in various shapes and sizes and face you in fight arenas that bear more in common with Doom and Quake then they do with any two-bit milsim. Quake 4 has a now-well known plot twist that has probably achieved Citizen Kane levels of osmosis by this point, but suffice it to say that your character undergoes a staggering change that is reflected in gameplay by increased movespeed, max health, a different hud and the ability to read text on and interact with certain environmental objects they could not before. The game isn't perfect. The grenade launcher has a habit of blowing you up instead, there's never enough ammo for the nailgun, the combat balance is slightly inferior to that of Doom 3, and it is for better or worse what we called a "Pipe shooter". You go from Point A to Point B, shooting bad guys and pushing buttons along the way. I don't dislike pipe shooters out of principle- games like F.E.A.R. or Clive Barker's Jericho I had a great time with. Most people would count its vehicle segments against it as well, though of course I see those as high points. I've never understood the prevailing opinion against things like vehicle or turret sections and find it typical of a reality where people parrot youtubers instead of formulating their own opinions. Maybe people never did like vehicular gameplay, and that's why there's dozens of games that harken back to Doom, Quake, Blood, Duke 3d and so on, and almost none that take after Tyrian 2000, Descent, HAVOC, or Fury3. When I last played Quake 4 in 2011, I wouldn't have hesitated to tell you to buy it on Steam and give it a try. These days I can't justify telling anyone to give Bethesda or Microsoft money. So set sail for open waters and go digging for it elsewhere, if you take my meaning. It's a good game.

When doors are opening enemies spot you before the door is even halfway open. Secondly enemies can shoot through each other and you can not. So if you are shooting down a tight corridor and there are multiple enemies lined up you will get shot. The reaction speed of enemies are insanely fast, coupled with how much damage you take at close range. During the last 3 episodes I was wondering if I had just gotten tired of the game because I was not having fun. When I started Spear of Destiny I realized why I felt that way. I wasn't tired of the game, I just did not enjoy how hard the game would get later on. In conclusion: The first 3 episodes are great, the last 3 are mostly frustrating and Spear of Destiny is good up until maybe the last 5 floors or so. Big credit goes to the people behind ECWolf for creating a really solid source port. Thank god for the added automap, I could not imagine playing without it. Before reviewing W3D, I'd like to give my brief thoughts on the first two games in the series- (I played the Apple II versions of both games, since the MS-DOS version was giving me trouble.) Castle Wolfenstein (1981) - I was surprised when I learned it came out the same year as Donkey Kong. I did like the stealthy atmosphere of the game and being able to blend in by wearing a guard uniform, and the mature theming of the game. But I don't like how it can take upwards of over 200 seconds just to open a chest, especially since you need to check every single one because the war plans could be in literally any one of them. Also, sometimes when you walk into a room you'll walk right on top of a guard, and just get caught before you can even react. You might need savestates in order to finish the game. Beyond Castle Wolfenstein (1984) - The game had some improvements over the first, like how the closets (functionally the same as chests) just open when you interact with them. And they can have a lot more stuff in them, like diaries and items owned by Hitler himself or people related to him. I also like how you're already undercover in the game, but the Nazis are wise to your scheme now, so you have to use passes to get through them. The problem is, you have only two chances to show them the right pass, and if you fail twice, they practically kill you on the spot. And they require a different pass on each floor, so that could just throw away the whole run. Honestly, I would love to see some kind of remake on the first two games. But now, Wolfenstein 3D review. Because, I'm sure none of the people reading this give any craps about the first two games. And I think id Software too, they probably said "Kids these days don't want to sneak past the guards, they want to massacre their way through the guards!" Kinda like Henry Stickmin: Stealing the Diamond, where you choose to either bust in or sneak in. My friend jokingly calls this game "Bootleg Doom". But I think it's cool to look at certain things in this game and see what evolved into stuff we see in Doom. By 1992 id Software had already dabbled into the art of 3D FPS games, with Hovertank 3D in 1991 (You can get that on Abandonware). Then earlier in 1992 came Catacombs 3D, which was a 3D FPS version of Catacomb and Catacomb II (Which you can get all of those and more on GOG via Catacombs pack), so they were also immersed in taking 2D games and making them 3D. I will say, I definitely do think Doom was a massive improvement over Wolfenstein 3D, mostly because of the enemies. After you beat episode 3, all the episodes onward just feature the same enemies: Guards, killer dogs, Stormtroopers, and Officers. You don't even see the mutants or fake Hitlers after that. The only new enemies were a really weird kind of enemy in one of the secrets floors. But beyond that, the extent of the new enemies are pretty much just the bosses. But I did like all of the German-spoken voice clips they made. Spear of Desinity- SoD was pretty much just more Wolfenstein 3D, but it still suffers from the same same-ish enemy problem the base game had. At least we had the mutants, bot not the fake Hitlers. HOWEVER... I think it made up for what you see in the very last level. But I shan't say more, for I will spoil the end. Admittedly I think Wolfenstein 3D tarnished the bit of realism the first two games had, but I can look past it. Great game if you want an old first-person shooter maze game. (Seriously this whole game was basically one giant maze.)

Installed and ran quickly just to leave a review. Contrarily to the anniversary jobs that have been done on later id Software titles, this is just the original on DosBox, so unless you want to just play the unadultered original (and even so, it's better if you take the files and set up DosBox better), getting a source port like ECWolf may be a good idea. Where would we be if Wolf3D never was, or was developed as originally intended, a stealth game in line with the 1980s inspirators? The FPS genre would likely still have emerged one way or another but it doesn't change that, in the timeline we live in, this is rightfully considered the title that codified it. It is still fun enough to play in short bursts but can't escape a fundamental issue: it's a game that was already dated by 1994. In that era of huge leaps and bounds forward for videogames, just 18 months later Doom came and it was such an amazing improvement in all aspects that Wolf3D immediately felt much older than it was. I have amazing memories of the game because I first played it in the Summer of 1992; was it two years later, you can be sure I'd have had a very different impression of it. It's not a matter of graphics but rather gameplay and especially level design; Doom benefited from the technical innovations in that aspect too, compared to the blocky grids you get here. That doesn't mean it can't be still fun, ironically even for its own simplicity, but there's simply so much better to play nowadays - even if all those other games, ultimately, have to thank Wolfenstein 3D for existing. Get a copy and keep it like a revered patriarch.

Wolfenstein 3D, developed by id Software and published on Steam by Bethesda Softworks, stands as one of the most influential titles in gaming history-a cornerstone of the first-person shooter genre and a defining moment in the evolution of interactive entertainment. Originally released in 1992, its arrival reshaped the industry, transforming the PC from a platform for puzzle and strategy games into a haven for fast-paced, visceral action. Even decades later, its impact is unmistakable. While its mechanics and visuals now feel primitive by modern standards, Wolfenstein 3D remains both a time capsule and a masterclass in elegant design, demonstrating how simplicity and focus can birth an entire genre. The premise is stark and straightforward. You play as B.J. Blazkowicz, an Allied spy captured by the Nazis during World War II, imprisoned in the labyrinthine depths of Castle Wolfenstein. Armed with little more than grit and a pistol, you must escape your captors, steal enemy secrets, and ultimately take revenge on the Third Reich. It's a plot as direct as its mechanics-one that reflects the game's single-minded commitment to action. There are no lengthy cutscenes, moral choices, or expository detours. Instead, the story unfolds through gameplay: the creaking of metal doors, the guttural shouts of German guards, and the echo of gunfire reverberating down dimly lit corridors. Every movement feels immediate, every encounter deadly, and every victory earned through reflex and instinct rather than cinematic spectacle. What made Wolfenstein 3D revolutionary was not just its premise, but its presentation. Using John Carmack's pioneering 3D engine, the game simulated depth and perspective in a way that was unprecedented for the time. The illusion of traversing fully realized 3D environments-despite being built from flat planes and repeating textures-was nothing short of mind-blowing in 1992. The sensation of running through corridors, hearing enemies around corners, and turning to face threats in real-time gave players an entirely new sense of immersion. The technical limitations of the era forced id Software to innovate, and from those constraints came design choices that defined the genre: fast movement, simple controls, and immediate feedback. These foundational ideas-combined with the smooth fluidity of motion-made the act of playing Wolfenstein feel thrillingly new. The gameplay itself is brutally efficient. Each level is a maze of rooms, corridors, and secret passages filled with enemies, treasure, and key-locked doors. Success depends on mastering the rhythm of exploration and combat: listening for enemy footsteps, conserving ammunition, and uncovering hidden caches behind false walls. The enemies are simple yet effective obstacles-guards who shout in German before attacking, vicious dogs that rush without hesitation, and later, heavily armed soldiers and mutants. Their AI is primitive by modern standards, but their relentless aggression forces the player to stay alert. The absence of complex enemy behavior is compensated by clever level layouts that keep the player guessing. One wrong turn can lead to a dead end; one missed key can force a desperate backtrack under fire. It's a design philosophy built around tension and immediacy rather than complexity. What makes the experience so enduring is its rhythm. The game moves at a relentless pace, encouraging fluid motion and quick reflexes. There is no stamina system, no cover mechanic, and no need to pause for reloading-only a constant push forward. The speed of movement gives the game an almost arcade-like energy, transforming the act of clearing a corridor into something instinctual and satisfying. Even today, few games capture that raw momentum. Each shot has weight, and the combination of simple controls and precise responsiveness ensures that even decades later, Wolfenstein 3D feels surprisingly playable. The shooting is tight, the hit feedback immediate, and the loop of kill, collect, and advance remains addictive in its purity. Visually, the game has aged, yet its aesthetic still carries a certain charm. The limited color palette, flat textures, and blocky environments contribute to a claustrophobic atmosphere that suits its premise perfectly. The pixelated portraits of guards, the stark steel walls, and the flickering lights all contribute to an uncanny sense of menace. The art style, though simple, captures a grim caricature of wartime horror, balancing cartoonish exaggeration with genuine tension. The sound design enhances this effect-enemies bark "Achtung!" when spotting you, and their cries of defeat punctuate the eerie silence of the castle's corridors. The music alternates between triumphant marches and ominous tones, reinforcing the feeling that you are both predator and prey in a deadly labyrinth. Beyond its mechanics, Wolfenstein 3D's importance lies in its legacy. It was the blueprint from which the modern first-person shooter evolved. It introduced conventions that became staples of the genre: health pickups, ammo management, secret rooms, and key-based progression. It also set the tone for countless successors, from Doom to Half-Life and beyond, proving that first-person perspective could create both tension and empowerment. More than that, it demonstrated that video games could elicit emotion through interaction rather than scripted storytelling. The fear of rounding a corner, the thrill of a well-timed ambush, and the satisfaction of finding a hidden cache-all of these feelings were born here. Revisiting the game today, especially through the Steam version published by Bethesda Softworks, can be both nostalgic and enlightening. It runs through DOSBox, preserving the look, sound, and feel of the original. The low-resolution graphics and dated mechanics serve as reminders of how much design has evolved, but also how much remains the same at its core. Modern shooters may have layered on narrative, spectacle, and technical complexity, yet they still draw from Wolfenstein's foundational formula: move fast, aim true, and survive. Playing it now is less about chasing thrills and more about understanding history-experiencing firsthand the birth of a medium's defining genre. Despite its age, Wolfenstein 3D's power endures in its simplicity. It's not just nostalgia that makes it worth revisiting-it's the purity of its design. The game wastes no time, makes no apologies, and hides no ambition. It simply asks the player to fight, explore, and escape. In doing so, it achieves something rare: timelessness through clarity. Its corridors may be narrow, its enemies predictable, and its world pixelated, but within those constraints lies the blueprint for everything that came after. Wolfenstein 3D is not just a piece of gaming history-it is the beginning of a revolution, and it remains, even today, a masterclass in how to turn technical limitation into creative brilliance. "Get Psyched!" Wolfenstein 3D is a FPS developed by id Software and released in 1992. It is the first major title of the genre, and a true pillar of video gaming. You play as B.J. Blazkowicz, a talented American spy tasked with infiltrating Nazi fortresses to thwart their plans and turn the tide of the war. This time, the objective focuses on Castle Wolfenstein, where some seriously shady stuff is going down. You'll need to face hordes of vile Nazis and navigate this stone maze in hopes of confronting the Führer himself! Once the first three episodes are completed, a second campaign of the same caliber extends the adventure. In reality, it's a prequel: the "Nocturnal Missions," where B.J. must sabotage the Germans' chemical warfare plans. The game contains a total of 60 levels, offering hours of fun!The fortress is heavily and effectively guarded, with numerous enemies lurking around. The soldiers you encounter most often are simple guards in brown uniforms, armed with a basic pistol. They shout "Achtung!" when they spot you and offer little resistance. Then come the SS, the "Schutzstaffel!" as they call themselves, tougher and equipped with a submachine gun. They cry "Mein Leben!" ("My life!") as they breathe their last. Even higher in rank, the Officers are almost identical but wear white uniforms. These enemies yell "Spion!" (Spy!) when they see you, move and shoot much faster, and scream "Mein Führer"" when taken down. Trust me, you're not going to like them much. But they're nothing compared to the mutant soldiers with a weapon in their chest, who spew purple blood when you kill them. Those are as fast as they are infuriating to fight. Oh, and they give a Nazi salute with each arm when they shoot. You'll occasionally come across dogs, which are just cannon fodder, almost insignificant. Each chapter ends with a boss that you'll need to shower with bullets to defeat. I should point out that the damage enemies deal increases the closer they are to you. To exterminate all these nasty Krauts, our dear B.J. Blazkowicz has only four weapons, but they get the job done: A simple knife with ridiculous range, a pistol (Luger), a submachine gun (MP-40), and a Gatling-type machine gun. Restoring health is done by finding medkits or eating food scattered around the mazes. I hope you like chicken and dog food! Expect labyrinthine levels, but relatively easy to navigate, most of which can be completed in a few minutes if you're on point. You'll need to find keys to unlock doors to progress. However, some levels are fiendishly complex and convoluted, and they'll melt your brain. Joking aside, the game is generally fairly easy, but things get tougher from the second half of the sixth chapter. The further you progress, the more numerous the enemies become, and the means to fight or heal grow scarcer. You'll need to show tenacity and patience, but it's far from insurmountable. Besides slaughtering Nazis, you can collect riches they've plundered: various treasures, gold crosses, and chalices, all of which boost your score. A little tip: you'll need to push certain walls to achieve your goals. I won't say more! The environments are relatively minimalist, even quite austere, but not without a certain quaint charm. You'll traverse corridors made of wooden, stone, or brightly colored brick walls, adorned with portraits of the Führer, Nazi flags, and swastikas, and some rooms are decorated with golden eagles, knight armor, and other old relics. But you'll often come face-to-face with skeletal corpses on the floor, trapped in cages, or hanging. The music is fantastic, and for good reason: it's composed by Bobby Prince. It's super catchy, almost addictive, and I can't stop humming it while playing! Now let's talk about a few things that annoy: The levels are very flat and lack any verticality. The graphics are ultra-pixelated, made worse by the very short draw distance. There are no quicksave or quickload buttons, and you have to strafe by pressing a dedicated button. There's also no minimap, which demands a lot of concentration (like the camps, get it?). I'm nitpicking, I know, the game is still super fun despite all this, but a remaster like DOOM 1 & 2 wouldn't hurt. If you loved Wolfenstein 3D, you can extend the fun with its expansion, Spear of Destiny, which adds nearly 20 levels that aren't very original but are still more convoluted and packed with enemies. Be warned, though-the difficulty ramps up steadily, and the developers didn't hold back. What more can be said about Wolfenstein 3D than it's a cult classic shooter? It's a true cornerstone of the genre! Would you dare call yourself a FPS fan if you've never played this classic?

[h1]GET PSYCHED ![/h1] [b]id[/b][i] /ɪd/n.[/i] [b]1.[/b] [i]The one of the three divisions of the psyche in psychoanalytic theory that is completely unconscious and is the source of psychic energy derived from instinctual needs and drives.[/i] Everything that could be said or analyzed about this iconic title has already been done. A revolution in its time, a pivotal step in the history of video games. Like it or not, it set the standard, shaping future games and establishing rules that are still followed to this day. [b]Wolfenstein 3D[/b] is nothing less than the very essence of "First-Person Shooter": fun, action, stimulation. You've got to admit, id Software chose their name wisely: their games have always stayed true to that spirit. Yet, until very recently, I never really dared to put my hands on it. I saw it as a grandparent with a rich life and many stories, but a bit boring and prone to rambling; the kind you're happy to visit at Christmas or birthdays, just to be polite and stay in touch. So I dove in with great motivation, and I was committed to seeing it through: [b]Wolfenstein 3D[/b], plus its "sequel" [b]Spear of Destiny[/b], and its two official expansions: [b]Return to Danger[/b] and [b]Ultimate Challenge[/b]. One hundred and twenty mazes to find and defeat the ultimate evil: Adolf Hitler. No joke. [h3]Wolfenstein 3D[/h3] The game was originally released in two phases. The first 30 levels present the main storyline. You're the legendary B.J. Blazkowicz, an American spy captured by Nazis and imprisoned in Castle Wolfenstein. The mission is simple: escape the castle, then hunt down Adolf Hitler to end the war. A problem quickly cropped up for the developers after the game's success. With Hitler defeated at the end, how do you continue a story based on fighting Nazi Germany...? By making a prequel. The next 30 levels then serve as a prequel, showing Blazkowicz's missions that led to his capture. The game offers four weapons: a knife, a pistol, a submachine gun, and a chaingun. The shotgun wasn't yet an FPS staple, and you'll also have to get by without projectiles. Each weapon more or less replaces the previous one, so once you have the chaingun, there's little reason to go back. Enemies aren't particularly smart, but they're numerous and well organized. [b]Wolfenstein 3D[/b] plays very differently from later classics. Enemy fire hurts, and you're no superhero: two bullets can take you out on higher difficulty. The challenge is largely about enemy placement and player reaction speed. Enemies respond to sound: a notable detail for its time, and you'll need to exploit that to survive. If you rush into Wolfenstein head-on, you're in for a rough time. Level design is probably the weakest aspect: complicated, yet limited. You'll trek down long hallways, visit countless rooms, and collect keys to open elevator doors. Luckily, no traps: your only foes are Nazi troops. The engine's limitations often feel annoying: few textures to differentiate rooms, very little decoration, and no automap in the original version. If you're after 100% completion like I was, you'll need patience, and a good memory. Secrets, hidden behind push-walls, are a pure torment. They were added late in development, and it shows. In [b]Doom[/b] or [b]Duke Nukem 3D[/b], you spot secrets by noticing cracked walls, misaligned textures, odd objects... Here, any wall could hide a secret, with no logical hints. Worse, finding some secrets in the "wrong" order can block access to others. The soundtrack by Bobby Prince paces the adventure well. The tunes are catchy and pleasant, but don't whistle the intro theme... it might annoy some folks. :) Honestly, I didn't expect to enjoy blasting SS soldiers so much. The game responds well, it's fast, stripped to the essentials, but masters its subject. Sure, its successors went bigger and better, so comparing wouldn't be fair, but [b]Wolfenstein 3D[/b] absolutely nails what it sets out to do, and this is what matters. [h3]Spear of Destiny[/h3] Released just four months after [b]Wolfenstein 3D[/b], [b]Spear of Destiny[/b] positions itself as its sequel, or rather, a prequel. This time, you must recover the spear of destiny, said to have pierced Christ's body. Adolf Hitler had the Nazis steal it and bring it to Nuremberg Castle, thinking it would help him to master dark forces... [b]Spear of Destiny[/b] doesn't improve the original formula, and is essentially identical, using the same engine with only minor tweaks. This "sequel" adds little beyond new levels, more action, a tougher difficulty, new music tracks, and a few fresh textures. Still, it'd be a shame to skip it: [b]Spear of Destiny[/b] is more focused and inspired than much of the base game. Its level design is noticeably better, action is constant, and its ending delivers a twist that is worth seeing... Trust me ! It's easy to see the direction the studio would take with [b]Doom[/b] after that...! [h3]Mission Pack #2: Return to Danger[/h3] Released two years after the original game, [b]Return to Danger[/b] is the first official expansion for [b]Spear of Destiny[/b]. It was developed by FormGen, not id Software, and that shows. The Nazis once again captured the spear and took it to Scandinavia, where they're trying to build their own atomic bomb… Gameplay remains unchanged, as do the music tracks. Where [b]Return to Danger[/b] tries something is in its visuals. Most sprites and textures were redone, but let's face it: not everyone has what it takes to be a designer. They clearly fell in love with bright colors, especially blue, repainting weapons, many walls, even dogs… blue everywhere! The result oscillates between passable and ridiculous, but at least it brings some freshness after [b]Spear of Destiny[/b] which stuck completely to the original game's visuals. The real problem is the level design. [b]Return to Danger[/b] is easier than [b]Spear of Destiny[/b], but levels quality is very uneven. Some maps can be finished in under twenty seconds, and many rooms are completely empty. Enemy placement also often feels off. Once again, many secrets have to be found in the 'right' order, but I appreciate the idea of marking some with hidden rat corpses nearby. An extension not as dreadful as some say, but forgotten over time for obvious reasons. [h3]Mission Pack #3: Ultimate Challenge[/h3] Released at the same time as [b]Return to Danger[/b], [b]Ultimate Challenge[/b] is the second and final official expansion for [b]Spear of Destiny[/b]. The Nazis once again stole the spear, this time taking it into Hitler's bunker, who just made a pact with a demonic force granting him knowledge of futuristic weapons... Gameplay, arsenal, and enemies remain unchanged, mirroring [b]Return to Danger[/b]. Graphics look nearly identical. The major improvement here is level design. The difference between [b]Return to Danger[/b] and [b]Ultimate Challenge[/b] is striking: the mapping is competent, even matching some of [b]Wolfenstein 3D[/b]'s better levels. Most feel inspired and concise, offering a much more pleasant experience. Secrets are once again hinted, this time by pools of blood, making the hunt less frustrating. Everything else is similar except for the ending: [b]Ultimate Challenge[/b] goes for surprise like [b]Spear of Destiny[/b] did, linking the Wolfenstein universe with... [b]Doom[/b]! I won't spoil it, but it's a fun, unexpected finale. [h3]Too Long ! Didn't Read lol.[/h3] [b]Wolfenstein 3D[/b] earned its rightful title as the grand‑father of FPS, and is still super fun and interesting to play, for its huge impact and the brilliant simplicity that still shines through. Patience is key to adapt to its technical limits and level‑design inconsistencies, but overall, Blazkowicz's adventure deserves players' attention just as much as its successors, which may age better, but share all its strengths. Now, you know what to do. [h1]GO BLAZKO ![/h1]

On one hand, this is REALLY impressive stuff for a game released in 1994, especially for a game running on DOS. That being said, when you look at it as a game and not as an art piece, it's not the best. I'd still probably recommend it for the historical factor (and it's only 5 dollars at the end of the day), but it's not super fun to play. - Probably the most important thing to know about this game going in is that it's a DIRECT port of the original DOS version. The game files literally come packaged with a build of DOS Box, and all of the little foibles that come alongside a DOS game should be kept in mind. - Other reviews have mentioned the controls, and the tank controls are definitely clunky, but I was surprised by the mouse controls, and how they were also just as clunky. If you've ever played TF2, held down ALT, and tried to move your mouse, that's very similar to how the mouse controls feel. They're very slippery, and the speed is uncapped (likely because most mice used trackballs around this time), so you can fly around levels in a way that doesn't feel very intentional. Though, to be fair, I definitely prefer it to how slow Wolf Guy's normal movement speed is. - The enemies are weirdly polarized (fitting for not-zis) in their mechanics, and especially in their damage output. Damage is distance-based, and if an enemy sees/hears you from around a corner and gets a cheap shot off, you're going to lose 50 health out of nowhere. Likewise, if an enemy shoots at you from a long distance, it'll do almost nothing. The same is true with your own weapons, and you can do some crazy things if an enemy doesn't see you first, but the enemies can definitely take advantage of it more, leading to some frustrating moments. - The level design is very serpentine and aimless, and it's shockingly easy to get lost, especially in levels that require keys. This would be much less of a problem if there was a map, but that doesn't get added until DOOM, so for now I hope you enjoy retracing your steps looking for the one door you haven't opened yet. - The game also has a lives system, and is also the originator of the annoying trait of this breed of game to respawn you with just the default weapon. When compounded together, it means you're likely to lose multiple lives in a row if you die once, and if you run out of lives entirely, you lose ALL of your progress. I'm very happy that this kind of design was left behind in the arcade era, but unfortunately this game is just old enough to still get caught in that cultural crossfire. Overall, I probably wouldn't recommend it to the average person, but if you're looking for a gaming history lesson, or you want to see where DOOM, John Carmack, and John Romero got their start, it's probably worth picking up.

Doom I + II is one of those games that just leaves you wondering whether it hates you or actually wants you to win. The games themselves are very fair, even if it constantly feels like you're backed into a corner, trying to gain ground against hordes of enemies who not only control space but actively use your own goals to ambush you at every step. Still, the mechanics quickly teach you that you can always work around them, no matter the situation you find yourself in as long as you go about it the right way (and have enough bullets). While there are sections that definitely test your ability to just "suffer" through them, the game doesn't throw you into that brutality from the start. There's a clear progression between every level and episode, and it genuinely feels like the game trusts you to learn from previous encounters as it becomes progressively more punishing. They've ported, rereleased, enhanced, remastered Doom so many times at this point, that it's gone from dated feeling game, and visually dated game, to something both unique in its gameplay and its visual/atmosphere. I was honestly one of those ppl who were on the fence of how much content has been added to this game and how much ppl keep playing said content despite it being essentially the same gameplay mechanics and confinements on repeat. But finally jumping into the larger OG Doom world with the most recent update/remaster of Doom, I finally get it. First off lets get some stuff out the way. Lets talk about the most important thing, the base game. With Doom + Doom 2, you get the definitive versions of the games with all they're additional dlc and add-on content. The visuals are polished up and look super neat and clear. When it comes to 2D artwork and sprites, when we talk about graphics you talk about the art direction, and quality, that's why in the same sentence you can say something like Cuphead has great graphics and The Last Of Us, it's all about if they're executing what they're going for and whether its visually interesting. So with that said, Doom holds up graphically. Its assisted by the fact the game had a clear vision and visual narrative. The art direction is cool, levels tell a narrative with their themes. However Doom + Doom 2 its a whooping game, to complete it, its about 70 stages long and both games (similar to games like OG RE1 and 2 or Crash Bandicoot 1 and 2,) the games essentially use the same exact hardware/engine/assets and it does in the long haul get visually repetitious. The games boil down to run down cities, research/laboratory facilities, and hell, and both games have you go through similar visual narratives. There's so much to talk about Doom and why ppl keep coming back. The next thing is the music. Doom at this point is essentially an interactive soundtrack. I deadass sometimes just leave Doom playing in the background while I play comp games, because the metal soundtrack and accompanying STs are that much of a banger. AND THE GAME HAS TONS MUSIC CONTENT. You can either play the original songs using the sfx of their 90s hardware, or play new version mixed with the latest music tech. Both soundtracks sounds amazing but I am particular found of the new arrangements, they simply slap dawg. On top there's a bunch of new music added via dlc, ranging from electronic, sci-fi, rock, metal, heck even Celtic music, YES YOU READ THAT RIGHT, CELTIC MUSIC. The game continues to see new tracks added and by actual talented/famous musicians, for example legendary artist Buckethead made music for the Sigil dlc, YEAH BUCKETHEAD, WHAT. And than you have artist Thorr who made the ST for Sigil 2 which came out a little over a yr ago. Doom music is an experience, and has become its own central thing. As I have the music playing, when the game im playing its trying to cue up a match, me and my friend will dive pick up the control and dive into Doom while we wait since the game is left on pause. And a great way to gradually progress through the huge amount of content this release has. Now the gameplay. Doom isnt a narrative game, the true focus of the game is the gameplay loop, that's literally where all the value is at, so if you play Doom, you play Doom because you want a challenging shooter experience, or you're an exploration junkie and want to find all the creative secrets. You progress your way through differently designed levels, some are linear, some are maze like, others are more open-worldish and require tons of exploration, some have a heavier focus on action and others heavier on exploration and unlocking the next path. The action boils down to fighting waves or groups of enemies with the devs finding ways to surprise you with encounters. Lower grunts alone dont pose much of a threat, its only when they gang up, and only higher level enemies pose a threat alone or in small numbers, here is the core of the game, groups require carefully dodging or finding cover, stuff like fireballs can be moved around, but bullets track and for that you need cover, so you're constantly having to move, or peak out of areas to kill and avoid dmg. Resources can be scarce, especially if you dont know how to manage them so this is one of those games where every shot counts. You have a decent weapon variety, and the game encourages to not only use them all but to swap between them regularly. For example you avoid using the super shotgun, as its better suited for higher level enemies and for lining up shots with said enemies, bullets can pierce and you can kill 2 or 3 enemies at the same time, saving precious ammo. Soon as the meatball enemy that spits fire gets close, I switch to the chainsaw, saves you ammo and it stunlocks them, and you end up using them as cover because they also stick to the chainsaw, than immediately switch to the machine gun or regular shotgun and kill the rest. There's a surprising amount of depth when it comes to not only using which weapon for the right moment, but also in how you manage your limited ammo resources. So because of that I feel Doom is designed to be played at Hard or above. On normal as you learn the game it starts to get easier, but on hard the true design of the game flourishes and puts your skills and mechanics to the test. Trying to get the highest score possible in a level makes things even harder, as enemy encounters and obstacles becomes so hard to deal with that you have to rely on alot of cheese to kill enemies without taking dmg or using too much ammo, and thats legit the crux of the game, avoiding dmg and saving ammo, as you need both for harder encounters. Another big part of the loop, is knowing when to grab resources, for example, shotgun pack gives you 20 ammo, even if you only need 10 ammo to max out, once you grab it, it goes away, the remaining ten ammo doesnt stay, cause of this when you need to get through a room where you can only rely on your shotgun, and there's 20 enemies requiring 40 shots, and you only have 20 rounds and a case of 20 near you, not only do you need to hit almost every shot to avoid melee combat, you gotta make sure you dont grab the ammo too soon, as you'll replenish it 14, get only 6 and lose 14 rounds, and now you dont have enough. Its the same with health packs, you're gonna want to count how many you see and avoid grabbing them, than when you have a tough group encounter where dmg is almost unavoidable, you're gonna want to receive as much dmg possible, than to retreat grab the pack and get as much value possible to beat the encounter. You can legit end up stuck in a stage because you end up with not enough health to fight something. Than there's the exploration, ignore or dont. Finding all the secrets is an experience itself, and if thats your thing, playing this game on normal is fine as action and getting the high score with enemy kills isnt your objective. The main objective is to get through every level. But there's secondary objectives in the form of clear times, finding and killing all enemies, finding all secrets and finding all items. The game is fun as af even by modern standards, its super simple but has so much depth. Its best experienced playing the game in chunks as the game is long and hard. But the true best way to experience Doom is via coop. The way coop has been added and than evolved in Doom has made the game an experience of its own. The OG Doom was a single player game, that was the design, but through the beauty of its design the game beautifully to a coop game and great one at that. Imo this is the biggest selling point, is the coop experience. If you're hardcore gamer, or a boom shooter enthusiast, sure Dooms action and challenge is what you want, but if you're just a casual gamer, and or coop enthusiast, than Doom I dare say is a must have. It's Doom. I feel like I shouldn't need to say more. I'm going to though out of sheer love for the game. I've played the original version of Doom on and off for nigh on 30 years. Through SNES and original PC to PlayStation versions. Once I saw this version was available I made it my mission to 100% it. Blimey, that was no mean feat! In some of the add ons the levels turn into a nightmare of ridiculous traps and demonic ambushes that you won't survive first time! Its taken patience and perseverance to finally finish it , but its a journey I'm so glad I undertook. The game plays like a dream. Even now the combat is tight, the enemies are as iconic as they are lethal and the weapons (including the Incinerator and the Calamity Blade, replacing the Plasma gun and BFG in Legacy of Rust) are simply perfect. I'll never forget that room on the Soul Vats level that lets you go mad with the Calamity Blade. For me, the Super Shotgun is the best pound for pound weapon, although I do have a fondness for the Chaingun and Chainsaw as well! The sound surprised me in this version. Its all the original music! Digitised and ripped off Metallica, Pantera and Alice in Chains riffs are amazing, but when you add the remixed versions in, the game changes. Metal guitars and double kick come screaming at you with as much danger as the demons you're killing! Several times I had to stop and have a little headbang! Where can I buy this soundtrack?? The rest of the soundscape still holds up too. Guns bark and demons growl in the darkness. The sound design is excellent and really plays on your fears. You know they're out there but you can't see them yet... Then you fire up the chainsaw with that beautiful, distinctive rasp. Heavenly. If I had to add a criticism, it's that some of the levels are too much exploring, platforming and puzzle solving. I don't mind a bit of distraction from the bloodshed but this is a shooter. The most prolific FPS probably. If I wanted puzzles galore I'd play Tetris! There's also a heck of a lot of platforming considering there is no jump button! This is minor stuff though. The game is an absolute classic and even if you only go through the core Doom and Doom II, you'll have a good time. And if you find it too easy, just crank up the difficulty. I guarantee you won't survive without a horrible death or 6! Boom. Chuck.... chunk..... Boom!!!

Note: Although Steam says I only have 27 hours on this game, most of my time spent playing Doom has been on community source ports or console ports outside of Steam, so my real playtime is probably at several thousand hours. There's nothing I can really say about Doom that hasn't been said past 30 years. The original games are perhaps [i] the greatest [/i] first person shooters ever created and have been kept alive by a strong spirited community over the past three decades. If you're looking for a game with practically endless amount of content, then Doom is your game. This port in particular is a great way for a more casual player to experience the original doom games and their expansions (Plutonia Experiment, TNT Evilution, Master Levels). It also contains the formerly console-exclusive expansion "No Rest For The Living", John Romero's "Sigil" and a brand new episode "Legacy of Rust". The port also has a built-in mod browser with access to a wide range of community-released content over the years. There also aren't any major glitches within the port that come to mind. Only ones I've encountered is the Bethesda.net login freezing/crashing the game on rare occasions and a strange audio issue within the port related to wireless headphones with built in microphones (causes the audio to become very muffled. Inputting playfab_shutdown in the console fixes this though it also disables multiplayer for the session) As for the new episode, it adds new weapons and enemies that manage to not feel too out-of-place from the regular roster and includes an outstanding soundtrack. Level design is solid too, although the game can get very uptight about ammo in certain stages. I highly recommend playing through the episode on a lower difficulty on your first go, as it was clearly designed with Doom community's higher average skill level in mind.

Doom. I really can't say anything more. It started everything related to video games. Every single FPS still has a strand or two of DNA in it that is directly ported from Doom. It was the first video game along with Ghosts N' Goblins (NES), and Super Mario Bros (1, 2, 3, and Super Nintendo all stars ports, super mario world) i've ever played. It has had such a massive cultural impact and proves to be such an incredible pioneering technical achievement, through it's sheer number of system ports and cross platform compatibility to how minimal of hardware the game can run yet it provides so much! The gameplay loop never gets tiring. It drops you in, no nonsense, no explanation, you do your thing. I recommend not looking anything up, and just experiencing the game. You won't get to experience it a first time all but once. Yes, it's simple. But it works. You want to see a masterpiece in video game design, this is it when nobody did this before. IT invented Multiplayer Deathmatch and cooperative play. Doom clones were Wolf3D raycasting engine knockoffs. They used the funds to invest into another developer of things that eventually started giving you the Call of Duty games you all know and love/hate... Raven Software. Yes there were First Person Shooters before this, Catacombs 3D being probably the first example, Wolfenstein 3D the first to gain international traction, Doom... yeah that started everything. These guys had the weight on their shoulders to come up with follow ups that either pushed the industry or it weren't worth coming to the party. Doom II, Quake, Quake gave you Half-Life, Half-life gave you steam. "heavily modified Quake Engine - Goldsource" It is the Quake Engine lmao so much so that quake content and half life content run with very little modification. BSP was invented with Doom to give it the fluid rendering it had with very efficient CPU usage. Everything uses BSP. I'm not trying to detract from valve lmao I'm rendering credit upon where they got their stuff and inspiration from because they'd say the same thing and we all know it. Half-Life, somehow managed to pull a doom like industry splash in 1997/1998... while Quake was still riding high. That aside, Doom... every weapon has a use and can be used, every map isn't a linear path, enemies are well balanced and you have to fight to survive. Exploration and curiousity reveals both challenge and reward. You will be teased with the prospect of a cool weapon hidden in a secret area to the original monster closets and traps. With five difficulty settings that affect enemy and item placement, you can adjust the game to your liking. The game being what it is, it is an easy game to pick up and play, save as you will, leave it be, and return to over and over and over again. All you have to worry about controlwise is turning/strafing, forward/backward movement, and your horizontal aiming capabilities. This will teach you the fundamentals of games and it's multiplayer, will allow you to learn the fundamentals of what really makes a pro player in games. Every FPS these skills will translate over to. But stripped of fluff, it's the only game that has really held up over 30+ years I can say and hasn't lost appeal. It's just the one that started them all. I'd like to see this game continue as is and am happy to see it get re-released and hold up such a community albeit we all scattered amongst the ports! But if you were to ask me the ONE game in the entire series everyone should play, it would be the original Doom. Those three episodes, define everything to be loved and enjoyed playing First Person Shooter video games. Everything else just took the torch in their respective directions. Honestly between these guys and valve along with a few others, the 1990-2010 period brought about the best video game experiences you could have ever asked for. IF you like doom, check out Descent (1995) and bring a joystick but be prepared for the installation of a new butthole on easy thanks to ONE enemy non-boss robot. DOOM + DOOM 2 is a game features the original DOOM, DOOM II, Master Levels, Evilution, The Plutonia Experiment, No Rest For The Living, Sigil 1 and 2, and the newly created, Legacy of Rust. All of these games were expansions created for either DOOM 1 or DOOM 2. So let's review all of them DOOM What is there to say about DOOM? it's a game that everyone has heard off. Beside's Wolfenstein, (which was released in 1992) it revolutionised the idea of First Person Shooter games and created it as a whole. the art style is iconic mixing 2d and 3d very well making players feel like their playing a 3d game. The weapons feel great to use, it's sound effects crunchy as well as other sound effects present in the game such as enemies groaning across halls. The music is iconic and the remixed music is even BETTER thanks to the amazing work of Andrew Hulshult. One complaint I have with DOOM is it's level design. Although feeling like a maze, most solutions to progress the level are either cryptic or poorly designed DOOM II To be honest, DOOM II doesn't change much to differ itself from the first game. Although there are additions. The Super Shotgun is God's divine weapons, it packs a punch and is easily the strongest weapon in the game (besides BFG9000). This game also introduces new enemies that would be featured in many other games such as the revenant. However the music and level design are a step down. DOOM II does have good music featuring 'Running From Evil', Into Sandy City, and 'Bye Bye American Pie' to name a few, but the majority of tracks are forgettable. The level design, ESPECIALLY the city levels are more cryptic and are badly designed and honestly not appealing. Despite it's flaws. DOOM II is a good game, but isn't better than DOOM 1 Evilution and Plutonia Experiment I'm combining these two for 2 reasons. One being that I haven't played these as such as DOOM 1 and 2, and secondly, because there both mixed bags. These two expansions are divisive among the DOOM community. Evilution has okay music but offers no remix tracks, Plutonia only has tracks from DOOM 1. The gameplay does not innovate and only offer more DOOM with more levels, with aren't well design and have enemies spammed across everywhere. Although my complaints overshadow the good, this is worth a little bit of time if you were attracted to DOOM 1 and DOOM 2 No Rest For The Living Okay to be real i didn't play this so were just gonna move on Sigil 1 and 2 First of all, the music is a fucking banger. Well done. The level design isn't that bad this time around but holy shit, Mr Romero really likes the colour red. I don't blame him, it's my favourite colour but it honestly makes my eyes hurt. Legacy of Rust is amazing. They've managed to capture almost Build-engine level of detail in the world. The environs are now immediately recognizable as the sci-fi locations they're supposed to be. It makes DOOM II's Earth levels look positively amateurish in comparison. While the engine has severe limits on how 3D the worlds can actually be (no level element can be directly above any other), the constraint becomes a feature in the Legacy of Rust level design. Each level starts off with a simple, typically hall based, layout. Then as you find more switches and unlocks, walls start to come down, transforming the level step-by-step into progressively larger open arenas to do battle with each wave of new hordes. By the time you make it to the last stand, the layout resembles nothing like what you started the level on, and yet the aesthetic of where you are supposed to be somehow always shines through. Each level an intricately designed mechanism revealing itself to you, in a way that I've never seen any other game do.

The best modern port of the most influential game of it's time. If you enjoy 90s shooters or are an FPS fan looking to get into them, you'll get lost in this one with so much content and maps you'll enjoy for a long time. DOOM changed pretty much everything at the time. But what about the game itself? You'll explore 3d, labyrinthian environments, with exploration, satisfying shotgun blasts, strategy between weapons and how to deal with enemies, and learn the patterns and layouts of countless maps. This collection comes with all of Final DOOM. The four episodes, and the map packs from the Casali brothers; TNT: Evilution and Plutonia Experiment. It also includes the unofficial fifth and sixth episodes, with SIGIL and SIGIL II. Finally, it includes an entirely new two-episode curated expansion, Legacy of Rust, with new textures, enemies, a new flamethrower weapon, and well thought-out maps. Basically, this is part of the recent Bethesda efforts alongside Nightdive and other studios, to put out the definitive port for mass audience of classic titles that they own the rights to. Should you still play gzdoom or another source port? Absolutely. But if you happen to pick up the 'official' version of the game, this is the best it'll get. The Kex engine has handled these remasters really well. If you enjoy this, do check out Heretic + Hexen, Quake, or the other remasters for more of stuff like this. Bonus point: if you owned the original Steam edition of any of these games, like Doom or Heretic, you will get these completely free added to your library. A source port like gzdoom might have more capability overall, but these offer a lot in the way of cross play multiplayer support, a built in add-on menu to play curated player made map packs, crosshair editor, and a brand new soundtrack (doesn't really fit the game, quite honestly, but its fun to try out. Legacy of Rust's style of soundtrack and Sigil had the right idea with their soundtracks.) Definitely an approve in my book.
