A lot of old games, even classics, end up becoming dated, whether it's because of technological advances, changing audience expectations, or developments in game design theory. They were "good for their time", maybe even exceptional, but hard to go back to today. Quake isn't one of these games; despite being 30 years old this year, the game remains as polished and responsive as the day it was released. It's good without qualifiers, and in 2026 is still more genuinely, honestly fun than most modern shooters of the last 10 or 20 years. The lighting and art direction means the game still looks good despite the low-poly models. The sound is impeccable. Controls are responsive. The game is fast, both in terms of performance (you can load it and be in a game in ten seconds from zero, and there is even a settings option to turn off opening cutscenes without having to manually rename or delete the files) and in speed of gameplay. The 2021 remaster touches up the graphics a little and adds some minor QOL tweaks (like achievements, a mod database, and mouse control of menus), and also includes the original Trent Reznor soundtrack that wasn't included in some other digital releases of Quake. It also includes both of the original official expansion packs and two new ones designed by the remaster developers. Dimension of the Past is the more amateur of the two, and features a lot of hard slogs through some ill-advised enemy placement, but Dimension of the Machine is beautifully realized, with a large variety of evocative new environments and excellent level design. The original gameplay mechanics are untouched even in the remaster, but if you really want to play the original versions without any changes at all, those are also included. This is a big step up in customer-forward design from remasters which try their best to pretend the originals didn't exist and prevent players from using or accessing them. (Note for achievement hunters: there is exactly one PvP-focused achievement, but it can easily be gotten in single-player deathmatch with bots. None of the achievements require multiplayer or other difficult-to-arrange circumstances.)

This is where it all began for me. The first FPS I ever played, or least the first one that got me hooked (I remember playing a few random shareware things like Nitemare 3D on my dad's laptop but can't remember specifically which came first!). This game is nothing less than legendary in my mind, and I've owned it on every platform it has been available on that I've owned ever since. Everything about it is done right, and the impact it had on the fps genre, just like Doom before it, cannot be understated. As far as I can tell, Quake wasn't the first true 3d game, but it seems to be the first 3D fps to appeal to the masses and register as a seismic event in the progression of the genre. Thankfully, whoever owns the IP now (Microsoft/ZeniMax/Bethesda I think) have remastered it and its two mission packs and I was able to replay it on my Steam Deck all the way through. Despite owning it, I've never actually put much time into it in adult life, so I've had a total blast playing it the whole way through again. What I love about it is its purity. It does one thing and it does it exceptionally well - and that is fast-paced first-person shoot-em-upping. Everything about it is designed to maximise fun in this regard. The weapons are really satisfying. There aren't too many, and each of them offers a really clear purpose. The shotgun is your trusty workhorse. The nail gun is when you need to deliver pain as fast as possible. The bouncing grenade launcher lets you gib the undead as well as bounce grenades off walls and round corners to clear a path ahead. The rocket launcher delivers huge damage at long range but be careful of using it in close quarters, and the lightning gun is saved for the hardest enemies but just don't use it in water. They are all fun, and sound and feel great. Ammo isn't overly generous so you're often having to switch it up based on what's available, and what pickups the level is offering you. Similarly, the enemies all play their parts. They range from the simple shotgun soldier to spider beasts the launch homing missiles. You learn your own strategy for taking down all of them, which weapons work best, which to prioritise etc. Soon you're zooming fearlessly round the map feeling like a true badass. Even the levels are designed to maximise shooting fun - their layout very often doesn't make a lot of sense if you stopped to think about it, but make total sense in the interest of shooting baddies and having fun. That's not to say they don't play a role in the cohesive feeling of the game - each of the four chapters have their own theme, and I found them much more believable than the levels of Doom and Doom 2. Like Doom before it, this game is about speed and carnage. This isn't a thinking-person's shooter. There are loads of baddies, and you survive by moving quickly and dishing out as much damage as possible int he shortest amount of time. You are rewarded for good use of movement, like circling an enemy via strafing. There is no reloading and no animated weapon switching - everything is instant in the pursuit of high-octane fun, and boy does it deliver. Graphics-wise it all just works. The remastered version means it runs smoothly but the textures all look the way they used to, and I really enjoyed it for that. It just looks great and again the graphics, textures and aesthetic all just work together perfectly. All-in-all, still just an incredible game. Now for me to play the DLC!

[h1] Straight up Quaking it [/h1] [b] Quake [/b] is the 1996 shooter basically responsible for the entire boomer shooter revival. And there's good reason for it. [i] This review primarily focuses on the 2021 enhanced version, though there's a short section regarding the original. Also, I have only played the Singleplayer, though note you'll need a bethesda.net account to play online. [/i] [h2] Gameplay [/h2] Quakes gameplay isn't that crazy or anything: get to the end of the level and blow to absolute smithereens anything that moves on the way, while also finding secrets. Basically, it's DOOM but actually 3D. To accomplish this goal, you've got a variety of weapons, Most of which share ammo types with another. Shotguns use shells, nailguns use nails and explosive weapons use rockets. Of course, it has a few differences compared to DOOM aside from the 3D stuff: you now walk into and shoot buttons to use them, with no dedicated use key being present, and three separate armour types that protect you more, with red having 200 points and protecting you from a whopping 80% of damage. Enemies are braindead, which makes sense for the kind of gameplay, they have limited attacks and basically no sense of self preservation, happily running towards you despite you repeatedly shooting them. That's not to say there isn't variety, but most enemies don't have particular tactics and bar a few glaring exceptions you can just double barrel shotgun them to death with ease. The two original expansions, Scourge of Armagon and Dissolution of Eternity, feature new weapons and enemies that do not appear in the later ones. While they're not terrible and I definitely enjoyed them, I can somewhat see why the MachineGames expansions didn't use them, even if it hurt variety a bit. [h2] Story [/h2] In true old shooter fashion, there is merely the suggestion of a story. You go to alternate dimensions to collect runes that, when all collected, will let you obliterate the big bad. Yeah there ain't much to it, there's more in a manual that came with the game but as for in game stuff there ain't much, which it doesn't really need. [h2] Graphics [/h2] Of course, being a 1996 game, Quake will not blow you away, but the art direction still has sauce, with its gloomy castles and military bases being arguably timeless despite the very basic textures and geometry. The Dimension of the Machine expansion, however, is a lot more advanced, with a lot more detail, smoother geometry and new textures, and it was definitely made for the graphical enhancements of this new version. As above, the enhanced version features a bunch of graphical improvements, mainly the implementation of more dynamic lighting. Alongside that, there's a bunch of toggleable ones, including dynamic shadows, fog, and enhanced models (basically smoother versions of the models). I kept most of these off, as personally they feel slapped on to the 1996 visuals (seriously I do like motion blur but it just does not fit in this game), but I did keep anti aliasing (for the image), depth of field (only appears while the weapon wheel is raised) and model interpolation (smooths out animations). Enhanced models in particular I kept off as the two original expansions did not receive this treatment, and as a lot of those expansions new weapons are slightly modified versions of base game weapons, the quality difference is obvious. I also kept texture filtering off, as I prefer my pixels C R U N C H Y As for performance, Quake runs [i] beautifully [/i], which honestly I'd fucking hope so for a game this old. It defaulted to 120fps, and while I usually end up lowering it to 60 as I think I can't handle it, boy I felt the difference and went back to 120. This hasn't ruined 60 for me tho, as in most games it feels a lot smoother. [h2] Original version [/h2] Aside from the enhanced version, there's the original version that was the default until 2021, running off the id developed Glquake source port. This version DOES work, you can play it direct on Windows 11 with no fiddling or external source ports, but it does have issues: - It does go up to 1440p, but you need to use console commands. By default it goes to 400p, which isn't unplayable but definitely a bit rough - No mouse in menus, but that's not surprising - You have to hold a button down to free look, otherwise moving the mouse up and down moves the player [h2] Verdict [/h2] I hereby declare [b] Quake [/b] as [h3] TIMELESS GOOD SHIT [/h3] Almost three decades on and it's STILL some damn good, pick up and play, monster shooting action. You can't really go wrong with this kind of stuff

It's about as simple as FPS's get, but The sheer efficiency and straight forward nature of the gameplay is honestly a good time. It's more like a really fast paced dungeon crawler; each level is a winding maze of switches to hit, enemies to shoot, and secrets to find, and the fun is less in the combat itself and more how the enemy placement forces the player to move around the environment. It's as much a twitchy navigation puzzle as it is a shooter. Sound is arguably just as important as sight, since enemies will often warn you of their presence before you ever see them with the noises they make. The vibes are also strong. The aesthetic is understandably pretty drab, but the NIN ambience does lend the game an incredibly distinct tone. It feels like you're somewhere uncanny that shouldn't exist, which fits the weird, vague story the game has. It never answers just what the thing referenced only as Quake is, and my theory is the entity Quake is the game itself. The base game is great. The longest level is about ten minutes, and with each episode having been designed by a single person, they manage to feel distinct despite the simple visuals. There's only one real boss fight, and it's not challenging in the slightest, but the mazes are fun to navigate and the flavor text at the end of each section is funny in how cheesy it is. Scourge of Armagon gives some new weapons to compliment the small base game arsenal. You get two new energy weapons, Mjonir, a hammer that will chain lightning between enemies that I didn't use much, and a laser cannon, which fires bouncing shots and is a lot more fun. The other new weapon is the Proximity launcher, which I pretty much never used since the regular rocket launcher is so damn effective in so many situations. There are a few new enemy types, and two brand new bosses (not overly challenging, just shoot them until they die, but the designs are cool as is the lore). Level design is uniformly excellent here, with plenty of great traps and a sense of progression as well as a vague industrial vibe that is apparently where Quake 2 jumped off of. Dissolution of Eternity is one of the most challenging parts of the game in my opinion. Instead of new weapons, you get two new ammo types; lava nails for the nail guns that do a bunch more damage, and a rocket that splits off into four. The increased firepower is incredibly empowering, and the new ammo types are common enough that they felt like key parts of the arsenal. And this is because the game compensates for the increased damage output with some of the most diabolical enemy combinations and traps in the whole game. Levels have much higher body counts and secrets to find. The final boss is pretty easy but an interesting gimmick for the tech the game runs on. Dimension of the Past is interesting because it is arguably just as hard or harder than Dissolution, but in a completely different way. Dissolution is tough in the sheer relentless amount of enemies and straight up evil enemy combinations. Despite that, I rarely felt low on supplies, be it the new ammo, health, or armor. Dimension of the Past has the benefit of 20 years of hindsight from when the game originally dropped, so rather than having the largest density of enemies, you instead have to really manage your ammo, because pickups are far more scarce than in any other part of the game. I think it was the second level that I had to shotgun a Shambler to death because I just hadn't picked up a grenade launcher and my nailgun was empty. Levels also have a new visual flair, really leaning into the gothic elements and having more complicated architecture. If Dissolution of Eternity was the twitchy player's hard mode, this is the planner's hard mode. I will say though, the aforementioned hindsight does let the developer be far more thoughtful with power up placements. Too often in the base game would I find invincibility after I'd already cleared a room, but when I got, say, a Quad Damage in DotP, I would run into a room filled with nearly two dozen soldier enemies and gun them down like Rambo. It's good stuff, if a bit anticlimactic. The final expansion, and the most recent, Dimension of the Machine, feels like the full realization of the unique mixture of gothic architecture, industrial elements, and cosmic horror the base game has. There are six dimensions with two levels apiece (aside from the one that has a secret level) but levels are huge and much more fully formed as real locations. The expansion's lore is also fairly coherent; you're dimension hopping, finding runes, and each new place is a world that's been ravaged by the mysterious forces of Quake. You'll explore full prisons, cathedrals, and a bunch of other cool places that feel a lot more "real" than other parts of the game without ever sacrificing the flow and pace that the best levels in the game have. It does a great job of modernizing mechanics that are 30 years old at this point by simply upping the fidelity to the absolute limit the engine can do and creating much more lived in environments. I love the otherworldly vibe the rest of the game has, but this expansion really does hit it out of the park with its level theming and lore. No new weapons, sadly, but you do get another showdown with one of the base game's bosses, and this time it's actually a threat. Great stuff, and a great way to end the game. Quake is honestly pretty great. It's simple compared to a lot of other boomer shooters, but the unnerving energy it gives off and its focus on challenge through complex labyrinths combined with the devious enemy placement honestly helps the game play well even today. It was ahead of its time in a lot of ways. The fun is less in seeing flashy new enemies or weapons and more in navigating the specific challenges of each individual level, and in that it entirely succeeds. It's that combined with the atmosphere and huge amount of great content in this edition of the game that makes it a great first person shooter x dungeon crawler.

Quake is one of the greatest games ever made, and more accessible than ever after this remaster. Not only has Quake's gunplay and feel aged flawlessly, but there is, to this day, nothing that feels exactly like Quake. The level progression, the weapons, the enemies - they're all completely unique and excellent. Now that Quake has been bundled with all the expansions, the whole package took me a bit more than 46 hours to beat. But, every moment was absolutely worth it. The expansions are also great, and I would go as far to say that the new one by Machine Games contains the best level design in all of Quake, pushing the engine to new, beautiful limits. I would recommend not only playing this game, but 100%ing it on Nightmare Mode. Of id Software's countless incredible singleplayer games, this might take the crown as the best. My only complaint with this remaster is that a game made by nine people has hundreds, maybe even thousands of names in the credits. There are now several company logos that announce themselves upon booting up the game in addition to entire employee databases being listed when you finish the game. Surely not every one of these people contributed to this project, and even if all of them did, 99% of these names likely had a marginal impact. This just comes off as needless game bloat. Anyway, this is a minor qualm. Otherwise, the remaster has been incredibly faithful. The remodels look great aside from the inconsistencies in the expansions, but otherwise feel perfectly in-place. Other visual remasters should take notes. Be subtle, more accessible, and optimize. Buy Quake.

Quake is a game that shouldn't exist. The feeling I get from playing this game is that a game had to be made so a game was made. Does a fancy new engine necessitate a game? A game in which none of its creators even really wanted to make? The answer is, of course not. John Romero was going for a gothic aesthetic while others at Id wanted military sci-fi and as a result we get an abortive assemblage of these two disparate visions. What does the title of the game "quake" even mean in relation to the game? 'Hardcore gamers' will respond to these points by saying that you just don't get it and that you're not supposed to expect coherence and that this is a good thing. I think this is obviously stupid. Doom was simple yet coherent and there's no reason why Quake couldn't have been likewise. Later official expansions would try to tell a coherent story so this obviously had to be on the mind of players back in the day before the 'hardcore gamer' became an identity. This game's skyboxes are rather enchanting but for the most part I don't care for this game's aesthetic although I do appreciate that the use of occult imagery made christcucks seethe. The soundtrack by Trent Reznor fits the more gothic levels very well although the same can't be said for the military sci-fi ones. The sound design is also really impressive at times. Besides some of Sandy Peterson's elder world levels, the game is very fun and the fancy new engine does feel incredible but does this redeem the experience entirely? I don't think so. Games have to do more than just be fun for me, Fallout 3 is the exception, not the rule. I hope this doesn't come across as polemical, these are my honest thoughts on the game.

Well.. It's kind of not DOOM in 3D that's for sure. Majority of my playtime hours came from the "Arcane Dimensions" mod because I found it to be a better Quake than Quake itself. I didn't think I would like that the weapons all had the "Super" variant because it sounded so strange. Why would I want to use the regular variation of a weapon when I can use the Super variant? The strange concept kind of grew on me after I realized that the Super variants are good for taking out enemies with a chunk of health while the normal variants are for weaker enemies (sometimes use super weapons) Enemies are top-notch and force you to be on your feet and utilize your moveset to the fullest potential even though its just WADS and a spacebar + your mouse. Quake is one of those old school must‑plays that shaped the history of shooters. Even with its simple polygonal look, the game oozes atmosphere: the dark soundtrack, the unsettling ambient noises, and the oppressive level design still hit hard today. Best played on an OLED screen IMO. Gameplay is fast, straightforward, and pure. The few switch "puzzles" barely deserve the name, but that's exactly the point - Quake is not about riddles, it's about relentless action. And it still delivers. What surprised me most is how little of its charm has faded. Running it on the Steam Deck OLED in 1080p, high settings, all effects on, and 60Hz via an external monitor feels absolutely smooth and faithful. It's a piece of history that plays like a dream with full Controller support of course. As for difficulty, "Normal" is the sweet spot: challenging enough to keep you on edge, but never unfair. Verdict: Quake hasn't lost a single drop of its magic. If you care about the roots of the FPS genre, this is essential.

The Internet's First True Arena There are few games that can truly be called a milestone, a title so influential it fundamentally changes the trajectory of its genre and the industry as a whole. Games like Street Fighter II for fighting games or Super Mario World for platformers hold this status. It was in this same rarefied air that Quake landed. While Wolfenstein 3D was a pioneer, and Doom introduced the thrilling chaos of multiplayer over LAN, it was Quake that truly took the internet by storm. Its impact is difficult to overstate, as it redefined the multiplayer experience and set the stage for competitive online gaming for decades to come. One of Quake's most significant contributions was its revolutionary graphics. The game was built on a true 3D engine, and its embrace of hardware acceleration, particularly with 3dfx Voodoo cards, allowed for a level of visual fidelity previously unseen. This graphical leap, combined with the frenetic gameplay, created an unparalleled immersive experience. But graphics were only part of the equation. The level design in Quake is arguably among the best in 3D shooter history. The maps are intricate, memorable, and expertly designed for fast-paced combat. While they were far from perfectly balanced-with scores like 20:-2 not being uncommon-this imbalance was a key part of the fun and unpredictability that defined the game. The multiplayer maps themselves are iconic. Levels like dm2 (Claustrophobopolis), dm4 (The Bad Place), and dm6 (The Dark Zone) are etched into the memory of every player who spent hours perfecting their rocket jumps and understanding every hidden route. They are a masterclass in level design, built for competitive play. The game's sound and music were equally as important. The sound effects are fitting and have become iconic in their own right; the satisfying thump of a rocket launcher, the distinct blip of a grenade launcher, and the definitive pop of a telefrag all sound fantastic. But what truly elevated the atmosphere was the industrial, foreboding soundtrack created by Nine Inch Nails, a perfect sonic backdrop for the game's dark and grim aesthetic. Quake's legacy extends far beyond its own success. Its engine and innovations served as the foundation for future titans of the industry, most notably Half-Life. From there, it paved the way for games like Counter-Strike, a title that continues to be played competitively to this day, a testament to the enduring influence of the original Quake.

[b] Quake is the true revolution that followed Doom, taking everything that was great about its predecessor and blasting it into a new dimension. It didn't just innovate - it redefined the FPS genre with groundbreaking level design, physics, and multiplayer mechanics that still set the standard for shooters today. [/b] [u] What did later shooters copy from Quake? [/u] Authentic 3D vertical mapping: Quake's insistence that "if a room could have been in Doom, the level designers had failed" ensured that every map took full advantage of height, depth, and multi-level geometry. Physics‑driven environmental interaction: Jump pads, moving platforms, elevators, underwater zones with adjusted movement and weapon behavior - these interactive mechanics became staples of modern FPS design Lightmaps and dynamic lighting; polygonal models: Replacing sprite-based constructs with real-time lit 3D environments raised atmospheric immersion, later replicated by countless engines. Encouraging modding with scripting and level editing: Quake's open tools (QuakeC, editors like WorldCraft) produced a modding ecosystem that other engines emulated - Valve's Hammer Editor for GoldSrc (Half-Life) traces lineage back to Quake tools. Rocket‑jumping and strafing quirks: These unintended physics exploits in Quake became beloved quirks, widely adopted in future shooters - adding both strategic movement and emergent gameplay

We're 29 years on from Quake's release (when I played it as a 16 year old) and not only do I still play it online today, it's still my favourite multiplayer shooter. It's extremely "basic" by modern day shooter standards; there's no progression systems, no cosmetics to buy, no weapon attachments, nothing to unlock through season passes, no lore to speak of. But, that's what I love and have always loved about it. It's simple, pure fun that's hyper-focused on skill, awareness, decision making and movement. There's no fluff, no BS, just a to-the-point, gritty and exceptionally fun game with a VERY high skill ceiling that makes you grin from ear-to-ear as you play. Quake got me hooked in 1996; it made me convince my folks to part with a serious amount of cash to buy me my first PC (under the guise of it being used for school work). It made me part with my modest life savings for internet use in a time where you paid by the minute on a dial-up connection with an average ping of 200ms. It was the first game I ever played online or joined a clan for (a group of folk that I'm still in touch with today) and play in competitive leagues in. Instead of listening to teachers in class, I'd be drawing the Quake logo, longing to run home to play 5 hours FFA or duels on DM4 (the best duel map of all time!) before bed. It got in my head, big time. I'm not that 16 year old boy anymore, I'm a 45 year old dad of two young girls, with a lot less time than I used to have back then. Yet, when I boot up Quake, it takes me back in time to a golden age of online gaming where time has stood still, even if my reflexes haven't. Eat my pineapples, b*****s. *** Note: I play Quake / QW off Steam via the EzQuake client, hence my low play time on Steam :-)

[Updated review] Quake is my favourite shooter of all time. Keep in mind that I'm approaching this game as someone who's played Doom 1+2 (also the remaster by Night Dive), i fell in love with ID's classic catalogue. These are the games that created and defined the genre. Despite being so old, this remaster by Night Dive studios is awesome, it did so much to modernize one of the defining titles of IDsoftware's classic era (Their Doom remaster is another conversation). Quake is still such an incredible title even after all these years. The Lovecraftian Horror Atmosphere, the haunting music by Nine Inch Nails, the amazing levels made by IDsoftware, the enemy designs & animations, all were put together to create a single truly great experience. This game is of course not without it's flaws. The designs doesn't feel coherent sometimes, mechanics appear and dissapear. The levels' designs could also be very confusing at times, such it the case with IDsoftware's classic titles. The dynamic between the abstract art directions ranging from Medieval Castles, other Dark fantasy places, and Industrial buildings are actually something i quite enjoy. It makes the game feel somewhat varied in this gritty horror package. The dynamic that's not consistent is how these episodes play out. One might be very simple and intuitive, another one might have complicated designs, and another may have cruel enemy placements. That part is the reason why playing through Quake almost feels like a chore--you have to re-learn how the game's design works every other episode. The great definitely outweighs the bad in the base campaign, but it's still something worth mentioning. The amount of levels that i enjoyed were super good, and they shrouded the bad ones. Much love for IDsoftware & Night Dive. [DLC 1 : Scourge of Armagon] This one was pretty good. a little more intense and difficult compared to the base game, but that's a plus. The soundtrack has a different direction compared to the tracks Nine Inch Nails made, but that's not necessarily a bad thing. I guess they were just going for a different vibe for this expansion. This DLC campaign also gives you some variations of the pre-existing weapons, which translates to more options on how to brutalize the fiends and the shambler. There's also the Mjolnir, which brings this game back to it's DnD origin. It's a pretty good crowd control weapon too. Also, some new fodder enemies, they're cool i guess. This DLC's highlight is the level design. It feels a lot like base campaign Quake, but it did more to show what the Quake engine could pull. A lot of cool set pieces could be found in this DLC. Really good overall, holds up well to the base game content. Easy reccomend if you want more Quake. [DLC 2 : Dissolution of Eternity] This one has the more interesting art diretion. You get to visit ancient places such as ancient Rome, Egypt, and even meso-america. This DLC is way more concerned in throwing the players into traps, just to abuse the new level themes i guess. This DLC just does tons of gimmicks in my opinion, it could be more frustating than fun sometimes. Also, a lot more new enemies. The Wrath is probably the coolest one here. The new weapons are just variations of the pre-existing ones, but the lava nails are legit life-saver when you're in a tight corner and a fiend or a shambler show up. This DLC also has the best boss fights. The Overlord and the Dragon was quite fun actually. Quake boss fights were never the most interesting things out there, but between DLC 1 & 2, the developers wanted to shake things up and bring more value to the Quake package. Which i appreaciate a lot. [DLC 3 : Dimension of the Past] This one might be the most simple official Quake expansion. It wasn't like DLC 1 & 2 where it was outsourced to other studios by IDsoftware way back during the game's original release. It resulted in 2 development studios doing their own take on Quake's blueprint, offering their spices and quirks. Dimension of the Past (DOPA) was developed by MachineGames, the developers of the new Wolfenstein games & Indiana Jones. Apparently it was mainly helmed by gustaffson, the creative director of said studio. it was made as a return-to-form Quake expansion, going as far as calling it the 5th episode. I could definitely feel that direction for the DLC. It didn't add anything new to the game, it just offers more harder levels for Quake players. Think Thy Flesh Consumed from (TFC) Ultimate Doom. Strictly talking about direction anyhow, DOPA is definitely harder than base Quake, but i don't know if i would say it's as hard as Doom TFC. The quality is very in-line with base campaign Quake by the way. Easy Recommendation if you want more challenging levels.

Quake is a classic, a cult game. It's one of the first 3D FPS games in history ( the most famous predecessors being Wolfenstein 3D, DOOM, Hexen: Beyond Heretic and Duke Nukem 3D.). It had great value in the year of release and years and years after that. It featured a very unique and dark (even occult) atmosphere, because the player was thrown in strange dimensions, controlled by evil, occult monsters and over-lords. It was fast paced and had a coherent level design and recognizable gothic locations. A positive aspect of this remaster is that it comes with all official expansion packs/DLCs ( 4 of them ), and that makes the campain much longer. Also fans made a lot of player-made levels and mini campains for those who want to continue playing ever further. Having said that, I just can't recommend this game in 2025 because it's incredibly outdated. Needless to say, the graphics is very outdated ( of course, it's a 1996 game ) but it's interesting to note how the fourth and last DLC "Dimensions of the Machine" comes with a much improved graphics. ( it was made in 2016 with the remaster ). I never played Quake before, so I wanted to give it a shot because I would like to play as many classic games as possible to widen my gaming general culture. I found it very boring and repetitive to be honest. It has no story whatsoever, which is a shortcoming because every shooter in the last 20 years has had a story and also has objectives/quest. In my opinion, the game is first and foremost a puzzle/labyrinth, and then only secondary a shooter. I will explain what I mean. In every level, what you basically have to do is this: 1- find the silver key, 2- find and pass the silver gate, 3- find the golden key, 4 - find and pass the golden gate and 5- find the exit. In some levels it's not a great problem, but in many levels (especially when the levels are big), that paradigm was a chore, as the game hasn't got a map. So you can expect a lot of searching, searching and going back and forth in every level. Furthermore, the combat is also bad. I played on normal and I found it very hard (especially the DLCs). In the 90's they made games much harder then now. They were made to last for years and years, because people couldn't afford many games. There is too little ammo in my opinion, the enemies are bullet sponges, there is a lot of unavoidable damage, unless you memorize everything and act accordingly knowing all in advance. The key to this game is memorizing the levels to perfection and knowing when and where the certain types of enemies will come so you can prepare with the right weapons and movements/tricks. When you watch any Quake longplay on youtube, you can clearly see those guys played Quake hundreds of times and they memorized every single detail in every level. Is this a shooter or a memory game? In every level there are secret locations that give you armor and ammo, but I could scarcely find any. They are very difficult to spot. Quake is thus, not very friendly to new players. As I said, it is made for people who will play it over and over for a long time. I didn't like the weapons (it's perhaps the worst weapons arsenal in any shooter in history). The base game (you have 4 episodes with 7 levels + 2 secret levels each) was not that brutal on normal difficulty. Only occasionally I had to use some ammo cheat. But the 4 DLCs are much harder and I found myself often using both ammo and health cheats, because without them it would take forever to plow through that already boring and frustrating experience. After every level I would think "thank god it's over", and that thought was especially in my mind after finishing the last expansion pack.

I started playing this after watching the Bloodthief dev logs from Blargis. I had never played the game until 2025 but my dad had always said it was good and it looked well made. It holds up incredibly well for a 30 year old game, although this is the updated version. The movement is incredibly smooth, the enemy placement keeps you moving and keeps things reasonably fast paced, weapon and enemy variety is great, levels wrap around on themselves and are consistently well designed. All in all a great game. I only really got into it after playing the first episode of the base game though. I think it took a little time to get into the flow of things. The thing that has surprised me most, is that, as one of the first fully 3d shooter games it is way better than a lot of shooters that came out after it and plays as well as many modern shooters. I think this is mostly down to hit having a relatively modern control scheme and having some great level design and movement. Each episode gradually introduces more enemies, concepts, and weapons. These each fit incredibly well into the game as a whole. The rocket launcher is probably the most fun but they all have their uses. Weapons without AOE damage are much better in close corridors while AOE weapons are great for clearing rooms with lots of enemies. My main problem is your weapon list gets cluttered with a few weapons that are just straight upgrades of weapons you already have. This isn't a major problem just a minor annoyance when trying to find the weapon you want. The game encourages movement by having a lot of back spawns or enemy swarms. At first this can feel a little annoying especially for someone who has come from games where slowly and methodically working your way through enemies is the best strategy. However, when you get used to this, I think it really encourages you to play the game in the most fun way. This is to keep moving all the time. By doing this you dodge enemy attacks, keep an eye on everything and don't get caught out. This keeps the action up and just makes for a fun game. The DOOM games new and old do this, which makes sense since this is by the same developers, as well as a few indie devs and Titanfall 2. Other than these this sort of movement isn't that common so I found it quite refreshing. Level design is also fun a varied. Despite having no map markers and very few glaring indicators of where to go I rarely felt lost, and when I did it was more of a puzzle than an annoyance. There are lots of secrets to find, hidden exits and unique level features. My favourite was the wind tunnels where you jump into pipes and they fire you around but there are lots of great levels and they don't really feel repetitive anywhere. It does iterate on the level design of the DOOM games that came before it but used its new mechanics to really add to the formula. Overall a great game that I would recommend to any fan of shooters young or old. It has aged very well and is a lot of fun. I will likely be back to try some fan made maps or replay on harder difficulties. For someone who has played some shooters hard felt like a good starting point which is what I played on.

Quake is a classic fast-paced shooter created in 1996 by id Software. Considered one of the top games of its genre for its 3D graphics and multiplayer, it holds a long-standing place in video game history, albeit a bit overshadowed by other big names. Following a simple formula, the player jumps straight into action, collecting guns and sparse ammo while running, gunning down monsters, and hunting for secrets.The stages are the crowning jewel of Quake. Each one is meticulously designed, with corridors and rooms crafted to avoid confusion while offering many interesting ways to use the 3D space.; hidden buttons, inventive traps, and angles perfect for sniping and be sniped. Special attention to detail is evident in the difficulty selection area, where each of the three standard levels has its own visual cues, and the nightmare difficulty is cleverly hidden behind a puzzle. The expansions add numerous new stages filled with secrets, weapons, enemies, and clever uses of the limited technology, offering a significantly tougher challenge. Unfortunately, after several hours of gameplay, the cracks in this classic begin to show, exponentially affecting enjoyment. The weapons are repetitive and uninspired: gun A, super gun A, gun B, super gun B, and more of the same for explosives. Some expansions introduce other duller versions of existing weapons, along with one or two new ones, but they lack the creativity one might expect in a world of demons and magic. Enemy variety is also lacking. Many enemies glitch around the stages and pose little real challenge, serving more as mild annoyances than engaging or fun opponents. You'll see the exact same enemies throughout the entire game and its expansions. While a few new foes are briefly introduced in the expansions, they are sparse. The shambler and the vore will consistently be your main ammunition sinks. On that note, Quake has a surprisingly limited ammo count compared to other shooters like Doom and Duke Nukem. You need to ration bullets and missiles carefully to eliminate all enemies. On higher difficulties, you may even not be able to kill all monsters without lucky shots. This limitation constantly undercuts the fast pace the game is built around. In terms of health, the game offers plenty of recovery and armor, yet many deaths still feel unfair, often caused by enemies randomly spawning behind you or unpredictable traps. I feel like we've lost something in the last 30 years, because I had more fun playing Quake for the first time than I ever did playing Overwatch or Valorant. It's so fun to blow up monsters while running at mach 5. I think it's the ruthless efficiency that's so fun. Clearing rooms while dodging enemy projectiles makes you feel like you're good at video games (and at times embarassingly bad). Running past enemies and skipping sections with the grenade/rocket launcher makes you feel like a racing monster (no demons here, this is Quake, not Doom). The art style really holds up too. Yeah, Quake is the progenitor of all puke-brown games, but it wears it on its chest, and at the time it was an innovation. I feel like this opinion is vindicated with Dimension of the Machine -- the new 2021 expansion -- as it's able to adapt Quake's art-style to curves and modern lighting. Quake has coherent, distinct environments: Egyptian, Medieval, Runic, Terracota, Sci-Fi, Underworld. As for each of the expansions: [list] [*]Quake: 9/10 -- nicely designed levels, though some sections are a bit dated. [*]Scourge of Armagon: 7/10 -- a cool expansion, but the level design isn't quite as good. Awesome set-pieces. [*]Dissolution of Eternity: 6/10 -- levels are long as !#@$, and a lot of the encounters don't feel fair. You go up elevators just to see 5 enemies in your face :/. [*]Dimension of the Past: 10/10 -- the levels feel like reboot Wolfenstein levels in the Quake engine (that's literally what they are). They include all the level-design innovations of the 20 years after Quake. Well paced, with great action; would make a 1996 gamer's mind explode. [*]Dimension of the Machine: 8/10 -- really cool to see new graphics in the style of Quake, but some of the level design suffers. I got lost several times in the loooong levels. Also, I ran out of bullets on all my weapons a few times, which happened because they put 10 high health enemies in a row :|. [/list] I recommend Quake. It's nice to return to the basics of just running and shooting. That's what the game is about, and it does it in the most satisfying way. If you do pick it up, you should probably play on nightmare difficulty -- shooter gamers have gotten a lot better since 1996 when they didn't even use WASD or vertical mouse-look. Have fun, and good luck, Ranger.

As a person who played Quake I since a very young age, this is the best remaster that id Software has to offer. I know I'm very late to the game, but it's always better than never. I really do wish they would give the Quake franchise the DOOM treatment, where it is rebooted into a modern first-person shooter masterpiece. Many people often overlook Quake's significance in the shooting game history as Quake is the first FPS game that comes with a 3D game engine that even stood out the test of time. Many people would return at least once in a while to play this game as if they were a kid growing in the mid-2000s. Talk about gameplay, the game engine is smooth as ever, like how I would play it back then, but it is optimised to a modern game feel. The Enhanced version features a new weapon swatch mode where you could switch weapons easily just like in any modern shooting games which I enjoy a lot. It also has the motion blur effect that enhances the gameplay immersion, adding tension to the gameplay. The one favorite improvement of mine when it comes to the gameplay is the 50% health handicap in Nightmare difficulty. This small change in gameplay has challenged my skill more than ever. While others might find it redundant or unnecessary, I personally think this change has made my achievements more gratifying than how I used to play it. It forced me to think harder and plan my ammo usage efficiently. The interesting thing about the in-game textures is that the new ones look subtly yet significantly different than the original ones where the devs gave the textures a high-definition look while retaining the aesthetic of the original textures. In other words, they managed to keep the models look more refined and detailed while keeping the low-poly aesthetic of the original Quake as if you were playing it 20 years ago. Soundtrack-wise, I have nothing to say much. Nine Inch Nails done a splendid job on creating the eerie atmosphere as well as the Industrial Metal the accompanies you when you're on a Quad Damage rampage. One major drawback from me is the fact that the main menu UI and HUD is reduced down to a cheap minimalist look which to me is the biggest disappointment in Quake Enhanced. It doesn't even offer to switch to the original look that is way more iconic. To sum this all up, if you haven't buy it, GO DO IT. You'll be happy.

Initially I planned to just write "What the hell am I supposed to say about Quake? It's a Quake, goddammit!" and call it the day. But then I was struck with realization: this is exactly the reason why I should write something more. Because time passes. Quake was released to the world in 1996 - next year will turn 30. Thirty! There are entire generations of people who were born, raised, finished school, got a job, got married and have kids after this game. Sometimes it's hard to understand that years fly by and we are no longer in a timeline where games are puny, niche entertainment, but a monolithic, big-ass industry slowly but surely dominating the entire free time segment of our lives. Soon on Earth there will be more people who play games than people who don't know what the hell FPS are. And a big chunk of today's gaming looks like this thanks to this one particular game. Majority of people cannot even understand how influential this Quake was. So, what did we get thanks to this little piece of code? How about a real 3D environment, without 2.5 D hacks from Doom? And I mean, fast paced, optimized 3D gameplay with decent frame rate albeit without smooth animation, where everything - literally EVERYTHING had three dimensions, monsters, weapons, even fire or light sources? 3D where you can create a vertical level with rooms built upon rooms? Now it's laughable, but back then, that was a real revolution, opening endless possibilities, limited only by imagination. And how about real multiplayer? That simple thing led to the creation of the entire E-Sport - and the first real tournament, with real money (Some dude named Dennis "Thresh" Fong even won a Carmack Ferrari) was made specifically for Quake. What more? Modding - yup, the first mods were created for Quake. From simple Doom's map conversion to engine to entire map packs like Arcane Dimension, and even more - the infamous grappling hook mechanic, implemented later in many different games, start as mod for Quake. You know Games Done Quick? It was inspired by Quake Done Quick - yeah, speedrunning was invented with Quake. Wants even more? Engine was bought by multiple other companies and converted into different games. One of said companies was Valve, and they used it to create a little game called Half-life. Later, the same engine was used as the foundation for their Source engine for HL2. And with HL2 Steam was created. Yes, today's shape of PC gaming is possible thanks to the Quake engine. Another company called Infinity Ward bought the Quake 3 engine license in 2003 and created Call of Duty. And yet another look on what Quake can achieve and said "we can create something better". And then Unreal Engine was born. Yes, Epic advertised Unreal as "Quake killer". And rest is history. But this is only scratching a surface. Because Quake showed us, showed the entire world, that games can be something more than pixelated, cartoonish graphics and silly, childish premises. Then games can - and are - a serious medium, atleast at the same level as movies, books or music. That they are THE entertainment. My point is - Doom is the grandfather of FPS, but Quake is something much, much more than being just another step in genre evolution, especially for PC gaming. But what about the game itself? Comparing it to today's standards it is redundant and stupid, because technology evolved so much that now you can do nothing more but laugh at Quake. But again, it's like comparing the Ford T to the newest Ferrari - yes, the former looks weak, because back then there were no today's advancements and everything was undiscovered territory. Yes, it still has this great, lovecraftian-like atmosphere, but mostly thanks to consistent art direction rather than technical aspects. So instead, useless criticizing, I will tell you, dear zoomers, what you can expect when booting this game. First of all - JANK. Don't get delusional, this is a very janky, clunky game, and you will experience it every second. Go, start the game, press WSAD, try to move. Your character moves like on ice - even when you stop pushing buttons, he will do those little extra 1 and half steps in every direction. Now imagine fighting or traveling on narrow edges, or jumping from platform to platform. You will feel like moving too much and start correcting mid walking, and therefore probably fall. I did it multiple times. Veterans will laugh at this, but hey, I can laugh also looking at a person playing only one game for 30 years. Another big thing are enemies hitboxes. They are gigantic and enormous. You can easily fire on some Ogre or Skag around the corner without even seeing a monster. But before you start cheering this, just remember - your character has the same problem. You can clearly see something like lasers passing around you and get hit anyway, because hitboxes of bullets and your character connect. It always pissed me off, no matter how many times I played Quake. Also - just look how many times enemies can block themself on the door frames or ledges, not being able to reach you. Yeah, I'm talking mostly about you, Fiends, with your stupid leap attacks. Thirdly - weapons. For me, the weapons of the Quake were always weak. Yeah, we have the legendary Rocket Launcher, an iconic weapon popular to this day, but looking beyond that you can clearly see a little cheating of some sort. Shotgun and Super Shotgun running on the same ammo, same with Nail Gun and Super Nail gun, Grenade launcher and RL. So we don't have 6 weapons (plus Thunderbolt as 7), we only have 3 weapons with different damage output and ammo consumption - oh yeah, and weird grenades angles when firing. God, I love weapons that can kill me instead of the enemy. I also really don't like SSG in this game - too weak, no reload animation, too wide spread. Lastly, levels - at some point, at least in vanilla games - they are all like this one big blurred image: all the same, without noticeable differences. They all are brown, grey, purple castles, dungeons and mazes, albeit not so much labyrinthian. Also with small numbers of enemies - aside from the dimension of the machine addon, you will witness no levels with more than a hundred monsters. You know, because back in 1996 that level of complexity would fry even more powerful PCs. You can easily end every level under 15 minutes, which is good, because always around 3 episodes I become a little bored with single player, mostly because at this point the game showed all of the tricks it can pull out from its sleeve. One more word about enemies - Fuck Vores. And Spawns. Fuck them, FUCK THEM TO THE CORE. They should be deleted from existence. Even Shamblers are better, especially in this port, because they finally fixed their attack animation on nightmare difficulty, so now it's alignment better with actual lighting projectiles. Ogres are cute, with their chainsaw (probably stolen by some time travel portal shenanigans from Doom 3) and grenade launchers, which in majority of cases damage enemies around them more than my actions. As for the rest - this more than standard menagerie from FPS games with strong emphasis on melee oriented enemies - fiend, knights, death knights, you know the drill; they run towards you swinging their claws and swords, but since you are faster, the only real threat is how small room where you fight are. Game also lack real boss fights - even ones from expansions are boring or annoying. idSoft's best game, my 2nd-favourite shooter ever made, and easily among the best in any case. Arena shooters (or "movement shooters") were midwifed by Quake; [i] this [/i] is where Unreal, Ultrakill, Severed Steel, and so many other games first found their footing. The most important change in the Remaster is that it makes Nightmare the unequivocally toughest difficulty-Quake is not the hardest shooter in general, so this is a welcome change as far as I'm concerned. Either way, the original is also included here, so this is without a doubt the best version of the game. Remaster also includes four mission packs; the original two packs of Scourge of Armagon and Dissolution of Eternity from 1997, along with two new ones: Dimension of the Past and Dimension of the Machines, from 2016 & 2021 respectively. The first two mission packs have clumsier design overall compared with base Quake, often falling into the same confusing, maze-like level design that Quake had already shed from its idSoft predecessors, along with suffering from some enemy spam, obnoxious platforming, etc. Probably the worst part is the music, which is a major step down from Reznor. They're not awful, but the latter two mission packs are significantly better. These are developed by MachineGames, with whom I have a minor grudge from their treatment of Wolfenstein, but regardless these episodes are genuinely good. DotP plays like a fairly standard homage to Quake, but DotM is a significant alteration of the formula, featuring enormous levels that are downright gorgeous (excepting only Realm of the Stonemasons), and immediately remind one of 2019's Amid Evil. The complex geometry does not always play that nice with Quake's dodging-focused gunplay, but that's a price I'm willing to pay for some of the most beautiful levels ever designed for the game. DotM would alone would be a good reason to play this, and with the mod support it's a no-brainer. Before playing almost any other shooter, there's always a good hundred things more you should do in Quake.

Dissolution of Eternity was largely a mission pack to let the player loose with plentiful ammo for the bigger weapons. Scourge or Armagon gives the player new weapons to blow things up with, but also introduces Spike Mines (f*ck Spike Mines), so the whole campaign feels fresh even when played immediately after the main Quake campaign. Quake is an absolute classic and I'm sure is a great source of inspiration for many of the modern retro "boomer-shooters", however, despite not only this but also me playing Half-Life in the beginning of 2024, I only got around to playing Quake in August 2024 using the Mark V source port, while I did buy the game on Steam, NightDive for some reason decided it would be a great idea to run this 1996 game on Vulkan and my really old computer doesn't even have that, so I could either only downgrade my game a lot for it to run or use Mark V, so Mark V it goes. Quake is an absolute blast, it feels very much like Doom but I actually prefer this much more over the 1993 Doom title, I'm not sure if it's because I grew up with GoldSrc and old games in general, but Quake still controls really smoothly despite being almost 30 years old. The ways that Quake takes similar steps to Doom is in the maze-like level layout, arcade-like stats for time; secrets and kills, HUD, etc. This makes the game really fun to play considering how you just pop-in a level, try your best, and get to see your score at the end. Trent Reznor composed the OST for this game and it's probably one of my favorite videogame soundtracks. Despite being similar to Doom, the only song here that might make you bang your head back-and-forth is the main title theme, the rest is a spooky ambient soundscape with brilliant sound design. I totally recommend you check over Trent Reznor's other works like The Downward Spiral and The Fragile, he's an amazing composer and producer. You can even see his band's logo (Nine Inch Nails) on the boxes for nailgun ammo. Quake is very smart with the weapon selection, you have eight weapons, most of them sharing ammo types, it really makes you think rapidly on which gun is more appropriate for each situation (besides the axe, that one's pretty useless, it's not even a "last resort" weapon considering how I've never found myself in a situation where my only option was the axe.) The enemy variety is good too, with its H. P. Lovecraftian inspired designs, *most* enemies feel fair to fight and feel like they require skill to master, take the Ogre for example, first time I played Quake I was stunned that an enemy as hard as them would be one of the first enemies introduced, I couldn't figure out how to beat them and almost always lost a ton of health, now I think they're incredibly easy to defeat! Most enemies pretty much include good movement and dodging abilities (even if that includes basically just circlestrafing), people often complain about the Vores but honestly they're pretty easy, just shoot them and find the nearest corner when they fire their homing attack. However, as I said earlier, only *most* of them seem well-balanced/designed, the Fiends are a cool enemy in concept but I don't like the absurd amount of health they take from you, sometimes they manage to take half of your health, I've heard that is a bug in the code but wow it really makes me hate this enemy, the Spawns are also horrible, they were designed late into development so they couldn't be retouched too hard, but I still think they could've at least not have made an enemy that jumps all over your face and blows up (usually in your face also) taking like 80 points of your health, it's not *too* bad if you quicksave and also know exactly where they are placed (and also because they die relatively quickly), but they still should've never been put into the game. And don't get me started in enemy-placement. It's alright up until Episodes 3-4, Episode 3 ends with a pretty "screw you" approach to enemy placement, right as the level is about to end, they spawn two Fiends, one in front of you and one behind you, just to catch first-players off-guard, worst part? Whenever you die in this game, you have to start the level from the *very* beginning, Episode 4 is even worse, with Spawns being placed often in corners or in completely dark places just for you to not notice them until it's too late, in one instance, they place Fiends in front of you and like 3-4 Spawns *behind* you, it feels like a very cruel joke to do this to the player and it just doesn't seem fair, it's one of the game's aspects that has aged the worst. Level design is pretty good, as I've said it follows the maze-like structure of Doom, each level is pretty short and they make it pretty obvious of where you have to go/what you have to do, so you don't get lost that often unlike Doom, and it's extremely fun to run around those places while bunnyhopping. Multiplayer is actually funny enough the aspect of this game I've touched the least, this is because the multiplayer servers in Mark V would just not work, or because the multiplayer that did work was stuck in the Steam version, you also need to make a Bethesda account and I wasn't in the mood to do that so I just didn't play. I did try Deathmatch with bots and it was fun! But I think they truly mastered Deathmatch in Quake III Arena, for me it always felt like the bots could kill me incredibly easy and I could almost never kill the bots, but the deathmatch maps are pretty good too! Despite the obvious flaws (Episode 4) I can't stress how good and important this game is, it was influential for modding/multiplayer/3D engines in general/the industry/etc. Doom might've been the first step into the rise of the FPS genre, but Quake truly nailed it. 9.5/10

[h1][b]Quake[/b][/h1] [h3][i][u]This game shouldn't require an introduction.[/u][/i][/h3] This is a legendary game in the PC realm for 1 huge thing. Real Time 3D graphics. I was there when this game came out, and despite only being 5 or so, I played a LAN deathmatch in a room with a bunch of my father's friends. I remember one of them named Tigger letting me 'frag' him until I won just to appease a 5 year old, and it was a core memory. I still think about that every time I boot this game up and hear the menu scroll sound effects. Anyways... You are Ranger. You are tasked with finding Runes (in the base game) to defeat a life form named Shub. After doing so, you have won! Until you realize there are more episodes that were released afterwards that I have yet to play, so I will update this review when I get around to that. The base game was a step up in the direction of PC game art and graphics. Nowadays, it doesn't look very high tech. Brown on brown on beige on grey was a critique I held frequently for Xbox 360/PS3 era games, due to everything trying to evoke an earthy realistically lighted feel. Back in Quake, I actually didn't mind. Gaming then was trying to be (sometimes literally) as flashy as possible, both in game and on the box art, to wow the player into spreading the word about how great the game was. As weird as it seems, the brown art direction Quake took was new, on top of the 3D rendering. The weapon lineup, the basic monster archetype, the twisted machined flesh graphical style, secret hunting, key hunting, and mixing FPS with platforming all became cemented as bonafide id tech staples here. The graphics and sound don't hold up to modern gaming, but modern gaming standards were built on what was done here. If you are a fan of boomer shooters, or a returning rocket jumper, you will %100 like this port's visual style and rendering enhancements over the original. Speaking of, the original game's files are included in this release in case you wanted to play vanilla or modded Quake and its expansions in software rendering. TL;DR: It's Quake, buy it. This is as close to a perfect FPS as you're gonna get. Quite possibly one of, if not THE, best FPS's I have ever played. I never grew up playing Quake, as I was born just a year after it's release, but nonetheless I was drawn to the game thanks in part to it's incredible atmosphere and dark fantasy style. Quake still absolutely demolishes damn near every modern FPS I have ever played, and it's combat loop, mechanics, weapons, enemy variety, sound design and masterful soundtrack put it at the top of my list of "games I find myself losing track of time while playing." I've played through everything Quake has to offer on the nightmare difficulty, and have actually moved to playing the game on the fantastic Ironwail sourceport(which I highly recommend as well). But I'll give some brief thoughts on all of Quake's expansions thus far, as I believe they all bring a unique flavor of gameplay to Quake and are worth your time playing. Scourge of Armagon: A fun romp, it feels like a natural continuation of the base game. It includes a few new weapons and some new enemy types. The real star of the show here are the levels, as they all flow extremely well and are never tedious to play through. The music is also great, and has a much more in-your-face industrial metal soundscape to it. Dissolution of Eternity: A great time all around, the only level I personally dislike is Elemental Fury 1 but that's just because of the annoying "earthquake" gimmick of the level. Also, whoever decided that Vore's should be turned into a flying enemy is a literal psychopath. The expansion has a unique mechanic of alternate ammo types that are all fun, albeit a tad overpowered, and fit in nicely with some of the heavier hitting enemies that'll show up later. My only gripe with this, is that the alternate rocket and nail ammo types are fairly plentiful and heavily outclass their normal counterparts and can trivialize a lot of combat encounters. But the alternate ammo for the Thunderbolt almost feels as if it's a prototype for the modern BFG design you see in Quake 2 and the modern DOOM games. My favorite aspect of DoE however, is the sheer variety of the locations you'll be fighting and navigating in. Dimension of the Past: A sheer test of your accuracy and resource management skills, ammo and health are NOT plentiful. Each shot missed, each ammo drop you accidentally pick up when you had more than enough, is punishing. Knowledge of where the secrets are located are VITAL to your survival and success, especially if you wish to go for all kills in a level. This expansion doesn't offer any new enemies or weapons, but it doesn't need to. It's more Quake, and that of in itself is perfect and good enough for me. The levels all flow extremely well, and all combat encounters are intelligently designed, with some fairly devious and malicious traps if you're not ready for them. Fairly difficult for the first timer, but gets more and more fun and satisfying to overcome once you know the levels tricks and where the secrets are located. Dimension of the Machine: Masterclass in level design and architecture, this is top-shelf Quake. While not as difficult and sadistic as DoPA, there are still plenty of hair raising moments and combat encounters that will get the blood pumping. The levels are also incredibly massive, and while that may be a complaint for some, I love having these massive levels to traverse and dissect. The high monster count, jaw dropping visuals and perfect level design compliments Quake to a T. By far my favorite expansion out of them all. And if you're still fiending for more Quake, then there is a plethora of fan made content that is of ABSURD quality and production. So much so, that there are actually some mods that I prefer to play over the base game such as Arcane Dimensions and Deathmatch Dimension. A perfect FPS that more than just stands the test of time, it continues to define the genre to this day.

Quake 2 is a competent FPS that introduced lots of welcome improvements over the earlier Quake, but unfortunately, Id Software seemed far more interested in showcasing their new innovations than adhering to the masterful design of Quake 1, resulting in a title that plays more like DOOM than Quake and feels like 1 step forward but 2 steps backward from the first Quake. Quake 2 still retains a lot of the best parts of Quake 1: the movement and shooting are still fantastic; the enemies are varied and challenging; the weapons are satisfying to shoot and feature different trade-offs; there are plenty of fun secrets to find in levels; 4x damage is as OP as ever; all multiplayer features are still present; and rocket jumping is still permitted. On top of this, there are many improvements over the first game. The enemy AI has been vastly upgraded - features include ducking beneath incoming projectiles, firing last stand shots before fully dying, and sidestepping incoming rockets and grenades. Enemies also have new mechanics such as soldiers protected with energy-shields and medics that can resurrect fallen foes, like the Arch-Vile from DOOM II. The weapon arsenal is rebalanced and expanded, and major highlights include the shotgun and double-barrel/super shotgun, which have much higher damage than their Quake 1 counterparts; the railgun, a hitscan + piercing sniper rifle that dominates in singleplayer and multiplayer; and the BFG 10K, whose energy ball now discharges green lightning bolts in all directions. There are more powerups - including more unique options such as the power shield (a game-breaking powerup that drains energy cells to increase armor while active) and adrenaline (permanent +1% max HP and full heal) - and you can store them in your inventory for later use. Id Software even tried adding a late 90s military sci-fi story in this game, which while basic and formulaic, does at least provide context to your actions and a nice sense of progression as you gradually dismantle the Strogg's military capabilities. I also appreciate the environmental storytelling, such as the captured marines in the research lab. The graphics are nice (for the most part; the explosion graphics still look atrocious), but admittingly, this game reuses the same sci-fi industrial art style the entire way through, and it gets very repetitive past the halfway point. (Everyone complains that Quake 1 has an 80% brown color palette, but at least that game introduced a dark fantasy + runic + eldritch horror aesthetic on top of the sci-fi to shake things up - even DOOM introduced the underworld tilesets so that you weren't looking at the same green and gray metal corridors all the time.) However, Quake 2 introduced tons of new severe flaws compared to Quake 1. The biggest issue is that there are more hitscan enemies this time around, causing combat to devolve into hiding behind walls and taking potshots from behind cover. The most egregious hitscan enemy is the Gladiator, a too common late game enemy who has high HP and a 50-damage railgun attack with no telegraph (at least the Shambler had an obvious attack animation before he fired his lightning bolts). Another major issue is that there are also way more bullet sponge enemies in this game too, such as the Tank and Tank Commander (tanky enemies are literally called tanks lmao) who can easily take 10+ rockets to bring down and bring the game's pacing to a crawl. The boss fights are worse, and all of them devolve into unloading tons of rockets/energy blasts/chain gun rounds/BFG balls into a slow-moving bullet sponge for several minutes. The level design is still good, but there are far more claustrophobic hallways and tiny rooms compared to the earlier Quake, which becomes extremely noticeable when you are hiding from hitscan attacks. Combining these factors, the result is a much slower-paced FPS that plays like a modern cover/corridor shooter, the opposite of what made Quake 1 so beloved. (Seriously, one of the best tactics in this game is to bounce grenades around the corner so you never expose yourself to incoming hitscan attacks lol.) I have a few minor complaints with the weapons - the grenade and rocket launchers are pretty weak due to their lower fire rates + slower projectile speeds compared to Quake 1; the starting pistol is still useless; the assault rifle is a little bit too strong in the early game due to its hitscan attacks (the hitscan is a big problem in multiplayer); [url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2KL89T9T9UA]the BFG programming is still over-engineered[/url]; the thunderbolt from Quake 1 is absent (although I hear the plasma beam from an expansion pack is a decent substitute); and I don't understand why the hyperblaster has a cooldown when you stop firing like the plasma rifle in the DOOM games. The weapon switch speed also used to be as atrocious as in DOOM, but fortunately the 2023 remaster sped it up (still too slow imo). The final boss is anticlimactic as well - it is just a 1v1 in a tiny arena against a slow moving mech with too much HP - and is a rehash of the final boss from the Scourge of Armagon Expansion Pack. (At least we don't have to fight that dreadful dragon from Dissolution of Eternity again.) [url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HpjO6KmiuDw]You can also bring a 4x damage + invulnerability powerup to this fight and use the BFG to melt the final boss in ~30 seconds[/url]. And maybe it's just me, but the Strogg just are not as iconic or memorable as the enemies from Quake 1, and Quake 2 never introduces anything as frightening or menacing as the Shambler [spoiler](hence why Nightdive brought them back in their Call of the Machine campaign).[/spoiler] This remastered version also includes an odious and anti-immersive compass system that displays a quest marker and a neon green path to your destination, because the labyrinthine levels are apparently too complex for modern audiences. I know backtracking is annoying and getting lost leads to lost of wasted time, but this compass is an awful solution that really insults your intelligence, so hopefully this system does not become a trend in future games. (I would have preferred a minimalist mini-map system like the DOOM games, but it would probably be too hard to implement in a true 3D engine.) And I know this is an unpopular opinion, but I think the soundtrack in this game is just ok and unremarkable, and a major downgrade from Reznor's ambient masterpieces from the Quake 1 OST. Quake 2 is divisive compared to Quake 1, and it's not hard to see why - Quake 1 is about diving head-first into the action and never standing still for too long, whereas Quake 2 favours hiding behind cover and taking fights at a slower pace - a massive departure from what players loved about original. Regardless, if you can go into this game with fresh expectations, Quake 2 is still a great and influential Boomer Shooter that holds up surprisingly well today. It is also a much more fitting sequel to DOOM II than the actual DOOM 3, that's for sure. 8/10
