I've not quite finished all the campaigns within Quake II Remastered, but I have finished the main campaign and the new 'Call of the Machine', which were the two main draws for me. I have a great love for Quake II after playing it in high school. Nowadays it seems to be a bit maligned as a game that's slower and less iconic than the first game, and not as polished or 'perfected' as the third entry (to the point where that game is more favourably renowned despite the singleplayer component being quite lacking). However, Quake II has a ton to offer and it does certain things better than either entry. The Remastered version brings some updates that only improve the situation in my eye. First off, the atmosphere is still fantastic. It's not as iconic as the first Quake's Lovecraftian setting, but it's still dark, gory and claustrophobic, with great use of ambient sound. A couple of things to mention here - this is id Software's final pixel art game. The textures in this game throughout the levels look utterly gorgeous, provided you play the game [b]without texture filtering[/b]. Quake II also introduced atmospheric and moody coloured lighting. Now, here's where the Remastered version is a definite improvement - you could [b]not[/b] have unfiltered textures and coloured lighting on at the same time in the original release of Quake II, as enabling software rendering locked the textures into filtered mode. Granted the filtered mode probably looked great in the 90s, but it smears over the detail in the textures. Now with the remastered version, you can properly configure the graphics to make the most detailed and best visually dating iteration of Quake 2 yet. There are also updates to weapon models and level geometry which makes things look a little more detailed. There are notable gameplay updates as well - here some are starting with my favourites: [list] [*]Shots are actually centred on the crosshair now. [*]Weapon switching is much, much faster now, closer to Quake 3's speed. The original release has quite ponderous animations between switching weapons which slows down the game a fair bit. [*]There's a quick select wheel. I didn't think I would actually use it, but Quake II has such an expansive array of gadgets and weapons I ended up really loving it. [*]There's an optional compass function that paints arrows on the floor leading to your next objective. I didn't use this once in the base game, which should attest to the quality of it's design. [*]The shield mechanic is more fleshed out now, and even enemies can be shielded. Not only this, energy weapons are now vastly more effective against shields, which adds another layer onto weapon switching and target prioritisation. I'm a bit torn on this - there are not that many energy weapons and the Hyperblaster already has the highest DPS in the game. The default Blaster could have been made a [i]bit[/i] more effective against shields though, then it would see more use. [/list] When I played Quake II back in high school I was really impressed with how modern it felt. From what I've read it was a big stride forward in terms of FPS level design, in terms of moving away from levels being unconnected sequential hubs. Quake II moves away from the sensation of FPS games consisting of "Level 1.. level 2..." - it has levels that function as miniature hubs that branch off and require you to backtrack. However, any backtracking is integrated utterly perfectly, and the game might be a masterclass on how to effectively utilise and arrange physical space in levels. You'll double up on yourself without realising it and it'll be a surprise every time. The weaponset in Quake II is absolutely my favourite, in terms of design and utility. The viewmodels of the other two Quake games might as well be tubes, and I was really disappointed going from Quake II to III in this regard. The animations and sound design are really imaginative and fun, especially for the time. Some of the weapons here are the VERY top of the top of the line for the FPS genre. THAT double-barrelled shotgun. THAT minigun. THE BFG10K. But my favourite might be the grenade launcher, which while nerfed compared to the other two games, has some of the most satisfying animation and sound design. The only reason I don't play through the whole game with it is because I run out of ammo. On top of weapons, Quake 2 is replete with gadgets to use as well, which greatly increase the amount of options you have for approaching situations. It just trounces the first game in this regard and I'm a big fan of this design ethos in games personally. The enemies are fun. The low-level grunts have lots of things going on with animations and AI that give them a lot of character, and their random last-stand shooting animations on death can trip you up. The enemies do seem to get dumber the bigger they are but they're fine. I've prattled on about details, but newcomers are probably think "Is the original campaign actually any good then?" In my opinion, it's really good, but like in the original release, [b]play it on Nightmare[/b]. Otherwise, it's a bit too boring without the stakes being higher. The game just doesn't really provide quite enough situations where you feel adequately challenged. The prospect of taking more damage forces you to play more carefully and smartly utilise your extensive array of weapons and fun gadgets. Story wise it's just a power fantasy of "bloke saves the day from nasty aliens", which is fine - not many revelations within this reverie. If there are moral themes in this game, it's in the horrors of hostile transhumanism and general cybernetic aesthetic in the levels and enemy design. Story-wise it's a bit mid and there are maybe not enough mind-blowing moments gameplay wise, but it's still very decent, just not quite on the level of something like Half Life (as for Unreal - I can't decide). Having a spruced up version of the original campaign is great, but another great draw of the appeal in this package is the new [b]Call of the Machine[/b] campaign. This campaign has been very obviously been created by fans with a great reverence for the original game and intrinsic understanding of how Quake II's design. I am going to be blunt. In terms of gameplay, it absolutely trounces the original Quake II campaign. And frankly, it might be one of the finest official Quake campaigns ever devised, if not the very best. It is STUPIDLY fun. The enemy count feels tripled from the original campaign, leading to a much faster paced, chaotic, and even more tactical experience, as target prioritisation and resource management take precedent. The campaigns are varied and packed full of little surprises and details and new novel tricks - it really helps that it's split into six parts designed by separate authors. It SLAPS Doom Eternal, and the comparative freedom you have with your extensive and generous weapon and gadget array really puts to death the idea that limiting resources and forcing players into illogical and unsatisfying combat loops is stifling and irritating. It's basically everything I wanted that could improve Quake II and it fucking ROCKS! This is the kind of remaster that is dreamt about. I've not even touched on the other campaigns or the multiplayer (which I always thought was underrated next to the other two games). The value in this package is insane and there's a lot here to bring you back compared to firing up a source port. Quake II fans should get it, Quake fans should get it, boomer shooter fans should get it.

A decent remaster for a dull game. I've always heard people say that Quake II is where id lost the magic, and yeah, it's almost like you can see the point where their soul fell out. It honestly feels like the shovelware Half-Life clones of the early 2000s, albeit not as bad as that makes it sound since it did come out nearly a full year before Half-Life, and there's clearly more meat to Quake II than to most of the later chaff. But even by the standards of its time, and even with the improvements of the remaster, the game just falls flat in so many important ways. I don't think I would call it bad per se, it isn't [i]not[/i] fun, howeverI'd only recommend it as a slice of FPS history (tbf this is probably the only reason you'd be looking at Quake II reviews lol), not as a retro shooter with great replay value to keep you busy for a while. Pretty much every other big game in the years before and after this will give you a better time. What does Quake II do well? - Graphically, it is pretty impressive for late 1997, although with modern eyes it's kinda hard to appreciate that. - Enemies take visible damage, that's cool and something which most games don't even do today. - They have some scripted sequences and environmental storytelling which is neat, a clear stepping stone on the way to Half-Life and similar games in the years to follow. The environments also feel more like real places than the abstract hellscapes of prior shooters, although it still predates the realization that people need doors to enter and exit buildings by many years lmao. - The soundtrack is full of nice soothing guitar riffs, even if they are generic compared to the first game's moody horror ambience. - The inventory system for powerups was a decent idea, although I forgot to use them most of the time lol. - The weapon selection is a bit better than Quake 1. The super shotgun is still a straight upgrade to the normal shotgun, and some of the guns feel like they do the same things with different ammo types, but for the most part everything has its uses. So, what does Quake II do poorly? Unfortunately, all the actually important bits, and more. - The movement feels slow and floaty, like you're sneaking around on ice. Quake 1 feels quick and crisp, Half-Life 1 feels quick and crisp, Doom feels quick, but this feels like a water slide covered in syrup. - Every enemy feels like an unflinching bullet sponge. You might think, well that's true of every game in the 90s, and yeah it is, but the good ones don't [i]feel[/i] like bullet sponges, they give you more feedback or some kind of interesting tactical play or weak spots to hit or whatever. This is just shooting things slowly until they die. - Also, welcome to hitscan hell. The combat has largely devolved into corner peeking and pressing ADADADADAD until one of you dies. - Kinda tied in to the above, the weapons all feel soft. Even the railgun, which seems like it should be the best non-BFG weapon in your arsenal, can only be described by comparison to that feeling where you have to sneeze but can't so you just kinda sit there feeling robbed of your time. - The art style is weak as hell, it's just so generic. It's like a cartoon parody of ugly old sci-fi games. The Strogg are horrifying on paper but the visuals do not do them justice at all. The sounds are also very meh. - The level design is awful even by 90s standards, I see what they were going for but it really plays terribly in practice. "Maze-like levels" is a common and often well-deserved complaint with all of these old shooters, yet Quake II somehow gets the worst of the new and old by making linear mazes where you walk down a few cramped identical corridors and then get lost for 10 minutes because they expect you to backtrack through two loading screens with no signposting or new enemy spawns to say you're on the right path. It's literally easier to find most of the secrets than to find the way forwards. - Even aesthetically, levels lack variety, there is one flavour of Strogg architecture and it gets boring very very quickly. Quake 1 did suffer from everything being kinda the same, especially in episode 4, but at least it had a vibe, this doesn't. If you really need a shooter from 1997 specifically, just play Dark Forces II. Or Outlaws. Or, idk, the Quake 1 mission pack which came out a few months earlier. Hell, I am sure there were some good Doom wads coming out around this time.

Quake II still absolutely holds up. The pacing, the gunplay and the feel of the weapons are all incredibly satisfying - every shotgun blast and railgun shot lands with real weight. I honestly forgot how much I love Quake 2. The past week I've found myself playing it for hours on end, going through the single player over and over. Once on hard, again on Nightmare, and one more on Nightmare without the use of the Super Shotgun. In 2023, the game got a free remaster release that provides you with plenty new features to go from. You have the main game, coupled with the mission packs, Ground Zero and the Reckoning released back in 1998, along side a new expansion called Call of the Machine - Along packed with the N64 campaign. They added some gameplay changes, such as: - An inventory and weapon wheel, that slows the game down upon opening. - They added a compass item for players to help guide players through the maps. - Nightmare mode is no longer hidden - AI has improved behavior patterns, such as dodging and running around projectiles, and will stubbornly follow the player rather than stand still or get stuck. Multiplayer now also provides public and private lobbies without the need of having to port forward. I decided I wanted to give the game one last go without the use of the Super Shotgun, because I feel like that weapon just carries you too much. More so than the one from Doom 2, if I'm gonna be honest. The fact that you can carry up to 200 shells after finding a couple of backpacks, leaves you not needing to ever come back and get the ammo later. I had MORE fun playing through the game without using it at all, sometimes less is just more. EITHER WAY In my opinion, this is one of the best boomer shooters you could try.

[TO NOTE: I'm basing my experience off of the Yamagi source port. I haven't played the Nightdive release much] It's fine. Not fantastic. A solidly fun but messy follow up that leaves a bit to be desired. I wasn't expecting an atmosphere on-par with the original but I also wasn't expecting the bleak, oppressive industrial aesthetic that exists to be drowned out by the soundtrack and general schlocky-ness of other parts of the game. It feels like the tone the game has and the tone it wants are clashing at every opportunity . The larger , more open level layouts give way to a lot of backtracking and samey design as Id struggles to make the nebulous industrial spaces feel like real locations. The enemy design is a lot less rigid and intelligent than the original and especially on normal staggering is way too generous - lategame enemies boil down to how many railgun shots you can put in them before they can ever attack. The Strogg are an interesting concept that's simultaneously too comprehensible and too vague to leave any sort of impact outside of being this games enemy lineup. That said, the gunplay is some of the strongest from Id , the Railgun especially is a blast to use. A decent number of areas accommodate for the increased scale nicely without letting the player get too lost. The aesthetic is genuinely wonderful despite the aforementioned tonal issues. The music can be a bit repetitive but mostly slaps. At it's core Quake 2 is a well-designed boomer shooter that feels like it's forcing itself to be less interesting than it wants to be, and it succeeds in that endeavor for better and for worse.

I was really excited to play this game after 100%ing Quake 1 on nightmare. But sadly i was disappointed. This is a good game but it just feels like a downgrade of quake 1 in almost every way. The Levels? There was genuinely no memorable level in my head. They all look and play the same. But it gets even better(worse)! Unlike in the original where the gameplay loop follows the formula: Level A -> Level B The levels now are interconnected with lots of different ways to get lost. Now you have stuff like: Level A -> Level -> B -> Level A -> Level B -> Level C -> Level A -> Level D. This is just incredibly tedious. Thank god this remaster has a compass. Because otherwise you get insanely lost. What even is the point of making the levels like a maze if you have to use an item which shows you the way? Thats just stupid. I was just spaming the compass all the time because i couldn't bother exploring because behind the most doors you risk going into the previous level again with a loading screen. Great. And then all these objectives. They aren't meaningful in any way. Get this Keycard, activate that Satellite, disable that lasergate, airstrike this and that, find entrace into bla bla bla. It genuinely adds no value compared to the original level formula in quake 1 where your goal is to exit the level. Thank god the Call of the Machine DLC has the best levels with lots of variety. How could MachineGames create a DLC 20 years after the release in which every level is better than the base game and its original 2 DLCs? How could the original level designers fuck up so bad? The Weapons? The Railgun is fun but besides that... the weapons just feel off. Sounddesign is bad, punchiness is gone. The new super shotgun isn't even able to follow the footsteps of the double barrel shotgun in the original. It sounds so shallow. Only exception is the minigun. Mowing down multiple low tier enemies is enjoyable. And MachineGames understood that! There are plenty levels in the dlc where you get a minigun and plenty of ammo dropped, before hordes of normal soldiers spawn. They just know. How about the enemies? They are just plain annoying. Do you enjoy getting two-shot by a Gladiator on Hard difficulty? Do you like parasite dogs which are incredibly hard to dodge because they don't have a clear animation when they hit you with their tail giving you no time to evade? Brains which hook you in the middle of the fight to their place, getting you stuck in a corner and slapping you in the face? Medics which revive enemies like the Gladiator in less than 2 seconds, all while spawning 2 low tier infantry simutaneosly every 2 seconds and thus making you unable to hit him? Berserkers who like to jump you in the face from all across the room? The icarus which has a ridiculously high amount of health for no reason? Oh and most low tier enemies can dodge projectiles. Which is random. Thus making fights even harder because you don't even know if you're able to reliably kill an enemy with your rocket even if your aim is 100% correct. Due to lots of verticality(which is a good addition) you don't always have the chance to kill enemies due to AoE damage. So shooting in their face is your only option. Lets see... the aesthetics? Literally every level looks the same. I'm serious. I'm not gonna go in that trent razor "quake 2 has no atmosphere" quote, because that's an misconception. He didn't say that. But the sentence itself has some truth. Compared to quake 1 the atmosphere is just... almost gone. To be fair: the levels in quake 1 also almost looked the same, but they just had more soul. At least that's my conception. Some gadgets just feel straight up useless. What the hell am i gonna use a silencer for? IR Goggles? And some weapons are completely redundant. Especially from the DLCs. You have so many different machine guns which feel the same but use different ammo. Amazing. And who thought it is a great idea to manually throw them grenades instead of just using the launcher? It takes ages to throw them. It just makes the duration from receiving the first grenades until you get your grenades launcher tedious. Proximity mines? Yeah... uh no. But WAIT! There is one thing i have to praise Quake 2 for. Can you guess it? The MUSIC! The Music is amazing. You start the first level and you're greeted by a fantastic track which introduces the game and the rest of the music direction for the soundtrack. Sonic Mayhem did an amazing job. Some Riffs are stuck in my head even years after playing this game for the first time. Don't get me wrong Nine Inch Nails did a great job for the first game to match the atmosphere.. but those are tracks are just Incidental music. Nothing you want to listen after playing the game. Except maybe the first minute of the first song. I'm also a bit dissapointed in Nightdive for adding such lackluster achievements. You get 100% for completing every level regardless of difficulty... How about a achievement for finding each secret level? Especially those in the DLC are pretty fun with their trial formula. Besides all that nightdive did an amazing job in remastering this game. Common Nightdive W. (And for implementing that compass thank you so much q_q) Maybe i'm just butthurt because i expected this game to be atleast as good as quake 1 but i was let down :/ I still recommend this game and im sure that you'll have plenty of fun with it regardless :3

The game's atmosphere, enhanced by its soundtrack, immerses you in its gritty sci-fi world. Overall, Quake II offers a satisfying experience for those looking to revisit a classic or explore it for the first time.

Speaking of projectiles, they come out of the weapon itself, so where the shot lands depends on your handedness. There's an option to change this in the remaster, but if you're playing on a source port, the command is "hand 2". Yeah, it hasn't aged too well, and the gun play is a bit finicky, but it's still fun to blast through if you can look past its flaws.

Having never played the original Quake II, I came into this without any strong feelings about the changes Nightdive made to the original formula in this remaster. They did a great job with the original Quake in 2021 and figured they'd do just as good a job in Quake II two years later. I was right. I think the changes made to gameplay are probably for the better; even on Hard the Remaster isn't all that difficult, so the original would have been even less difficult, so I think the thoughtfulness with which Nightdive approached rebalancing the whole package was great. And QoL things like the Compass make traversing multiple maps within a Unit way more tolerable instead of aimlessly wondering about when confused about where to go to progress. Speaking of package - there's a metric tonne of stuff in here to enjoy: [h3]Quake II[/h3] The base campaign is a complete shift away from the Lovecraftian fantasy of the first game. For me, this is probably for the better. And whilst I appreciated the Trent Reznor soundtrack for its ambience, Sonic Mayhem's bangers are more up my street too. Core gameplay was strong back in 1997, it's clear. And it's still punchy and fun today. The Units are really well designed and introduction of new weapons and enemies was handled really well to keep things feeling fresh later on. [h3] Mission Pack: The Awakenening [/h3] We get some new toys to play with that, unfortunately, don't quite pack the same punch as the original weapons, so they don't get much use. There's a couple of new enemies too, which add some variety and richness to the attempts at storytelling. Other than some new powerups as well, it's pretty much more of the same. Which is absolutely fine with me! [h3] Mission Pack: Ground Zero [/h3] Undoubtedly the weakest of the bunch. The difficulty is isn't really an issue, but it's more about how irritating that slight difficulty is to overcome. Constantly checking for turrets doesn't make for a particularly enjoyable experience. I'm given to understand that Nightdive nerfed them from the original, making this a a tolerable campaign to undertake rather than one to be avoided at all costs. [h3] Call of the Machine [/h3] Machine Games return after the disappointing Ground Zero with what can only be described as an epic campaign. After Quake's Dimension of the Machine, wherein Machine Games exploited the Kex engine for all it's worth, I was really looking forward to this. The game is no longer continuous, but broken into discrete mini-campaigns for each Unit. This gives each a very distinctive feeling, direction and design philosophy that works incredibly well. This is the hardest campaign in the package, but it's probably also the best, with a finale dripping with fan service. The maps are ambitious in terms of scale, aesthetic and challenge, with some very high enemy counts and [usually] some good firepower to get the player through it. One Unit was definitely trickier than the others, with a lack of resources making it slightly less enjoyable. But overall, probably worth the price of admission on its own. [h3]Quake II 64 [/h3] I came into this expecting it to be a doddle, with low enemy counts necessitated by 1990s console hardware limits. But some cunning use of enemies in these very compact maps, coupled with Nightdive's tweaks made this short campaign more difficult than I'd anticipated. I'll likely not remember much about this in the near future, which speaks to it's "good-but-not-great"-ness, but it's definitely worth a go, and it's not like it'll take long (and the road to platinum trophy is pretty easy as well). [h3] Overall [/h3] Brilliant.

To me Quake 2 was just as boring and completely outdated as Quake 1. An improvement is that Quake 2 has a coherent sci-fi story, you know who you fight against = an alien race (the Strogg), you even have some story cinematics from time to time, they give you objectives and the enemies make more sense. In Quake 1 all the elements were all over the place. You were wondering in both some occult and sci-fi dimensions and the enemies were of all kinds (human, monsters, aliens). It's clear Quake 1 is the compilation of many different ideas put together. In Quake 2 you still don't have a mini-map but you have a compass that tells you where to go and what to do at all times. On one hand, it's way better then the tiresome searching in Quake 1, but at the other hand, now it's all even more bland and boring. You just follow that line and kill enemies in the way. Isn't it better to give players a map so the players can navigate the levels/locations by themselves? Because in this way it's easy to miss some parts of the level because the compass just points to the next main objective. Quake 2 is even harder then the predecessor. Enemies are still bullet sponges but the damage they inflict is way higher. Now some enemies can one-shot you. I found the game hard on the "normal" difficulty. Ammo is still scarce, so I was continuosly adding some ammo with cheats. If you don't add ammo with cheats it's a tiresome puzzle game. You have to carefully think where to spend which type of ammo. "Oh I need to use this weapon here on this enemies, but then I have to use that weapon on those enemies, but I have to save some of the stronger ammo on those stronger enemies later". The DLC's are even harder then the base game so without the health cheats I could never beat them, to be honest. The game comes with all 3 DLC's included, and that prolongs the story a lot. It's just for the biggest fans of FPS games. I found the game soul-less. In Quake 1 you had an interesting atmosphere and gloomy locations, while here it's all some brown-grey silos in some spaceship ( but some DLC's added some more locations and color, and better graphics ). To conclude, there is in my opinion 0 reasons to buy this game in 2025 with so many interesting FPS titles out there.

This is not me hating on Quake 2 but rather the Quake 2 remaster. Many elements were changed; they were changed not in order to improve the game, yet rather to make the game more obnoxious. Such as: making some enemies more unbalanced and more difficult, making ammo limits more of a thing (particularly with the grenades/land mines), and changing the effectiveness of certain weapons (some are better than others). While I enjoy that the Remaster looks and feels smooth, the gameplay changes are not something to adore aside from the compass and the weapon/ inventory wheels. The enemy balance change that I hate the most is the one enemy that used to only have a short-ranged melee attack, but now has a much harder-to-avoid long-ranged dashing melee attack. In my opinion, this is more of a Quake 2 re-imagination collection or a remake. The Quake 1 remaster felt like a semi-ugly but real remaster considering that it didn't change any gameplay mechanics other than adding a weapon wheel, while the Quake 2 remaster felt like it was trying to become more of a remake. The plus-side is that there's a free Remaster of Quake 2 64 found in-game, a PSX version of Quake 2 found on MODDB, and in September of this year there's supposed to be a prequel mod to Quake 2 called Call of The Void which attempts to add cohesion between Quake 1 and Quake 2 coming to Quake 2 Remastered and modding sites. I usually like remasters made by Nightdive but this one, while feature-rich, seemed to try to change the game rather than just remaster it. Remember to eat your QUAKEr Oats!

What is awfull though is "Ground Zero", which is a horrid DLC. Quake 2 and Call of the Machine have a certain type of level design which you can still see in the new Doom releases: Open arenas to fight the enemies in which you are given the space to take advantage of the movement and of explosive weapons. Ground Zero DOES NOT, 90% of it is crammed corridors with twists and turns with enemies hidden behind every corner, and I am not exaggerating, this is how most of this DLC is like, which results in a tiring gameplay loop of: "Enter room, retreat, wait for enemies to follow you down the corridor, shoot at them" or "peak behind wall, shoot and repeat.", you don't get to jump around and dodge enemy attacks or do trick shots with grenade or rocket lanuchers, its literally antithethical to what makes the game good. To add on to this, in a corridor hitscan weapons are obviously the best, which means you oversue them and get left without ammo, which means you have to rely on grenade launchers and rocket lanuchers in these jam packed corridors which is just frustrating and boring. To top it off, it has the worst enemy selection out of all the DLCs and main game: a whole lot of Flyers, Gladiators, stalkers and parasites and gunners, a toxic ass combination of hitscan enemies that can also bridge distance quite easily, which adds to the frustration when using explosive weapons. Not to mention you also have the turrets and the ocasional enemy spawning RIGHT BEHIND YOU IN A CORRIDOR. And it missed so much of the main game aesthethic! None of the gothic elements are there, its all blue and grey, the enemies are all red and green for some reason and its missing the classics like barracuda, mutant, shambler. The Reconing felt like the devs had no budget, but this one Its like the devs made the DLC bad on purpose or something. Its a shame too, since it adds some very cool weapons, but you dont get to enjoy them, since no matter what weapon you are using you are forced in the same playstyle, you also don't get too much ammo for them and imo some of the old weapons should have been removed from the DLC, less weapon selection means you can enjoy the new ones more ( except for the chainfist which is useless for some reason ). Theres also Quake 64, which is not as bad as Ground Zero, it does do some of the annoying corridor shooter bullshit and surprise enemies, but it also has some interesting levels towards the end. I'm making this review in the hopes that if Devs see that even 20+ years later people are attached to the game they might try giving it another update! As they did in 2023, which was amazing, they added new areas and new secret areas, besides the newest DLC, so I don't see why they shouldn't go further and change some things in these old DLC's to improve them. With all that being said, it is Quake 2, it is amazing, I love it, BUY IT BUY IT BUY IT.

Quake II was on of the games I always wanted to try since I started gaming. For context, I started playing games in 2010. I just never played games for the previous 14 years of my life. That meant that I missed out on a lot of the retro greats. Quake II was one of those. I decided to get it in 2015 but couldn't figure out how to use sourceports or getting the soundtrack working. SO I just never played it but thought about it and even tried again but I just couldn't get everything working so I left it in my library. Then in 2023, the masters of remasters, Nightdive Studios released a remaster, with all the DLC, the N64 version and a new campaign. This review will be from a person who played the game for the first time after the release. Quake II is about war. and killing and stuff. I never bothered to follow the story. The level design was unique for it's time. You had a few levels connected to each other to form a hub (Or "unit" as the game calls it) with objectives to complete. You had to move between the levels to open doors in other levels within the Unit. It was probably tough to figure it out back in the day but the new version has a compass feature to use whenever you got loss that points you to the next objective. You can also spam it continuously if you want to but that's no fun. The weapons in this version was fun to use and varied, with the expansions having some unique weapons. What should be noted, based from reviews made before the remaster's release is that the weapons have been adjusted. The machine gun had way more recoil in the original version. The enemies are fun to fight for me but there is a lack of variety. While the look different there are a few types with different weapons. Small guys with guns (Hitscanners, I think), bigger guys with explosives, flying guys with lasers and melee dog like enemies. There were a few enemies that stood out, like the Tanks (big guys on tank tracks), some okayish bosses. What makes the combat fun, engaging and challenging is the combination of enemies thrown at you. It's fair (most of the time and I never felt like a situation was impossible to overcome. The updated graphics looks great, with a lot of stuff added. I'm not sure if the touched the sound but the soundtrack is included and works right out of the box. If you like retro shooters or have ever been curious about the amazing game, this remaster is the best way to play it. P.S. I have since gotten better with sourceports and stuff like that so I put in a few playtroughs with different soureports and still prefer this release.

Quake 2 is my favorite FPS, at least concerning the main campaign. It gets underwritten as a game with less atmosphere than Quake and I think that's unfair. It has a very cohesive and consistent world, the Strogg are a grotesque foe, and the levels tell a story of escalating human misery in the way people are recycled and eaten by the Strogg. The soundtrack would be repetitive if it weren't for the fact that it's simply EXCELLENT, and although it lacks the sheer ambience of Quake, it fits better with the badass marine theme Quake 2 is hitting. I love the enemies in the game, although they are all decidedly Strogg in design and often have a pretty similar palette making them less distinguishable than enemies in other FPS titles, the variations in their attacks and weapon types are what makes them fun to fight, and the remaster doubles down on this by restoring some attacks and animations that were missing from the original. I'm a long time Doom fan and I have played a large variety of map packs from Plutonia to Eviternity and Sunlust, and have become accustomed to the doom dance over time and fare decently in Ultraviolence in all of the standard Doom 1 and Doom 2 WADs. But despite having spent so much more time with Doom, after really sitting down with Quake 2 after so many years and devoting real time too it, I understand the cleverness in its design. The levels being broken up into manageable units while still having some backtracking and areas that cannot be explored until later objectives are completed was a great choice because while it is possible to get lost, you are never going so in the weeds that you can't find your way back. The new compass feature alleviates this as well but I try not to use it, and also it is not always completely helpful or accurate. I have clocked 18 hours on the PC version but many more on the Xbox and PS5 versions, and the control on all of them is exemplary. The once thing I like more about the console version is the fact that on PS5, sound effects come through on the controller and that can be pretty impactful when you are unloading a full round of chaingun ammo into a Tank Commander. Online multiplayer is great, it certainly has a lower skill ceiling than Quake Live if you just want to enjoy some matches, but servers are scant as is to be expected from a game that is now decades old. My favorite addition is Nightmare mode. Called Hard + and removed from the game originally, Nightmare removes enemy stagger and enemies also fire more often. It's a great challenge with a small handful of stages proving to be extremely tricky on it until you learn how they flow. It is nothing compared to Nightmare in Doom, being more comparable if anything to Ultraviolence. But it demands that players be pretty adept with all ammo types, especially grenades which I kind of bypassed in previous runs until I got the launcher for them. Ammo management here is great - if you play smart, you should never really run out of it completely, which is good because the blaster is tough. Strategically saving health pickups is also a boon, and in the later stages, power armor is essential. The visuals are absolutely beautiful. If you are into mapping you can configure Trenchbroom to make levels for the remaster as well, so that's a huge plus. All in all, Quake 2 is hands down my favorite shooter, and with the remaster, this is the absolute best way to enjoy it out of the box. The new campaign Call of the Machine is a spectacle, with Doom-like enemy counts in some situations, and is extremely challenging and well designed. The fact that you also get Ground Zero, Reckoning, and Quake 64's campaign as extras is just icing. Quake 2 should be more well loved and remembered than it is because in my opinion, the multiplayer at the time was so good it completely overshadowed what was by then a fairly rudimentary Doom Clone with some extra meat. But if you look deeper and really take the time to play through and enjoy the campaign, it's clear that they were not slacking in the single player department by any stretch.

Quake II is shockingly different to the first game, and that's a good thing. I didn't love the first Quake, but Quake II is so f*cking good. Enemy variety is better, guns are better, levels are better and a little more varied. There is some backtracking unfortunately, but the compass which is a fantastic addition makes it easy to know where to go next. There is much more purpose to each level this time. You have objectives you need to do, and after completing each mission you are given a quick brief on your next objectives. I have to mention the Chain Gun, it feels so f*cking good to shoot. Probably my favorite weapon. The soundtrack is incredible, although the music starts getting repetitive after a while. There is a lot of care put into small details. Enemies can duck their heads to dodge rockets. Enemy corpses attract flies. There is visible damage on their models the more you shoot them. Enemies actually react to being shot by either falling over or getting staggered. Some enemies will continue shooting even after you blow their head off. Enemies splatter into pieces if you use an explosive weapon or a shotgun up close. I will always prefer animated enemy deaths over ragdolls, they just have so much more character. Such a big upgrade to the first game in every single way. Credit to Nightdive Studios for updating the game and making it run like butter on modern systems.

Quick review from Quake 2 speedrunner (Top 30 atm) [h3] Review [/h3] To begin with, this is proper remaster. I can't be hundred percent sure but this is not per-se [i]original[/i] experience of the game. First-time players will get extremely good old-school game, crisp multiplayer and tons of good time. For Quake 2 freaks, like me, who played original for years and years - there are a lot of changes, yet, they can be somewhat divisive. This is a nitpicking territory, Nightdive and others have done absolutely stellar job with remastering this game for casual audience. What is written after this is for Quake 2 veterans. First of all, the engine got tweaks or this is totally different engine / fork. Movement is different, the speed is slightly off, the physics are working in a different way and there are bugs introduced that never were a problem in an original. Finally, there are ways to get out-of-bounds in a game that had no out-of-bounds of any kind. Speaking from "speedrunner" perspective, this version is actually worst way to speedrun the game - a lot of small details in combination makes the game totally different per se. I will also cram here the new enemy AI - it is more developed and have more dynamics, yes, it is also RNG-fest and they're also far more aggressive, even on "Easy" difficulty, the Any% one. Second thing, maps. A lot of original maps have been expanded in some ways. Some changes are fine - base1 has separate area outside, some maps are beautified and so on. Some changes are "fixes" - power2 skip is no more, fact2 laser grid can't be skipped and so on. Some changes are head scratching - fact2 got moving platforms over lava before last area, like, huh okay. New expansion is 100% worth it, great content and is total apogee of Quake 2 mapping. Basically, it's a fresh look on Quake 2 from the prism of modern gaming perspective. Thing is, I am not exactly sure, do old games need this kind of "refreshment".

Funny thing, this antinomy - a contradiction between two statements that seem equally reasonable. Like when you say "This statement is false". People listen to this sentence, they sit and start thinking, and soon enough their brains will start to melt. Or like when you say "There is no absolute truth" and then you put your bare hands into the fire. Ten out of ten times you will end up burning your fingers. So we can say that the sentence "you will get burned when you put your bare hand into fire" is always true. 100%, work like a charm, every time. But there is still no absolute truth in the universe. Quake 2 is an antimony in the video games world. Because this game is - at the same time - an experience that is extremely good and painfully mid. To understand why it's extremely good, we need first understand flaws and lows of Quake 1. First game was revolutionary from a technology perspective, but very, very jank from the technical side - the fully 3D environments and characters in the game world with fast, stable frames and zippy action speed was something never seen before 1996. But it was also very janky, clunky game, with little unresponsive movement (you was moving more like on ice than on solid ground) and broken hitboxes; It has atmosphere, but no story; It was surreal, labyrinthian experience without cohesive direction rather than grounded, more realistic approach to topic. Weapons - aside rocket launchers - were meh, enemies were too spongy and too simple. Playing on Nightmare was more like torture slog rather than fun time. All this was fixed in Quake 2. Movement is more tight and responsive, so you have a better feel of control of your character, and mouse look is way, way smoother and better. Weapons are also much, much better designed and tuned with damage and rate of fire, so now you do not need to spend eight (!) shells to kill the most common, low tier enemy, and guns like super shotgun or even machine gun (thank God Nightdive decided to remove knockback from this one!) are more satisfying to use - hearing loud "Boom" and seeing how a cloud of pellets turn the enemy to bloody pulp is always nice to experience; Enemies are way way better balanced and sophisticated rather than just simple melee and range difference with wider range of damage output - and with introducing more hit scanner types they can put a little bit of pressure on player; hit boxes are also better implemented, albeit there are still instances of shooting enemies without seeing them, but mostly bigger ones; There is also a story and clear direction in level design without absurdly complicated mazes, and with more realistic approach dealing with progression is less frustrating. All this improvement makes Quake 2 a better experience from a gameplay perspective. And yet, at the same time, this game is painfully mid. Why? Maybe because worldbuilding, enemies and premise is generic and shallow to the bone? Forget about fighting monsters and cosmic abomination in surreal, eldritch worlds. Now you have a simple story about space marine fighting with alien cyborgs in their homeworld. How many times have we seen this already? Even in 1997 it was so overused tropes in video games, books, movies in comics. None of this is memorable and has even a pinch of character. Story doesn't matter, because it's a boomer shooter, and yet we are constantly exposed to its bits, through scripted sequences (which mostly are reduced to blowing things up or fighter jets flying above heads), radio chatter or even multiple objectives, which you can do by accident when you are fighting with enemies. No one cares about it. And look at enemies. When I see Shambler in Quake 1, I feel threatened. In Q2 I am put against some small metal dudes who are shooting at me from afar. Yeah, they may have different guns, but that all - the biomechanical horror of Strogg empire does not work on me, because I can simply dispatch even the biggest, meanest looking tin-can soldier with ease. Which is a good segway to difficulty - rebalancing works TOO WELL in this game. The fact that enemies stop being too spongy makes them less threatening. Playing vanilla game was like walking in the park. I died maybe less than 5 times, all of which was in the end game, where you fight tank commanders in tight corridors and cannot circle-strafing around them. They are so without character that I even refuse to analyze them further. My advice - just point a gun and shoot, from time to time run away or in circles around them. What is more hilarious is that the people apparently have troubles with Berserkers. You know guys that you can jump when they land their jump attack to avoid damage? Different story is in expansions, which are more difficult, but in a bad sense, because using cheap tricks to catch players off guard is a sign of incompetent design. Or maybe it's about level design? You thought levels in Q1 were monotonne blur of the same structures? Q2 is even worse. We have military bases, prisons, Industrial factories, citadels, maybe from time to time mines and caves. All of them look exactly the same, and they are even simpler, so your smooth FPS brain cannot feel lost. And gimmick with traveling back and forth between levels to accomplish different objectives is a poor excuse to extend game time, forcing you on multiple occasions to run through empty levels, because you forgot about pressing one damn switch. Pro tip - if music (which is great heavy metal stuff BTW) stops playing suddenly after doing things like blowing something up or pressing a lever, it's a subtle hint that you are done and time to GTFO from place. Cohesive structure of Q2 is a blessing and a curse at the same time. It makes gameplay a much better experience, but on the other hand makes the game more generic and shallow, more forgettable and less impactful. There is this famous quote from Trent Reznor, dude from Nine Inch Nails, who made music from Q1, about the second game - "This game has no atmosphere". This was debunked later by Sonic Maychen, the person behind Q2 music as being fake, but I think it's a good summary of Quake 2. More I say: I feel we can make this sentence even more perfect: This game has no soul. It's like watching your favorite indie game going mainstream. You witness how everything that was unique and memorable is slowly turning into a well designed, corporate machine. Yeah, it works, even better than before and makes tons of fun, but something is missing, some personal touch, some spirit. It's more about excel spreadsheets rather than having fun. Or like watching your daughter growing up only to become an OF model. And now, little about campaigns. Vanilla Q2 it's a great power fantasy. You are this one badass dude, dropped behind enemy lines, who just deletes everything that is moving around you from existence. It has great pacing, good enemies placements, but lacking in difficulty. In the last unit, the palace section, I was just swimming in ammo, swapping between weapons for my amusement, never feeling threatened or in danger, aside when fighting the tank commander. I died to them mostly because I was too greedy with peeking around corners and forgetting about timings. The Reckoning is too long. It has too many levels with little to none new textures, and has lost pacing. And alternative weapons suck ass, new enemies are just reskins with different weapons, posing zero real threat. Game really should end after starport, but it drags, and drags, wasting player time mostly.

My palace. My Stroggos. My Quake II. Circa ~2014, I was a junior in high school. Instead of going to prom that weekend, I stayed home and played Quake and Quake II. At the time, I didn't know anything about the games or patching them, so I played the Steam ports with no music. Since then, I've replayed Q2 with Yamagi on Nightmare and found it to be too easy. I've now played the 2023 remaster on Nightmare, and I've got to say this is a class act remaster in every single way. The new graphics are exactly how your mind remembers playing Q2 while retaining the original atmosphere. You can tell that the developers lovingly improved every texture. The guns look sharper than ever, especially the BFG10k. The enemies look meaner than ever, and they pack a nasty punch. Vanilla Q2, while it had an amazing cohesive industrial design, lacked a challenging difficulty and fell into obscurity as it was overshadowed by its bigger brothers DOOM and Quake. Nightdive's overhaul of the gameplay has turned it into one of the very best shooters of its time. On vanilla Nightmare, you can fly through the game with little to no challenge. On the remaster's Nightmare, you will begin struggling around Unit 6: Power & Cooling and spend the rest of the game fighting tooth and nail to survive. You're juiced to the gills, but so are your enemies. The tight movement and gory fights creates some truly refined gameplay. My playthrough ended with me in the final showdown with the Makron, out of power-ups and fighting him in a Mexican standoff with my railgun, praying that I last longer than he does. Which is exactly how a great game should end. My playthrough took me 8 hours. While I think you've experienced everything the game has to offer around the 6th hour mark, there's no denying that Q2 has a fantastic linear campaign with a much more cohesive design than its predecessor. The remaster also includes a tutorial, The Reckoning and Ground Zero expansions, Call of the Machine episode, and N64 port. My favorite is The Reckoning by Xatrix Entertainment - thank you Drew Markham (Xatrix founder) and may you rest easy. The id Vault is absolutely worth checking out as it includes the playable E3 97 and ECTS 97 demos, loads of development artwork and backstory, and model previews. I'm forever thankful to Yamagi Burmeister (Yamagi developer) and hope he's taking it easy these days, but Nightdive's remaster adds so many quality of life improvements that it's truly the definitive way to play Q2. Make sure you find the secret level in Unit 8: Hangar - Outer Hangar to play the best level in the game. :) Quake II will always rule the cosmos!

Quake II Remastered - A Perfect Balance of Nostalgia and Modern Enhancements Quake II Remastered is not just a visual upgrade - it's a full-fledged enhancement that stays true to the original while improving on nearly every aspect. As someone who played the original, I can confidently say that the quality-of-life improvements, like the compass, make a significant difference. Navigation feels smoother, and this small addition alone makes progression more intuitive. I played on moderate difficulty, and it strikes the perfect balance - challenging enough to stay engaging, yet not too punishing for a busy gamer. The gunplay and movement are still fantastic. The arcade-like mechanics demand skill rather than randomness, making every encounter feel satisfying. The visuals are fantastic, modern yet retaining that classic feel. If you remember the old PC gaming days, this remaster hits the perfect nostalgic sweet spot. On PC, everything runs smoothly, and I didn't experience any performance issues. The Call of the Machine expansion is the highlight of this remaster. Bloody Good Time is a darkly humorous first-person multiplayer game developed by Outerlight Ltd. and published by Ubisoft, released in 2010 as a spiritual successor to the cult classic The Ship. Built on the Source engine, it inherits the same mix of stealth, social deception, and unpredictable violence that made its predecessor so unique, but it wraps those ideas in a more accessible, fast-paced, and gleefully chaotic framework. The setting is a satirical take on Hollywood's obsession with horror and fame: players assume the roles of aspiring actors competing for a part in the latest film by the notorious Director X. Each round unfolds like a twisted audition, where the only way to impress the director is to eliminate your assigned target - and avoid being murdered by someone else in turn. It's a concept that immediately sets a tongue-in-cheek tone, combining slapstick absurdity with a layer of tense strategy. The premise unfolds across a handful of movie-themed sets - from a lavish beach house to a grimy motel and a creepy horror mansion - each designed to evoke a sense of playful carnage. These maps serve as the backdrop for rounds of murder and misdirection, where up to eight players stalk, sabotage, and deceive one another in pursuit of fame, fortune, and survival. The rules are deceptively simple: every player receives a contract to kill a specific target, while another player has a contract on them. The challenge lies in pulling off the perfect kill without attracting attention from guards or security cameras. Each weapon, from frying pans and baseball bats to electric traps and explosives, carries different point values, encouraging creative kills rather than repetitive brawls. This dynamic scoring system pushes players to improvise and take risks, ensuring that every match unfolds differently and rewards ingenuity over brute force. The balance between chaos and cunning is what gives Bloody Good Time its distinctive edge, making every kill feel both ridiculous and strangely satisfying. Outerlight's sense of humor permeates every corner of the game. The characters - a colorful cast of archetypal movie stereotypes like the surfer, the goth, and the nerd - lean into caricature, emphasizing the game's B-movie atmosphere. Director X's sardonic commentary and the exaggerated performances of each character reinforce the idea that you're part of a grotesque production, where every death is just another scene to be filmed. The slapstick tone makes the violence feel comedic rather than grim, transforming murder into performance. Combined with the stylized visuals and exaggerated animations, this creates an aesthetic that feels like a parody of both horror films and competitive shooters. The result is an experience that never takes itself too seriously, even when the stakes of each round start to feel personal. It's as much about laughing at the absurdity of the situation as it is about actually winning. Gameplay-wise, Bloody Good Time builds on the mechanics of The Ship but trades some of its slower, more deliberate pacing for a snappier and more action-oriented style. Players still have to manage their needs - hunger, fatigue, hygiene, and entertainment - which forces them to move through the map and expose themselves to risk, but the pace is faster and more forgiving than in its predecessor. The inclusion of guards and security cameras means that careless aggression can backfire spectacularly, adding a layer of tactical restraint to what might otherwise be pure chaos. The best moments often come from tension rather than combat - stalking your target through crowded hallways, waiting for the perfect opportunity, and striking just before someone does the same to you. The interplay of hunter and hunted keeps every round unpredictable, as you're constantly juggling offense and defense while trying to read other players' behavior. Even when you fail, the unpredictability of it all makes each match entertaining in its own way. However, while Bloody Good Time's concept is brilliant, its execution sometimes struggles to keep up. The game launched with only three maps and a limited selection of modes, which can make it feel repetitive after extended play. The controls and weapon handling, while functional, lack the smoothness or precision of larger FPS titles from its era, and the AI in single-player bot matches never truly captures the tension of playing against humans. The game's reliance on online multiplayer also means that its long-term appeal lives or dies by the activity of its community. Unfortunately, over time, player numbers dwindled, leaving the online lobbies sparsely populated or completely empty in many regions. While it's still possible to play with friends through private matches or local network play, the absence of a steady player base limits the spontaneity that made it so exciting at launch. It's a reminder that even the most clever multiplayer concepts can struggle to endure without consistent support or updates. Despite these limitations, Bloody Good Time remains a fascinating piece of gaming history - a snapshot of a developer experimenting with ideas well ahead of their time. Its blend of asymmetrical gameplay, stealth, and comedy anticipated the rise of social deduction and sandbox party games that would gain popularity a decade later. What makes it special is how effortlessly it combines humor and tension, turning murder into a theatrical spectacle. The Source engine's flexibility allows for vibrant lighting, quirky animations, and environments that still hold up surprisingly well for their age, giving the game a distinctive, cartoonish charm. The sound design adds another layer of personality, with dramatic stings and exaggerated screams punctuating the absurd violence. Every element - from the exaggerated deaths to the tongue-in-cheek commentary - contributes to the game's self-aware personality, ensuring that even when it falters mechanically, it never loses its sense of fun. As it stands today, Bloody Good Time is more of a hidden gem than an active multiplayer hit. It's the kind of game that thrives when played among friends rather than strangers, where its chaotic mechanics and dark humor can fully shine. While its limited content, aging design, and lack of updates prevent it from achieving lasting popularity, it remains an underrated experiment in multiplayer creativity. Outerlight's unique approach to blending comedy, tension, and unpredictability deserves recognition for pushing boundaries at a time when few mainstream games dared to. For players willing to overlook its rough edges and seek out a group of like-minded friends, Bloody Good Time still delivers exactly what its name promises - a violent, hilarious, and refreshingly original experience that never forgets to have fun. It's a reminder that sometimes the best games are the ones that don't aim for perfection but embrace chaos with a grin and a machete. Rating: 7/10

Bloody Good Time has charm, sure, but this party ended years ago... This is a multiplayer-focused shooter set on a Hollywood backlot, where players take on exaggerated B-movie roles and compete in a series of elimination-based game modes. The premise is built around absurdity. Matches revolve around earning points through stealth, aggression, and survival, while also managing basic needs like hunger, sleep, and bathroom breaks. The movement and shooting felt standard for a Source-engine shooter, but what stood out most was the added layer of survival management. Having to monitor bodily needs mid-match introduced a unique kind of tension. It did not feel serious or strategic, but it added pressure in a way that briefly made the game more engaging. I found myself thinking this kind of mechanic could add depth to more traditional shooters if implemented well. Here, it was played for humour, and that mostly worked. I played the game solo and quickly ran into the core issue. Bloody Good Time is built for PvP, but the multiplayer scene is completely dead. Bots are available, but they lack the intelligence and unpredictability needed to keep matches interesting. Without real players, the game's systems fall flat. The lack of challenge and interaction made it feel repetitive and hollow. There is very little guidance or on-boarding, and the weapon system was initially disorienting. Each slot contains multiple options, but without explanation or progression, the variety does not add much. It felt like a set of disconnected tools rather than a system you grow into. The aesthetic fits the concept but was not enough to carry the experience. By the 45-minute mark, I found myself watching the clock. The premise has charm, and the absurd mechanics do offer a few standout moments, but the lack of players and poor bot design mean that whatever this game once was, it is no longer functioning as intended. Final Rating: 4/10 The concept is fun to explain, but the experience no longer holds up.

Shadowgrounds, developed and published by Frozenbyte, is a top-down sci-fi shooter that blends fast-paced combat with a tense, atmospheric setting. Set on the moon Ganymede, the game places players in the role of Wesley Tyler, a maintenance engineer who becomes the unlikely hero tasked with surviving a violent alien outbreak that has overrun a research colony. From the very first moments, the game establishes a sense of isolation and danger, using a combination of claustrophobic environments, dynamic lighting, and relentless alien encounters to immerse players in its world. The gameplay in Shadowgrounds revolves around intense, tactical combat viewed from a top-down perspective. Players must carefully navigate corridors, rooms, and open spaces while managing ammunition, health, and resources. The arsenal includes standard firearms as well as more specialized weapons, each with distinct characteristics and upgrade paths, giving combat a layer of strategic depth. The game's flashlight mechanic adds a constant element of tension, as dark areas hide lurking threats and players must balance illumination with vulnerability. Enemy encounters are varied and often overwhelming in numbers, encouraging players to plan their movement, prioritize targets, and make split-second decisions under pressure. Visually, Shadowgrounds excels in creating a dark and foreboding atmosphere. The industrial, futuristic environments of the colony are richly detailed, from abandoned labs and machinery to dimly lit hallways and cavernous storage areas. The lighting system is particularly effective, casting deep shadows and forcing players to navigate partly blind, heightening the horror and suspense. Alien designs are grotesque and diverse, reinforcing the game's sense of danger and unpredictability. The art style combines realism with stylized exaggeration, producing an eerie yet visually compelling experience that complements the gameplay. While the narrative in Shadowgrounds is not its primary focus, it effectively supports the gameplay and enhances immersion. The story unfolds through environmental storytelling, in-game communications, and occasional scripted events, gradually revealing the scale of the alien outbreak and Tyler's role in combating it. Character development is minimal, keeping the focus on action and survival, but the story's pacing aligns well with the intensity of the gameplay, providing enough context to maintain engagement without interrupting the flow of combat. Critically, Shadowgrounds has been praised for its ability to capture the tension and excitement of classic top-down shooters while introducing its own atmospheric flair. Reviewers have highlighted its challenging combat, compelling use of lighting and darkness, and overall immersion. Some criticism has been directed at the potential for repetitive encounters, as the game leans heavily on combat sequences, but many players appreciate the straightforward and satisfying gameplay loop. Its blend of horror, strategy, and action makes it appealing to fans of both shooters and sci-fi adventure games. In summary, Shadowgrounds is a memorable top-down shooter that effectively combines intense action, strategic gameplay, and a dark, immersive environment. Its mix of weapon variety, tactical combat, and atmospheric design provides a challenging and engaging experience for players. While the narrative is secondary to gameplay, it offers enough context to enrich the world and motivate the player's progression. For those seeking a shooter that balances tension, action, and suspense, Shadowgrounds remains a compelling and enjoyable title that has aged well within its genre. Rating: 8/10

The RIP trilogy is a franchise that starts out as a top down tower defense game and evolves to a twin stick shooter in its sequels. This collection includes 200 levels in total which sounds like a lot, but some of them are short and a couple of them are variations of the previous levels. Nevertheless, I think that for 5€ it is a good deal. The third game in particular has a lot to offer. [h3] RIP 1 [/h3] - Tower defense game where you operate a turret and kill incoming waves of enemies. The levels mostly consist of what seem to be ruins of different types, some are rocky surfaces and other snowy with a few obstacles and explosives. There are 3 different characters which in my opinion only make a minor difference - the turret looks slightly different and when upgrading each hero has their own special ability. The upgrades after leveling up don't do that big of a difference, except the ones that stun or push enemies. There are also weapon pick ups and power ups which are RNG, but some levels will only drop 1 weapon ( because the dev wants you to play with that ) which is kinda annoying. One thing I find kinda weird is that they added dogs in the waves, it could be something else like zombies. No story, the game says that you gotta kill " Pigman's forces " and that's it. [h3] RIP 2 [/h3] - An improvement from the first game, players can now see their character who is no longer stuck in his turret but can move. In other words RIP 2 is where the game became a twin stick shooter. Still no story but I like the changes they made here. The upgrades have a bigger impact and I like that weapon pick ups carry over to the next mission ( assuming you didn't die ). You can also drop a weapon if you picked it up by accident. New enemies were added as well as boss fights to make things more interesting. (gameplay spoilers) VtMB is clearly the shining star of Vampire games, and completely leans into it's greatest strength: playing as a hardcore vampire in a grungy world. There is nothing quite like opening this game and roaming the world while hiding in the shadows, or talking crazy, or operating as a seemingly normal person, the many gameplay styles VtMB offers really allows the player to get into their idea of how a vampire should operate. It's classical RPG style leveling system is also great, allowing a lot of control over what you want your character to do, and the many interesting characters, dialogue options, computers and locks forces you to choose what you want your character to focus on, and encourages playing again to revisit something you may not have been able to access. However, VtMB falls apart in its final sections, with it's unbalanced combat skills making some builds that have been viable so far borderline impossible, and completely blocking off any non combat builds from being able to complete the game. Tie that in with it's sloppy and boring combat mechanics and the game forces you to go through many long, tiresome sections of repetitive battles before you can get to the parts that are actually enjoyable. And this is without mentioning any of the bugs, which are mostly remedied by the unofficial patch, but still show up to cause problems (some of which are admittedly hilarious). Conclusion: VtMB is a great RPG that is well worth playing, especially if you like vampires, but is definitely weighed down by its sloppy combat, often confusing and unintuitive puzzles, and buggy gameplay. 8/10

Actual Review: Lore Explanation: If you like anything Vampire themed and D&D themed, this is THE game for you. Pretty much everything you expect from D&D campaigns but add the plot twist of White Wolf's "World of Darkness" popular series "Vampire: The Masquerade" into the mix! This game focuses purely on VTM, but does have tie ins and allusions to White Wolf's other franchises: "Werewolf: The Apocalypse" and "Mage: The Ascension" These three universes collectively make the entirety of The World of Darkness as they exist within each other. Gameplay: It's literally Half Life 2 before HL2 was even released lol. Thanks to Activision's tomfoolery in rushing the original 2004 release, this game plays pretty much the as any source engine game. Melee, weapon and shoot your way through, but adding VTM into the mix adds something... DIFFERENT. Your blood powers (Depending on how you build your character) ranges from Seduction, Persuasion, Regenerative Healing, buffing melee and bullet resistances, blinding, Intellect, Fighting Skill and other things like hacking computers, weapon proficiency, Lockpicking, and Research. You can allocate things specifically in you character sheet to specialise, or balance things out a bit, THEN specialise as you get to the later parts in Downtown, Hollywood, etc. Story: Heaps of fun playing it, but you can see where Activision forced Troika Games' hands with the tight deadline and some parts of the endgame felt empty, hence why the Unofficial Patch fixes everything! Right down to that patch restoring critical things like your Ghoul being able to be spared being killed during the Blood Hunt sequence by telling her to "Stay indoors" or release her from her blood bond to you so she goes back to her normal life. Plenty of characters that you get to experience, and then there's the Malkavians. Word of advice: DO NOT play as a either a Malkavian or Nosferatu as your first playthroughs, they are notoriously difficult due to Nosferatu being ostracise by humanity and Vampire Kindred alike (Human police will attack on sight) hence why Nosferatu characters are limited to the sewers. Malkavians are BATSHIT INSANE. Their brains (Or lack thereof...) are both there, and not there at the same time. Even your player dialouge as a Malkavian speaks in riddles and prose and the text has the "2Sp00ky4U" style font and NPC's HATE dealing with Malkavians because of the impending insanity they have to put up with. Graphics: Its a Half Life engine based game from 2004. Its graphics are somewhat dated and shows its age, but was still groundbreaking for a 22 year old game. This game is also moddable so the graphics can be modernised. Moddabilitly: Almost on par with Skyrim, but not as diverse. Currently over 300 mods on Nexus Mods (https://www.nexusmods.com/games/vampirebloodlines) and even more on ModDB (https://www.moddb.com/games/vampire-the-masquerade-bloodlines) Like full on Nvidia RTX complete remasters and such. Overall for my playthroughs, I had fun and definitely recommend it. Just please install the unofficial patch first and use the plus version. It still gets updated to this very day.

Note: I played the Plus version of the unofficial patch and so I can't speak for the original game. Bloodlines is a must play if you're a fan of the immersive sim genre. While it doesn't have the most complex main quest, the worldbuilding and environment of the game is incredibly imaginative. I love the small open world locations that really feel like they could exist. For the most part, if you see a building, you can enter it and there will be something or someone to interact with in there. So many open worlds don't get this and they feel dead and lifeless without it. Strange that the best implementation I have seen of this is in a game nobody's heard of before from 2004. The worldbuilding is grounded and rarely breaks it's own rules. I easily found myself liking different factions and clans better than others and was excited to influence the outcome of the story in their favor. Unfortunately, there isn't much opportunity to do that throughout the game, but still better than most other RPG's I've played. Mechanically, the game holds up surprisingly well for it's age. The controls make sense out of the box (something I've found is rather uncommon especially among older titles) and the mechanics of sneaking, interacting, lockpicking, etc. are intuitive and work well together if not perfect. The combat is serviceable, but definitely not great. I'd say it's better than Deus Ex (from 2000) but that's really not saying too much. Overall, I'd highly recommend it and may end up playing it again some day to see what it's like to be a different faction. It's by no means perfect, but clearly had a lot of heard put into it and was genuinely enjoyable for the majority of my playtime.

Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines is a classic, and a fantastic action RPG, made back when Activision wasn't the corrupt, disgusting giant company it is now. Additionally, Bloodlines 2 does not hold a candle to this game, aside from modern combat improvements. Overall, this original Bloodlines entry is still the best. Pros: + Various different play-styles, attributes, vampire types and weapon types to choose from, along with a decently sized tree to invest additional points in + Fantastic industrial/goth vibe, art direction and overall aesthetics + Great overall 'people vs. the elite' plot, with interesting quest lines, sub-plots, characters and places + Fantastic writing. It is not bound by political filters and is not afraid to offend with its dialogue, dark themes and humor + Great voice acting + Combat has aged well, for the most part. There are attribute checks for certain things, as there are no sprint, dodge or block mechanics. Gunplay and melee combat isn't bad, as hits must still land for damage-based skill checks + Other playstyle options available, such as stealth, lockpicking, charisma/persuasion, hacking, investigation, romance/seduction, etc. + The characters are delightfully and noticeably expressive in their facial expressions and movements + A lot of attention to detail and more involvement than you will find even in modern RPGs + Not too long and not too short, at around 28 hours if side quests are completed + Great licensed soundtrack from artists such as Ministry, Lacuna Coil, Die My Darling and more + Still the best Bloodlines entry in the series Cons: - Requires the community mod 'Unofficial Patch 11.5' to be installed, for the game to run on modern hardware. The game has not been officially patched in quite some time. Note, the link to the download can easily be found pinned in the game's discussion page, and installation is very straight-forward, quick and easy - The camera is uncooperative in tight spaces, due to the fact that some weapons force 3rd person perspective while equipped - One of the final boss fights (tentacle monster) was rushed in development and is nearly impossible to beat with any build, without cheesing or using all available blood packs if you have them - Corpses despawn and NPC movements don't always track between different scene/area transitions Mixed: ~ This RPG uses skill checks, which may or not be everyone's cup of tea. However, combat-based skill checks only decide damage, as each hit/shot still must make contact with the enemy from your own skill and aim ~ Five possible different endings, depending on who you choose to side with throughout the game In conclusion, I would definitely recommend this game to anyone who enjoys RPGs, even to those who haven't found themselves liking the vampire genre, for I myself don't usually and still had a lot of fun with this game. Overall Rating: 4.5 out of 5
