Troika's first and only try at making a 3D CRPG, VTMB plays less like the vampire action/survival game you were probably expecting and more like an urban fantasy Deus Ex with even more quests to solve. Make sure to grab Wesp5's Unofficial Patch (also recommend enabling Plus Patch) as this game has major problems running on modern systems otherwise. For starters, the game is dripping with atmosphere - whether it's the stormy streets of Santa Monica, or the gothic skyscrapers towering far above Downtown LA, or the myriad of neon nightclubs and idyllic business (with a touch of depravity) beneath the enchanted skies of Hollywood, or the exotic Chinatown hub that feels like stepping into another world, the artists managed to make even the run-down slums of LA feel so mystical and ethereal. I think the graphics hold up today, and of course, Rik Schaffer's soundtrack is as peerless as ever. Set in a 2000s gothic Los Angeles where supernatural entities must blend into human society to avoid extermination, VTMB presents one of the most believable, immersive, and rich worlds in any CRPG. You meet a wide cast of characters from all classes of undead society, including ruthless club owners, Thin-Blooded outcasts, anarchic rebels, megalomaniacal elites, and tons of unaware humans caught in between, all with eccentric personalities, deep backstories, and unique perspectives on the world. The cast is brought to life through stellar dialogue, superb voice acting, and some of the best facial animations in any video game ever, so talking to them never gets dull. The story is engrossing as you get involved with the diverse factions and supernatural races vying for control of LA and excellent supernatural political drama ensues. Granted, the plot ultimately boils down to running a bunch of errands (many dialogue options lampshade this) and remains very linear until one dialogue tree at the end, but the memorable characters and superb quests will give you more than enough reason to replay. Sprinkled throughout this vibrant world are some of the best and most creative quests in any CRPG. Each quest is discovered through natural dialogue, is internally consistent with the world, and tells its own self-contained mini-story, like an episode in a TV series. Look at the variety: there are combat-focused quests (the plague bearer quest chain, Grout's mansion, the Gargoyle boss fight); a few stealth-oriented quests (the Elizabeth Dane, the LA National Museum); lots of social-themed quests (resolving Therese/Jeanette Voerman's rivalry, convincing a food critic to leave a bad review, retrieving the B-writer's screenplay); plus a few other surprises (Ocean House Hotel, Griffith Park). Best of all, you can be assured that the devs considered and accommodated every playstyle: quests have many solutions; lots of unique outcomes; plenty of skill checks, hidden routes, and secrets that only specialized builds can leverage; and tons of opportunities for character expression (wow, proper GMing!). Sure, there are a few frustrating quests here and there (the Elizabeth Dane, Romero's graveyard w/o guns, the SchreckNet quest chain…), there's a bit too much backtracking, and most locations are never visited again once their related quest is completed, but when the quests are this entertaining and reactive, you will hardly notice these faults. There are plenty of ways to approach a problem, including unarmed/melee, guns, blood disciplines/spells, sneaking around (extremely buggy though), hacking, lockpicking, and talking to NPCs to persuade, intimidate, or seduce them into doing your bidding (you can even use some spells in dialogue). There are also side systems to manage such as the masquerade, humanity scores, and criminal violations for breaking the law to keep you vigilant. Perhaps the most interesting design choice is that there are no health potions in this game - you must instead feed on humans/rats, which is the main way to restore mana and (more importantly) HP. This mechanic definitely encourages you to take more risks with fights, that's for sure. Most impressively, there are the 7 playable clans (Brujah, Gangrel, Malkavian, Nosferatu, Toreador, Tremere, Ventrue), analogous to D&D classes, with different playstyles, spells, and tradeoffs. Most impressively, the characters and factions have wildly different reactions to each clan, as if the world is being reshaped to fit your character. One of the great strengths of Arcanum was how wildly your race affected character reactions, and I am glad VTMB continues this tradition. Of course, VTMB is far from perfect. The combat is as awful as it looks in the YouTube videos, and none of the options (unarmed, melee, ranged) are pleasant. Melee forces you into an awkward 3rd-person view and devolves into a boring button-mash fest based around a repetitive 3-hit combo. Unarmed is even worse: it has the same problems as Melee and deals less damage, has no weapon unlocks, and has way worse hit reg. The guns are not much better - early game firearms are worthless, many have unbearably slow reloads, they are all very inaccurate, the ammo system is fucked, and the automatic guns have the worst muzzle climb I have ever experienced (the MAC-10 is especially abysmal). At least guns become serviceable once you fully max out the feat (it must be 10, it cannot be less), but this often occurs well into the end game. Fortunately, you do not have to engage with the combat too much… for the first 3/4 of the game at least. VTMB completely falls apart in its last 1/4: it's all tedious combat challenges in claustrophobic rooms, everyone is armed with automatic guns, enemy density is at least 2x what you can handle, side quests are few and far between, and all non-combat-focused builds become useless here. Take your pick: Nosferatu Warrens, the Chinatown story quests where everyone has MAC-10s, the Society of Leopold, Hallowbrook Hotel, the Ming Xiao temple + boss fight, the Ventrue Tower where everyone has Steyr AUGs - they're all miserable no matter how strong you are, and they suck out nearly all the joy accrued in the first 3/4 of the game. The boss fights are especially egregious - they all have bloated HP + armor and annoying gimmicks like teleportation or flight. Worst of all, because there is nothing to feed on, there is no way to heal during a boss fight (especially when the boss deals aggravated damage). The worst offender is Ming Xiao, who has obnoxiously high armor and is one of the worst boss fights in any game. The game rushes through the rest of story, too - major antagonists like Andrei and Bach are discarded in anticlimactic boss fights, while major battles like the Sabbat raid and the Kuei-Jin invasion are resolved off screen. There are other minor issues, too. There are unfinished levels everywhere - the sewers are just a series of empty, bland-looking corridors with no combat or loot, and half of the building interiors look like run-down apartments cobbled together in 15 minutes. The progression system is vastly inferior to the one in Arcanum, and most feats are skill check fodder: the intimidate, persuade, and seduction feats are all different flavours of the same speech check (with persuade being stronger than the other two), for instance. And like in every other CRPG, beware of all the useless feats: melee, ranged, lockpick, computers, and persuasion are essential, while haggle, research, inspection, intimidation, and seduction are underwhelming at best. Overall, VTMB is a buggy, frustrating, and unfinished mess that is still ahead of its time in world-building, quest design, reactivity, and character expression. These are not minor achievements - I cannot stress enough that the story and worldbuilding are just as important as, if not more vital than, the combat and looting in a proper CRPG. VTMB is certainly the best urban fantasy first/third-person CRPG in gaming, and it's always a great time to replay it. 8/10

Download this game, install the unofficial path and play it (either on Basic or Plus, whichever you fancy, or both one after the other). Just trust me on this one, if nothing else. So where do the maudlin ramblings begin? Here. I love this game, I really do but it can be a fickle mistress at tines, and sure, I can acknowledge that I love it as seen through the blindness of a hopelessly infatuated, naive young lover. It just has things that no other game I know has: 1. It's the best adaptation of the original White Wolf property. If you loved the table top RPG, you should probably try this game at some point, unless you don't like computer games, in which case why are you reading this on Steam? Just be tolerant of its flaws, and a great story, characters, voice acting and atmosphere shall be delivered unto you. 2. That makes it, for all its flaws, one of the best vampire RPGs of all time. That doesn't necessarily mean it's worth buying, though. I mean, you have to be really quite tolerant. 3. In some ways, it's a brilliant RPG. It's just that anything not the actual RPG basically sucks to some degree. 4. Knowing the game well by completing it a few times, then playing it through as a Malkavian for the first time is simply one of the best things ever to exist. 5. Let's divert onto a few of the distinct different playthroughs you can do with this game: a) Brujah or Gangrel killing machine. Straight forward, but watch that humanity, the beast lurks shallowest here. b) Ventrue manipulator/seductress. See how powerful Persuasion is, find alternate ending to quests, always have a blood doll within reach in any location. Fortitude goes a long way towards enduring the end game. d) Tremere blood sorcerer, and probably social artist. An alternative to Ventrue, mostly, although you do get one of the two unique different havens to the rest of the rabble. c) Toreador sword artist or gunslinger. Sword artist recommended, guns are for idiots, but still, you know. Or, Brujah sword artist, just for funsies. d) Nosferatu stealth. A completely different experience, but very capable of finishing it all, potence and obfuscation are a great combo. Also, the second unqiue haven. e) Malkavian. Oh, how we laughed. Oh, how we found out things that no other clan can find out. Peak RPGing. Considering there's several different ending dependent on choices made, there's some replayability in there for hardcore fanatics like me. However, the suck: 1. Controls. I think I've wrestled them into submission, or been wrestled into submission, and can live with them nowadays, but still get touches of frustration occasionally. Minor suck, all things considered. 2. Graphical glitches. Game is old, and the Unoffical Patch repairs the story and stuff under the hood but not as much in visuals. I lost count of the million miles per hour pedestrians seen on this run through, and still Skyeline Apartments can get so buggy that I'd be mad if some of the end results weren't actually quite funny. Thank god a save and reload sorts it out nowadays - back in the day, once it glitched it was like that for rest of the game, often making that haven unusable. Minor suck nowadays, as long as you appreciate that game is old. 3. Combat. If you can tolerate the controls, fists and weapons are okay. Guns are totally meh. Game was not designed to be a FPS. Can be quite fun with celerity, but generally best avoided. Which brings us onto . . . 4. The end game. Just when things should all be coming together, the end of this beautiful, wretched, wondrous, awful game becomes an unavoidable slug fest. Such a brilliant RPG takes you to ecstatic peaks then dumps you like a used plaything. From around the Hallowbrook Hotel onwards, it's more or less just a war of attrition, and if that's not what you came for, then sure, this game really sucks. See third paragraph (above) about stopping this playthrough at Ming Xiao. It's like the way someone once described the end game of Dark Souls - how their casual runs stopped at Anor Londo so many times, with Lost Izalith being particularly hated. This game is a bit like that. 5. A personal one this one - it pains me for what it could have been. In my opinion, as good as Half Life 2, better than Half-Life 2 (one of the best games of all time) except reasons. They're well documented elsewhere, and I see no reason to rehash old territories here. 6. A not directly connected but still personally painful memory, the cancellation of CCP's (the maker of E.V.E) adaptation of the White Wolf's property into an MMORPG, brought to an end in 2014 after nine years of development. Oh, the things we could have had . . . In closing. VTMB:2 doesn't look like my kind of thing, but I'll probably try it one day if it's discounted enough. And so, back to start a new run, the second of this purchase, and to see if Ming Xiao's boss fight is any more bearable this time round. Double sigh. Recommended because I love it, still, despite it all.

I play this game at least once each year. It has become a tradition. VTMB is as much a flawed gem as it is a part of video game history. It was the first game built on the source engine and the last game by Troika (a pill as bitter as the cancellation of Firefly). It stands virtually alone in the field of satisfying vampire games (which is baffling in and of itself). It adapted the World of Darkness into an immersive, engaging, and deliciously stylized vehicle that kept true to the lore and themes in the source material. Impactful choices, freedom to play as you like, and a wealth of solutions to most problems made it a uniquely freeing experience in a time when most games were extremely linear. A balance of crude humor and scathing social commentary as delivered by a politically underinformed friend ranting on your couch at 1AM who you love enough to enjoy his company and laugh along, the narrative is comfort food for the rebellious underdog inside us all. It is a paradoxically beautiful and ugly game. A time capsule of the era, caricaturing the fashion, sound, and style of the early 00's and creating a venue closer to a dream or fleeting memory than reality. The levels are often winding or crafted without a sense of flow, leaving the player endlessly oscillating between immersion and awareness of the hands that made these unreal spaces. Stiff animations, clumsy cutscenes, and buggy physics scream "this is a video game" at every opportunity and sometimes feels as if this game was simply ahead of its time; a victim of inadequate technology in the face of wild ambition. The story is good, the characters are intriguing, and there are very few quests that aren't worth engaging with. The drama is there, but a little pulpy. The action can be repetitive, but it doesn't ruin the experience. The Clans have meaningful impacts on how you play (Malkavian and Nosferatu especially so). I love this game for all its flaws and for all the beautiful heights it sought, but barely fell short of. It has become part of nostalgia for many, myself included, and in that rose colored retrospective I will always recommend it. Play it and play it again.

🩸 Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines I meant to write something short… and then I didn't. Returning to Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines was… overwhelming in the best way. I first played it as a kid, from a CD, at a time when simply installing it without errors felt like an achievement - and finishing it was a heroic feat. Even then it left a massive mark. Now, with fan patches and restored content, the game becomes a completely different experience. 🔧 Important note: Without fan patches it's almost unplayable today. The original release had tons of cut content and game-breaking bugs. Its development story is tragic: huge ambitions (basically a 2004 Cyberpunk), genius writing, genius atmosphere, genius mechanics - and a fatal studio collapse in 2005. But over time, Bloodlines became a cult legend. A vampire Blade Runner. 🧛‍♂️ What Makes Bloodlines Special? 🔥 A world that feels alive (even if everyone's dead) You're a vampire - but the world around you is surprisingly alive: NPCs, atmosphere, music, clubs, back alleys, offices, sewers. Every tiny location is used for quests. Developers squeezed 90% of potential out of every street and building. 🔧 Combat & Playstyle Variety You can play however you want: • stealth • brute force • persuasion / social dominance • hacking (with actual command input!) • melee • firearms • clan abilities The game gives you complete freedom to craft your build and approach. ⚙️ Character Progression One of the best leveling systems of its time: your stats affect dialogue, combat, quest solutions, alternative routes. You also can find: • skill-boosting books • unique items • clan powers • restored content (in patched versions) 👥 Characters Jeanette Voerman - the legend herself. Wild, charming, dangerous - easily one of the most iconic characters in RPG history. Every major NPC feels memorable thanks to style, voice acting, writing, and design. 🏙️ Clubs - An Entire Culture Dancing. Music. Atmosphere. Interaction. And yes - "cocktails" are humans. The game never lets you forget that you're a predator. 🩸 Masquerade Mechanics Break the rules - and there are consequences: • civilians panic • hunters appear • enemies become more aggressive This makes the role of being a vampire deep and believable. 🎬 Story & Endings Multiple endings depending on your choices. They don't rewrite the entire game but you feel their weight. Side quests are like small indie films: atmospheric, dramatic, weird, sometimes hilarious. The main plot feels cinematic and dark. 👁️ Horror & Mystery Bloodlines excels at atmospheric horror: • dark alleys • broken souls • grotesque monsters • unhinged vampires • the legendary ghost house mission Some scenes outperform modern horror games. ✅ Pros: ✔ Phenomenal Los Angeles atmosphere ✔ Memorable characters & brilliant dialogue ✔ Huge freedom in playstyle ✔ Excellent progression system ✔ Stylish, unique quests ✔ Many vampire clans with different gameplay ✔ Iconic soundtrack (clubs, main menu, ending) ✔ You truly feel like a vampire ✔ Even today - completely unique and irreplaceable ❌ Cons: ➖ Without patches - the game is barely playable ➖ Even patched: occasional bugs and crashes ➖ Combat can feel clunky ➖ Second half is weaker (lots of content was cut) ➖ You can feel the lack of time, money, and polish 📝 Conclusion Bloodlines is not just a game. It's a dark, stylish, poetic experience. Beautiful, grimy, atmospheric, emotional. A story where good and evil are long blurred, and humanity is the only thing separating a monster from a person. 👉 Recommended for everyone who loves vampires, noir, mystery, horror and deep RPGs. 👉 If you want polished AAA smoothness - this is not it. 👉 If you're ready to accept flaws for the sake of brilliance - welcome to LA at night. Rating: ⭐ 9/10 with fan patches ⭐ 6/10 vanilla (Without patches - survival impossible 🙂) 🎮 Fan Facts: • Developed by Troika Games, founded by three creators of Fallout. • Released on the same day as Half-Life 2, which destroyed its sales. • Made by the same people behind Arcanum. • Launch version was so broken that some quests couldn't be completed. • Troika Games closed soon after the failed release. • Jeanette is the most iconic character of the entire franchise. • The unofficial patch has been maintained for over 15 years (!). • Many quests and areas were cut but later restored by fans. • One of the most quoted RPGs in Reddit and modding communities. • The 2024 sequel is made by a completely different studio - expectations are cautious.

You should only play this game if the setting absolutely hooks you to put up with anything and everything. The writing starts off strong, the game is filled with interesting set pieces and characters, the "urban vampire" concept is executed very well, really leaves you wanting more. But what everyone will tell you is that the actual gameplay is this game is godawful. It's something of a strange stealth RPG, but the stealth is just a bunch of corridors, the AI is terrible and there's little in the way to interact with. The game gives up halfway through and forces you through a bunch of dungeons and gauntlets filled with extremely generic first-person shooter combat and basic puzzle solving, which I honestly preferred to the stealth segments. Note that it should remain a first-person shooter; never feel tempted to engage with the melee combat in this game. There's ammunition everywhere, and no matter how high your melee skill is, your college student muscles will outshine your vampirism to make you flail around like an idiot. If you're willing to put up with that thanks to the story's promises, you'll discover the reason the gameplay is so bad: this game is extremely rushed. Past the first two chapters, the game completely falls apart. Any idea of solving quests in an interesting way with outcomes that will follow you throughout the game vanish, everything is now you walking back and forth a hallway with buildings painted on it, talking to heads, going to a location and either shooting it up or spamming vampire abilities to get around the next fork in a plain white hallway with a security guard walking in a circle. You might even discover that some of the mechanics promised to you at the start of the game, like Humanity, don't actually exist because the developers didn't have the time to implement them properly. The writing tries its hardest to hide the fact that you no longer have any impact on the story or what quests or missions you're going to do next, but the veil is impossible to maintain once the japanese schoolgirl comes out fighting a demon and one of your dialogue options is a tentacle joke. I have fond memories of the first few hours of my playthrough, and also the game crashing incredibly frequently if you don't use the Unofficial Patch (which skewed my playtime to say only 3.7 hours). Past that, this game is either a bad version of Deus Ex or a bad version of Half-Life. If you haven't played either of those, and the vampire concept doesn't sound that cool to you, just play one of them instead.

This game is considered a cult classic. Clearly I am not part of the cult. I can see how this game is highly regarded as, when it came out over 20 years ago, it was one of a kind. However, games have evolved and VtMB has not kept up. It's truly just a tabletop RPG in a 3D space. The main focus of the game is your choices, reactions, keeping up with politics, and choosing character skills/builds. Choices matter but it's still a linear game. Actual game [i] play [/i] is clunky, slow, and tedious. Additionally, the game being sold today is literally the same one released over 20 years ago. It does not run on modern PC's without some form of finagling (tweaking launch options or just installing the unofficial patch). It is still full of bugs and glitches even after installing the unofficial patch. Speaking of which, be careful where you get the unofficial patch, as even the correct file is heavily flagged as possibly harmful. If you are interested in trying this game here's a few things worth noting: -There is no controller support -There is no visual/cosmetic character creation -There are no quest compass markers -There is very little explanation of skill points/attributes (i recommend looking up a guide before you make your character sheet) -There is a skill that determines how well you aim with firearms -There is lots of lockpicking and stealth -There are many skills that only affect dialogue Maybe this game is for you, or maybe not. The writing/narrative is fantastic but gameplay falls short. I suggest looking at gameplay videos before purchasing. It took me many years to finally get to this game, but I can confidently say that I understand why Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines (VTMB) is seen as an RPG classic. It has aged heavily, but if you can get around that, then there is a lot of fun to be had here. As an initial note, generally, when I write reviews, I am opposed to reviewing a game based on a modded experience. Not everyone will want to mod the game, and as such, it should be reviewed without them in my opinion. However, this game is hard to get running well on modern hardware without some modifications, and a few quality-of-life improvements really do make this game more palatable nowadays. I used [url=https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2909531565] this [/url] Steam guide and played version 11.5 of the Unofficial Patch (the most current version available at the time of play). I made no other adjustments to the game as I wanted to have as close to the vanilla experience as I could. I do recommend that you have at least the unofficial patch, but there is a lot that can be done to make the VTMB experience better for modern players if you want to get rid of all of the jank. I wanted most of the jank, though, it is part of the classic gaming experience in my opinion, and I wouldn't have had it any other way. With that out of the way, VTMB does something that many other games of the era were trying to do: make a game using tabletop gaming elements as part of a 3D fast-paced action game. KOTOR is well known for doing this with dice rolls being done behind the scenes and stats and leveling being done like a tabletop RPG. VTMB does this by utilizing the World of Darkness RPG system that the series comes from, and it does it pretty damn well. With this philosophy at the heart of VTMB, the core intrigue of this game is the RPG elements over everything else, in my opinion. The combat is rough, moving around the map is annoying, and there are plenty of tedious fetch quests. If you wanted a Vampire combat simulator, this is not the game for you; however, if you want to play a character, make interesting choices, uncover a unique story, and have more of an "experience," this game is fucking great. I did enjoy things like combat, but I always felt it slowed down the story of the game, so it really did become a means to an end sort of mechanic. By the way, tabletop RPG is supposed to be played a lot like this as well. It straight up has rules for skipping combat, it is called down and dirty combat in the rulebook that I am most familiar with, and it exists so that combat does not get in the way of the story. So, it is kind of neat, but annoying, that the game puts the story first even when there is a lot of action. As far as the RPG elements go, this game is well known for having a lot of ways to play that are all fairly valid. You are railroaded a bit, though; stealth in particular is pretty much essential for a few main story missions, but in a lot of cases, you have several different ways to solve a problem with subterfuge, violence, and charm being core ways to get what you want. One thing that is legendary about this game is the option to play different Vampire clans, with the Nosferatu being particularly interesting because you have to make sure that like 90% of people don't see you because you are a horrific monster. It changes the story and the way you play so much. It does suck for the RPG side of things, though, that you are not able to customize a character. I felt less connected to my character because of this, but given the era the game came from, it is not surprising. Overall, I would say that the gameplay in VTMB is dated, but as an RPG, it is great. There is a lot I could say about the story, but honestly, the less you know, the better, and it is not like I have all the time in the world to explain the lore either. I will note that this game has a generally dark and gothic vibe and as someone who never grew out of their emo phase I love it, the lore of the vampire clans is complex but you do not have to understand it because your character doesn't either so this game is a great entry point so don't worry about playing a game with such rich lore, and also, VTMB does a great job handling morality in its own way, after all you (probably) want to stay human but you actively feed off of and kill them. I found that the most interesting choices were not related to the main story, and when they were, they often were related to side characters rather than the main players in the Vampire politics. Overall, I was so interested in the story this game had to tell, I felt that the rest of the game was just slowing me down the entire time, and it is not because I didn't enjoy everything else; the story just actually carries the game that well. If you are a fan of games for their stories, I think that this game is a must-play. The sound design for the game is clearly dated. A lot of the combat sounds are simpler than you see nowadays; they are clearly a bit compressed at times, and NPC voice lines are very limited. However, the vibe is great, the line reading is wonderful, and it has a great cast of voices. And if you are nostalgic for the sound flaws, like I am, then it is pretty darn great. But what really sells the game is the soundtrack; it has a synthetic vibe that feels dark and dreary, the use of strong drums and liberal use of the electric guitar with lots of reverberation in many of the songs gives off that goth vibe, and the energy and theming for each zone it is used in is great. If you want to get a feel for the game's vibes, just look up the soundtrack; it is fantastic. Graphically, this game has aged a lot; textures are blurry and messy, lighting can be a bit hit or miss (though some of that was the glitches present on modern hardware and modded with the lighting), models move oddly, and everything is low-poly and very flat. That is to be expected with a game this old, but what is still good to this day is the facial animations. Even with the low-quality models, characters are really expressive, and it sells the character interactions a lot. Yeah, sure, they still look janky as hell, but you can really read characters. Not everyone will like how this game looks, but it is nostalgic to me. Overall, I love VTMB; it is an absolute treat, and I am so glad I finally got myself to play it. It is an experience that holds up even today. If you like old games, a good story, and/or just love the dark and gothic atmosphere this game has to offer, I think VTMB is an easy recommendation.

a tiktok edit popped up on my fyp, clips from the game set to "rot daughter" by sophie woodhouse, and i instantly vibed with it. i saved it right away. that whole trashy 2000s punk vampire-in-the-city aesthetic? so good. when i finally played the game myself, it didn't just meet my expectations, it actually exceeded them. the only thing that kinda bugged me was the movement. it's a little too sensitive; your character keeps gliding for a second after you stop moving, like you're on ice. but other than that, it was exactly what i hoped it'd be. does it still hold up today? honestly, i think so. but i get that most people now expect games to be perfect; hyper-realistic graphics, quest markers telling you where to go, all that. i'm a sucker for older games that weren't perfect, didn't have crazy graphics, and didn't hold your hand. so yeah, maybe i'm biased, but i really do think it holds up. i love that it actually makes you figure things out. it throws you into side-quests right away, which keeps it fun. a lot of rpgs get too focused on the main story early on; you spend forever learning the mechanics, and by the time side-quests open up, you feel stuck on the main path. this one avoids that. right after the tutorial, it already gives you options. it sucks the game's basically been abandoned, because it's such a gem. the 2000s punk fashion, moody level design, the humor - it's all there. it's just annoying that you need a fan patch to make it run better lol. i really wish the devs would clean it up a bit, fix the bugs, and drop an update. after less than an hour of playing, it instantly became one of my favorite games ever... and i haven't even finished it yet!

Writing this right after I beat VTMB, it was really really good. Really jank, to be expected of a RPG built on a beta version of the Source engine. Very nice and fun RPG mechanics, lots of side quests and a decently lengthy campaign. Honestly for a game that was rushed to shit to come out alongside HL2, the game offers a lot. I feel bad for the crunch that must've happened to get the game out the door with the amount of content and polish for back in that day. The early 2000's/late 90's styles were really nostalgic to seeing that sort of stuff as a kid. I was also reminded that I was told about this game loooooong ago but I didn't wanna play it for one silly reason or another. A decent amount of the humour and such still holds up and sounds like stuff that would be written these days, hard to tell if that's unofficial patch plus content or what though. I did find it funny that over the course of the game, melee becomes much less useful and guns actually pick up a lot late game. You'd think that a vampire that's rapidly gaining power would get better at melee, but no, a lot of the encounters are based around shooting. The shooting is also decent, I hated the aiming at first but came to appreciate it, taking the time to aim my shots and using auspex to speed it up. it was a fun little balance between fps and rpg. Honestly my biggest complaint of the game is the fact that it has that early 2000's/late 90's sensibilities. A bit insensitive and stuff here and there, I was expecting Chinatown to be a lot worse than it was. Though it was still a bit *eeesssshhh* here and there. Beyond that, having the weird midpoint between goldsource and source jank had me grumble every once in a while once the novelty of essentially playing on modified version of the hl2 beta engine wore off. The game really was overall fun and interesting, and got me to dip my toes a bit into the whole world of darkness stuff. the game is rough and old but if you can stick with it it's real fun. the game isn't afraid to be crass, rude, raunchy, and funny while still managing to have a balance of taking itself seriously enough, fairly dark in some places, and just not really pull many of the punches it sets out to give. its a shame another game was never made.

I love this gane, but I have to be fair. I'll throw the BS at your first and if you're still here, then you can read the essay I left which will explain more about the game. Summary: Game comes with work to do after installation, lots of reading, puzzles, backtracking, etc. Huge recommend to people who love RPG's, but I'd say look the other way if you aren't willing to learn how to fix and make it playable after purchase. I'd also say don't get this game if you get bored after not fighting stuff every 5 minutes. At that point, you'd be better off just watching someone else play the game and getting the story experience that way. Like I said, lots of reading. BS 1: If you're willing to spend a solid 10 to 15 minutes going through youtube to learn how to set this game up properly, or are on the tech savvy side of things, then go ahead and ignore this portion, however if you are not and simply want to find a game to install and play, no BS, then avoid this one. BS 2: This game is buggy, visual bugs, cutscene issues (rare but present), and may require you to invest a bit more time learning how to install fixes should you wish to polish the game. BS 3: I've had very few but nearly detrimental saving issues, where a save might get corrupted and simply not allow you to continue. Make MULTIPLE saves of the same run within a similar time frame to ensure if this were to happen, you don't get set back or straight up lose a run. End of BS, essay incoming. This game is a gem, it's given me a similar experience to playing Skyrim for the first time. If you're here because the 2nd bloodlines game came out and you're a bit disappointed, I welcome you to try the original. This is not a game where you simply spawn in and do whatever, you'll spend a good bit of time making your character and putting points into skills. The combat at first can feel a bit clunky, but in time it gets manageable. The most important point you'll hear about this game and what i'll share here is it's a roleplaying game first, and a fighting game second, meaning the dialogue, story, lore, etc is prioritized and takes the lead on the experience more than the fighting, some missions you won't be fighting at all, or maybe you'll be hiding. A good handful of levels you'll notice are mazelike in design, some quests you might not even be able to figure out until you bite the bullet and pull up a tutorial, only to find out you did 99% of it, and simply couldn't find the last thing. Your race/clan is very important, and if you're first starting out, AVOID Malkavian and Nosferatu. Malkavian's dialogue to someone who hasn't played the game might be discouraging as you won't necessarily mean what which option means or what it will lead to unless you had the knowledge of prior runs and the context you get from them. Nosferatu unlike the others, cannot simply walk around the map, you have to navigate the sewers underneath and basically hide 65% of the time so you'll feel very restricted, additionally if you enjoy exploring the setting and map of the new game you just bought, because of course you do, well can't really do that as easily as Nosferatu. Towards the end of the game, it feels unfinished, you'll feel gridlocked if you didn't choose specific skills to help you like lockpicking for example, and certain boss fights are nearly impossible if you didn't have the know how of what to expect beforehand, which will leave you with 2 choices: 1. Assuming you saved before (which for a first playthrough I wouldn't expect you to save that far back) and are willing to lose 30 minutes of progress, or 2. Just enable god mode and BS the boss down, and actually experience the ending and then prepare for it in your next run. I hate BS'ing my way through games and enjoy challenges, but 1 particular fight is just so unbearably unfun and needs you to be absolutely perfect to overcome which for a first playthrough will likely not be possible. Other than that, I absolutely love the story, the replayability of the game is heavy, and by your 2nd run you'll see just how different each quest and interaction can go based on the skills and race you chose. There are multiple endings you can work towards, and you'll find that no matter if you choose the same race as last time, or choose a new one, or even eventually play all of them and replay them, you can still make the run unique with different builds or quest line choices. PS: Jack is great, and my favorite character, but when he says "guns are useless, he's wrong, guns are very nice (if you put points into firearms).

I have played through the first part of the game several times, but always stopped for whatever reason. If you were to play this game until the end of the Hollywood section, you'd probably come away thinking this game is great, and I'm fairly certain that is all people remember of this game. However, from the end of Hollywood section (specifically the sewers) until the end of the game, it's utter trash, and very clearly is being blocked out like a repressed trauma from peoples memories. Starting from the sewers section, there are these long and gruelling, unavoidable combat sections, during which you spend literally hours fighting enemies that you cannot avoid, nor drink from to regain blood for your combat abilities (only rats scattered around). The combat in this game is awful, even by 2004 standards, and is by far the worst part of the game. When you are able to play stealthily, the game is great, but as soon as you're forced into combat it's becomes an awful experience. It's very clear that after the Hollywood section, the developers were rushed for time until release, because area design, as well as the writing suck comparatively, in addition to forcing all those combat sections. The areas in the latter half of the game all become huge, and very repetitive. So, even if you manage to stealth through successfully, you still wasted a ton of time because the areas were just bloated in size. During the Sabbat Hotel section, I actually uninstalled the game for a couple of days because I hated it so much. I ended up cheating to get through the rest of the game because I just wanted to finish it by ignoring the combat. I'd hoped that doing so would improve my opinion of the game, but it didn't. The Chinatown section is meh, the endings are meh and the combat is infuriatingly bad. I'm fairly certain that was my last complete play through, though I may play to revisit Santa Monica, because genuinely the twins story line is fantastic. To conclude, up until end of Hollywood it's an 8/10, but you should stop there and uninstall the game. After that it's 2/10, maybe 3/10 at most. Genuinely the worst gaming experience I've had in years. Overall 5-5.5/10 and so I can't recommend. VTMB is what happens if you take the original Deus Ex and replace the "conspiracy theories" with vampire lore. Unfortunately it suffered from a tumultuous dev cycle and was rushed out the door by their publisher, only to release on the exact same date as Half-Life 2. This is one of those rare older games dripping with soul that is frustratingly rough around the edges; you can see the dev's passion for the project, but you might not appreciate the actual gameplay if you didn't grow up during the early 2000s. This is a time capsule of the culture at the time, from the art style, outfit designs, music, dialogue, and technology used in the game [do kids know what VHS tapes are?], so a lot of it will be lost on post-9/11 people. A random YouTube comment I read recently about this game summed it up best: this is really feels like a fan game with a budget. Even with over a decade of fan patches and fixes, there's still issues from top to bottom, but it's unlike (almost) anything else you'll ever play. The hub areas are all very atmospheric and push the technology at the time... and then you'll be forced through a terrible "dungeon" sequence like the warrens or the entirety of last two levels. No reasonable amount of additional dev time or funding could've fixed the bad level design, awkward weapon handling, or how much they leaned into forced combat sequences in the second half of the game. VTMB holds a special place in my heart among other random boxed games I bought on a whim that blew my mind back in the day, but it's difficult to recommend to modern gamers. If you're an Electronic Old Man like me and you never played this, grab Wesp5's patch and enjoy the ride. With all the new content available in his patch, it's worth playing through once with the fixed vanilla version, and a second time with all the restored content. Also, don't play Malk or Nosferatu on your first playthrough: everyone raves about Malk but it's a joke campaign and Nosferatu will have you eating rats in the sewer most of the game (with a lot of stealth above ground). It requires patience and an understanding of the game design of the time, but once you look past its flaws you'll find it's a rare memorable journey with plenty of replay value.

TLDR; Despite the janky combat it's one of THE best RPGs ever made. It's a dark comedy based in the World of Darkness, where you play as a fledgling vampire learning about your new unlife and navigating the politics of the powers that be. One of the greatest strengths of the game is the amazing story (side quests included) where player choice matters. Many factions will attempt to persuade you see things their way and the endings reflect these worldviews. It has many interestingly written characters and every npc line of dialogue is voiced with great acting (shout out to Neil Ross as Gary Golden). The game is short but sweet, perfect for replayability and it is quite recommended to do so. There are 7 clans and 2 of them play completely differently than the rest. To the point where all dialogue is unique with the Malkavian (Though it can be a bit spoilery but mostly confusing and it is widely considered to be the New game+ clan. I certainly recommend to play the game as a different clan first, but then the Malk is an absolute must play). And People freak out and it is a straight up violation of the Masquerade if you even show your face as the Nosferatu it requires you to take alternate routes to places as you normally would. The rest of the clans mechanically play similarly, but the flavour is completely different if you look at the certain clans lore and different approaches to problems. There are many ways to play the game, you can shoot or talk your way out of trouble, be a sneeky-breeky, boil enemies's blood in their bodies, or share your own madness with them (once again, Malkavian supremacy, Dementation is best discipline, I WILL fight you over this :D). You can also hack a door, pick a lock, or go around the back climb a ladder and go through the vents, so it's the usual 'immersive sim' gameplay styles. Every club in game has it's own banging track to go with, and the sounds and ambience of L. A. at night is proper goth mood. It has a soundtrack that consists of licensed music that fits the setting perfectly. And the other tracks on it? Let's just say that the Hollywood theme is burned into my very soul. It's a 2 decade old game that still looks great, mostly due to it's charm and aesthetic design. The locations are varied and interesting even in the game's restrictive urban setting. There are also plenty of mods and HD textures out there to modernize it. Speaking of mods, some of those are true love-letters to the game improving on many aspects, balance, bugs, and even new quests and clans to play as. Like the Unofficial patch plus or the Clan quest mods. I can only sing praises of this game, it's one of those 'if you mention it, someone will reinstall it' kinds of titles. After all this time it still has a cult following and I've got to say I am quite glad to be one of them.

A flawed masterpiece that still stands tall two decades later. Bloodlines may have launched in a buggy, incomplete state, but thanks to the dedication of fans and the strength of its writing, atmosphere, and roleplaying systems, it has become a must-play classic-not just for vampire enthusiasts, but for any fan of immersive RPGs. Few games offer this level of narrative reactivity, player freedom, and unforgettable characters. Story & Writing: 10/10 The writing in Bloodlines is masterful. Dialogue choices feel meaningful, and each NPC oozes personality-whether it's the seductive Jeanette, the Prince LaCroix, or the completely unhinged Jack. Every clan's playthrough offers a unique narrative voice and perception of events, making replayability feel organic and rewarding - this is especially true when playing as a Malkavian in the second playthrough, as the dialogue options are very prophetic. The game doesn't hold your hand. You're dropped into the political underbelly of undead society and expected to navigate complex allegiances, moral ambiguity, and personal ambition. The plot feels reactive, and your decisions feel like they genuinely affect the ending. The Malkavian and Nosferatu playthroughs, in particular, deserve special mention for completely changing how the game world responds to you-from psychic ramblings to literal back-alley sneaking due to NPCs fearing your appearance. Atmosphere & Immersion: 10/10 Few RPGs capture a setting as well as Bloodlines captures the World of Darkness. The game drips with dark, moody atmosphere-rainy neon-lit streets, creepy apartment complexes, underground clubs, and bloodstained back alleys. You feel like a creature of the night not just through mechanics, but through tone, music, and presentation. Locations like the haunted Ocean House Hotel are still talked about today for their tension and design. It doesn't rely on cheap jumpscares-it unsettles through tone. Even club scenes feel alive with ambient conversations and reactive NPCs. Sound & Music: 9/10 The soundtrack is iconic. Gothic rock, industrial beats, and ethereal synths create a hypnotic mood that perfectly fits the vampire theme. Tracks like "Isolated" by Chiasm and "Swamped" by Lacuna Coil are legendary in the gaming world and instantly transport you back into the world of Bloodlines. A personal favorite of mine is the track "Festival" by Rik Schaffer from the game's OST (I can't tell how many times I've listened to it in my freetime). Voice acting is solid across the board-even minor characters have distinct voices and deliver convincing performances. Only some NPCs have more dated or overacted lines, but given the age of the game, that's forgivable. Gameplay & Mechanics: 7/10 This is where the cracks show. The combat system was never the game's strongest aspect-it's serviceable at best. Melee and ranged weapons can feel clunky, and enemy AI isn't very smart. However, where the game truly shines is in its clan abilities and how you approach encounters: stealth, persuasion, domination, seduction, or brute force are all viable. You can talk your way out of fights, manipulate NPCs to do your bidding, or stalk silently from the shadows. That said, Bloodlines suffers from bugs and balance issues, especially in the late game. Boss fights are often frustrating and underwhelming, and unless you mod the game, some disciplines are far superior to others. Thankfully, fan patches and community mods have addressed many of these issues over time. Replayability & Roleplaying: 10/10 Bloodlines is one of the most replayable RPGs ever made. Each of the seven clans offers unique experiences, from the political Ventrue to the beastly Gangrel to the enigmatic Malkavians. Not only do your powers change, but so does how people talk to you, treat you, and what options are available in quests. The sheer amount of roleplaying variation is staggering. Want to seduce and manipulate your way to power? You can. Want to never be seen and silently feed from the shadows? Go Nosferatu. Want to embrace insanity and uncover hidden truths? Malkavian is a surreal experience in and of itself. Visuals & Art Direction: 6.5/10 (2025 standards) At launch, Bloodlines was visually impressive for its time. In the year of writing this - 2025, it's clearly dated, though the art direction still holds strong. With mods, HD textures, and widescreen support, it can look fairly decent. Environments remain atmospheric, and character models-while stiff-have expressive animations. Don't expect photorealism or fluid modern animations. Instead, focus on the tone, lighting, and creative design that still make this game feel alive. Technical Stability: 5/10 (Without patches), 8/10 (With Unofficial Patch) Bloodlines was infamously released unfinished due to Troika's shutdown. Bugs, crashes, broken quests, and balance issues were common. Fortunately, the community-created Unofficial Patch has kept the game alive, fixing hundreds of bugs, restoring cut content, and improving compatibility. If you're playing unmodded, prepare for a rough ride. With the Unofficial Patch (which is considered essential), the game runs well on modern systems. Conclusion: Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines is a flawed gem, but one whose brilliance shines brighter with each passing year. It offers an unmatched vampire roleplaying experience, blending mystery, politics, horror, and freedom in a way few games have ever managed. Though the mechanics and visuals may show their age, the narrative depth, atmosphere, and replayability ensure that this game remains a crown jewel of the RPG genre. If you haven't played it yet, you owe it to yourself-especially if you're a fan of immersive storytelling and moral complexity. Hopefully The Chinese Room does this game justice by delivering a solid Bloodlines 2. Final Score: 94/100

With Bloodlines 2 in less than a week away as of writing this post I felt obligated to write a review of this game. Short, sweet, and to the point because that's what this game deserves. This game is easily THE MOST 9/10 game you will ever play. Period. Why? Vampire the Masquerade: Bloodlines is a tabletop-to-videogame adaptation of World of Darkness' Vampire the Masquerade 20th edition. Think of something like Baldurs Gate 3 or Fallout in nature where it's made from the ground up with TTRPG mechanics in mind. You start character creation by choosing your class, known in game and lore as a clan, and choosing your characters features. Granted, I am playing on the Unofficial Patch so some things may be different. After doing so, you start the game. (This is about to be typed out as if the player knows nothing about VtM so keep those thumb down buttons at bay) You play as a young illegitimate spawn born into the world of vampires in Santa Montica by your sire who did not get permission to do so. In a political power move, the lead vampire decides to spare your life after a outburst in the court. As such, the games story plays as a "rags to riches" where you earn your right to be a vampire, learn about the world you were born into and it's vast intricacies, and gain power in your own story. The story going this way is brilliant. For one, the player *and* the player character being new to this world means both can learn the world together, and for those already familiar can brush up on lore and sometimes even learn new things or just things specific to Santa Monica. On the other hand, it makes the progression of power and responsibility go hand and hand and it feels fun at all turns! The game play can either be first or third person. As you go through the game there is no "leveling up" in the tradition sense. Instead, you get points every time you do a task as a reward and you can allocate those points according to how you want to build your character. All classes share the same stats, some restricting certain stats due to their lore or a specific feat you have chosen, but one major thing that is different is Disciplines. They are powers (typically) unique to YOUR clan respectively, and while some are shared and in very RARE instances you can actually learn a new one, they are esscential to your characters playstyle. (SPOILERS AHEAD UNTIL LAST PARAGRAPH) Now for the finale; the bad. Why is this the most "9/10 game." For starters, the game is very linear. For the time it is ASTOUNDING, but by the past two decades that have passed it the results can be frustrating. For example there is no other way to leave the first zone without doing the ghost quest for Therese Voerman no matter what, and you cannot just find Bertram Tung without her help even if you know where he is. There are many other questlines that you will notice this with and it gets very frustrating on your 4th playthrough when you just want to experience a different story. Another big problem is the end game. Once you get to Chinatown the games quality nosedives rapidly in both quality and playtesting. The Chang Brothers can go die of erotic asphyxiation, Ming is one of the worst bosses of any games I have ever encountered, and "Hot Stripper Assassin Action!" is so broken not even the VTMBUP team could save it. I had to personally console command it to life and even then I have to fix some flags that didn't even count it. And even worse then all of that combined? The ending of this game is so horribly disappointing I don't even know where to start. THE FUCKING COFFIN WAS JUST FULL OF C4??? I have heard rumors the game suffered time restraints and budget cuts but holy shit nothing justifies this lackluster, piss-poor ending to me. Most of the endings are kinda trash with only the Tremere ending seeming kinda satisfying. On top of that I know La Croix is supposed to be portrayed as a bitch but NO LA CROIX BOSS FIGHT???????? Side note, no character customizer is lame :( I get it for the time there were not many games that let you but sometimes it really hits me where it hurts (SPOILERS OVER) 9/10, this game is god tier up until the very last minute. A game absolutely worthy of it's cult classic status. I know I didn't cover much of the story other than the tutorial story, or explain a bunch of the fun stuff in this review that seems jarring to VtM fans, but I promise for those new people this world and story is so interesting you just have to experience it for yourself. I also love how stylized the game's world is, it's a more sleazy and depraved version of our world. My only complaints is it feels like you only get a superficial look at the world of [i]Vampire: The Masquerade[/i], and I wanted to dive in much deeper. Ultimately, the game is a perfect introduction to the [i]World of Darkness[/i] franchise, as it shows how amazing it's world is. The game also gives you so many options to how you want to play it. The most obvious are the starting clans, that can make you more predisposed to certain builds, or fundamentally change how you play the game. This is also helped by the game's quests that give you many options with how you want to tackle them. The game's problems are it's linear main quest and combat. The game's main quest is one of the most linear quests I've ever seen in a RPG. Given how much freedom your given with your character's build, I went in thinking you'd be able to decide what factions you align yourself with throughout the whole game. However, no matter what you want to do you're stuck with a single path for the main quest, all given to you by a specific faction, no matter if it aligns with your character. It isn't until the very end when you're finally able to decide who you side with. The second, and most glaring problem is the game's combat. It's not good, but for most of the game I found it fine as you only do it in short intervals and can be forgone based on your character's build. However, at the end of the game you are forced into long combat sections back-to-back, and it ultimately gave me a sour taste when finishing the game and makes me kind-of dread doing it again when I decide to replay the game with a different starting clan. If you want to play Deus Ex as a vampire with pretty much just as much political conspiracy, you should try this. If you want to play skyrim, this isn't for you. To explain, this game is roleplaying first, that means you can carefully tune your character's personality through the dialogue, carve your specific path through the story in a few unique ways, and get rewarded for doing things that aren't outright stated as an option, as well as be punished for doing things the wrong way. This comes at the cost of everything that isn't dialogue and story. ⚡The combat.⚡ I am personally someone who doesn't mind bad combat. [b]Score: 2/10[/b] A now-cultish classic, VTMB's relative obscurity, even in light of its development-plagued sequel, is what masks the fact that this game absolutely sucks. Yes, the first half is a unique, and plenty enjoyable saunter down Santa Monica streets, chock full of a well-realized and decidedly campy southern California vampire pulp setting. All the girls have big boobs, all the guys are edgy or pathetic losers, the only posters are pinups, and the sexual innuendos are so obnoxious for a video game that you do laugh a little for the full-send efforts of writers that are seemingly knocking their neighbors. The voice acting is actually extremely laudable, and if you grew up in the late 00s you'll recognize a handful of timbres that you didn't expect to do game work. The quest design in this fabled first half isn't... insane, but it's solid. The music and club environments and general atmosphere, yeah, it's giving vampire. It's easy to see why the game had a niche audience. But... but! The moment the second half starts, it takes a horrific shift. The combat, by far the worst part of the game (aside from an abysmal third person camera, terrifyingly softlockable leveling, irritating gunplay, and lack of polish), is suddenly made the ultimate focus, with a previously balanced gameplay loop absolutely sledgehammered and pushed all the way over to melee and ranged builds only. You are absolutely screwed if you attempt to beat the game as a stealth or speech character, period. It loses the general RPG tag, for me, and becomes an action RPG. Even then, by ARPG standards, the last 30% is a nightmarish slog through labyrinthian tilesets, densely packed with frustrating and pointless enemy variations, stacked layer upon layer upon layer... You get a couple interesting visual designs, yes, but it's not even remotely worth it. I did not find the endings to be diverse enough to encourage second playthroughs, either, or even satisfying in the case of the one I got. Yes, it's true that VTMB does satisfy a certain savouring, but once you bite down, it turns rotten, putrid, and wholly inedible. Put this thing back in the coffin and leave it six feet under.

Just a quest log and your sense of exploration, looking at signs on buildings in the gritty streets and using your actual brain for direction. The story itself was engaging and I did my play through as one of my favourite clans, a Tremere. Which are known for being Vampire mages that use blood magic. I played everything in big screen mode with a controller and a HDMI connecting my PC to my large TV. The game takes place in Los Angeles and has 4 main areas. My favourite missions were The Ghost That Haunts Midnight in Santa Monica early in the game. The vibes in the house were very atmospheric and super immersive. It's pretty good, but it really does depend on what you want out of this game. There are a lot of people who will tell you that this game is one of the best rpgs of all time. I don't think I can agree. No matter what your build is, you will be fighting a lot. The midpoint onwards is basically just a series of fights. I went into this game wanting to play a speech/stealth character, and neither is particularly viable. Not only is it impossible to talk your way out of or sneak past most major fights (although stealth can be useful for a few side quests), but speech is strangely split into three separate stats, which weakens it further. Even for the few encounters you can use speech to bypass, you probably won't have the necessary stats, since not only do you need to invest heavily into combat, but your speech investment is also split, so it's unlikely that any of your speech skills will ever get high enough for the checks without following a guide. Additionally, the lock-picking and hacking skills are annoyingly necessary. While there are a few keys and passwords that you can find in the level, a frustrating amount of doors and computers require lock-picking and either hacking or just looking up the password. This contributes to the feeling that you're not building a character, but rather just trying to meet skill checks to unlock more game. Despite this, though, I'd argue VtMB does succeed in providing a great, varied vampire fantasy. While everyone has to fight, different clans will fight entirely differently. The defining mechanic of the combat is the clan discipline system. Disciplines being supernatural powers, and while most disciplines are shared between two to three clans, no two clans share the same set of three. This means that every clan feels very different to play, and the specific combination of disciplines creates a very different playstyle. The combat itself is pretty terrible, but it's fun in the same way traditional MOBA combat is fun. Even if you're mostly just left clicking, the fun comes from making your own build and eventually becoming an unstoppable killing machine. Overall, it might not be exactly what I expected or even wanted, but I think it does have something for a lot of players. I'd keep in mind, though, that it's less of a great rpg, and more of a great vampire game.

Alright, here's my take after finishing Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines for the first time: This game is what I would call a flawed masterpiece. For what it is, it's phenomenal. It does things that most modern RPGs don't even attempt, and it does them with personality, atmosphere, and writing that's rarely matched. But at the same time, it's held back by rushed development, underfunding, and being built on early Source engine tech that just wasn't quite ready. The highs of this game are really high. Santa Monica in particular felt like the most fleshed-out, atmospheric hub. Exploring it, talking to every character, checking every door - it was exciting and rewarding. Chinatown, despite some questionable English-Asian accents, also stood out to me as one of my favorite locations, with its own strong atmosphere and questlines. The Ocean House Hotel mission deserves a special mention: it's hands-down one of the best haunted house levels I've ever played in any game. Genuinely creepy, brilliantly designed, and it sticks with you. On the flip side, there are parts of this game that don't hold up. Hollywood was a big letdown compared to Santa Monica and Downtown. It felt undercooked and lacked the energy of the other hubs. The infamous sewer section was a slog - a confusing maze padded out with repetitive enemies, and I eventually just turned on god mode and noclip to get through it because it wasn't fun anymore. And the endgame as a whole… it kind of overstayed its welcome. Instead of building to a tight, impactful conclusion, it dragged on a bit, and I found myself pushing through it just to reach the end rather than feeling excited about what was happening. Character-wise, this game is packed with standouts. Jeanette and her sister Therese are an amazing early highlight (I do wish they played a bigger role later on, given that Jeanette is literally on the cover of the game). Nines, Gary, and even random side characters left impressions that stuck with me. The writing, the dialogue, the worldbuilding - it's all top-tier. This is where the game shines brightest: it makes you feel like you're part of this strange, dark world full of politics, manipulation, and monsters trying to pass as human. As for gameplay, let's be real: the combat isn't great. I ended up focusing on a persuasion build, and that felt like the most rewarding way to play. Talking my way through situations, using the dialogue options, persuading enemies to back down instead of fighting - it all felt powerful and satisfying. The actual fighting sections, though? Janky and unfun, and honestly, if you're here for combat, you're not going to find much to love. If you're here for story, choices, and atmosphere, you're in the right place. In terms of a score, I'd give this game a 7.5/10. I'm tempted to rank it higher, but here's my breakdown: I take one point off for Hollywood being a dud, another point off for the bloated endgame, and half a point off for some of the mechanics and systems that have aged poorly (though I don't hold that too hard against it - it's very much a product of its time). Still, those flaws don't erase the fact that this game has some of the best writing, atmosphere, and roleplaying opportunities I've seen in an RPG. If this game were remade today, with modern tech, proper funding, and developers who had the time and passion to see it through, it could easily be one of the greatest RPGs ever made. As it stands now, it's already something special - a cult classic that earns that title for good reason. So yeah: a flawed masterpiece, but one absolutely worth experiencing. If you love RPGs, storytelling, and atmosphere, you owe it to yourself to play this.

The WoD setting includes not only vampires, but also werewolves, witches, and magic, all tied together with a rich hierarchy system and layers of alternate history. Vampire: The Masquerade Bloodlines stays true to this world with remarkable authenticity, offering players the chance to join iconic clans, make impactful choices, and experience dynamic combat. I immersed myself in the lore and characters, finally grasped the intricacies of the Masquerade system, and from then on I became fully invested in the World of Darkness universe. Despite its technical shortcomings, I strongly recommend patience and tolerance toward its outdated mechanics. Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines is a cult classic that has earned its reputation as one of the most ambitious and atmospheric RPGs ever made, despite a troubled development and a notoriously buggy release. Developed by Troika Games and released in 2004, the game adapts White Wolf's Vampire: The Masquerade tabletop RPG into a dark, immersive, and narratively rich experience that continues to resonate with fans decades later. It offers a unique blend of first-person and third-person gameplay, deep character customization, multiple story paths, and an unforgettable cast of characters-all set against the backdrop of a twisted, nocturnal version of Los Angeles ruled by vampire politics and ancient conspiracies. From the opening cinematic, Bloodlines pulls you into a world of shadow and secrecy, where vampires coexist with humans under the veil of the Masquerade-a code that ensures their existence remains hidden. You begin the game by creating a character from one of seven clans, each with its own strengths, weaknesses, and playstyle. This initial choice has a massive impact on how you experience the game, from the dialogue options available to you, to how NPCs react, to the very way you traverse and interact with the world. Whether you're playing as a suave Toreador, a monstrous Nosferatu, or the reality-bending Malkavian, each clan provides a fresh lens through which the story unfolds. Gameplay is a fusion of RPG progression, immersive sim mechanics, and narrative-driven design. You explore different urban hubs-Santa Monica, Downtown L.A., Hollywood, and Chinatown-each teeming with side quests, hidden secrets, and factional intrigue. The dialogue system is exceptionally well-written, with options tailored to your clan and stats, encouraging multiple playthroughs. Social manipulation, stealth, hacking, persuasion, and raw intimidation are all viable means of advancing objectives, and you're rarely forced into a singular approach. This freedom is one of Bloodlines' most celebrated features, allowing you to truly roleplay your character in a world that feels reactive and alive. Combat, on the other hand, is where the game's age and limitations show. Melee, firearms, and vampiric disciplines are all available in combat scenarios, but the mechanics feel clunky by modern standards. Gunplay is imprecise, and AI behavior is inconsistent, which can make certain sections more frustrating than enjoyable-especially in the final third of the game, where combat becomes increasingly unavoidable. Still, the diversity in abilities and approaches-especially with disciplines like Dominate, Obfuscate, or Blood Buff-gives players plenty of tools to overcome these shortcomings creatively. It's also a testament to the game's narrative and atmosphere that even the weakest gameplay elements don't significantly diminish its overall impact. Where Bloodlines truly shines is in its world-building and character design. Every major NPC you encounter feels memorable and distinct, from the dual personas of Jeanette and Therese Voerman, to the enigmatic Prince LaCroix, to the anarchic smuggler Jack. These characters aren't just exposition machines; they're flawed, dangerous, manipulative, or endearing in their own ways, often leaving you guessing about their true motives. The writing is layered with political subtext, moral ambiguity, and psychological complexity, reflecting the nuanced tone of the tabletop source material. The game rarely offers clear-cut choices-there are no obvious heroes or villains, only factions vying for power and survival in a web of lies and half-truths. Atmospherically, Bloodlines is masterful. The soundtrack by Rik Schaffer, combined with licensed tracks from artists like Chiasm and Lacuna Coil, creates a moody, immersive soundscape that perfectly captures the nocturnal melancholy of the setting. Each district in the game has its own distinct flavor, from the eerie beachfront sleaze of Santa Monica to the decaying glamour of Hollywood. The level design, while dated in some aspects, does an impressive job of creating interconnected urban spaces that feel grounded and lived-in. Quests often unfold in unpredictable ways, and there's a consistent sense that danger could lurk around any corner, whether from rival Kindred, rogue vampires, or things even older and darker. Perhaps the most infamous aspect of Bloodlines is its technical instability. At launch, the game was riddled with bugs, performance issues, and incomplete content due to a rushed release and financial troubles at Troika. Many quests were broken, NPC behavior was erratic, and certain features were underdeveloped or missing altogether. However, the fan community quickly stepped in to preserve the game's legacy. Over the years, extensive unofficial patches have restored cut content, improved stability, and fixed countless bugs, making the current version of Bloodlines far more playable than the original release. This ongoing support has helped keep the game alive and relevant long after its initial commercial failure. In hindsight, Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines represents a rare kind of RPG-one that prioritizes player agency, moral complexity, and narrative depth above all else. Its flawed brilliance, combined with its enduring atmosphere and character-driven storytelling, has solidified its place as one of the most beloved cult classics in gaming history. It's a game that manages to feel personal and impactful, where your choices matter not just in terms of outcomes, but in how they reflect your evolving identity as a creature of the night. Despite its imperfections, or perhaps because of them, Bloodlines remains a landmark achievement-a haunting, seductive, and endlessly fascinating descent into darkness. Rating: 9/10

2025 Bloodlines still bites hard. It thrives in the tension between ambition and execution, and honestly, that's where its magic lies. The dialogue and character writing are sharp, memorable, and deep. Despite its age, this game can still outshine many modern RPGs when it comes to world-building, immersion, and choice. With multiple vampire clans to choose from, branching paths, faction allegiances, and four different endings, the replay value is through the roof. The atmosphere is unmatched. Los Angeles feels both lived-in and otherworldly, with a gothic-punk tone that oozes personality. The voice acting still lands, and it does a lot of heavy lifting to keep the immersion strong. That said, it's far from perfect. Visually, it's aged, and the combat, especially melee, feels clunky. Firearms are sluggish and underwhelming unless upgraded. The final portion of the game starts to feel more linear, as if it was rushed toward the finish line, but it's still fun. Technical issues are present, but the community has fan patches that make it perfectly playable in 2025. It's a flawed gem, no doubt, but if you're into RPGs that prioritise atmosphere, dialogue, and real choice, this is a must-play. Bloodlines is one of my all-time favorite games, it's practically a core memory. Not just because it's good, which it absolutely is, but because it pulls off something most games still can't: making you truly believe your character belongs in its world. The atmosphere, the writing, the insane clan-specific dialogue options that still slap harder than most modern RPGs, this game shaped my taste in everything from character builds to eyeliner. You're not just role-playing. You are your clan. Whether you're brooding as a Ventrue, unraveling as a Malkavian, or obsessing over your own reflection as a Toreador, Bloodlines lets you live the Masquerade like no other game has ever managed. Yes, it's old. Yes, it was broken on launch. But that's where the modding community swoops in with a passion usually reserved for cults or small indie religions. The Unofficial Patch, does more than fix bugs. It restores cut content, rebalances gameplay, and keeps this gothic trainwreck alive. Then there's the Clan Quest Mod, which adds new quests and dialogue tailored to your clan, and the Antitribu Mod, if you want to throw canon out the window and dive into chaos. Steam shows only 40~ minutes played. That's because mods launch the game through a separate executable, and I never bothered with the fix that tracks playtime properly, there is a guide made by the community for that though. Every time I replay it, I find something new. A bit of cut dialogue, a weird NPC animation, a random alley that somehow scares me more than most horror games, and that werewolf, fuck that guy. This game isn't perfect, but it kinda is? If you're even remotely interested in vampires, RPGs, or storytelling that's more than "kill ten rats", you owe it to yourself to play Bloodlines, and always with mods. Trust me, mod the hell out of it.

It might be considered a good game back in 2004; however, it's not up to the standard of modern games in 2025. The vampire abilities the player possesses require blood to cast, but it is difficult to suck the blood out from the enemies during a fight; hence relying on those abilities in the boss fight is unpractical. In addition, there are no hot keys for the said abilities, and you can't pause the game to pick an ability to use; instead, you may get hit several times before you finally find the ability you want to cast via rolling the mouse wheel. Also, guns are ineffective against enemy vampires in this game. As such, most of time the player will use the basic melee attack to fight both the standard enemies (b/c we want to save blood for boss fights) and bosses (b/c we have limited blood). In other words, the fighting in this game is quite boring. The game suffers further from its poorly-designed quest-tracking system. The game does not come with any map that the player can carry. Instead, the player must go to the bus stations to check the city map. Moreover, the quest locations are not marked on the map, and from time to time the quest log does not really tell you what to do or where to go next. Consequently, the player needs to try every building in the city or every door in a building in hope of triggering the follow-up event in a mission/side quest. It's nearly impossible to complete some of the missions without looking up the solutions in Youtube videos or game wiki websites. What makes VTMB iconic is not just that it's an excellent game. Don't get me wrong- it absolutely is. Although many systems feel janky and the graphics dated by contemporary standards, the game's RPG elements hold up really well. You get a compelling narrative with a colourful cast, and a lot of choice in how you want to approach both individual 'quests' and the game's overarching story. The game is great. But it's not mainly that which keeps drawing me back. What makes VTMB truly iconic to me is how well it paints the turn-of-the-millennium pop culture picture of the World of Shadows. More than anything, VTMB pulls you in and makes you feel like you're [i]part[/i] of that distorted mirror image counterpart to our own world. Even with the dated, pixellated graphics, I can stand in the heights overlooking LA and [i]feel[/i] like the night-time traffic of this conspiracy-laden world is unfolding below me. For the world-weary, ironic teens of the late 90s and early 00s, this hit a special nerve. And it remains, to me, a pop culture icon of the era.
