A cult classic, which deserves all the praise and all the criticism that it receives. For anyone coming to the game fresh, be prepared for the mechanical shortcomings. This game is buggy and contains more than it's fair share of jank. The early game is phenomenal but some of the later game segments are underdeveloped and linear owing to the game being shipped out before it was ready. There are patches maintained by the community that address some of the biggest issues and even restore content. Look for it online. The game truly succeeds on the atmosphere, ethos and story telling. There are a couple of cringe performances here and there, but the nature of WoD and the VtM setting, make some eccentricity work better than it otherwise would. Otherwise voice acting and script are damn solid, even to this day. The story is engaging and sits nicely in the lore of the franchise. It doesn't seem out of place in the least. Various factions are lovingly and accurately portrayed, perhaps with the exception of the Sabbat, who are slightly caricatured. But the game needs villains and you can't beat shovelheads for that role. The lore of the world isn't dumped on you either, atleast not too much so. If you are unfamiliar with the world of darkness or Vampire the Masquerade in particular you will be overwhelmed with the lore right out the gate. Equally, if you are a returning fan of the IP, you'll find all the little details here, with the meta plot referenced here and there if you go out of your way to look for it. The sound design is on point, atmospheric and grungy and helps to set the tone. Voice acting is incredible, though no voiced protag. This was before that time when voiced MC's was common. I think, that for some people the age and jankiness of this game will prevent them from enjoying this rough diamond. But for those that can look past the shortcomings, you'll be treated to what can perhaps be considered the best computer game adaptation of the WoD ever made.

Cult classic that dared to be different, delivering a brutally raw, mature, and richly layered RPG experience. Released in 2004 by Troika Games, it was undeniably ahead of its time-a game brimming with bold ideas that stumbled only because of the technical limitations and a rushed launch. Set in a dark and twisted version of modern-day Los Angeles, Bloodlines thrusts players into the violent, seductive underworld of vampire society. It doesn't hold back-there's sex, nudity, drug dens, shady nightclubs, and enough political backstabbing to rival a Shakespearean tragedy. You don't just play a vampire-you live as one, navigating clan politics, manipulating humans, feeding to survive, and hiding your true nature from the world ("the Masquerade"). The game masterfully blends RPG mechanics with immersive storytelling. Dialogue options shape your path, your clan choice alters gameplay (e.g., the insane Malkavians or grotesque Nosferatu), and missions often allow for stealth, persuasion, or full-on violence. It's heavy on investigation and dripping with dark humor-sometimes grotesque, often witty. Combat is rough around the edges, but enemy variety-from humans and vampire hunters to supernatural horrors-keeps things tense. One moment you're seducing a clubgoer, the next you're battling twisted monstrosities in haunted hospitals or sewers. A brooding, broken gem that gleams with personality and world-building most modern games couldn't summon with all the Vitae in Los Angeles. It oozes style, menace, and that wonderful feeling of playing something that absolutely wasn't made for mass appeal. It's flawed. It's glorious. It's Vampire, dammit. The setting? Immaculate. VtM Bloodlines is in equal parts an underrated gem and a hot mess. The game is pretty rough if you don't play with the unofficial patch, but aside from that it's pretty stable if you do go out of the way to download it. As a whole, the game thrives with its writing, atmosphere, and roleplaying opportunities. There aren't many games that manage to really get me immersed in their dialogue systems, but Bloodlines is just genuinely very well written and presents a wide variety of different character types for you to try out. You're given ample opportunities to play the kind of vampire you're interested in without ever being given choices that feel tacked on or immersion breaking. This game immediately ranks up there along with other titles like Fallout: New Vegas, Baldur's Gate 3, and Disco Elysium as experiences that I was able to truly immerse myself in and become somebody else. Any game that can do that is worth a shoutout. With all of that being said, the gameplay is definitely the game's weak point. Combat is clunky and unsatifying, with some really poor balancing with regard to specific build types such as stealth. The AI can often be comically bad, although this is only super noticeable if you try to avoid combat in most cases. I'd also like to highlight that in terms of enemy layout and level design, the last stretch of the game is legitimately pretty terrible and feels like a punishment for wanting to reach the end. The sewer level in particular feels like an unfinished Garry's Mod map you'd use for playtesting, rather than something that should be in any sort of finished project. It's sort of a shame that Bloodlines sputters out in the end, because it sort of leaves a bad final impression even if you've managed to appreciate the game's strengths. As I said at the start, VtM Bloodlines is a game defined by duality. It ranges from being a genuine masterpiece to unfinished garbage that I really did have to force myself to get through. However even keeping the bad in mind, I still think it deserves its status as a cult classic and is a must play for fans of TTRPG and WRPG experiences.

Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines is one of the best RPGs I've played. Set in the World of Darkness universe, the game is based on White Wolf's role-playing game Vampire: The Masquerade. The writing and characters are excellent, keeping you invested through the 30-40 hours it takes to complete (depending on how many side quests you take on). There are choices to be made about who you side with, leading to different story arcs and side quests. The choice of vampire clan for your character gives you unique powers that often come in very handy in completing your missions. I played as a member of the Tremere clan, which gives you some very cool blood magic. There are some difficult bosses towards the end of the game, which will really punish you if you haven't got your build just right, so spend your experience points wisely! The world is also not as fleshed out in the later levels, probably a consequence of the game being released before it was really ready. Playing with the Unofficial Patch is mandatory to avoid the bugs.

A flawed masterpiece. Although pretty much requiring modding in order to achieve a playable state (the unofficial patch). Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines provides one of the best role-playing experiences a player could ask for. This game basically begs the player to replay as everything concerning the stats you choose to invest in, your race, and clan you side with will greatly affect your experience. For example if you chose to be a Nosferatu NPC's will treat the player completely different as well as how you traverse the world will be completely different. (NPC's will comment on the players appearance with disgust and the player will be left to traverse the world out of sight through the sewers feeding on rats to survive) Player choice is heavily emphasized meaning, experiment with your approach, seduce, intimidate, and persuade to get the result you want. Amazing quests, setting, lore, music, atmosphere, and by far the strongest point of the game are the characters. I couldn't believe how expressive the character models were for a game that runs on the Source engine released in 2004. Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines is a game you could only dream of releasing in this generation of games. What this game provides that others that have since released do not is soul. The world is palatable with the amount of care and detail painstakingly put in every line of code and dialogue. For a game this size, I couldn't believe how consistently good the voice acting was. I couldn't even list all of my favorite characters if I tried, as the list would be too long. Games I've played that have been released in recent years have NPCs that feel like floating talking heads with no individuality. The gothic, edgy, vampire underworld of Los Angeles is something I've never experienced, and I'm convinced Troika Games couldn't have made it more interesting. Each character you encounter reinforces the politics, factions, races, and history of this world. The story gripped me in a way that kept me up late seeing what would happen next. The plot twists had my jaw on the floor, the humor had me in stitches, and the drama floored me. Now this is a game that can be unbearably frustrating at times. At some points of my playthrough, I had to enable god mode/noclip to progress. There are bugs and glitches, and the combat is serviceable at its very best. This could be a deal breaker for many, but if you take a step back to experience the kind of game that this is, it's like no other. This was the high I've been chasing that Fallout and The Elder Scrolls gave me. I'm skeptical for the sequel as a different developer has the responsibility of making it, and the constant delays are not a good sign. Regardless, I'm ready to experience more of what this world can offer. For as rushed as the game was, the hardware limitations, and the year it was released it completely makes sense the kind of cult following and support it has garnered. The game also features a hacking mechanic that is crazy addicting and satisfying. Like a fine wine, this game only appreciates in value as more and more commercial games fail to emulate a tenth of the kind of experience this game provides. P.S. DON'T OPEN IT

Install the unofficial patch. Playing without it is impossible. It's free, less than 1GB and pretty much installs itself so there's no fuss. My favourite part about this game is that the quickload button is also Steam's screenshot button, so I have a lovely gallery of me fucking up along my playthrough. You can manually change it but it's very innovative. It does atmosphere quite well. You really feel like this newborn vampire belonging to this secret society where fuck-ups are NOT tolerated. You have to follow people into alleyways to feed, you can covertly use your vampiric traits to guide conversations your way, among other really neat features that I can't think of right now. I really wish characters were expanded upon more. Jeanette (cover girl) shows up for the first few hours, then never comes up again. Same thing with multiple other characters throughout the game. I like these characters and want to interact with them more but the game just doesn't let me. Combat is average early game, and steadily gets worse as the game goes on. Knocking enemies over with melee weapons gives them i-frames while they stand up, pretty much negating your advantage and making this whole knock down system pointless. Melee also forces you to engage at close-range (obviously), which become a MAJOR disadvantage late-game as more and more enemies become ranged. Stealth also becomes worse as time goes on, as enemies just start being able to see through invisibility for some reason. So just walking up to enemies guarantees a fuckton of damage. Ranged is just as bad though. There is forced weapon spread, so you have to stand still and crouch to get a half-decent shot on target. Automatic weapons have too much recoil to use (both for the player's aim, and the weapon spread mechanic). Last but not least is your own health regen. It slowly goes up over time, but regens faster if you munch on somebody. But some enemies are completely immune to this (making some section of the game a slog as you have to frequently go afk to wait for health regen), and the hit detection is beyond broken while in combat. This makes it very inconsistent and a struggle to use. Maps are small, but somehow still too big in certain areas. Santa Monica and Chinatown were decent, but Hollywood and Downtown had far too much walking distance between objectives. Some dungeon segments are fucking horrible. The Nosferatu Sewer section in Hollywood, and the late-game Hotel section especially. Just wave after wave after wave of enemies copy-pasted everywhere. If I have to hear those Geodude-looking losers lunge at me one more time I'll cry. Also a lot of extremely tedious puzzles, like trial-and-error maze areas and that stupid vent room in the sewers. I have a lot of bad things to say, but it's a 9/10. Loved the world and characters. Level-design was usually fine. The story was just ok. The combat was meh.

Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines is a difficult game to review in 2025. The game is very, very dated. It absolutely needs the Unofficial Patch to even be playable. Usually that's enough for me to apply the thumbs down for any game. But I'll make an exception here because where this game doesn't suck, it's incredible. Taking a leaf from contemporaries like Deus Ex, this action RPG grabs you with the excellent recreation of the tabletop vampire abilities you'll be used to if you played the pen and paper RPG, with the fan favourite clans from Ventrue to Brujah available for players. As well as all the crazy abilities, like domination and mind control all the way to making people's blood boil until they explode. It's also let down by the combat which comes across as unpolished, although in 2004, there wasn't a lot to compare to. TTK ranges from way too long to instakill and it's balanced rather poorly. However what drives this game is world class narrative combined with meaningful choices that impact all the way through the game, just like with Deus Ex, you get that whole vibe... what you do in this game and the way you do it has consequences, and it makes it all the more immersive and enjoyable. It's also something developers rarely manage to grasp... I can't think of many examples beyond Baldur's Gate 3 where such excellent game design philosophy has been so successfully applied. If you can pick this up for $5 or less, and you like retro gaming, and can handle the dated, rough edges, this is worth a play-through.

GUN, developed by Neversoft and published by Activision, is a gritty, cinematic portrayal of the American frontier that captures both the freedom and savagery of the Old West. Released in 2005, it arrived at a time when Western-themed games were rare, making its ambition stand out even more. The story follows Colton White, a rugged frontiersman whose life of hunting and survival is upended when his adoptive father, Ned, is killed during a brutal ambush aboard a riverboat. Left with nothing but vengeance and unanswered questions, Colton embarks on a journey across a violent and morally ambiguous frontier. What begins as a quest for revenge slowly unfolds into a broader narrative of corruption, greed, and the dying age of the untamed West. It's a familiar tale of blood and betrayal, yet told with enough cinematic weight and authenticity to make it compelling even today. The gameplay in GUN blends the raw action of a third-person shooter with the open exploration of an early sandbox design. Players can freely traverse vast stretches of wilderness, desolate mining towns, and bustling frontier settlements on horseback, with seamless transitions between mission-based storytelling and side activities. The gunplay is tight and satisfying, with a clever "Quick Draw" mechanic that allows players to slow down time, lining up precise shots in the heat of battle-a feature that captures the essence of a gunslinger duel while adding a dynamic rhythm to firefights. Whether you're facing down bandits in a dusty street, raiding a gang's hideout, or defending settlers from Apache raiders, the combat feels immediate and visceral. Every encounter reinforces the lawless brutality of the world Neversoft set out to recreate. What elevates GUN beyond its action sequences is its sense of place. The game's environments-sprawling canyons, snow-capped mountains, and sun-baked plains-paint a vivid picture of the untamed frontier. Each settlement feels distinct, from the corrupt town of Empire to the mining camps and trading outposts scattered across the map. The open world, though not massive by today's standards, was ambitious for its time and still succeeds in evoking the spirit of freedom and isolation that defines the Western genre. Traveling on horseback across the open land, with wind sweeping through the grass and vultures circling in the distance, carries a quiet majesty that contrasts beautifully with the violence that punctuates the story. The sound design reinforces this atmosphere-guns crack with sharp authority, saloon pianos play in the background, and the haunting score perfectly captures the melancholy tone of the frontier's twilight. GUN also benefits from strong voice acting that breathes life into its characters. Thomas Jane's portrayal of Colton White conveys both stoicism and simmering rage, while Kris Kristofferson's gruff performance as Ned adds emotional weight to the game's opening tragedy. The supporting cast, including Ron Perlman and Brad Dourif, lends credibility to the world, grounding it in a realism that matches its mature themes. The writing, while leaning on classic Western archetypes, treats its subject matter with seriousness and respect. There's no attempt to romanticize the frontier; the world of GUN is harsh, unjust, and rife with moral compromise. Slavery, greed, and religious exploitation are all touched upon, giving the story a more somber and reflective tone than the average action game of its era. Despite its strengths, GUN is not without limitations. The game's biggest drawback is its brevity-most players can complete the main story in under ten hours, and while side missions like bounty hunting, gold mining, and law enforcement provide optional distractions, they lack the depth to extend the experience much further. The world, though open, feels underpopulated at times, with fewer interactive systems compared to the more expansive sandboxes that would follow in later years. Still, these constraints reflect the era in which the game was made; GUN's focus on narrative pacing and mechanical polish makes it feel purposeful rather than hollow. Its concise structure allows the story to unfold without filler, maintaining a steady sense of momentum from start to finish. Looking back, GUN can be seen as a precursor to later genre-defining Westerns like Red Dead Redemption. It laid much of the groundwork for how developers could translate the mythology of the American West into an interactive experience-balancing personal drama, historical grit, and moral complexity. It's a game that understands that the West was never just about adventure and heroism, but about survival and the slow death of an era. Even years after its release, it remains a vivid depiction of a world in transition, where progress comes at the cost of blood and innocence. Ultimately, GUN endures as one of the most memorable Western action games of its generation. Its combination of tight gunplay, evocative world design, and morally charged storytelling makes it an experience that still holds up remarkably well. Though brief, it delivers its tale with conviction, never overstaying its welcome. It captures the essence of the Western mythos-loneliness, vengeance, and the fading glow of a brutal frontier-with cinematic precision and unflinching honesty. For players who crave a concentrated dose of Western grit wrapped in fast-paced gameplay and cinematic flair, GUN remains a classic worth revisiting-a raw and unpolished gem that helped shape the digital frontier that came after it. Rating: 9/10

Worth playing for nostalgia reasons, and fine as an early exploration into open-world shooters, but has a small map and other limits compared to modern titles in the genre. The plot is gritty, and includes unflinching violence, sexism, and racism (but although the game portrays these things, that does not mean to say that the game promotes them). Culturally, the game was successful at opening a dialogue about problematic history that had been glossed over in the past. By having the protagonist change allegiances between colonial and native powers, we at least get some exposure to the idea that the "good guys" simply aren't that from another perspective. However, some stereotypes persist, the Chinese immigrants are not given a voice, and you will see some offensive content. There are plenty of things to call out in your cultural studies thesis. In a way, the fact that the game is culturally outdated is a good sign that we're making social progress. Did I enjoy the game when it came out? Definitely. Did I enjoy replaying it recently for nostalgia? Yes. The gameplay is smooth, the writing is witty, the sound is good. The graphics are definitely legacy. Would I recommend it to others in general? Probably not, unless you have a specific reason you're interested. I ended up playing with keyboard and mouse, because even though my controller was supported and played okay (8bitdo SN30 pro), I didn't have enough buttons on the controller to assign all the keybinds that the game expects us to use. My classic playthrough was on the Gamecube version which consolidated some control schemes (walking, crouching, weapon switching) to fit on a controller. This version assumes keyboard and has a lot of independent binds. I encountered a few crashes (easy to manage by saving regularly) and one technical issue where I was able to change the game resolution to a setting that my monitor did not support, which then got locked in to some config file somewhere and did not revert upon game restart or uninstall / reinstall (without deleting save files). Since the game did not confirm and automatically revert the setting if no confirmation is provided, as soon as I applied the setting, it took some work to navigate the menus blind and back out the change. I'm not sure that anyone else will encounter a similar issue, though. Overall, you probably want to play another game like perhaps Red Dead Redemption.

Call of Duty (2003) - The Grandfather of Scripted Chaos Score: 7.5/10 Before the jetpacks, the battle passes, and the slide-canceling sweats, there was just Call of Duty. Playing the original game today is like visiting a museum; you respect the history, even if the exhibits look a little dusty. The Ultimate Nostalgia Hit If you grew up in the early 2000s, booting this up will instantly transport you back. The Campaign Structure: The idea of playing through three different perspectives (American, British, Soviet) was revolutionary at the time and still feels cool today. The British campaign with Captain Price (the grandfather of the Modern Warfare Price) is pure classic charm. Stalingrad: The opening of the Soviet campaign is still one of the most atmospheric moments in gaming history. crossing the Volga River without a rifle, just holding a clip of ammo while waiting for your comrade to die so you can take his gun? That is cinematic gold that modern games struggle to replicate. Squad Feeling: Unlike Medal of Honor where you felt like Rambo, this game made you feel like just another soldier in a massive army. Hearing the chaotic shouting of your squadmates still adds to the immersion. The Reality: It Has Not Aged Well However, take off the rose-tinted glasses, and you have to admit: this game feels old. No Sprinting: This is the hardest thing to get used to. You move at a brisk jog at best. Trying to cross an open field under machine-gun fire without a sprint button feels agonizingly slow by modern standards. Health Packs: There is no "hide behind a wall and heal." You have to hunt for health kits. It creates tension, sure, but it can also be incredibly frustrating when you are stuck at a checkpoint with 10 HP and no way to heal. The Gunplay: The weapons feel stiff. There is no real recoil control or weapon weight; it's just point-and-click. The iron sights are functional, but compared to the snappy responsiveness of newer titles, it feels a bit like shooting a potato gun. Verdict Call of Duty (1) is a mandatory history lesson for FPS fans. It is a fantastic nostalgia trip that reminds you where the juggernaut franchise started. It's clunky, it's ugly, and you can't run, but storming the Reichstag or holding Pegasus Bridge still sparks that specific joy that only 2003 gaming can provide. Status: A classic, but bring your patience (and search for medkits). 🎖️👴

Single-player only review. Played on Hardened difficulty. [h2]Quick Verdict[/h2] Call of Duty remains a mechanically engaging and historically important shooter whose strengths lie in its squad-based combat and AI scripting, even if aging gunplay systems and a weak narrative presentation hold it back. [h2]Score: 3/5[/h2] [hr] [h1]The Review[/h1] A review of the original Call of Duty in 2025 feels unnecessary, but here we are. Starting with technical details, the game still runs very well. Any crashes I encountered were easily resolved by changing a line or two in a configuration file under the advisement of PCGamingWiki. I first played Call of Duty around its original release, and at the time of this review I have completed the campaign four or five times over the last twenty-two years. Nostalgia is certainly a factor, but I do believe the game holds up surprisingly well given how much time has passed since its release. What still stands out most is the dynamic feel of its squad-based gameplay and enemy encounters. The AI scripting in Call of Duty does a remarkable amount of work. Enemies can be suppressed by covering fire, allowing your AI teammates to advance and take ground. When an opportunity to flank presents itself, cutting down a dug-in enemy line to push your squad forward feels genuinely rewarding. AI design in the early 2000s elevated many otherwise simple point-and-click shooters. I would argue that Halo is built almost entirely around how enemies react to the player and the emergent gameplay that results from engaging mixed-unit squads. Call of Duty belongs firmly in that same lineage. There are, however, a few frustrations built into the game, and two of them stand out as the most detrimental to enjoyment. First, health is restored exclusively through health packs scattered throughout levels. Enemies often seem to know your position at all times and can instantly snap to your location the moment you become visible. On harder difficulties, this means you will become very familiar with your quick save and quick load keybinds. Some damage is simply unavoidable, whether from artillery, grenades, or scripted moments. If your health is already low from previous firefights, you may find yourself reloading through no real fault of your own. Second, guns do not always shoot where you think they do. Aiming and firing can sometimes feel like an RPG where your accuracy stat is under-leveled. I may not be the best shot in the world, but I know that when I'm stationary, iron sights lined up directly on an enemy's head should result in a kill nearly every time. In Call of Duty, it can feel like a gamble whether your bullet will connect at all. This is most noticeable at longer ranges, but it can occur even in situations where accuracy feels like it should be guaranteed. The bullet spread outside of iron sights is wider than expected, which can make otherwise simple engagements feel unnecessarily tedious. Weapon sound design also shows its age. Many guns sound flat or outright bad when fired, and sound design improves dramatically even by the next entry in the series. Narratively, the game has never particularly grabbed me. The story is delivered primarily through text on loading screens and dry slideshow transitions between character arcs. These explain who you are, where you are going, what you are doing, and how you are getting out, but they do so in one of the least engaging ways possible. The campaign places you in the roles of an American paratrooper, a British special forces soldier, and a Russian infantryman. I won't lie, I tuned out one of the slideshows and didn't realize that I had switched to a British protagonist until the 2nd or 3rd mission in the arc. Everyone around me had British accents, but I figured we were in Europe, whatever, checks out. Overall, the narrative is fairly lackluster, but that has never been the main draw. You are here to push forward under artillery fire, explosions tearing through the battlefield, clicking on enemies while trying to get your squad to the next objective. As a brief aside, the game oddly evokes the feel of early Doom. This is coming from someone who has not played much Doom at all, but after checking, it makes sense. Call of Duty runs on the id Tech 3 engine, developed by id Software. Despite its flaws, this is an easy recommendation. Call of Duty is worth playing even today, if only to experience a foundational milestone in the evolution of first-person shooters.

[h1] Call of Duty - an unpolished diamond [/h1] [b]Prelude[/b] The first Call of Duty is undoubtedly an FPS classic which, along with the Medal of Honor series, gave rise to the subgenre of games with more cinematic campaigns, grounded stories about war or special ops - rarely going beyond the modern era, nearby future or WWII, only occasionally stepping into sci-fi territory. Speaking of the gameplay aspects of this subgenre, these shooters share some usual traits: usually 2-3 weapon types instead of a full arsenal; a small variety of enemies, typically limited to different types of soldiers; linear levels where exploration ends with a couple of tiny side alleys; HP regeneration or lots of medkits; checkpoints, etc. The list could go on. I'm not insisting on this categorisation as final - as in any art form, genres blend, and CoD-like FPS games may borrow something from retro shooters (hello F.E.A.R., RAGE). Long story short: compared to what came before it, Call of Duty revolutionised the genre - whether for better or worse is a matter of taste, but as the fact it must be acknowledged. Now all that's left is to examine the game itself: did it manage to pull this off on the first try? [b]Review[/b] Short answer: yes, it succeeded, but with some rough edges The first thing that catches the eye is the graphics. Unfortunately, even at its 2003 release, the graphics didn't produce much of a wow effect. Enemy models, by the standards of the time, look somewhat more detailed in comparison to RTCW: characters actually have polygonal pockets, folds and little bumps on their uniforms, but the textures drag down the overall impression. The weapon models are quite decent, though the iron sights are too thick and not really comfortable to use. The levels range from «wow, that's impressive», like the unique german battleship or the dam, to generic villages with identical house interiors that often repeat themselves (some locations are reused for two missions, day/night). The soviet campaign with its gray ruined walls and snowy forests ending can make you feel upset too. As for gameplay, the gunplay is very pleasant and not very realistic, but reasonably accessible. It's hard to say there's a great variety of guns: most missions are completed either with your standard issued kit or the MP-40 & Kar98k combo. Still, it's always exciting to pick up an FG-42 or StG-44 though you'll rarely find much ammo for them. As already mentioned, the game's key feature is its cinematic nature. Every mission feels like «Saving Private Ryan», where you feel your involvement, your role in the operation. The levels are full of military bravado - there's no room for deep reflection here, but that is Call of Duty, and that is why we do love it. There are chases on car, stealth infiltrations, dangerous landings, assaults. And the defence of Pavlov's House alone is worth mentioning - the best and the hardest level in the game. Overall, it's a real thrill-ride. However, there are a few things that personally disappoint me. Some levels are repeated and it's understandable that reusing a map with different lighting is easier than building a new one, so this isn't a critical issue. The biggest drawback for me are the stationary weapon sections, where you don't have an opportunity to hide, and the first enemy can shoot your entire face off with a couple of accurate hits - leaving you stuck like that unless you restart the level. I understand it probably has to do with AI behaviour and the lack of health regeneration. The developers just threw in a few medkits, but once you use them up, the enemies can just blast you again in the same way. Speaking of AI: the machine gunners are extremely annoying. They instantly switch focus to you and suppress you with heavy fire. If you've run out of health and medkits, you're forced into pure save-scum process and boring peeking from a cover, waiting for enemies to "forget" you. And sometimes friendly fire happens - but that's a minor issue :D The absence of health regeneration. The developers added it only in the second game, and it was a great change, it made the gameplay much smoother and eliminated the need for save-scumming when medkits were gone. And one more minor drawback about the graphics: this is the only FPS where I genuinely struggle to distinguish enemy silhouettes. I don't know why, but the camouflage here blends with the environment a little too well. [b]Epilogue[/b] The first Call of Duty is definitely a good, though not perfect, game, and many of its rough edges can be forgiven, considering it was an experiment. Is it worth playing at least once? Definitely yes. I've replayed it many times, and every time, the game delivers enjoyment. This is one of those cases where an old game can truly be called a classic - not outdated junk. 7 Captain Price moustaches out of 10.

The AI doesn't always work perfectly, and most of the guns have problems, either in accuracy, damage, or ammo capacity. For example, the Garand can't be reloaded mid clip and isn't very accurate. The best weapon in the game is easily the MP40, which I used 90% of the time. Some levels are completely unfair, but with patience, you can work your way through them. My favorite mission is Pavlov's House, also the hardest one. You really have to think strategically-clearing the building, destroying tanks, and surviving wave after wave of enemies. This game on Veteran difficulty is definitely not for beginners. It's extremely punishing, and you'll die many times, making the learning curve feel harsh. But on lower difficulties, where you have health packs, the balance feels much better. What makes this game truly unique is its three weapon inventory, the non regenerating health system, the fast paced movement, and the ability to crouch or go prone, add a decent story and plenty of historically inspired missions, and you've got one of the best WWII shooters of the early 2000s right up there with Call of Duty 2. There's a lot of variety too! you get to play as Americans, British, and Soviets, each with different weapons and maps. I do wish there were more enemy types but you only fight the Germans. The game also adds creative moments like tank missions and using anti air guns. The only real downside is the vehicle sections, they're a unfair but still manageable. Overall, I can absolutely recommend this game to new players, and if you want a true challenge, play it on Veteran. Simply a great FPS.

Call of Duty (2003), developed by Infinity Ward and published by Activision, is one of the most influential first-person shooters ever created-a game that reshaped how war could be represented in interactive form. Released at a time when World War II shooters were abundant, it managed to stand apart through its realism, pacing, and cinematic presentation. What distinguished it most was its perspective: instead of placing players in the shoes of a single heroic figure, it divided its story across multiple Allied soldiers from the United States, the United Kingdom, and the Soviet Union, creating a mosaic of experiences that together captured the scale and chaos of global conflict. It was a game that didn't glorify war as much as it made you feel its intensity-bullets whizzing overhead, comrades shouting for cover, explosions shaking your screen. Two decades later, it remains a striking testament to the power of atmosphere and design over spectacle. From the very beginning, Call of Duty establishes an uncompromising tone. You are not the lone super-soldier single-handedly winning the war, but part of a squad, a small piece of a much larger machine. The game's revolutionary use of AI allies-an uncommon feature at the time-helps to sell that illusion. Your fellow soldiers fight alongside you, calling out enemy positions, suppressing fire, and even dying in unpredictable ways. Their presence gives every mission a sense of authenticity, making you feel as though you're in the middle of a desperate battle rather than simply playing through a scripted level. This shift from the individual hero narrative to a collective experience was groundbreaking. The developers wanted players to understand the terror and confusion of war from the ground level, and they achieved that through the game's remarkable pacing and dynamic mission design. From storming enemy bunkers in France to defending the crumbling streets of Stalingrad, each mission captures a different face of the war, blending cinematic storytelling with raw, moment-to-moment intensity. The game's structure across three distinct campaigns-American, British, and Soviet-creates a sense of global scale that few shooters at the time managed to achieve. The American missions emphasize large-scale assaults and frontal combat, immersing you in the chaos of Allied offensives. The British missions, often featuring smaller, specialized commando units, focus more on stealth, sabotage, and precision strikes. Then comes the Soviet campaign, perhaps the most harrowing of all, as you're thrust into the Red Army's desperate defense against the German invasion. The Stalingrad sequence, in particular, stands as one of the most iconic moments in early first-person shooter history. Stripped of weapons and forced to scavenge from fallen comrades while artillery shells rain down around you, the game drives home the helplessness and horror of war more powerfully than any cutscene could. Each faction's story is tightly interwoven, not through direct connection but through tone and theme-the shared sense of sacrifice, exhaustion, and determination that defined the Allied war effort. One of Call of Duty's most enduring innovations is its focus on realism within its gameplay mechanics. The two-weapon limit, the ability to aim down sights, and the lethal damage model were all designed to make players think tactically rather than charging blindly into battle. You can't simply carry an arsenal; you must choose carefully, adapting to the battlefield by scavenging weapons from fallen enemies. This system keeps every engagement tense and personal, reinforcing the game's grounded approach. Combat is loud, visceral, and chaotic, and yet the controls feel precise enough to give you full agency within that chaos. The sound design plays a massive role in that immersion-gunfire cracks through the air, explosions deafen your ears, and the cries of your squadmates echo through ruined buildings. The orchestral score swells at key moments, driving home the emotion without ever overpowering the realism. Even today, the audio atmosphere of the original Call of Duty remains remarkably effective at evoking both adrenaline and dread. Visually, the game has naturally aged, but at its release, it was a technical showcase. Built on a modified version of the id Tech 3 engine, it featured environments that felt alive with activity: dust rising from explosions, smoke curling through the air, and soldiers charging across battlefields littered with debris. The level design was tight and deliberate, guiding players through a series of carefully choreographed encounters that balanced linear storytelling with enough freedom to make each firefight feel organic. While the graphics no longer impress by modern standards, their clarity and cohesion still make the game easy to play and appreciate. The animation of reloads, weapon handling, and character movement all retain a certain weight that helps ground the experience. It's a reminder that visual fidelity alone doesn't define immersion-design, composition, and pacing matter just as much, and Call of Duty delivers all three. Another aspect that defined the game's legacy was its multiplayer mode, which provided a fast-paced, competitive experience that would later evolve into one of the franchise's hallmarks. In 2003, online shooters were still developing their identity, and Call of Duty's multiplayer stood out for its balance, speed, and accessibility. Matches were small but intense, emphasizing skill, reflexes, and teamwork over gimmicks. The weapon handling carried over faithfully from the single-player campaign, and the map design encouraged both tactical positioning and improvisation. While the multiplayer framework was modest compared to what the series would later become, it laid the foundation for the global phenomenon that followed. In its day, it was a thrilling extension of the campaign-an arena where the chaos of war could be experienced competitively, one firefight at a time. What makes Call of Duty (2003) especially remarkable is how well its design philosophy holds up after two decades. It doesn't rely on elaborate systems or cinematic excess; it builds immersion through authenticity, pacing, and sound. The missions are short, sharp bursts of tension, rarely overstaying their welcome, and the variety between them keeps the momentum alive. Even now, its campaign can be completed in a few hours, yet it remains memorable because every mission feels distinct and purposeful. The game's difficulty can be punishing-especially on higher settings, where a few bullets can kill you-but that risk is part of the experience. It forces you to value cover, teamwork, and patience, emphasizing survival over heroism. For players used to the regenerating health systems of later Call of Duty titles, revisiting the original is a humbling reminder of how fragile you are in a real firefight. In hindsight, Call of Duty (2003) stands as both a time capsule and a foundation stone. It captured the spirit of wartime shooters at their most immersive and set a precedent that would define the next two decades of the genre. Modern players may find its graphics primitive and its scope modest, but beneath those dated surfaces lies a game that understood the essence of immersion before technology made it easy. It's an experience that values tension over flash, precision over chaos, and authenticity over heroics. Playing it today is like returning to the roots of a cultural phenomenon-a reminder that before the bombast of modern warfare, there was a simple idea executed perfectly: that the most powerful stories of war are told not through invincibility, but through vulnerability. Rating: 9/10

The origin of the insanely popular but somewhat polarizing FPS franchise. For a first attempt I think this game is well made for the time and an overall enjoyable experience. The game takes place during World War II with you playing as 3 different soldiers from America, Britain and Russia. Over the course of the game, we get to experience the battlefields of World War II and see how the allied countries fought back against the Nazi regime. The campaign is quite by-the-numbers if you look at the game from a modern-day standpoint. There is no real story or character development going on and no conclusion at the end, not even an anti-war message or anything it just stops abruptly. That being said however, I feel that the game is going for more of a historical snapshot vibe rather than focusing on character development etc. so the story can take a back seat. Although I am not a historian, I believe that the game depicts World War II with some degree of accuracy which will keep history buffs happy. The gameplay feels good enough on a keyboard and mouse although some strange design choices may frustrate players who are used to more modern controls. One example of this is having crouch and lie prone being assigned to different buttons. There were several times during the campaign when I wanted to lie prone but forgot that I needed to press the CTRL key. It's not a major issue but takes a little bit of time to adjust. The shooting feels good for a game developed in 2003 although I would personally like more feedback when hitting enemy soldiers. One criticism I have for this game would have to be the AI of both friendly and enemy soldiers. First of all, your squad mates are next to useless, they will frequently stand around out in the open while a machine gun nest is tearing them to shreds with no reaction whatsoever. They will often not even check certain rooms filled with enemies just running past and then leaving you to get shot later. Enemy AI is hyper-focused on killing you with pinpoint accuracy they can track through walls and start firing almost the instant you make an appearance. The constant respawning of enemies is also a problem where sometimes you will seemingly clear an area only for two soldiers to spawn behind and kill you. Admittedly this only really becomes a major issue in a few levels such as "Pavlov`s Apartment" but it`s still a nuisance. The gameplay doesn't really provide much variety, most levels have you just clearing out enemy camps, houses and bunkers with a rifle and machine gun and that's it. The Russian levels where probably the highlight being focused on long-range sniping and a few levels where you get to control a tank however these levels were near the end of the game and in my opinion would have been much better being spread out across the course of the campaign. Overall, I feel I would recommend this game to people who are curious about the series roots but be warned that some parts won't really hold up to modern standards. I look to playing the rest of the series and seeing how it evolves (or devolves).

Having played just one other CoD game in my life (Black Ops), I'm pretty sure this sort of ultra-cinematic, frenetic FPS is not my jam. I'm too deliberate and methodical to be railroaded through the cultivated mayhem that defines Call of Duty as a series, even if I can recognize why tens of millions thrive on it. Going back to the beginning of the series, it's easy to see how this upped the ante for the WWII genre - it's essentially the D-Day mission from Medal of Honor Frontline stretched out the length of an entire game. Even now, nearly 25 years later, the sense of overwhelming chaos and desperate combat still rings true, especially when it more than compensates for an almost total lack of plot and character (they do exist, but are best ignored completely). The guns have the right oomph, the levels are relentlessly paced, and the scenarios are varied enough to not become tiresome (with one major exception). It's easily the closest you could get to feeling like you were in the midst of battle, and so many entries later, Activision still has a knack for capturing that. Of course, there are obvious first-time flaws, as well as things that personally irritated me. I get the appeal of on-rails vehicle missions, but I largely found them nauseating with the whiplashing of your viewpoint and the sheer amount of things happening made it difficult to follow at times. Missions where you have to stand your ground (Pavlov's House in particular) represent almost infuriating spikes in difficulty, particularly when you are apparently the only person who can deal with tanks while enemies respawn endlessly and overwhelm your comrades. And the auto-save system is as much a hindrance as a help - twice it saved in the instant before I was killed, which meant that every subsequent quick-load only resulted in me dying again and again. Still, these minor annoyances can't blunt the impact this series has had and, I'm sure, will continue to have. They've spent the last two decades honing and refining their technique, and while the series will never be art, it will always know exactly how to give its audience what it wants. Just don't be offended if I choose not to heed the call.

A classic FPS game. Graphics are decent (recommend a retexture mod), gameplay can be hit or miss as the game is a bit dated. The recoil and bloom for automatic weapons are a bit on the heavy side, I would recommend burst shooting at longer ranges and resorting to full spraying at close range. Also, because of the large muzzle flash on automatic weapons, sometimes it felt better to hip-fire rather than aim down sights (ADS). The ADS inaccuracy could have been due to the funky resolution issue I had as well since this game was made for older systems. Unfortunately, the sprint feature is absent in this entry. Also, the health bar mechanic is a bit annoying but it is somewhat more realistic since normal people cannot just regenerate damage just by resting a few seconds (as seen in the newer Call of Duty games). Furthermore, playing on Veteran difficulty is quite challenging because there are no health packs to heal at all. Luckily, manual saving is allowed especially considering automatic checkpoints do not trigger a save if health is too low. If you've never yelled "Cover me, I'm reloading!" in a dramatic fashion while crouch-walking through Stalingrad, did you even have a childhood? Call of Duty (the original, the OG, the pixelated legend) is not just a game, it's a full-blown historical time machine powered by 2003 graphics and pure WWII grit. Before the series became a jetpack-fueled Michael Bay simulator, this was the game that made you feel like a tiny cog in the terrifying machine of war and it did it brilliantly. What still holds up ?: - AI Squadmates that actually help. They suppress enemies, flank, and occasionally die heroically (RIP random British guy #3). - Sound Design: That slaps from the ping of an M1 Garand to the terrifying buzz of an MG42, it's all deeply immersive. - Mission Variety: From storming bunkers in Normandy to surviving ambushes in snowy Soviet towns, each level has a cinematic flow that rivals even today's shooters. Graphics: Yes, it's from 2003. No, it doesn't have ray tracing. But somehow, your imagination fills the rest. Call it "retro immersion." Fun Fact: This is the only game where crouching in tall grass and throwing a potato masher grenade can feel both heroic and hilariously underpowered. Also, Price has a mustache that could conquer continents. Pro Tip: Play it on Hardened for the best balance of challenge and chaos. You'll feel like a war hero but one who occasionally gets stuck behind a jeep. Final Verdict: This isn't just a shooter. It's a historic relic, a masterclass in atmosphere, and most importantly the granddaddy of modern FPS campaigns. 🔟/🔟 would storm Normandy again.

[h1]Review of Call of Duty[/h1] I don't think anyone would have expected what a monster of a franchise Call of Duty would become when they first slipped their disc copies in, when 2003 rolled around. What was originally meant to be a direct competitor to the already established first person shooter set in World War 2, Medal of Honor, Call of Duty gave us larger conflicts with squads and reactive enemies. This was the one to start it all. I didn't get a chance to play the original Call of Duty myself until around 2013. Jumping back in for what I think is my third playthrough to do this review was exciting. Despite being over twenty years old, it's actually quite impressive just how smooth and playable this game is. [u]Authenticity in Humanity's bloodiest conflict[/u] When compared to the later titles in the series, the original Call of Duty games spent a lot more time and effort trying to recreate historical events. Giving you a sort of first person perspective of its combat. With some liberties taken to provide a fun gameplay experience. Missions often begin with a briefing & journal entry from one of your three playable characters across the game's three main campaigns. Being shown real WW2 footage/photos backed by what feels like actual tactics and discussion over your objectives really helps sell that you're playing a World War 2 game, and not just a game set in the Second World War. Rather than having a traditional story, Call of Duty gives you three distinct "Campaigns" & finishes with a 3 mission long epilogue, each one playing immediately after one another. Kicking things off as Martin of US Baker Company during the invasion of Normandy, followed by stepping into the shoes of Evans who joins the British SAS shortly after, and ending as Soviet conscript Alexei as he's thrown straight into the Hellish Stalingrad battlefield. None of these, or the supporting characters, are as important as later titles in the series since there's no overarching plot line, but you may come to enjoy the company of a few. Such as, but not limited to, Captain Price. The actual missions themselves take place across multiple major events throughout the duration of WW2. So the experience is what you'd call episodic. It's hard to choose a favorite, but I really enjoyed a lot of the British & Soviet missions. Some of my absolute favorites were sneaking aboard the Tirpitz and the Stalingrad sequences, which are heavily based on the film "Enemy at the Gates". [u]Gameplay[/u] As mentioned before, I am pleased with how smooth the game plays, in spite of its old age. Gunplay doesn't feel overly clunky or unresponsive. Enemies react to being hurt, even retreating at times, and it only takes a well placed bullet or two to bring them down. Being a WW2 first person shooter, you can expect a pretty wide variety of era-accurate weaponry. From the US Tompson & M1 Garand, the British Lee-Enflied & Bren, the Russian PPSh & Mosin-Nagant, all the way to iconic German weaponry like the MP44 or MG42. Scoped weapons, emplacements, explosives, it's got a little of everything. There's even as much as different firing-modes you can select for various guns. Not even later games in the series have that functionality. The missions themselves also implement a lot of things that at the time, were probably not as over-saturated, but are still fun. Like a tank mission where you control a T-34-85. Or jumping onto a quad 20mm anti-aircraft turret to take down Stuka dive bombers. One noteable mission that caught me by surprise originally was the event that follows the dam mission in the British campaign. You're escaping on the back of a truck while being chased down. It's almost identical in feel to Call of Duty 4's finale, I wonder if that was intentional. Other soldiers will often run alongside you, help you in combat, and even follow you around like a squad. Although annoyingly, they tend to get in your way. Though they do move, doorways are constantly being blocked by them. I believe it's possible to be on the receiving end of friendly fire to boot. Don't expect any sprinting as the game has one movement speed. You can bash with the butt of your weapon, or crouch and even go prone, but no sprinting. This took some time to adjust to, but the game doesn't punish you for lacking it. There's plenty of ways to maneuver and deal with enemy tanks or bunkers. Including the extremely useful ability to lean around corners. Health is finite, being an actual bar that needs to be refilled with medkits found around each level. I quite like this over the regenerating health. The game also supports a multiplayer mode. [u]Visuals, Audio & OST[/u] Graphically Call of Duty might seem a bit dated by today's standards, but that's okay. Some of the textures are a bit flat or muddy. Character models are segmented, and a few animations are awkward looking (I cannot get over how stupid other soldiers look when they're crouch-running), but that never stopped me from getting immersed regardless. Some of the most cinematic moments the game pulls off are the opening to the Soviet campaign, when you're crossing the river into Stalingrad. Or the epilogue while storming the Reichstag. I'd say that for the most part, the game's audio is really good for the time. Maybe it's just a bit too loud? I had it down to like 35% and it was still blasting my eardrums. Especially certain weapons like the MG42. Often subdued, but still thematic, the OST does a fine job setting the scene for a WW2 FPS. [h1]Conclusion (Pros & Cons)[/h1] All in all, the original Call of Duty that birthed the titan of a franchise, is well worth checking out for WW2 game fans, FPS fans, or even just CoD fans looking to see what it was like back when. My entire playthrough took about 4-5 hours, but higher difficulties can provide an even tougher experience for those who're worthy. [b]Pros:[/b] +Classic WW2 FPS +Smooth gameplay +Good mission variety +Tirpitz wasn't forgotten [b]Neutral:[/b] ~Some annoying AI ~Extra steps to get running on newer PC's (Although it's very easy) [b]Cons:[/b] N/A - No serious issues [h1]Disclaimer[/h1] Thank you for taking the time to read my review. Please remember, that this is just my opinion. We don't have to agree, one thing I love you may hate, and one thing I hate you may love. Hopefully this gave you an idea of what to expect. [b]Review lengths have been greatly compressed due to the character limit.[/b] 06/03/2025

Playing Call of Duty from 2003 today, more than twenty years after its release, was quite a unique experience. Right from the start, I couldn't expect anything groundbreaking graphically: this was an era of flat textures, simple animations, and polygon models as jagged as an old pixelated JPEG. The smooth movement of modern installments, with acrobatic jumps, slides, and parkour that would make an Olympic athlete jealous, is just a distant dream here. If you can jump and prone, consider yourself lucky. Yet, in its extreme simplicity, this Call of Duty managed to surprise me. The story isn't exactly a masterpiece of writing or innovation, but the presence of the legendary Captain Price - now an iconic, familiar figure in the more recent games - brought me back in time with a bittersweet nostalgia. Seeing that familiar face and those old mechanics brought a tear to my eye, reminding me why this series has endured and won over millions of fans throughout the years. Another thing that struck me was the difficulty. I always thought that as a kid I couldn't finish these games simply because I wasn't very good with shooters. Now that I'm older, I realize the challenge level was genuinely high. I played on "soldier" difficulty and still had to sweat buckets to complete the campaign. A very different experience from more recent titles, where the story often feels like a walk in the park. In conclusion, playing Call of Duty (2003) in 2025 was a real lesson in humility and respect for the series' roots. Despite obvious technical limits and simple gameplay, it still manages to move you and truly challenge the player. A trip down memory lane that I recommend to all fans of the saga and anyone who wants to understand where it all began.

Call of Duty started here in 2003 during a time of heavy competition with the Medal of Honor series and Wolfenstein series among others. Coming in new they had to innovate, and innovate they did! The training section is much better than in Medal of Honor Allied Assault which came out the year before, but that game had the famous D-Day mission on Omaha beach. Allied Assault also had a paratrooper mission in the expansion pack Spearhead, also released before Call of Duty. CoD innovates by enabling aiming down the sight, and making you part of a team when attacking - allied soldiers being constantly replaced. The gameplay is frantic and exciting and the level design varied. We also see the campaign from 3 different perspectives, the American, British and Soviet. AMERICAN (took about 1h 20 minutes) The introduction, but still my least favorite of the bunch. I never like this type of trench warfare which was common in WW2 games. The car scene is legendary and something that MoH just didn't have. My favorite mission is still rescuing Captain Price which comes at the end. This campaign is a lot easier than I remember it, maybe a bigger screen makes it easier to play? Most notably the "rescue mission" in the camp was something I thought was excrutiatingly difficult as a teenager, but now I simply thought "Oh, was that it?" I like the journals in the beginning explaining what I'm doing and overall it's an OK campaign in CoD, and way better than Medal of Honor's campaign, in spite of being the worst CoD campaign. BRITISH (took also about 1h 20 minutes) Good campaign, but a bit artificially stretched. The 1st and 2nd missions are played twice which seems kind of lazy. The beginning does have some resemblance with the movie "A Bridge too Far" which is kind of cool. The "lorry" mission is a classic, and much better than the American equivalent. Here we have Captain Price true start. The final missions seems a bit "extra" almost DLC like, but that's fine by me. Overall a great campaign! SOVIET (Around 1h 30 minutes) The beginning of this game is of course ripped straight from Enemy at the Gates, a movie which was popular at the time but these days it's rather obscure. The opening is great, but followed by an awful "city level". Next up gave me deja vu, a sniper level in the sewers with the enemy propaganda spouting out. CoD 2 had exactly this which is rather lazy of the sequel. The Polish tank factory assault is just lazy. Tons of enemies and no backup. I remeber dying like crazy here when I was 15, but this time it went quite quickly. This part ended with a tank assault, just like... Medal of Honor Allied Assault but more open. Kind of forgettable, but still... varied. Overall the Soviet campaign was something i remember being my favourite campaign, but this time around it was about on par with the American. COMBINED (Total around 30 minutes) Just when I thought the game ended, we get a bonus part. Just like... CoD 2 lol, but from all 3 perspectives around 10 minutes each more. These last missions were pretty good! Destroying V2 rockets as both the Americans and British and then storming the Reichstag as the Soviets. Funny, I remembered that mission from CoD WaW (again with the repetition), but not from CoD 1. CONCLUSION CoD 1 is better than CoD 2 in my opinion, with the exception of smoke grenades being an enormous improvement in CoD 2. There's no regenerating health, but there's tons of health packs all over the place, so maybe not that necessary. It has some laziness like no scoped Lee Enfield so the British get a Kar98K scoped instead, and the maching gun that the Soviets use to gun down their own people is an MG42 which is like "dafuq"? What made me baffled was the fact that I remember this game being longer, but nope! It clocks in at 4.5 HOURS, just like every CoD campaign ever made. And that... is kind of sad.

I played the single-player campaign completely blind and vanilla. Most of the missions were fun but some mostly in the British campaign did not hold up well (specifically the one where you have to hold the bridge for 5 minutes). The health system does not lend itself well to defending a siege. NPCs cannot switch weapons, but can throw grenades. NPCs will crouch and go prone when needed, and that is nice when in combat. Most will find cover, and can flee to find it if hurt. The Soviet campaign did an excellent job at showcasing the brutality the Soviet infantry had to go through. The Atmosphere for the Stalingrad mission was great, even if the rubble was lacking in polish due to the age of the game. I cannot speak much to the multiplayer aspect. In 2025 the game is completely dead, there is a mod for adding bots that I tried to add but could not get the bots to spawn. At the time of writing there are four servers that someone is hosting with bots and I tried each of them out. I was surprised to see the Carentan map (which now I know the CoD: WWII Carentan is a remake). I think there are modernization mods out there, but honestly playing vanilla is pretty fun. I know there are texture upscalers and sound mods available, but while neither were great in vanilla it wasn't bad enough for me to go mod it. I recommend to pick this up the next time it is on sale if it is on your wishlist. I will be doing that with the United Offensive expansion.

Call of Duty 2 - The Birth of the Modern Shooter Score: 8/10 If Call of Duty 1 was the prototype, Call of Duty 2 was the revolution. This is the game that practically invented the modern console shooter as we know it. Booting it up today is like stepping into a time machine-it's clunky, it's loud, and it hits you right in the nostalgia bone. The Nostalgia Hit is Unmatched Even 20 years later, the atmosphere in this game is incredible. The Battle Chatter: I forgot how alive this game sounds. Hearing your squad scream "Get a smoke out!" or "Jerry by the truck!" was mind-blowing in 2005, and it still creates a chaotic war vibe that few games match. Pointe du Hoc: Climbing those cliffs on D-Day while artillery rains down is still one of the most cinematic moments in the entire franchise. The Smoke Grenade: This was the first game where smoke grenades actually worked. Throwing one to cover your cross across a street in Stalingrad feels just as tactical and cool now as it did back then. The Reality: It Has Aged Like Milk (In Some Spots) However, we have to be honest: time has not been kind to everything here. The "Grenade Spam": If you play on Veteran, you will cry. The enemy AI doesn't try to outsmart you; they just turn into professional baseball pitchers. You spend half the game running away from grenade indicators rather than shooting. The "Whac-A-Mole" Gameplay: The enemy AI is very dated. They pop their heads up from behind the exact same sandbag every 3 seconds, making the combat feel like a repetitive shooting gallery rather than a dynamic fight. Brown on Brown: The graphics were amazing for the Xbox 360 launch, but today? The color palette is 50 shades of brown and gray. It can be hard to see enemies against the muddy textures. Verdict Call of Duty 2 is a flawed masterpiece. It introduced the "Regenerating Health" system (bye-bye health packs!) that defined the genre for a decade. It's a bit repetitive and the grenade spam is infuriating, but storming the beaches of Normandy or fighting through the desert in North Africa still feels epic. It is a perfect weekend nostalgia trip. Status: A legendary relic (watch out for the potato mashers!). 🥔💥

[h1]Review of Call of Duty 2[/h1] With the success of the first game, it was a no brainer that a sequel would be greenlit and ship under two years later. Being a fair improvement on just about everything that original title did, from better visuals to more variety in its retellings of notable World War 2 battles. Much like with many other series' out there, this one has its dedicated fans who swear by it, and it's not hard to see why. I firmly believe that Call of Duty 2 is the better of the two original games, but there's no reason you can't play and enjoy both of them. [u]Establishing Call of Duty as a Franchise[/u] Going from the first game to the second feels so natural. Like you've stepped into more of what made the original so likeable. Merely with higher quality. Once again, historical events are remade with some flare for the sake of gameplay. Missions are similarly opened with journal entries from the playable characters, and preceded with real footage of World War 2. However, instead of retreading the same grounds with the conflicts showcased, we focus on new perspectives and battles not shared in the first game. I must make it clear though, that I do not mind game sequels that keep an established formula. Where both the first & second titles are most similar, is the way the game is structured. This was clearly what they intended to stick with for a while, as quite a few of the old school CoD games did this. There's a total of 10 playable missions, split between three unique nation's campaigns. This time beginning in the shoes of a conscript of the Soviet Union in the Hellish Winter on the Eastern Front (Primarily Stalingrad), followed by the British story that sees you spending most of your time in Northern Africa. Then finally, invading France with a company of United States Army Rangers as you push towards the Rhine on the Western Front of the European Theatre. The game remains episodic in format, from the early 1940's to 1945. If you're a fan of film, you'll notice plenty of references, just like the original game. One of the things I enjoyed a lot about Call of Duty 2 was the battles depicted in the campaign. Don't get me wrong, I would gladly charge the beaches of Omaha a thousand times in a thousand different games. To me that will never get old, but it's always really nice to see other parts of the war shown off. For example, instead of the iconic Omaha beach landings, we get to see the lesser known scaling of the cliffs in Pointe du Hoc. Grapnels were fired from landing craft up 100+ feet sheer cliffs, then climbed by soldiers to take the ridge and push inland. It was nowhere near as bloody as Omaha, but everybody's efforts were critical, and I'm so happy to see more of these depictions. It's genuinely difficult to pick a favorite mission, as many of them are fantastic. I love the British mission in Eygpt, one where you're surrounded on all sides and watch as German troops pour over the sand dunes with trucks & tanks to support. Climbing, taking, and then holding Hill 400 is an absolute highlight for me as well. [u]Gameplay & Criticisms[/u] If you've played the first game, you'll slip right into this. As it's practically identical. Some of the weapons that are in both games have changed slightly, but movement & gunplay feels the same. The roster of useable weaponry is relatively similar to the previous game. With some differences. For example, the FG42 doesn't reappear here, which is sad. However, plenty of the other iconic firearms from the PPSh to the MP/StG-44 return. According to the wiki, Call of Duty 2 actually has more guns. However, I've actually been unable to find some of these guns.. maybe they're just for the multiplayer? Like the M3 Grease Gun or the Trench Gun. The biggest change this game made though, is removing finite health. Instead of health pickups, you now regenerate health over time when not receiving damage. I don't mind this feature, but I feel like it lead to some rebalancing in the combat I could have done without. There's no shortage of variety in missions and objectives again. It's easy to see some staples forming. We get another vehicle mission, but this time controlling a British Crusader in North Africa. Being able to take control of infamous 88mm gun emplacements and use them against enemy armor, or choose to flank them and place explosive charges. One interesting feature is that you can either choose to immobilize the tank to make it easier to flank, or just destroy it outright. I'm almost positive that the AI must be the same between this and the first game. Squads still follow you around during objective missions. Naturally taking cover, and helping in combat. They're fully capable of taking down enemies without much issue. Which is GREAT. I can't stress enough how much that helps immerse me. Unfortunately though, this means that your squad mates still bunch up and block your path. It's a minor issue. Okay, so for my main issues with the gameplay. These do not by any means ruin the game for me. By far the greatest problem I have is the grenades. What in the living Hell is up with grenades in this game. There's more being thrown than there's bullets being fired. It's clear that it's meant to flush you out of cover for gameplay reasons, but it just feels a little too over tuned. Press the crouch button? Here's three grenades for you. Take cover behind one singular sandbag? Here's two more grenades. Stop moving for 2 nanoseconds? A box of grenades for you. Scripted grenades too? Got you covered! I thought World at War was cursed with this, but apparently it was born here. It would help if enemies weren't perfectly accurate with them (Sometimes they'll be facing away from you, but still toss a grenade backwards right to your feet). Beyond this though, I really didn't have too many other annoyances that got on my nerves. Mission checkpoints are forgiving, so dying isn't too much of a setback. The last thing I would say felt a little off, was the campaign pacing. Missions are broken into different parts separated by loading screens. The 3 Soviet missions are over in an hour or less, and then the first two US missions seem to go on for three times the length of the entire Soviet campaign. Only to end with the "Crossing the Rhine" mission which is like 10-15 minutes to complete. This game supports a multiplayer mode too. [u]Visuals[/u] I think one of the standout parts of the sequel was its jump in visual quality. The game is "larger" in the sense that mission areas have far more detail and props. Textures & lighting are improved, and effects from explosions and debris are impressive compared to the original. The game is also far more cinematic than the first. The opening to the mission in El Daba, is probably one of the best examples. The emotional music, with the city under siege in the distance. As bombers roar over head with British fighters hot on their tails, while your convoy slowly approaches. [h1]Conclusion (Pros & Cons)[/h1] I know World War 2 games of this era became "over saturated" and a lot of people lost interest in them. I've never found that an issue personally, and could endlessly enjoy great games based on the largest Human conflict to date. Call of Duty 2 is a great sequel to an already great game. It's pretty short, but still a good time. I'd give anything to see my first CoD game, Big Red One, come to PC some day. [b]Pros:[/b] +Great Sequel +Smooth gameplay +Expanded battle variety [b]Neutral:[/b] ~Some annoying AI [b]Cons:[/b] -Grenade Hell [h1]Disclaimer[/h1] Thank you for taking the time to read my review. Please remember, that this is just my opinion. We don't have to agree, one thing I love you may hate, and one thing I hate you may love. Hopefully this gave you an idea of what to expect. Single-player only review. Played on Hardened difficulty. [h2]Quick Verdict[/h2] Call of Duty 2 is a clear step forward from the original game and United Offensive, refining its mechanics and encounter design into a far more consistently engaging shooter.| [h2]Score: 4/5[/h2] [hr] [h1]The Review[/h1] Call of Duty 2 is a noticeably stronger experience than Call of Duty (2003) and the United Offensive expansion that followed it. Playing on Hardened, every push toward an objective felt earned. The game consistently pressures the player without tipping into unfairness, striking a balance that earlier entries struggled to maintain. One of the most important improvements is the introduction of regenerating health. This adds much-needed breathing room to combat encounters, allowing the player to disengage briefly, reassess the situation, and reenter the fight without being permanently punished for every mistake. It makes firefights feel more fluid and less dependent on save-scumming. Grenade indicators are another major addition. They are so standard now that it is easy to forget how critical they are, but they were sorely missing in the first game. You will need them here, as enemy AI uses grenades aggressively to flush you out of cover. Smoke grenades also make their debut, and their importance cannot be overstated. Blocking enemy lines of sight and advancing under cover becomes essential, and success in the campaign often depends on smart and frequent smoke grenade usage. Gunplay sees meaningful refinement as well. One of my major complaints with Call of Duty (2003) was that bullets often did not land where you expected them to. Even with iron sights lined up, shots could feel unreliable. Call of Duty 2 significantly improves hit registration, making headshots more consistent and firefights feel far more responsive. Enemy AI has also been expanded with new behaviors. Downed enemies can continue firing pistols, and others will aggressively charge the player at close range. On multiple occasions, I was rushed in tight indoor spaces, which made submachine guns feel far more viable and situationally necessary. Sound design is another standout improvement. Weapon audio is punchier and more distinct, and environmental sound plays a much larger role. I frequently found myself listening for footsteps inside buildings, tracking enemy movement through walls before committing to a room. Speaking of buildings, clearing towns house by house became the highlight of the campaign for me. A line from The Expanse kept coming to mind: "Doors and corners. Always check doors and corners." These missions demand careful movement and awareness. Even on Hardened difficulty, taking two quick hits is often enough to send you back to the last checkpoint. Those sequences feel fantastic. Slowly advancing through a town, repositioning your squad, clearing a building, then immediately having to defend it against counterattacks creates some of the most satisfying moments in the entire series. It feels tactical, deliberate, and appropriately tense. One feature I found myself missing was sprint. It was introduced in United Offensive, and while limited, it allowed the player to cross open areas much more quickly than the slower movement speed in Call of Duty 2. Its absence is noticeable, even if it does not break the experience. Narratively, the game still does not fully land for me. That said, it is an improvement over the first game. Missions flow more cleanly into one another, creating a better sense of continuity. At this point in the series, though, the gameplay and scenario design are clearly the focus, and Call of Duty 2 delivers strongly on both fronts.
