Call of Duty 2, released on Steam as a remastered version of the classic 2005 World War II shooter, remains a significant and influential title in the history of first-person shooters. Developed by Infinity Ward, the game builds upon the foundations laid by its predecessor, delivering an intense and cinematic portrayal of the Allied campaigns during WWII. Even years after its initial release, Call of Duty 2 still holds up remarkably well thanks to its compelling single-player narrative, immersive audio-visual design, and solid multiplayer modes that helped shape the modern FPS genre. The single-player campaign in Call of Duty 2 is structured into multiple perspectives, allowing players to experience the war through the eyes of soldiers from different Allied forces, including the American, British, and Soviet armies. This variety adds narrative depth and diversity to the missions, which span iconic battles such as the Battle of Stalingrad and the Normandy invasion. The storytelling is presented through cinematic cutscenes and well-scripted in-game events that create a strong sense of urgency and realism. Unlike many modern shooters, the game favors authentic squad-based tactics and fluid AI behavior, requiring players to rely on their teammates, use cover effectively, and think strategically rather than run-and-gun. Graphically, Call of Duty 2 was groundbreaking at the time of its release, and its remastered visuals on Steam still impress. The game utilizes dynamic lighting, detailed environments, and realistic particle effects to bring battlefields to life. Smoke, explosions, and weather effects like rain or dust storms aren't just visual flourishes; they impact gameplay by obscuring vision and forcing players to adapt. This environmental immersion intensifies combat encounters and enhances the emotional weight of the campaign. Character models and animations have a gritty, believable quality that adds to the authenticity, making the war's harshness palpable. The sound design is another highlight of Call of Duty 2. The roar of gunfire, explosions, and shouted commands from squadmates combine with a stirring orchestral score to heighten the tension and drama. Weapon sounds are carefully crafted to feel powerful and distinct, helping to differentiate firearms and adding to the tactical depth. The voice acting is strong and adds personality to the soldiers, reinforcing the camaraderie and desperation felt during the war. These audio elements work in tandem with the gameplay to create a fully immersive and intense experience that draws players into the chaos of battle. Multiplayer, while more modest compared to modern standards, still provides engaging and competitive gameplay. The modes focus on classic team-based objectives like capture the flag, deathmatch, and territory control, encouraging cooperation and tactical play. The weapon selection and map design reflect the WWII setting, requiring players to master period-appropriate tactics rather than relying on futuristic gadgets or abilities. Though the multiplayer community has diminished over time, the game's influence on later entries in the Call of Duty series and other shooters is undeniable, laying the groundwork for many popular mechanics still used today. One aspect that stands out in Call of Duty 2 is the game's pacing and mission design. The developers avoided repetitive gameplay by introducing varied objectives that range from stealth infiltration and sniper missions to all-out assaults and defensive stands. These shifts in tempo keep the experience fresh and engaging across the campaign. The AI, while not perfect by today's standards, intelligently coordinates attacks and retreats, creating dynamic encounters that require players to adapt on the fly. This makes the single-player campaign feel less scripted and more like a genuine combat experience. However, there are some limitations. The game's narrative, while effective, is relatively straightforward and sometimes leans on familiar war movie tropes. Some players may find the mission linearity restrictive, as there is little room for exploration or alternative approaches. Also, despite the strong AI, moments of clunky pathfinding or occasional enemy predictability can detract from immersion. The multiplayer, while solid, lacks the depth and customization options modern gamers expect, and without an active community, finding populated servers can be a challenge. In summary, Call of Duty 2 remains a benchmark for WWII shooters and a testament to Infinity Ward's early prowess in creating engaging, cinematic FPS experiences. Its blend of immersive storytelling, authentic combat mechanics, and atmospheric presentation ensures it still provides a satisfying experience for fans of historical shooters. While some aspects feel dated, the game's core strengths shine through, offering both nostalgia and a well-crafted glimpse into one of the most brutal conflicts in history. For players interested in classic war shooters or those curious about the roots of the Call of Duty franchise, Call of Duty 2 on Steam is a worthwhile and enduring experience. Rating: 9/10

Back in 2005, while the world was still figuring out how to burn CDs properly, Infinity Ward dropped a bombshell and it wasn't just in-game. Call of Duty 2 delivered cinematic warfare, unforgettable voiceovers yelling "Grenade!" every 5 seconds, and some of the most intense trench fights gaming had ever seen. Why it's still legendary: Hit-reg? Crisp. Guns? Iconic. Kar98k headshots hit harder than your ex's last message. Dynamic smoke grenades that made you feel blind and alive at the same time. Three different campaigns, each one a gritty history lesson with bullets. Surprisingly smart AI - enemies actually flank you. In 2005. Madness. Sound design that screams "war movie" more than actual war movies. And let's not forget multiplayer - the chaotic LAN parties, the no-scope duels in Carentan, and the classic "who threw that smoke" moments that ended friendships. This game didn't need battle passes, skins, or killstreaks to keep you hooked. It just gave you a rifle, a war, and the will to fight. COD2 isn't just a game - it's a time capsule of when FPS was raw, real, and ruthless. Replaying it in 2025? Feels better than 90% of modern shooters. 🫡 10/10. Would charge Pointe du Hoc again.

After the difficulties I had with the expansion of the first chapter, I thought I had finally gotten past the technical obstacles of playing old games. But Call of Duty 2 put my patience to the test once again: figuring out a way to launch it without making my PC crash was incredibly frustrating. Luckily, by tweaking some game files, I managed to get around the issue. Given how much time and effort it cost me, I even made a guide to help others in the same situation. From a graphical standpoint, I didn't notice a major leap forward compared to the expansion of the first chapter, even though there's a one-year gap between the two titles. But back in the early 2000s, hardware limitations were far more severe than today, so it's understandable that there weren't huge improvements. That said, it's still a solid-looking game for its time, with well-constructed and varied environments. The story, in this case, was noticeably longer than in the previous chapters. You can tell there was a real effort to create a richer, more complete campaign. The downside is that, despite the longer runtime, I ended up finishing it in roughly the same amount of time as the earlier games-mainly because of how much easier the gameplay was. The earlier games had fewer missions, but they were way more demanding. Here, the abundance of checkpoints seriously diluted the challenge. Practically every ten meters the game saved your progress, and that made it easy to just charge into the action knowing you wouldn't be set back far if you died. In the previous titles, dying could mean repeating half the mission. It was punishing, yes, but also way more immersive. Here, it often felt like I was brute-forcing my way forward. As for difficulty, it felt significantly toned down. After finishing the Russian campaign on "Soldier" difficulty, it became clear I wasn't going to experience the same level of tension and frustration from the previous chapters. I cranked it up to "Veteran" hoping to get a proper challenge-and while I got it, it came with its own set of problems. The screen shake when taking damage was so extreme it became nauseating, and enemies instantly landed shots the moment I peeked out from cover. It stopped being immersive and turned into a test of sheer endurance. If I had to pick out memorable moments-memorable in a frustrating way, really-it would be the last mission and the hill defense mission. Playing them on Veteran, with an absurd number of enemies all coming from one direction, made it almost impossible to engage in proper gunfights. At times I had to rely solely on grenades and a lot of patience, hoping the AI teammates would thin out the crowd enough to let me move. Still, I have to admit the technical improvements were surprising. Smoother animations, more realistic enemy reactions, better ally behavior-these were all welcome details I didn't expect to see already in the second chapter of the series. And of course, there's the legendary Captain Price. While he doesn't yet have the narrative weight he carries in the later games, seeing him here again brought a smile to my face. A small but meaningful nod to what the series would eventually become. When it comes to audio, I haven't paid much attention to sound design or effects in these early titles, and I don't think it's worth diving into that just yet. I'd rather wait until I come across a game where the audio work truly stands out before discussing it properly. Overall, Call of Duty 2 is an important chapter in the series. It has its flaws, and many of them are quite noticeable, but the ambition behind it is clear. I didn't come away fully satisfied, but I can appreciate the effort to push the series forward.

I haven't played CoD2 in many, many years and wanted to see if it still holds up. CoD2 is famous for inventing the auto generative health and skipping health packs which were prevalent in all games of old. CoD2 is a game that has many "set pieces", bombastic music and drowns you in wave after wave with enemies while you play together with your own squads of enemies, no more single soldier Doom style. This is war! I play only for the campaign and it is split up in 3 distinct segments, Soviet Union, Great Britain and USA. The campaign took almost exactly 6 hours to complete, much shorter than I remember it. SOVIET UNION Really didn't care too much for this one, and it's sad that they have such a weak beginning to this game. The Soviet campaign took me around 1h 20 minutes to complete, and it's all the same, just fighting through residential areas and factories, clearing out ze Germans with a variety of weapons. Of course the "potatoes instead of grenades" in the beginning is classic, but I don't care too much for this campaign at all. Quite uninspired, an very short. After replaying CoD 1 I realized that a lot of the Soviet Campaign is rehashed from the first one, what the...? Sewer sniper level with propaganda... really lazy. GREAT BRITAIN The British campaign got way more love. Split into two sections, first the desert and then Europe it has more locations and variety, but above all the set pieces are much more inspired. In the beginning we radio in artillery on tanks, and later on we get to control a tank ourselves. Lots of fun! Captain Price is of course great as usual, but also the banter between soldiers is much better. This campaign was given a lot more love than the Soviet one and took around 2.5-3 hours to complete, twice as long as the Soviet campaign. USA The US campaign begins with a grand opening at Pointe du Hoc. Important to notice is that there was an abundance of WWII games at the time and movies like Saving Private Ryan and Band of Brothers lead to showcases of D-Day from both Omaha and the Airborne (in Medal of Honor Allied Assault). This new way of doing it was very refreshing! Only weird thing is that this is the scene on the cover of the box and it takes over 4 hours before we see it. The American campaign has some slow missions, but then comes the assault of Hill 400 which is extremely intense. A very well done mission. My memory told me that was it, but nope - we're going amphibian! The "ending" of the American campaign should have been Hill 400, but for some reason they throw in one final mission. Not sure why, but then it's over. Took around 2 hours to complete. VERDICT CoD 2's campaign is classic and revolutionary and parts of it hold up to this day. The British campaign is probably my favourite, with the US campaign a close second and the Soviet campaign being kind of bad and forgettable (and short). CoD World at War and CoD WW2 have much better campaigns than this and I can really only recomend it for "historical reasons". As it stands on its own, I guess I'll give it a 7/10, but only if you're a fan of old school shooters and WW2 games.

[h2]Quick Verdict[/h2] Call of Duty: United Offensive delivers more of the original game's squad-based combat with a few meaningful mechanical additions, but it rarely distinguishes itself enough to feel essential. [h2]Score: 3/5[/h2] [hr] [h1]The Review[/h1] United Offensive tells nearly the exact same kind of story as the original Call of Duty. If you are looking for more of that experience, this expansion delivers it cleanly and without surprises. The structure, tone, and pacing are immediately familiar, and it feels less like a new campaign and more like an additional set of missions built directly on top of the base game. The most noticeable additions come in the form of new weapons and combat roles. Mounted machine guns make their first appearance, requiring the player to commit to a fixed position before firing. These moments can feel powerful and satisfying, especially when holding a defensive line or suppressing advancing enemies. Semi-automatic rifles are also a welcome inclusion, offering more flexibility and precision than many of the original game's weapons. Despite these additions, the core gameplay remains largely unchanged. Squad-based encounters still rely heavily on AI scripting, suppression mechanics, and coordinated advances. These systems continue to work well and provide moments of genuine satisfaction when everything aligns correctly. However, because the expansion does little to evolve these ideas, they feel more iterative than transformative. Enemy behavior and level design are competent but rarely memorable. Most encounters blend together, and few missions stand out in the way the strongest moments from the original campaign do. The pacing is consistent, but it lacks the sense of escalation, novelty, or a central villain needed to make the experience feel distinct. I enjoyed my time with United Offensive. Let's start with something simple yet frustrating: to play United Offensive, you need to have the original Call of Duty installed. I know, that might seem obvious now, but losing an hour in 2025 just figuring that out definitely got me into this expansion with some early irritation. Once it finally launched, though, I have to admit - Call of Duty: United Offensive is surprisingly impressive. Even though it came out just a year after the original, the graphical leap is clear and quite decent for a 2004 title. It's still very much old-school, of course, but that initial visual punch is there. The story, just like in the base game, throws you into World War II from multiple perspectives: American, British, and Russian. But compared to the original, I felt less emotionally invested. Sure, some missions were genuinely well-made - intense, action-packed, well-paced - but others felt slapped together, frustrating, and at times straight-up unfair. Speaking of frustration: let's talk about that. In United Offensive, enemy soldiers feel like helmet-wearing Terminators, the guns sometimes shoot like they're loaded with confetti, and the "normal" difficulty feels like something you unlock through a secret passage in hell. There were moments where I was cursing in every known language just trying to get through a single mission. But honestly? That's exactly what I was looking for. That raw, unforgiving, brutal challenge only early Call of Duty titles seem to deliver. Even though it doesn't demand any advanced technical skill - no fancy movement, no perks, no min/max builds - United Offensive still pushes your patience and tests your ability to adapt under pressure. It's gritty, it's hard, and at times it's flat-out unfair… but it's also gloriously authentic.

RollerCoaster Tycoon 3: Platinum! is a comprehensive and immersive amusement park simulation that stands as one of the high points in the genre. Originally released in the mid-2000s and later brought to Steam with all its expansions included, this version offers players a full-featured experience that blends creativity, strategy, and management in equal measure. With both the Soaked! and Wild! expansion packs bundled in, the Platinum edition turns an already robust simulation game into an expansive sandbox for park-building enthusiasts. At its core, RollerCoaster Tycoon 3 tasks players with designing and managing their own amusement parks, complete with custom roller coasters, themed attractions, food stalls, and staff. The shift from the isometric, sprite-based graphics of the earlier titles to a fully 3D engine marked a major leap forward for the series. This not only improved visual fidelity but also opened up new gameplay possibilities. One of the most beloved features is the ability to ride the roller coasters you create, putting players in a first-person seat to experience their own designs in motion. This adds a unique layer of engagement and reward, as it's not just about profit margins and guest satisfaction-there's a genuine sense of amusement and pride in crafting thrilling, well-engineered rides. The game's management systems strike a careful balance between depth and accessibility. Players need to monitor guest happiness, ride reliability, staff workload, and overall park finances. While not as punishingly detailed as some hardcore sims, there's enough complexity here to satisfy fans of the genre. Dynamic weather, time-of-day changes, and seasonal variations also affect guest behavior and park operations. The economy can be micromanaged through pricing strategies, advertising campaigns, and careful investment in research and development. The challenge modes offer structured scenarios with specific goals, while the sandbox mode gives players limitless freedom to build the park of their dreams without financial constraints. The included expansions in the Platinum edition greatly enhance the gameplay. Soaked! introduces water park elements-wave pools, flume rides, custom water slides, and even choreographed water shows. It transforms your standard amusement park into a full-fledged aquatic wonderland and brings new guest needs like swimwear and lifeguard staffing. Wild! adds a zoo management element, allowing players to build animal enclosures, manage breeding programs, and design safari-style attractions. These additions don't just feel like extra content-they meaningfully expand the simulation with new mechanics, more guest types, and additional challenges to consider when running your park. Graphically, while the game does show its age compared to modern titles, the art direction remains charming and functional. The 3D models are bright, colorful, and full of character. The user interface is clear, though not always as intuitive as it could be-some of the menus and tools feel clunky, especially when working with terrain editing or fine-tuning coaster tracks. That said, once the learning curve is overcome, the game's building tools offer impressive flexibility. Whether you're constructing a towering steel monstrosity or a gentle family-friendly ride, the coaster builder allows for creativity and precision. The inclusion of day-night cycles and customizable scenery adds another layer of immersion and thematic flair to your creations. Performance on modern systems is generally stable, although occasional bugs or graphical glitches can occur, especially with large parks or complex ride setups. The Steam version has been updated to run on current operating systems without needing compatibility tweaks, but the game still lacks some modern conveniences like high-resolution UI scaling or mod support baked into the launcher. However, the modding community has kept the game alive over the years, offering custom scenery, improved textures, and even user-made rides for those willing to explore fan-made content outside of Steam. The audio design adds to the nostalgic appeal. From the excited screams of guests on coasters to the cheerful background music and theme park ambience, the soundscape enhances the feeling of being in a living, breathing amusement park. Each ride type has its own effects, and there's a clear attention to detail in how audio feedback reflects guest mood and ride operation. RollerCoaster Tycoon 3: Platinum! remains a benchmark for amusement park simulation. Its combination of open-ended creativity, strategic depth, and visual charm makes it a standout title even many years after its original release. While it may not have the polish of more recent entries or the ultra-modern graphics of newer sim games, it more than makes up for that with content, personality, and freedom of expression. For newcomers and nostalgic veterans alike, this Platinum edition delivers countless hours of amusement park management and roller coaster mayhem. Whether you're in it for the economic challenge, the ride design, or just the joy of building a park packed with happy guests, it's still one of the most satisfying simulation experiences available on Steam. Rating: 9/10

Click "Advanced system settings". Go to the "Performance" settings and click "Settings". Select the "Data Execution Prevention" tab. Choose "Turn on DEP for all programs and services except those I select". Click "Add" and navigate to the ACTOFWAR.exe file to exclude it from DEP after that it worked perfectly.

A pretty fun RTS and while similar to C&C generals it does enough to be different and in some ways better (mainly in terms of campaign gameplay and storytelling). The campaign is pretty fun and builds up pace nicely with more advanced units being introduced across time so as not to overwhelm with in which way to kill the enemy and every unit does have its place though some are better than others but without any glaring redundancies in the rosters. In terms of how it plays as an RTS, its pretty generic and while a bit thin on the building an economy side, the urban combat, terrain acquisition and combat mechanics are done well and are simple enough for anyone to get into and reward tactical play. I don't really want to say negative points as I don't think this game really commits any cardinal sins so things that could have been better: - More context in the story, villain is very one note who gets too many lucky escapes with their infinite supply of back up plans - Lack of campaign for the antagonist is a missed opportunity however the campaign we have is just long enough for a good experience and ends on a tough challenge without wearing out its welcome - Economy is pretty flimsy with all factions effectively making bank off taking prisoners of war, the oil is good but since it runs out quickly, everyone goes for a POW economy instead - Feels like there's a missing fourth faction such as a Middle Eastern faction or Russia to aid the mixed consortium forces.
20 years and this game deserves a remastered or a remake.
